calin.text: The câlin practises the trade of weaver in the Cholet area, whose textile industry — notably the famous Cholet handkerchief — made the region's reputation from the 18th century onward.

calmendier.label: Calmendier
calmendier.summary: Weaver making calmande (or calemande), a satin-finished twilled wool fabric.
calmendier.text: The calmendier weaves calmande (or calemande), a twilled woollen fabric, sturdy and satin-finished, used for clothing and furnishings from the 17th to the 19th century. A textile trade related to weaving but specialized in this particular weave.

calottier.label: Calottier
calottier.summary: Craftsman making skullcaps, small round caps covering the crown of the head.
calottier.text: The calottier makes skullcaps, round fitted caps worn notably by clerics, craftsmen, or under other headwear. A trade close to that of the hatter.

calvanier.label: Calvanier
calvanier.summary: Farm worker employed only for the duration of the harvest and threshing, to stack sheaves and thresh wheat.
calvanier.text: The calvanier is a seasonal farm worker, hired only for the duration of the harvest and threshing, responsible for stacking sheaves of grain and threshing wheat. Supplementary labour typical of the great harvests before mechanization.

camelot.label: Camelot
camelot.summary: Itinerant merchant selling small items on the public street or door to door.
camelot.text: The camelot hawks and sells small items, bazaar goods or newspapers, on the street, at markets or door to door, often crying his wares. The term still today denotes a street vendor and, in Quebec, a newspaper delivery boy.

camelotier.label: Camelotier
camelotier.summary: Maker or merchant of camelot, a fabric of goat hair or wool.
camelotier.text: The camelotier makes or sells camelot, a fabric woven originally from goat hair and later from wool, used for hard-wearing clothing. The word gave rise to the term "camelot" later denoting the street vendor, through a shift in meaning from the product sold to the seller.

camerier.label: Camérier
camerier.summary: Ecclesiastical dignitary responsible for serving the papal or episcopal chamber.
camerier.text: The camérier provides the personal service and stewardship of the chamber of a pope, cardinal or bishop, an honorific office of the papal court. The title still exists today in the papal household.

camionneur.label: Camionneur (lorry driver)
camionneur.text: The camionneur drove a lorry and carried goods by road, a trade that appeared with the development of the motor vehicle in the 20th century and gradually replaced the carter ("charretier") and the carrier ("voiturier").

campanier.label: Campanier
campanier.summary: Bell-ringer, or person walking ahead of funeral processions ringing a small bell.
campanier.text: The campanier rings the bells of a church, or walks ahead of funeral processions ringing a small bell to announce their passage.

campaniste.label: Campaniste
campaniste.summary: Person responsible for the upkeep of belfries, steeples and bells.
campaniste.text: The campaniste maintains belfries, steeples and the bells installed in them, a trade related to bell-founding and its mechanical maintenance.

campardon.label: Campardon
campardon.summary: Steward collecting the champart, a seigneurial due in kind.
campardon.text: The campardon is a seigneurial steward responsible for collecting the champart, a due in kind owed to the lord on harvests.

campiere.label: Campiere (Sicilian estate guard)
campiere.summary: In Sicily, a mounted armed guard who watched over a large estate, its crops and its livestock.
campiere.text: The campiere, employed by the gabelloto or the landowner, rode across the lands of the estate to prevent livestock theft and crop damage and to enforce the farming agreements. Unlike the municipal field guard, he was a private employee.

campino.label: Campino (mounted herdsman, Ribatejo)
campino.summary: Mounted herdsman who tends bulls and horses on the floodplains of the Ribatejo.
campino.text: The campino guards and drives, on horseback and armed with a long goad (pampilho), herds of fighting bulls, cattle and horses on the floodplains and fields of the Ribatejo. Recognisable by his traditional costume (green and red stocking cap, red waistcoat, blue breeches, white stockings), he has become an emblematic figure of the region.

cancelier.label: Cancelier
cancelier.summary: In Normandy, maker of fences and trellises.
cancelier.text: In Normandy, the cancelier makes fences and trellises surrounding a house or garden.

canneur.label: Canneur
canneur.summary: Craftsman practising caning, the weaving of rattan strands to seat chairs.
canneur.text: The canneur weaves strands of rattan or rush to seat and back chairs, a technique known as caning. A furniture trade, often complementary to that of the chair-maker.

canonigo.label: Canónigo (Spanish canon)
canonigo.summary: Cleric belonging to the chapter of a cathedral or collegiate church.
canonigo.text: The canónigo was a member of a cathedral or collegiate chapter, which assisted the bishop, celebrated the divine office in the choir and administered the church's property. Some canonries carried specific duties (preacher, legal adviser, scripture lecturer, penitentiary) and were filled by competitive examination.

canonnier.label: Canonnier (gunner)
canonnier.summary: Soldier specialized in serving artillery pieces.
canonnier.text: The canonnier serves in the artillery, responsible for operating and firing cannon, both on land and aboard warships. A rank or role very frequently found in military service records.

canotier.label: Canotier
canotier.summary: Boatman driving a canoe or a light craft.
canotier.text: The canotier drives a canoe, a light rowing or sailing craft, to transport passengers or goods on calm waters. Not to be confused with the hat of the same name, which appeared later.

cantastorie.label: Cantastorie (street ballad singer)
cantastorie.summary: Itinerant singer who told stories in verse in town squares, with an instrument and illustrated boards.
cantastorie.text: The cantastorie went from fair to market singing about news events, legends and the deeds of bandits, often illustrated on a large painted board, and sold printed sheets of the texts. The tradition was particularly alive in Sicily, Emilia and Tuscany in the 19th and 20th centuries.

cantinier.label: Cantinier
cantinier.summary: Person responsible for collective catering, notably within an army on campaign.
cantinier.text: The cantinier keeps a canteen, providing food and drink to a community, a garrison or troops on campaign. The cantinière, a female presence attached to regiments until the early 20th century, held an emblematic role in the French army, selling provisions and tobacco to soldiers and sometimes assisting them in combat.

cantonnier.label: Cantonnier (road mender)
cantonnier.summary: Municipal employee responsible for maintaining the roads of the commune.
cantonnier.text: The cantonnier is a municipal employee responsible for maintaining the roads and lanes of the commune: repair, snow clearing, upkeep of ditches and verges.

canut.label: Canut
canut.summary: In Lyon, a worker in the silk industries.
canut.text: In Lyon, the canut is a worker in the silk industries; the term "ferrandinier" was adopted by silk workers after the canut uprisings of 1831 and 1834, in reaction to the word's increasingly derogatory connotation.

caoutchoutier.label: Caoutchoutier
caoutchoutier.summary: Factory worker coating fabrics with rubber to waterproof them.
caoutchoutier.text: The caoutchoutier works in a factory where he coats fabrics and other objects with rubber to make them waterproof or airtight.

caparaconniere.label: Caparaçonnière
caparaconniere.summary: Maker of caparisons, cloths protecting horses from the weather and insects.
caparaconniere.text: The caparaçonnière makes caparisons, cloths used to cover horses to protect them from the weather or insects.

capataz.label: Capataz (Spanish foreman)
capataz.summary: Person who directed and supervised a group of workers.
capataz.text: The capataz directed a group of workers or day labourers on behalf of the owner or contractor, on an estate, a building site, a mine or a workshop, assigning tasks and overseeing their execution. On farms, the capataz de labor organised the day-to-day work.

capellan.label: Capellán (Spanish chaplain)
capellan.summary: Priest holding a chaplaincy benefice or serving a chapel, hospital, convent or noble house.
capellan.text: The capellán was the cleric holding a capellanía, a foundation endowed with property whose income paid for a set number of Masses for the founder's soul, often reserved for his relatives. The term also designates the priest serving a chapel, hospital, convent, regiment or private household. Chaplaincy files often contain genealogical information.

capitaine.label: Capitaine (captain)
capitaine.summary: Military officer or commander of a ship.
capitaine.text: The capitaine commands a company of troops or a ship, depending on the military or maritime context of the record. An intermediate officer rank, frequently cited in records concerning soldiers and sailors.

capitao_donatario.label: Capitão-donatário (lord-proprietor of a captaincy)
capitao_donatario.summary: Holder of a captaincy granted by the Crown in the Atlantic islands or in Brazil, with wide powers of settlement and government.
capitao_donatario.text: The capitão-donatário receives from the Portuguese Crown, by a deed of grant, a captaincy (capitania) — in Madeira and the Azores from the 15th century, and in Brazil from 1534 — with the duty of settling and developing it. He held wide judicial and fiscal powers, including the right to allot land as sesmarias. The office was generally hereditary.

capitao_mor.label: Capitão-mor (commander of the ordenanças)
capitao_mor.summary: Commander of the ordenanças, the territorial militia of a municipality.
capitao_mor.text: The capitão-mor commands the ordenanças of a municipality, a territorial militia enrolling able-bodied men not enlisted in the regular troops, organised from the regulation of 1570. Usually chosen from among the leading men of the locality, he enjoyed great prestige and local influence, and had under his orders the sargento-mor and the company captains. The ordenanças were abolished in the 19th century with the liberal reforms.

caporal.label: Caporal (corporal)
caporal.summary: Non-commissioned officer of the first rank, at the head of a squad.
caporal.text: The caporal is the first non-commissioned rank in the infantry, commanding a squad of soldiers. A rank frequently mentioned in military records.

carabinier.label: Carabinier
carabinier.text: The carabinier is a horseman armed with a carbine, a light cavalry unit attested as early as the 17th century.

caravanseraskier.label: Caravanseraskier
caravanseraskier.summary: Person responsible for receiving and watching over travellers at a caravanserai.
caravanseraskier.text: The caravanseraskier manages a caravanserai, an establishment offering lodging to travellers and their pack animals along the trade routes of the Near and Middle East. A rare term in French, Gallicized to denote this function of Eastern origin.

carcanier.label: Carcanier
carcanier.summary: Rare term of uncertain occupational use, possibly linked to making iron collars.
carcanier.text: The little-attested term carcanier may denote a maker of carcans (iron collars used as an instrument of punishment) or another activity close to it by the word's root. Its precise use remains uncertain.

carcassier.label: Carcassier
carcassier.summary: Craftsman making carcasses, internal structures serving as a support for various manufactured objects.
carcassier.text: The carcassier makes carcasses, frames or support structures (wood, metal, wicker) intended to receive a covering or trim, for example in hat-making, saddlery or furniture-making.

cardeur.label: Cardeur (carder)
cardeur.summary: Textile worker teasing out and aligning fibres of wool, cotton or flax using cards.
cardeur.text: The cardeur teases out, cleans and aligns textile fibres (wool, cotton, flax) using cards, tools fitted with metal points, preparing the raw material for spinning. An essential and very common step of craft textile-making.

cardeur_de_filouzelle.label: Cardeur de filoselle
cardeur_de_filouzelle.summary: Carder specialized in processing filoselle, silk waste or tow.
cardeur_de_filouzelle.text: The cardeur de filoselle cards filoselle, a coarse thread drawn from silk waste and tow unfit for fine spinning, used for lower-quality fabrics. A carding specialty linked to the silk industry.

cardeur_de_soye.label: Cardeur de soie
cardeur_de_soye.summary: Worker carding silk to prepare the fibres before spinning.
cardeur_de_soye.text: The cardeur de soie ("soye", old spelling) teases out and aligns silk fibres before spinning, a preparatory step specific to the silk industry, notably developed in the Lyon region.

cardier.label: Cardier
cardier.summary: Craftsman making cards, boards fitted with points used to tease out textile fibres.
cardier.text: The cardier makes cards, boards bristling with metal points used by carders to prepare textile fibres. A trade distinct from the carder, who uses these tools rather than making them.

cargador_de_indias.label: Cargador de Indias (Spanish transatlantic merchant)
cargador_de_indias.summary: Merchant registered to ship goods to the Americas with the fleets of the Spanish Indies trade.
cargador_de_indias.text: The cargador de Indias was a merchant enrolled in the register of the Consulado of Seville, moved to Cádiz in 1717, who was entitled to ship goods on the fleets and galleons of the Carrera de Indias. Often organised in family networks linking Andalusia and the American ports, these merchants dominated colonial trade until its liberalisation in 1778.

carillonneur.label: Carillonneur (bell-ringer)
carillonneur.summary: Musician playing the carillon, a set of tuned bells.
carillonneur.text: The carillonneur plays the carillon, an instrument made of several tuned bells, installed in a bell tower or belfry, a tradition especially alive in northern France, Flanders and the Netherlands.

carreleur.label: Carreleur (tiler)
carreleur.summary: Craftsman laying terracotta, stone or ceramic tiles on floors or walls.
carreleur.text: The carreleur lays tiles — terracotta, stone or ceramic — to cover floors and walls. The variant "carlier" denotes the same trade in certain regions.

carrelier.label: Carrelier (tile-maker)
carrelier.summary: Craftsman making terracotta, faience or ceramic tiles.
carrelier.text: The carrelier makes tiles intended for floor or wall covering, to be distinguished from the carreleur, who lays them. A trade linked to local tileworks and faience workshops.

carrie.label: Carrié
carrie.summary: Cemetery keeper responsible for its upkeep and burials; the closest modern equivalent is the monumental mason.
carrie.text: The carrié maintains a cemetery and takes part in burials, a modest function whose closest equivalent today would be the funerary monumental mason, responsible for monuments and graves.

carrier.label: Carrier (quarryman)
carrier.summary: Worker or operator specialized in extracting stone in a quarry.
carrier.text: The carrier extracts stone in a quarry, by hand or with explosives depending on the period, to supply building sites with rubble stone or ashlar. The regional variants "carreur", "carriéreur", "pierrieur" or "quarriereur" denote the same trade.

carronier.label: Carronier
carronier.summary: Itinerant brickmaker making bricks directly on the building site.
carronier.text: The carronier is an itinerant brickmaker who makes bricks ("carrons") directly on the construction site, rather than running a fixed brickworks, thereby avoiding the transport of heavy materials.

carrossier.label: Carrossier (coachbuilder)
carrossier.summary: Craftsman making, repairing and decorating vehicle bodywork.
carrossier.text: The carrossier builds, repairs and decorates vehicle bodywork — coaches and horse-drawn carriages originally, then automobiles from the 20th century. A demanding art trade, combined with joinery, saddlery and painting.

carruyer.label: Carruyer
carruyer.summary: Porter loading and unloading goods, notably on quays or in warehouses.
carruyer.text: The carruyer is a porter, a worker responsible for loading and unloading solid goods on his own back, an activity close to that of the hook-porter or unloader in ports and market halls.

cartier.label: Cartier (card-maker)
cartier.summary: Maker of playing cards and, sometimes, cartographer.
cartier.text: The cartier makes playing cards, printed and coloured according to techniques codified by guild as early as the 15th century. The term could also, by extension, denote a drawer of geographical maps.

carton.label: Carton
carton.summary: Driver of covered, horse-drawn wagons used to transport goods.
carton.text: The carton drives vehicles fitted with tarpaulins and drawn by horses, used to transport goods by road. A regional term related to the trade of carter.

cartonneur.label: Cartonneur
cartonneur.summary: Worker making cardboard and cardboard packaging.
cartonneur.text: The cartonneur makes cardboard and cardboard packaging, in an industrial cardboard mill, an activity booming from the 19th century with the development of packaging.

cartonnier.label: Cartonnier
cartonnier.summary: Craftsman making objects out of cardboard by assembly and decoration (boxes, cases).
cartonnier.text: The cartonnier assembles and decorates cardboard objects — boxes, cases, various cardboard items — unlike the cartonneur, who produces the cardboard itself in large industrial quantities.

caruso.label: Caruso (sulphur-mine carrier boy)
caruso.summary: In Sicily, a boy employed in the sulphur mines to carry the ore to the surface on his back.
caruso.text: The caruso, often a very young boy, carried on his shoulders the lumps of ore cut by the hewer through the galleries and up the steps of the mine to the surface. Bound to the hewer by a cash advance paid to his family (the soccorso morto), he endured extremely harsh working conditions, denounced by inquiries in the 19th and early 20th centuries.

caseiro.label: Caseiro (resident tenant farmer of a quinta)
caseiro.summary: Tenant who lived on a farm (quinta or casal) owned by someone else, farming it and looking after the property in exchange for rent.
caseiro.text: The caseiro lives on and farms a quinta or casal on behalf of its owner, to whom he pays a rent in money or in a share of the produce, while also guarding and maintaining the property. The figure is very common in northern Portugal, where large houses and town-dwelling owners entrusted their lands to caseiros. Leases and notarial deeds often make it possible to follow successive families of caseiros on the same estate.

casero.label: Casero (Basque farmstead tenant)
casero.summary: In the Basque Country, Navarre and Cantabria, tenant who lived on and farmed a caserío.
casero.text: The casero was the farmer who lived on and cultivated a caserío, the scattered family farmstead typical of the Basque Country and neighbouring areas, as a tenant or sometimes as owner. The caserío usually passed intact to a single heir, and tenancy contracts were often renewed within the same family for generations.

caseyeur.label: Caseyeur
caseyeur.summary: Fisherman using pots or traps to catch shellfish and fish.
caseyeur.text: The caseyeur fishes using pots or traps, a technique used notably to catch shellfish (lobsters, crabs, spiny lobsters) along the coast.

casquetier.label: Casquetier (cap-maker)
casquetier.summary: Craftsman making caps and peaked headwear.
casquetier.text: The casquetier makes caps, soft headwear fitted with a peak, whose use spread notably in the 19th century among working-class and military circles.

casse_moute.label: Casse-moute
casse_moute.summary: Itinerant miller collecting grain at people's homes to grind it.
casse_moute.text: The casse-moute travels from farm to farm to collect grain to be ground, bringing back the flour in exchange for a milling fee. An itinerant variant of the miller's trade, in regions lacking a nearby mill.

casseur_de_voitures.label: Casseur de voitures
casseur_de_voitures.summary: Forerunner of the modern car breaker, specialized in dismantling and salvaging parts from horse-drawn vehicles.
casseur_de_voitures.text: The casseur de voitures dismantles worn-out horse-drawn vehicles to salvage and resell reusable parts — wood, ironwork, wheels — an activity that is the direct forerunner of the modern car breaker.

castaldo.label: Castaldo (Italian land agent)
castaldo.summary: Agent who managed landed property for a lord, a church body or a private owner, especially in Veneto and Friuli.
castaldo.text: Of Lombard origin (the gastaldo was a royal official), the term later designated the agent who managed an owner's lands, collected rents and dues in kind and supervised the tenants. In Veneto and Friuli the castaldo often appears in records as the manager of a country estate or a farm.

castanera.label: Castañera (Spanish chestnut seller)
castanera.summary: Woman who sold roasted chestnuts in the street during autumn and winter.
castanera.text: The castañera roasted and sold chestnuts at a street stall with a small stove during the cold months. A traditional figure of Spanish towns, in Catalonia the "castanyera" is associated with the All Saints' festival.

catechiseermeester.label: Catechiseermeester (catechism teacher)
catechiseermeester.summary: Teacher who instructed children and young people in the faith according to the catechism.
catechiseermeester.text: The catechiseermeester taught catechism to children and young members, on behalf of the consistory or on his own account, usually from the Heidelberg Catechism. They were often laymen, sometimes also schoolmasters or readers, who earned additional income in this way.

catisseur.label: Catisseur
catisseur.summary: Textile worker handling the glazing and finishing of fabrics through catissage.
catisseur.text: The catisseur practises catissage, a finishing operation that smooths and glazes a fabric (notably wool) under a hot press, to give it a shiny, even appearance.

catraeiro.label: Catraeiro (harbour boatman)
catraeiro.summary: Boatman who carried passengers and goods in a catraia, in harbours and on rivers.
catraeiro.text: The catraeiro handles a catraia, a small rowing or sailing boat used to cross rivers, link the two banks and serve ships at anchor in harbours, carrying passengers, crew and goods. The occupation was common on the Douro at Porto, on the Tagus and in other Portuguese ports.

caucheteur.label: Caucheteur
caucheteur.summary: Craftsman who made stockings and tall shoes of cloth or soft leather.
caucheteur.text: The caucheteur made hose or ankle boots, a term derived from "chausse" used in certain regions of northern and western France. He is close to the hosier or the shoemaker depending on whether he worked cloth or leather. The word occasionally appears in civil records to denote a craftsman of leg and foot wear.

caussetier.label: Caussetier
caussetier.summary: Farmer working the arid limestone lands of the Causses, notably in the Quercy.
caussetier.text: The caussetier is a farmer adapted to the poor, stony soils of the causses, those limestone plateaus of southwestern France (Quercy, Larzac). Farming there was traditionally geared toward sheep raising and drought-resistant crops. The term, regional, is found mainly in the records of parishes located on these plateaus.

cauteleiro.label: Cauteleiro (lottery ticket seller)
cauteleiro.summary: Street seller of lottery ticket fractions (cautelas) and tickets.
cauteleiro.text: The cauteleiro sells in the streets, cafés and fairs the cautelas, fractions of lottery tickets, calling out the numbers and prizes. A typical figure of Lisbon, Porto and Portuguese towns since the 19th century, he often carried on this trade on behalf of a dealer who supplied him with tickets on commission.

cavalier.label: Cavalier (horseman)
cavalier.summary: Man fighting or travelling on horseback, in the military or civil sense.
cavalier.text: The term cavalier most often denotes a soldier serving in a mounted unit (cavalry), but it can also simply describe a man riding a horse in civilian life. In old records, it generally indicates mounted military service, as opposed to the foot soldier. The word is also sometimes used as a courtesy title for a gentleman.

cavalier_dans_une_compagnie_de_remonte.label: Cavalier dans une Compagnie de Remonte
cavalier_dans_une_compagnie_de_remonte.summary: Cavalry soldier assigned to buying and training troop horses.
cavalier_dans_une_compagnie_de_remonte.text: The cavalier dans une compagnie de remonte is a soldier of a cavalry regiment assigned to the unit responsible for buying and training the mounts intended for the troops.

cavelier.label: Cavelier
cavelier.summary: Keeper of an establishment offering food and drink for payment.
cavelier.text: The cavelier kept an inn, a tavern or an alehouse, offering food and drink to travellers and local residents. The term is a regional variant close to cabaretier or tavernier. It appears in some records from western and central France.

cavetonnier.label: Chavetonnier
cavetonnier.summary: Shoemaker specialized in making shoes from sheepskin.
cavetonnier.text: The chavetonnier (sometimes spelled cavetonnier or çavetonnier) is a leather craftsman close to the cobbler, specialized in shoes made from sheepskin, a less costly leather than calf or cattle hide. This regional term is found in some records from western and central France, often under fluctuating spellings.

caveur.label: Caveur
caveur.summary: Docker responsible for lowering casks with pulleys into the holds of ships.
caveur.text: The caveur worked on the quays and in ports, operating the pulleys and tackle needed to load or lower casks and heavy goods into the holds ("caves") of ships. A demanding port trade, related to that of the stevedore.

cazerotier.label: Cazerotier
cazerotier.summary: Craftsman making the wooden moulds and forms used to drain and shape cheese.
cazerotier.text: The cazerotier made "cazerottes" or "cazes", perforated moulds of wood or rush used by cheesemakers to drain the curd and give the cheese its shape. This craft trade, linked to the regional cheese industry, is found mainly in dairy-farming areas.

ceinturier.label: Ceinturier (belt maker)
ceinturier.summary: Leather craftsman specialized in making belts and matching accessories.
ceinturier.text: The ceinturier made belts, civilian waist-belts and small leather accessories, a craft close to saddlery and fine leatherwork. He is distinct from the ceinturonnier, who was geared more towards military equipment.

ceinturonnier.label: Ceinturonnier
ceinturonnier.summary: Maker of military belts and leather equipment for soldiers.
ceinturonnier.text: The ceinturonnier made the belts and leather equipment worn by soldiers (baldrics, pouches, scabbards), linked to military supply. This trade is distinguished from the civilian ceinturier by its essentially military clientele.

cellerier.label: Cellerier (cellarer)
cellerier.summary: Monk responsible for managing the monastery's provisions and material goods.
cellerier.text: The cellerier held one of the most important monastic offices after that of the abbot: he administered the provisions, cellars, lands and revenues of the community, in accordance with the Rule of Saint Benedict. The term is also found more broadly to denote a steward responsible for provisions in a great household or a chapter.

celnik.label: Celnik (customs officer)
celnik.summary: Official or guard collecting customs duties and inspecting the transport of goods.
celnik.text: The celnik collected duties on goods carried across borders or through customs houses and checked for smuggling. After the partitions, borders between the partitioning powers cut across Polish lands, so that the customs and border services employed many inhabitants of the border areas.

cendrier.label: Cendrier
cendrier.summary: Craftsman who recovered and processed wood ash for the soap and glass industries.
cendrier.text: The cendrier collected wood ash from domestic hearths to resell it to makers of lye, potash, soap or glass, who needed it as an alkaline raw material. This recycling trade was an important link in pre-industrial craft production.

cendrilleur.label: Cendrilleur
cendrilleur.summary: Worker responsible for removing the ash produced by hearths, forges and industrial plant.
cendrilleur.text: The cendrilleur carried out the regular cleaning and removal of ash accumulated in forge hearths, kilns and boilers, an arduous but necessary task for the proper running of the plant. He differs from the cendrier, who valorized ash as raw material rather than simply removing it.

censal.label: Censal
censal.summary: Financial broker trading in annuities and credit operations, a Mediterranean-usage term.
censal.text: The censal is a financial intermediary, attested notably in Mediterranean ports such as Marseille, who traded in constituted annuities ("censales") and various credit instruments, on the model of the well-documented Catalan censal in Barcelona's trade. The term reflects the influence of Catalan and Provençal commercial practices on the financial vocabulary of the Midi.

censeur.label: Censeur
censeur.summary: Officer or official responsible for examining and controlling writings, morals or seigneurial rights depending on context.
censeur.text: The term censeur covers several realities depending on period and context: a royal official responsible for approving publications before printing, but also, in an older sense linked to the word "cens", one who assesses or collects a due. In schools, it also denotes a supervisor responsible for discipline. The precise meaning thus depends heavily on the source document.

censeur_royal.label: Censeur royal (royal censor)
censeur_royal.summary: Royal official responsible for examining manuscripts and authorizing their publication.
censeur_royal.text: Under the Ancien Régime, the censeur royal (or censeur des livres) was a man of letters appointed by the crown to examine manuscripts before granting the royal privilege, a necessary condition for their legal printing. This function of prior control over publishing, entrusted to specialists recognized in their field, structured the whole of the French book world until the Revolution.

censier.label: Censier
censier.summary: Holder or collector of the cens, an annual due owed to the landed lord.
censier.text: The censier collected, or owed, the cens, a fixed due paid annually by the tenant (censitaire) to his lord in recognition of the latter's eminent ownership of the land. This system, inherited from the medieval cens-based tenure, durably structured land relations in the French countryside until its abolition in 1789-1793.

cercayres.label: Cercayrès
cercayres.summary: Professional mushroom gatherer, notably in the Périgord.
cercayres.text: The cercayrès (or cercaïre) denotes, in the Périgord and neighbouring regions, a professional gatherer of mushrooms — ceps chief among them — resold at local markets. This small seasonal gathering trade often supplemented other farming activities.

cercleur.label: Cercleur (hooper)
cercleur.summary: Coopering worker who fits and adjusts wooden or metal hoops onto casks.
cercleur.text: The cercleur takes part in making casks and barrels by fitting and tightening the hoops — bands of split wood and, later, iron — that hold the staves together. He is distinct from the cerclier, who shapes the hoops themselves, fitting and manufacture being two separate steps in the cooper's trade.

cerclier.label: Cerclier
cerclier.summary: Maker of wooden or metal hoops used to hold casks and barrels together.
cerclier.text: The cerclier shapes the hoops — rings of split wood (hazel, chestnut) and, from the 19th century, iron — that encircle casks and barrels to hold the staves together. The trade is distinct from that of the cercleur, who fits the hoops onto the cask rather than making them. The term is found under many dialectal spellings (cercillier, cerqueleur, cerquelier, cerquemaneur), all formed on the root "cercle" (hoop).

cerenceresse.label: Cerenceresse
cerenceresse.summary: Regional synonym for filassière, a female worker who combed tow to prepare it for spinning.
cerenceresse.text: The cerenceresse is a female worker who combs tow (flax or hemp fibres) with a hackle, a comb with iron points, to disentangle it and make it fit for spinning. The term, with the "-eresse" ending characteristic of feminine occupational names in Old French, is attested as a regional synonym for filassière.

cerisier.label: Cerisier
cerisier.text: The cerisier is a fruit grower devoted to growing cherry trees and selling their fruit. The term denotes either a specialized grower or simply a farmer owning a cherry orchard in certain producing regions.

cerusier.label: Cérusier
cerusier.summary: Maker of ceruse, a white lead-based pigment used in paint.
cerusier.text: The cérusier produces ceruse (basic lead carbonate), a highly opaque white pigment used in paint and formerly in cosmetics to whiten the complexion. Its manufacture, by exposing sheets of lead to vinegar fumes, exposed workers to severe lead poisoning, making it a notoriously dangerous trade before its regulation and gradual prohibition.

cervoisier.label: Cervoisier
cervoisier.summary: Brewer of cervoise, a fermented grain beverage, ancestor of beer.
cervoisier.text: The cervoisier brews cervoise, an unhopped beer made from barley or other grains, consumed since Gaulish antiquity and throughout the Middle Ages. The term gradually gave way to "brasseur" as hops became widespread from the late Middle Ages onward.

cetereau.label: Cétéreau
cetereau.summary: Pit-saw sawyer working in the Forez region, cutting tree trunks into planks.
cetereau.text: The cétéreau is a pit-saw sawyer of the Forez region: he cuts tree trunks into planks with a saw, work carried out in a team of two, one sawyer (the "chevrier") standing on the trunk itself set on a trestle (the "chèvre"), the other (the "renard" or "renardier") pulling the saw from below.

chableur.label: Chableur
chableur.summary: Forest worker who fells or moves trees using a cable and a winch.
chableur.text: The chableur uses a "chable" (cable or winch) to fell trees in a controlled manner or to move them to points of floating, a technique used notably in forestry and in transporting timber by water. The term also gave rise to "chablis", denoting trees felled by wind.

chableur_de_pertuis.label: Chableur de Pertuis
chableur_de_pertuis.summary: Worker responsible for handling cables at the pertuis, narrow passages of navigable rivers.
chableur_de_pertuis.text: The chableur de pertuis worked at the "pertuis", the narrow passes or sluices of rivers developed for navigation or timber floating, where he handled cables and ropes to get boats or timber rafts through. This specialized river trade was particularly present on the rivers of the Massif Central and the Paris Basin developed for floating.

chabretaire.label: Chabretaire
chabretaire.summary: Player of the chabrette, a traditional bagpipe of the Limousin, often an itinerant musician.
chabretaire.text: The chabretaire plays the chabrette, a traditional mouth-blown bagpipe of the Limousin and Poitou, fitted with a bone blowpipe mount. He livened up dances, weddings and village festivals, often travelling from town to town for his performances.

chagrinier.label: Chagrinier
chagrinier.summary: Craftsman specialized in making shagreen, a grained leather used in luxury fine leather goods.
chagrinier.text: The chagrinier works shagreen, a grained leather obtained from goat, sheep or ray skin, treated to achieve its characteristic granular texture. This leather was highly prized for luxury bookbinding, cases and small leather goods in the 18th and 19th centuries.

chaideur.label: Chaideur
chaideur.summary: Metalworker responsible for crushing iron ore before processing.
chaideur.text: The chaideur works in a metallurgical operation, where he crushes and grinds iron ore to prepare it for smelting in the blast furnace or forge. This trade belongs to the pre-industrial iron-production chain.

chainetier.label: Chaînetier
chainetier.summary: Maker of chains and small chains, often for decorative or light use.
chainetier.text: The chaînetier makes small chains, notably fine chains used in jewellery, clockmaking or light domestic use. He is distinct from the chaînier, who is geared toward producing heavier metal chains for industrial or maritime use.

chainier.label: Chaînier
chainier.summary: Maker of metal chains, notably for industrial, agricultural or maritime use.
chainier.text: The chaînier forges or assembles larger metal chains intended for heavy uses: mooring, lifting, agricultural traction. The trade developed particularly with the industrialization of the 19th century.

chainiste.label: Chaîniste
chainiste.summary: Worker specialized in making or maintaining chains and chain mechanisms.
chainiste.text: The chainiste works on chains and chain mechanisms, a term that covers both the traditional craft of the forged chain and, more recently, mechanical and industrial applications (transmission chains, for example).

chaintrier.label: Chaintrier
chaintrier.summary: Medieval craftsman specialized in setting up fences and trellises around plots of land.
chaintrier.text: The chaintrier takes his name from the "chaintre", an Old French term for the strip of unploughed land bordering a field. He would have been responsible for laying out and marking these agricultural borders and fences, a role close to that of the fence-maker in medieval countryside.

chaisier.label: Chaisier (chairmaker)
chaisier.summary: Craftsman specialized in making chairs, stools and seats of wood and straw.
chaisier.text: The chaisier makes chairs and various seats, assembling a turned-wood frame fitted with a woven-straw, rush or solid-wood seat. This trade long constituted an important local craft specialty in certain rural regions of France.

chalandon.label: Chalandon
chalandon.summary: Boatman driving a chaland, a flat-bottomed craft used for river transport.
chalandon.text: The chalandon (also spelled chalandou in certain regions, notably on the Loire) drives a chaland, a flat-bottomed boat typical of French river navigation, used to carry goods and materials along rivers. This river trade declined with the rise of the railway in the 19th century.

chaliste.label: Châliste
chaliste.text: The châliste weaves shawls, those large pieces of cloth worn over the shoulders, whose fashion boomed considerably in the 19th century with the craze for cashmere-style shawls. This specialized textile trade developed notably in wool- and silk-producing centres.

chalmandrier.label: Chalmandrier
chalmandrier.summary: Weaver specialized in making glazed woollen fabrics with a satin finish.
chalmandrier.text: The chalmandrier wove woollen fabrics called "chalmandes" or "calmandes", glazed fabrics with a satin-like finish obtained by a particular pressing, used notably for clothing and furnishings in the 17th and 18th centuries.

chaloupier.label: Chaloupier
chaloupier.summary: Builder and repairer of longboats, small craft used at sea or on rivers.
chaloupier.text: The chaloupier builds and maintains longboats, medium-sized rowing or sailing craft used for coastal fishing, transport, or as tenders for larger ships. This specialized naval-carpentry trade is found in ports and along coasts.

chalupnik.label: Chałupnik (landless cottager)
chalupnik.summary: Villager owning a cottage but no arable land, or only a tiny plot.
chalupnik.text: The chałupnik owned his own cottage but had no arable land, or only a scrap of it. He lived from hired work, village crafts or labour on the manor farm. In the village hierarchy he ranked below the zagrodnik and above the komornik, who did not even own a house.

chamarreur.label: Chamarreur
chamarreur.summary: Craftsman who adorned clothing and objects with showy, colourful braid and trimmings.
chamarreur.text: The chamarreur applies chamarrures — braid, embroidery and brightly coloured ornaments — to clothing, uniforms or ceremonial objects, a skill close to passementerie. The term gave rise to the verb "chamarrer", which today somewhat pejoratively denotes an excess of showy ornament.

chambellan.label: Chambellan (chamberlain)
chambellan.summary: Noble officer responsible for the service and administration of a sovereign's or great lord's chamber.
chambellan.text: The chambellan is a high-ranking officer responsible for the personal service and organization of the private chamber of a king, prince or great lord, a prestigious court office often reserved for the high nobility. The title survived, in honorific form, into European courts of the 19th and 20th centuries.

chambrier.label: Chambrier
chambrier.summary: Steward officer of the King's Chamber, responsible for archives and the treasury.
chambrier.text: The chambrier is a steward officer of the King's Chamber, responsible for keeping the archives and the royal treasury; the title also existed in great seigneurial households and abbeys.

chambriere.label: Chambrière
chambriere.summary: Servant, generally in the service of persons of modest condition.
chambriere.text: The chambrière is a servant generally employed by persons of modest condition, responsible for ordinary domestic tasks.

chamoiseur.label: Chamoiseur
chamoiseur.summary: Tanning craftsman specialized in preparing chamois-dressed leather, soft and absorbent.
chamoiseur.text: The chamoiseur treats hides (goat, sheep, chamois) by chamoising, an oil-tanning technique that produces a soft, porous, absorbent leather, used for glove-making, clothing and cleaning cloths. This process differs from classic vegetable-tan tanning used for stiffer leathers.

champarteur.label: Champarteur
champarteur.summary: Collector of the champart, a seigneurial due levied in kind on harvests.
champarteur.text: The champarteur collected the champart, a feudal due levied directly on the harvest (often a tenth or a twelfth of the sheaves) for the benefit of the lord, distinct from the ecclesiastical tithe. This levy in kind, made at the very moment of harvest, required an agent present on site during the harvest.

champartier.label: Champartier
champartier.summary: Holder or manager of champart rights over farmland.
champartier.text: The champartier is the holder of the champart rights over a piece of land, that is, the lord or right-holder collecting this due in kind on harvests, as opposed to the champarteur, who rather handled its concrete collection in the field.

chandelier.label: Chandelier
chandelier.summary: Maker of candles for domestic lighting.
chandelier.text: The chandelier makes candles, most often from tallow (rendered animal fat) poured around a wick, the most common lighting in modest households before wax candles or paraffin oil became widespread. He is distinct from the cirier, who works wax, a more costly material reserved for liturgical use and wealthy households.

chandelier_de_sieu.label: Chandelier de Sieu
chandelier_de_sieu.summary: Specialized maker of tallow candles, the most common material of popular lighting.
chandelier_de_sieu.text: The chandelier de sieu ("sieu" being the regional, notably Occitan, form of "suif"/tallow) specifically makes tallow candles, the rendered animal fat that was the most widespread and least costly raw material for domestic lighting before the 19th century.

chanevacier.label: Chanevacier
chanevacier.summary: Weaver making coarse cloth woven from hemp fibre.
chanevacier.text: The chanevacier weaves chanevas (canvas), a coarse, sturdy cloth obtained from hemp fibres, used for sailmaking, sacks, tarpaulins and certain work clothes. The English word "canvas" indeed derives directly from this French term. He is distinct from the chanvrier, who grows and sells raw hemp, and the chanvreur, who extracts its fibres by breaking.

chanfraineur.label: Chanfraineur
chanfraineur.summary: Craftsman who makes chamfers, bevelled surfaces on the sharp edges of a material.
chanfraineur.text: The chanfraineur bevels the sharp edges of wood, leather or stone to soften its profile or ease an assembly — a common operation in joinery, saddlery and construction. The term denotes a technique more than an autonomous trade, practised within other crafts.

changeur.label: Changeur (money changer)
changeur.summary: Professional in currency exchange and the appraisal of precious metals, forerunner of the banker.
changeur.text: The changeur converts currencies, appraises precious metals and carries out various credit operations, an essential role in merchant towns where numerous local and foreign coinages circulated. Changeurs, often organized into a sworn guild from the Middle Ages, are among the direct forerunners of modern bankers.

chanteur.label: Chanteur
chanteur.summary: Person practising singing, professionally or in a religious setting.
chanteur.text: The chanteur practises the vocal art, whether as a professional artist (opera, theatre, music hall) or in a religious setting, where he is then close to the chantre responsible for liturgical singing. The precise sense depends heavily on the context and period of the document.

chantre.label: Chantre (cantor)
chantre.summary: Cleric responsible for leading liturgical singing in a church or parish.
chantre.text: The chantre directs and performs the liturgical singing during religious services, a church office often combined with other minor parish duties such as keeping the registers or assisting the parish priest. In great churches and cathedrals, the "grand chantre" held an important dignity within the chapter.

chanvreur.label: Chanvreur
chanvreur.summary: Worker who breaks hemp to separate the textile fibres from the stalk.
chanvreur.text: The chanvreur performs hemp breaking, an operation consisting of breaking and then combing the dried stalks to extract usable textile fibres, later intended for spinning. This seasonal, physical work is distinct from that of the chanvrier, who grows the plant.

chanvrier.label: Chanvrier
chanvrier.summary: Grower and merchant of hemp, a textile plant once widely grown in France.
chanvrier.text: The chanvrier grows and sells hemp, an essential textile plant before the rise of cotton, used for cloth, cordage and sails. Certain regions such as Anjou or Brittany made it a specialty crop, sustaining a whole chain of breakers (chanvreurs) and weavers (chanevaciers).

chapacan.label: Chapacan
chapacan.summary: Municipal officer responsible for catching stray dogs in the streets.
chapacan.text: The chapacan (or chiapacan), a term of Occitan origin combining "chapar" (to catch) and "can" (dog), denoted the municipal officer responsible for catching stray dogs for hygiene and public-safety reasons, notably during rabies outbreaks.

chapeletier.label: Chapeletier (rosary maker)
chapeletier.summary: Craftsman making rosaries and other devotional objects of wood, bone or glass.
chapeletier.text: The chapeletier makes rosaries, as well as other small devotional objects, by stringing beads of turned wood, bone, mother-of-pearl or glass. This trade, organized into a guild as early as the Middle Ages under the name "paternôtriers", was particularly active in pilgrimage towns.

chapelier.label: Chapelier (hatter)
chapelier.summary: Craftsman specialized in making hats and other headwear.
chapelier.text: The chapelier makes hats, most often of wool or fur felt (rabbit, beaver), a craft organized into a guild as early as the Middle Ages and subject to strict rules on the quality of materials. The mercury-felting process, used to soften the fur, frequently caused poisoning among workers, the origin of the English expression "mad as a hatter".

chapelier_de_coton.label: Chapelier de Coton
chapelier_de_coton.summary: Hatter specialized in making hats of cotton or plant fibres.
chapelier_de_coton.text: The chapelier de coton makes hats from cotton or other plant fibres, a less costly alternative to wool- or fur-felt hats, intended for a more modest clientele or for summer wear.

chapelier_de_feutre.label: Chapelier de Feutre
chapelier_de_feutre.summary: Hatter specialized in making hats of wool or fur felt.
chapelier_de_feutre.text: The chapelier de feutre is the "classic" hatter, making hats by felting rabbit, hare or beaver fur, the most widespread and sought-after technique of hat-making from the Ancien Régime into the 20th century.

chapelier_de_fleurs.label: Chapelier de Fleurs
chapelier_de_fleurs.summary: Hatter specialized in hats trimmed with flowers, bordering on the milliner's trade.
chapelier_de_fleurs.text: The chapelier de fleurs trims hats, notably women's, with artificial flowers of cloth, feathers or wax, a skill that brings this trade closer to that of the milliner than to traditional men's hat-making.

chapelier_de_paon.label: Chapelier de Paon
chapelier_de_paon.summary: Hatter specialized in hats trimmed with peacock feathers.
chapelier_de_paon.text: The chapelier de paon trims hats with peacock feathers, highly prized for their brilliance, as part of the plume-trade fashion that enjoyed great success in the 19th century for luxury women's hat-making.

chapuis.label: Chapuis
chapuis.summary: Old name for the carpenter, a craftsman working structural timber.
chapuis.text: Chapuis is an old form of the word charpentier, denoting the craftsman who cuts and assembles roof and structural timber for building construction. This term also gave rise to the surname Chapuis, still common today in France and French-speaking Switzerland.

charbonnier.label: Charbonnier (charcoal burner)
charbonnier.summary: Producer of charcoal, obtained by the slow combustion of wood in earth-covered stacks.
charbonnier.text: The charbonnier makes charcoal by slowly burning, without flame, piles of wood covered with earth and moss (the "meules"), an indispensable fuel for forges and fire-based trades before coal became widespread. Often set up deep in the forest in temporary huts, charcoal burners formed a separate itinerant community, sometimes a source of suspicion — hence the name later given to the secret society of the "Carbonari".

charcutier.label: Charcutier (pork butcher)
charcutier.summary: Craftsman turning pork into prepared products: hams, pâtés, sausages.
charcutier.text: The charcutier, whose name comes from "chair cuite" (cooked meat — chaircuitier, chercuitier in old spellings), processes and sells pork in the form of prepared products — hams, sausages, pâtés, rillettes. The medieval charcutiers' guild held the exclusive monopoly on selling cooked and salted pork, other meats falling under the butcher.

chargeur.label: Chargeur
chargeur.summary: Worker responsible for loading and unloading goods.
chargeur.text: The chargeur handles goods during their loading or unloading, on quays, in warehouses or on transport vehicles. A generic handling term, found in various port, rail or industrial contexts.

charpagnate.label: Charpagnate
charpagnate.summary: Basket-maker of Lorraine specialized in working willow.
charpagnate.text: The charpagnate works willow according to the traditional basket-weaving techniques of Lorraine, making baskets and woven objects for farm or household use. The term, of regional form, is found mainly in records from this region.

charpentier.label: Charpentier (carpenter)
charpentier.summary: Craftsman specialized in building and assembling wooden roof frames and structures.
charpentier.text: The charpentier cuts and assembles the large timbers that form a building's frame — roof structures, floors, load-bearing structures — as opposed to the joiner (menuisier), who does finishing work (doors, windows, furniture). Organized into a guild as early as the Middle Ages, with its own journeymen of the Tour de France, this trade remains one of the most documented in old civil records.

charpentier_de_barriques.label: Charpentier de Barriques
charpentier_de_barriques.summary: Carpenter specialized in making casks and barrels, close to the cooper.
charpentier_de_barriques.text: The charpentier de barriques makes casks, barrels and other bent-wood containers, work close to that of the cooper but designated here from the angle of wood carpentry rather than coopering proper.

charpentier_de_grosses_oeuvres.label: Charpentier de Grosses Œuvres
charpentier_de_grosses_oeuvres.summary: Carpenter specialized in large building structures and major civil-engineering works.
charpentier_de_grosses_oeuvres.text: The charpentier de grosses œuvres builds large-scale timber frames — public buildings, market halls, civil-engineering works — as opposed to the "small works" of everyday carpentry. The expression "gros-œuvre" still today denotes, in construction, the major structural work of a building.

charpentier_de_haute_futaie.label: Charpentier de Haute Futaie
charpentier_de_haute_futaie.summary: Carpenter working timber from high forest, from large, superior-quality trees.
charpentier_de_haute_futaie.text: The charpentier de haute futaie uses timber from the "haute futaie", a forest-management method that lets trees grow over a long period to produce large, high-quality trunks, as opposed to coppice worked in short cycles. This nobler, sturdier timber was reserved for demanding roof frames.

charpentier_de_navires.label: Charpentier de Navires (shipwright)
charpentier_de_navires.summary: Craftsman specialized in building and repairing the wooden structures of ships.
charpentier_de_navires.text: The charpentier de navires (also called charpentier de nefs, "nef" being the old French word for ship) builds and repairs the hull and wooden structures of boats in shipyards and arsenals. This highly skilled trade was one of the essential crafts of shipbuilding before the age of iron and steel.

charretier.label: Charretier (carter)
charretier.summary: Driver of carts handling the transport of goods by land.
charretier.text: The charretier drives a horse-drawn cart, most often with one or two horses, to transport goods, harvests or materials. A very common term in rural records, also found in the contracted form "chartier".

charretier_paysan.label: Charretier Paysan
charretier_paysan.summary: Farmer who supplemented his income by hiring out his oxen and cart for transport work.
charretier_paysan.text: The charretier paysan is a farmer who, in addition to his farm work, makes use of his team of oxen and his cart to carry out paid transport on behalf of others, a common supplementary activity in the countryside.

charreur.label: Charreur
charreur.text: The charreur drives a char, a vehicle heavier than the cart, used to transport large loads such as timber, stone or harvested sheaves. The term is close to charretier while more specifically denoting the use of a high-tonnage vehicle.

charrieur_d_eau.label: Charrieur d'Eau (water carrier)
charrieur_d_eau.summary: Water carrier delivering to homes water drawn from public fountains.
charrieur_d_eau.text: The charrieur d'eau transported and delivered drinking water to homes, drawing it from public fountains and wells before running water became widespread. This urban trade, very present in Paris into the 19th century, was long practised by emigrants from the Auvergne, forerunners of the later "bougnats".

charron.label: Charron (wheelwright)
charron.summary: Craftsman who makes and repairs wheels, carts and animal-drawn vehicles.
charron.text: The charron builds and repairs the wheels, axles and bodies of carts, wagons and carriages. He works closely with the farrier, who fits the iron tyres (bands) onto the wooden wheels he has shaped.

charroyeur.label: Charroyeur
charroyeur.summary: Person handling the transport of goods by cart-haulage, as a trade or supplementary activity.
charroyeur.text: The charroyeur practises charroi, that is, the transport of goods by animal-drawn team, a term close to charretier but emphasizing the transport activity itself rather than driving a particular vehicle.

chartrier.label: Chartrier
chartrier.summary: Keeper of the charters and official documents of a lordship, an abbey or a noble family.
chartrier.text: The chartrier has custody of the chartrier — that is, the archive depository — of a lordship, an abbey or a great family, preserving deeds of ownership, contracts and legal instruments. The word denotes both the function and the place or the archival holdings itself, a term still used today in archival science.

chasan.label: Cantor (Chasan)
chasan.summary: Prayer leader and cantor who led the service in the synagogue.
chasan.text: The Chasan leads the congregation's prayer in the synagogue, chants the liturgical texts and performs the traditional melodies on holy days. In larger communities he was a trained cantor, often with a choir; in small rural communities the prayer leader (Vorbeter) usually held the office together with that of religious teacher and ritual slaughterer.

chasse_coquins.label: Chasse-Coquins
chasse_coquins.summary: Officer responsible for chasing off vagrants and petty offenders, sometimes in the service of a parish.
chasse_coquins.text: The chasse-coquins was a subordinate officer responsible for pursuing and driving off vagrants, beggars and petty offenders, whether in the service of the urban police or, in certain parishes, to maintain order around the church during services.

chasse_manee.label: Chasse-Manée
chasse_manee.summary: Rural intermediary organizing the door-to-door collection of grain for milling.
chasse_manee.text: The chasse-manée (also spelled chasse-maisnié depending on region) is a rural broker or intermediary who organized, often door to door, the collection of peasants' grain to carry it to the mill, for a fee. This type of intermediary service was common in certain areas of the Massif Central and southwestern France.

chasse_maree.label: Chasse-Marée
chasse_maree.summary: Carrier who rushed fresh fish from the coast to inland markets.
chasse_maree.text: The chasse-marée carried, at high speed by relays of horses, fresh fish caught on the coasts of Normandy and Brittany to the markets of Paris and other large cities, before the railway appeared. This demanding trade, mentioned in classic French literature, required speed and endurance to deliver a highly perishable good.

chasse_moute.label: Chasse-Moute
chasse_moute.summary: Miller or itinerant agent who collected grain at people's homes to process it at the mill.
chasse_moute.text: The chasse-moute (from "moute", a regional variant of "mouture"/milling) went from farm to farm collecting peasants' grain to take it to the mill, a common intermediary service in certain rural regions before everyone travelled there themselves.

chasse_mulet.label: Chasse-Mulet
chasse_mulet.summary: Miller's assistant responsible for auxiliary mill tasks, notably transport by mule.
chasse_mulet.text: The chasse-mulet assisted the miller with secondary mill tasks, particularly transporting sacks of grain and flour by mule between farms and the mill.

chasse_poche.label: Chasse Poche
chasse_poche.summary: Worker responsible for collecting and handling grain stored in sacks.
chasse_poche.text: The chasse-poche handled the collection and handling of grain kept in large sacks ("poches"), as part of the activities of a mill or a grain trade.

chasserat.label: Chasserat
chasserat.summary: Miller's assistant helping with milling and handling tasks at the mill.
chasserat.text: The chasserat helped the miller with the daily tasks of the mill — handling sacks, overseeing milling — a role of apprentice or auxiliary worker within the rural mill.

chasseron.label: Chasseron
chasseron.text: The chasseron worked alongside the miller in the various grain-processing operations of the mill, a regional term of the same family as chasserat, chasse-moute and chasse-mulet, all linked to the small staff of the rural mill.

chasseur.label: Chasseur (hunter)
chasseur.summary: Person hunting game, or, in a more modern sense, an employee handling errands or reception duties.
chasseur.text: In the most common sense, the chasseur hunts game, an activity of subsistence or leisure depending on period and social milieu. The word also denotes, in a more modern sense, a hotel or establishment employee responsible for errands and small services (the liveried "chasseur"), as well as certain military corps (chasseurs à pied, chasseurs alpins).

chassissier.label: Châssissier
chassissier.summary: Glazier specialized in making the lead frames encasing window panes and stained glass.
chassissier.text: The châssissier makes the lead frames (the lead "réseaux") used to set and assemble the pieces of glass in windows, glazed doors and stained-glass windows, a technique inherited from medieval glazing still used today for art stained glass.

chastreux.label: Chastreux
chastreux.summary: Itinerant castrator, specialized in castrating farm animals (pigs, bulls, horses).
chastreux.text: The chastreux (or châtreur, chatraire in Occitan) practises the castration of farm animals — pigs, calves, horses — a technical act requiring experience and dexterity. This trade was often practised itinerantly and seasonally, castrators travelling the countryside from farm to farm, a tradition particularly associated with southwestern France.

chasublier.label: Chasublier
chasublier.summary: Maker of chasubles and other liturgical vestments worn by priests.
chasublier.text: The chasublier makes chasubles and other liturgical ornaments (stoles, copes) worn by the clergy during services, often embroidered with gold thread and religious motifs. This specialized textile trade worked closely with parishes, chapters and religious communities.

chatelain.label: Châtelain (castellan)
chatelain.summary: Officer or lord dispensing justice and administering a châtellenie.
chatelain.text: The châtelain administers a châtellenie, a seigneurial district organized around a castle, where he dispenses justice in the lord's name and collects certain feudal dues. He is distinguished from the simple noble owner of a castle by this effective jurisdictional and administrative function.

chaucier.label: Chaucier
chaucier.summary: Medieval maker of hose, the garments covering legs and feet before the invention of the knitted stocking.
chaucier.text: The chaucier makes hose, a medieval garment covering the leg and sometimes the foot, cut and sewn from woven cloth — to be distinguished from the knitted stocking, later, which the chaussetier would produce. This old trade declined with the evolution of clothing fashion from the 16th century onward.

chaudronnier.label: Chaudronnier (coppersmith)
chaudronnier.summary: Craftsman who shapes copper and other metals into cauldrons, pots and kitchen utensils.
chaudronnier.text: The chaudronnier hammers sheets of copper or brass to make and repair cauldrons, pots and kitchen or industrial vessels. Many practised this trade itinerantly, going from village to village to repair copperware — a practice long associated with certain traveller communities.

chauffe_cire.label: Chauffe-Cire
chauffe_cire.summary: Officer of the royal chancery responsible for heating the wax used to affix the great seal.
chauffe_cire.text: The chauffe-cire is an officer of the Grande Chancellerie de France responsible for preparing and heating the wax needed to affix the great royal seal to official documents, a technical but prestigious function within the royal administration of the Ancien Régime.

chauffeur.label: Chauffeur
chauffeur.summary: Driver of a motor vehicle; originally, a worker responsible for feeding the firebox of a steam engine.
chauffeur.text: The word chauffeur, literally "one who heats", originally denoted the worker responsible for supplying fuel to the boiler of a steam engine (locomotive, boat, then steam automobile). The meaning shifted at the turn of the 20th century toward that of a motor-vehicle driver, the common sense today.

chauffeur_de_rivets.label: Chauffeur de Rivets
chauffeur_de_rivets.summary: Riveting-team worker responsible for heating metal rivets before they are driven.
chauffeur_de_rivets.text: The chauffeur de rivets is part of a riveting team in a shipyard or a metal-construction workshop: he heats the rivets red-hot before throwing them to the riveter, who inserts and immediately hammers them to join the plates. This teamwork, typical of 19th- and early-20th-century shipbuilding and railway construction, vanished with the spread of welding.

chaufournier.label: Chaufournier (lime burner)
chaufournier.summary: Operator of a lime kiln, producing the quicklime used in construction and agriculture.
chaufournier.text: The chaufournier operates a lime kiln, where he fires limestone at high temperature to produce quicklime, an essential material for building mortars and for improving farmland soils. This often-seasonal trade was practised near limestone quarries.

chaulier.label: Chaulier
chaulier.summary: Merchant or user of lime, notably for construction and improving land.
chaulier.text: The chaulier sells or uses lime, whether for preparing building mortars or for liming farmland, a practice aimed at correcting soil acidity. He is distinct from the chaufournier, who himself produces lime in the kiln.

chaumier.label: Chaumier
chaumier.summary: Roofing craftsman specialized in thatched roofs made of straw, reed or heather.
chaumier.text: The chaumier thatches roofs, using rye straw, reed or heather depending on the region, a traditional roofing technique particularly widespread in Normandy, Brittany and Sologne before tile and slate became widespread. In Auvergne and the Cantal, this same trade is denoted by the Occitan term cludjaire (from "clujaire", itself from "cluja", to thatch).

chaunier.label: Chaunier
chaunier.summary: Lime-stone extractor, responsible for the limestone quarry before firing by the chaufournier.
chaunier.text: The chaunier extracts limestone from the quarry, a step upstream in the lime-production chain, distinct from that of the chaufournier, who fires it in the kiln, and the chaulier, who sells or uses it. The term is uncommon and found mainly in limestone-quarry regions.

chaussetier.label: Chaussetier
chaussetier.summary: Maker of socks and stockings, notably knitted hosiery.
chaussetier.text: The chaussetier makes socks and stockings, originally cut and sewn from cloth, then, from the invention of the knitting frame in the 16th century, knitted as hosiery. This textile trade developed particularly in certain specialized regions such as Champagne (Troyes).

chausseur.label: Chausseur
chausseur.summary: Merchant and sometimes maker of shoes.
chausseur.text: The chausseur sells, and sometimes makes himself, shoes.

chaussier.label: Chaussier
chaussier.summary: Maker of shoes, a shoemaking craftsman.
chaussier.text: The chaussier makes shoes, a trade close to that of the cordonnier, also denoted by the regional forms chaussunier or chaussumier.

chaussonnier.label: Chaussonnier
chaussonnier.summary: Maker of slippers and indoor footwear.
chaussonnier.text: The chaussonnier makes slippers, light indoor footwear, a shoemaking craft distinct from making town or work shoes.

chavetier.label: Chavetier
chavetier.summary: Shoemaker specialized in repairing old shoes, close to the cobbler.
chavetier.text: The chavetier repairs worn shoes, a role close to that of the cobbler, as opposed to the cordonnier, who makes new ones. The term, of regional form, is found in certain provinces under related spellings.

chazan.label: Chazan (cantor)
chazan.summary: Leader of prayer and singer in a synagogue.
chazan.text: The chazan led prayers in the synagogue and performed liturgical chants, especially on holidays. He was employed and paid by the Jewish community, and in smaller communities often combined this role with others, such as ritual slaughterer or teacher.

chef_cuisinier.label: Chef cuisinier (head chef)
chef_cuisinier.summary: Person in charge of a restaurant's or establishment's kitchen, leading the team and the cooking.
chef_cuisinier.text: The chef cuisinier leads a kitchen brigade, designs the menus and supervises the preparation of dishes in a restaurant, a hotel or an institution. The title "chef" covers a precise hierarchy inherited from classical fine dining (chef de partie, sous-chef, executive chef).

chef_d_antenne.label: Chef d'antenne
chef_d_antenne.summary: Person responsible for the programming or presentation of a radio or television channel.
chef_d_antenne.text: The chef d'antenne directs the programming and broadcasting of a channel or station, ensuring the coherence of the programme schedule. In some usages, notably in Quebec, the term rather denotes the star anchor of the television news.

chef_de_place.label: Chef de Place
chef_de_place.summary: Officer responsible for commanding a stronghold or a strategic site.
chef_de_place.text: The chef de place (or commandant de place) leads the garrison and defence of a stronghold or a strategic military position, a local command function distinct from field command.

chef_de_production.label: Chef de production (production manager)
chef_de_production.summary: Person responsible for organizing and overseeing production in a company or a shoot.
chef_de_production.text: The chef de production oversees all the human, material and financial resources needed for a production, whether a factory, a film shoot or a show. The title covers very diverse realities depending on the industry.

chef_de_projet.label: Chef de Projet (project manager)
chef_de_projet.summary: Person responsible for planning, tracking and coordinating a project.
chef_de_projet.text: The chef de projet coordinates the human, financial and technical resources needed to carry out a project, in sectors as varied as IT, construction or industry. A common title of modern work organization, which appeared with the spread of project management.

chef_des_ponts.label: Chef des Ponts
chef_des_ponts.summary: Person responsible for building and maintaining bridges, often attached to the Ponts et Chaussées corps.
chef_des_ponts.text: The chef des ponts directs the construction and maintenance work of bridges, a technical function attached, from the 18th century, to the royal and then national Ponts et Chaussées corps, more broadly responsible for the road network and public infrastructure.

chemineau.label: Chemineau
chemineau.summary: Vagrant travelling the roads from village to village, with no fixed home.
chemineau.text: The chemineau is a vagrant or itinerant worker with no fixed home, travelling the roads from village to village in search of occasional work or charity. Not to be confused with the cheminot, the railway employee, despite the similarity of the two words.

cheminot.label: Cheminot (railwayman)
cheminot.summary: Railway employee, whatever the post (driver, signalman, maintenance worker).
cheminot.text: The cheminot works for a railway company, whether as a driver, signalman, station employee or track-maintenance worker. The term spread with the rise of the railway in France from the mid-19th century, and should not be confused with the chemineau, the road vagrant.

chevalier.label: Chevalier (knight)
chevalier.summary: Noble who has received the accolade, fighting on horseback in the service of a lord or the king.
chevalier.text: The chevalier belongs to the nobility of the sword, having received the accolade authorizing him to fight on horseback and bear arms in the service of a lord or the king. Both a noble title and a social status, it constitutes one of the rungs of the feudal hierarchy, below the titles of baron, count or duke.

chevalier_banneret.label: Chevalier banneret (knight banneret)
chevalier_banneret.summary: Knight of higher rank, authorized to raise and command his own troop under his own banner.
chevalier_banneret.text: The chevalier banneret is distinguished from the simple chevalier bachelier by the right to fly his own banner (square, unlike the bachelier's triangular pennon) and to command a company of vassals and men-at-arms recruited under his authority. This intermediate rank of medieval military nobility required sufficient financial means to maintain a troop.

chevalier_du_guet.label: Chevalier du Guet
chevalier_du_guet.summary: Officer commanding the guet, the night police responsible for the security of towns.
chevalier_du_guet.text: The chevalier du guet commanded the guet, an urban police corps responsible for night surveillance and keeping order in towns, notably in Paris where this office existed as early as the Middle Ages. He is one of the direct forerunners of the modern police, before the creation of the lieutenance générale de police in 1667.

chevalier_royal.label: Chevalier Royal
chevalier_royal.summary: Noble knight attached to the direct service of the king.
chevalier_royal.text: The expression chevalier royal generally denotes a knight attached to the sovereign's personal service, without constituting a well-defined official title like that of chevalier banneret. It is found mainly as a descriptive phrase in certain documents rather than as a precise institutional office.

chevaucheur_de_l_ecurie_du_roi.label: Chevaucheur de l'Écurie du Roi
chevaucheur_de_l_ecurie_du_roi.summary: Royal mounted messenger, attached to the King's Stable, responsible for carrying official dispatches.
chevaucheur_de_l_ecurie_du_roi.text: The chevaucheur de l'Écurie du Roi is a royal mounted courier, attached to the administration of the King's Stable, responsible for quickly carrying dispatches and official orders across the kingdom, before a regular postal service was established. This corps of mounted messengers is one of the forerunners of the royal postal service.

chevaucheur_royal.label: Chevaucheur Royal
chevaucheur_royal.summary: King's messenger responsible for carrying royal letters and orders within the kingdom and to embassies.
chevaucheur_royal.text: The chevaucheur royal carries, on horseback, the king's letters and orders across the kingdom and as far as foreign embassies, an official messenger service of the Ancien Régime.

chevillard.label: Chevillard (wholesale butcher)
chevillard.summary: Wholesale butcher, buying carcasses at the slaughterhouse to supply retail butchers.
chevillard.text: The chevillard buys livestock or carcasses directly at the slaughterhouse, where the meat is hung on "chevilles" (hooks), to resell it wholesale to retail butchers. This intermediary role between slaughter and retail sale became structured with the development of large urban slaughterhouses in the 19th century.

chevrier.label: Chevrier (goatherd)
chevrier.summary: Breeder and keeper of goats, often also a producer of goat cheese.
chevrier.text: The chevrier raises and keeps a herd of goats, driving the animals to pasture and often also handling milking and turning the milk into cheese. The term is found under various regional spelling variants.

chicoratier.label: Chicoratier
chicoratier.summary: Grower and processor of chicory, used notably as a coffee substitute.
chicoratier.text: The chicoratier grows chicory and processes it (roasting, grinding the root) to produce an inexpensive coffee substitute, an industry that boomed in northern France (the Lille, Orchies area) from the 19th century, particularly during coffee shortages such as the Continental Blockade.

chienneur.label: Chienneur
chienneur.summary: Dog groomer, responsible for clipping dogs.
chienneur.text: The chienneur is a dog groomer, a small service trade for pet owners, attested in old and rare occupational registers.

chiffonnier.label: Chiffonnier (ragpicker)
chiffonnier.summary: Gatherer of rags and old objects, resold to papermakers or scrap dealers.
chiffonnier.text: The chiffonnier walked the streets, basket on his back and hook in hand, to salvage rags, metal, glass, bone and other waste later resold to recycling industries, particularly to paper mills, which used rag as a raw material before wood pulp became widespread. An emblematic figure of 19th-century working-class Paris, the chiffonnier inspired many writers, including Baudelaire.

chiffonnier_tisserand.label: Chiffonnier (tisserand)
chiffonnier_tisserand.summary: Weaver using shredded rags as textile raw material.
chiffonnier_tisserand.text: The chiffonnier-weaver uses wool or cotton rags, shredded into reusable fibres (the shredding process), to weave inexpensive fabrics, a textile-recycling industry that developed notably in northern France in the 19th century.

chiffrier.label: Chiffrier
chiffrier.summary: Accountant or bookkeeper responsible for commercial entries and calculations.
chiffrier.text: The chiffrier keeps the accounts and account books of a business or an administration, a role close to that of the modern accountant, at a time when mastery of commercial arithmetic and calculation was not universally widespread.

chignoleur_de_lavoirs.label: Chignoleur de Lavoirs
chignoleur_de_lavoirs.summary: Worker responsible for the upkeep and proper operation of public wash-houses.
chignoleur_de_lavoirs.text: The chignoleur de lavoirs handled the routine upkeep, repairs and operation of public communal wash-houses, the fitted basins where washerwomen came to wash their linen before private laundries and running water at home became widespread.

chiourme.label: Chiourme
chiourme.summary: The body of convicts sentenced to the galleys, referred to collectively.
chiourme.text: The chiourme collectively denotes the crew of convicts rowing on a galley, sentenced to forced labour and chained to their bench. This penal workforce was overseen by the comite, an officer responsible for discipline and setting the rowing pace. The term is sometimes found in records to denote an individual who had belonged to this population of galley slaves.

chiqueteuse.label: Chiqueteuse
chiqueteuse.summary: Female worker preparing the fur used to make felt hats.
chiqueteuse.text: The chiqueteuse prepares and sorts the fur (rabbit, hare, beaver) used in hat-making for felting, a step that sometimes included "secretage" or carroting with mercury nitrate, a process that made the fur more felt-able but gravely exposed workers to mercury poisoning.

chirurgien.label: Chirurgien (surgeon)
chirurgien.summary: Practitioner performing bloodletting, minor procedures and difficult childbirths, distinct from the learned physician.
chirurgien.text: Under the Ancien Régime, the chirurgien practises a manual trade descended from the barber-surgeons' guild, performing bloodletting, tooth extractions, amputations and assistance with difficult births, as opposed to the médecin, university-trained and confined to theory and diagnosis. The Latin term "chirurgus", used in parish registers written in Latin, denotes the master surgeon.

chocolatero.label: Chocolatero (Spanish chocolate maker)
chocolatero.summary: Person who made or sold chocolate.
chocolatero.text: The chocolatero made chocolate by grinding cocoa with sugar and spices, traditionally by hand on a heated stone, and sold it in tablets or served it as a drink. Until mechanisation in the 19th century many chocolateros worked in customers' homes, going from house to house with their tools.

christalier.label: Christalier
christalier.summary: Glassworker specialized in making crystal objects.
