christalier.text: The christalier shapes crystal objects, a lead glass particularly brilliant and resonant, a luxury craft that boomed in France with the creation of great manufactories such as Baccarat and Saint-Louis in the 18th and 19th centuries.

churrero.label: Churrero (Spanish churro maker)
churrero.summary: Person who fried and sold churros.
churrero.text: The churrero fried a dough of flour, water and salt in oil to make churros, which he sold at a stall, in a churrería or in the streets, especially in the mornings and at fairs and festivals.

cidrier.label: Cidrier (cider maker)
cidrier.summary: Craftsman making cider from fermented apples or pears.
cidrier.text: The cidrier presses and ferments apple juice (or pear juice, for perry) to produce cider, a traditional drink of apple-growing regions such as Normandy and Brittany, where it often replaced wine in everyday consumption.

cigariere.label: Cigarière (cigar maker)
cigariere.summary: Female worker hand-rolling cigars and cigarettes in a tobacco factory.
cigariere.text: The cigarière worked in a tobacco manufactory, hand-rolling cigars and cigarettes. The great French state manufactories (Marseille, Toulouse, Morlaix, Nantes) employed an overwhelmingly female workforce, which was behind several notable social movements at the end of the 19th century.

cinquantainier.label: Cinquantainier
cinquantainier.summary: Medieval municipal officer commanding a group of fifty men within the town watch.
cinquantainier.text: The cinquantenier commanded a company of fifty men within the bourgeois watch, the urban militia responsible for the security and night surveillance of medieval towns, under the authority of a quartenier responsible for a district of the town.

cinuronnier.label: Cinuronnier
cinuronnier.summary: Craftsman making cuirasses and armour pieces of reinforced leather.
cinuronnier.text: The cinuronnier makes cuirasses and armour elements of boiled or reinforced leather, a lighter and less costly protection than metal armour, used notably by the infantry and men of war of lesser means.

cireur.label: Cireur (polisher)
cireur.summary: Person who cleaned and shined shoes, on the street or in an establishment.
cireur.text: The cireur cleaned and polished passers-by's shoes, often set up on a street corner with his shoeshine box, a small urban trade long practised by young boys. The related term "décrotteur" denoted a very similar function, ridding shoes of street mud before the age of asphalt.

cirier.label: Cirier (wax chandler)
cirier.summary: Maker of candles and wax objects, notably for liturgical use.
cirier.text: The cirier works beeswax to make candles and tapers, in particular the liturgical candles used in churches. A more costly material than the tallow used by the chandelier, wax was reserved for religious use and wealthy households. The term ciergier, used more specifically for making church candles, denotes the same trade.

cirquassien.label: Cirquassien
cirquassien.summary: Itinerant performer appearing in a travelling circus.
cirquassien.text: The cirquassien performs in a travelling circus, doing various acts (acrobatics, animal training, juggling) over the course of tours from troupe to troupe, a nomadic way of life characteristic of the fairground entertainment world.

ciseleur.label: Ciseleur
ciseleur.summary: Metal craftsman who decorates and shapes goldsmith's pieces with hammer and chasing tool.
ciseleur.text: The ciseleur works and decorates precious metals with hammer and chasing tool, repoussé-working or engraving the metal to create raised motifs, an art closely linked to goldsmithing and art bronze-work.

citoleeur.label: Citoléeur
citoleeur.summary: Instrument-maker or musician playing the citole, a medieval plucked-string instrument.
citoleeur.text: The citoléeur makes or plays the citole, a medieval musical instrument with plucked strings and a short neck, a distant ancestor of the cittern and the guitar. The term can denote either the instrument-maker who builds it or the musician who plays it.

civile.label: Civile (southern Italian gentry status)
civile.summary: In southern Italy, a person of comfortable means who did no manual work.
civile.text: In the records of southern Italy and Sicily, the description civile designated a person who lived on private income or practised a liberal profession without doing manual work: the class of the galantuomini, distinct from peasants and artisans. A social rank rather than an occupation, it often appears alongside the title don.

clapteur.label: Clapteur
clapteur.summary: Cooper's craftsman making clappes, small pieces of wood used in coopering.
clapteur.text: The clapteur makes clappes, small pieces of wood used as assembly or closing elements in building casks, an auxiliary trade of coopering.

clautrier.label: Clautrier
clautrier.summary: Craftsman specialized in making fences and enclosures.
clautrier.text: The clautrier (or claustrier) builds fences and enclosure devices, a term whose root refers to the Latin "claustrum" (enclosed precinct), also the origin of the word "cloître" (cloister).

clavellier.label: Clavellier
clavellier.summary: Locksmith, maker of locks and keys, an Occitan-usage term.
clavellier.text: The clavellier makes locks and keys, a regional term derived from the Occitan "clavèl" (key, lock), itself from the Latin "clavis". It is the Occitan equivalent of the serrurier of northern France.

claveteur.label: Claveteur
claveteur.summary: Craftsman making clavettes, small metal pieces used as pins or assembly pegs.
claveteur.text: The claveteur (or clavetier) forges clavettes, small wedge- or pin-shaped metal pieces used to fix an axle, a wheel or any mechanical assembly, small-forge work sometimes conflated in sources with nail-making.

clayonneur.label: Clayonneur (hurdle maker)
clayonneur.summary: Worker building woven structures of branches, used in masonry or land management.
clayonneur.text: The clayonneur makes wattlework, woven structures of flexible branches (willow, hazel) used as a support for earth cob when raising walls (wattle-and-daub technique), reinforcing riverbanks or marking off plots.

clerc.label: Clerc
clerc.summary: Originally an educated member of the clergy, then, by extension, an employee of a notarial or judicial office.
clerc.text: The clerc originally denotes a churchman who has received at least the tonsure, often a man of letters, hence its later use to denote any educated employee working in a notarial office, a court registry or a lawyer's office. This semantic shift, from the ecclesiastical clerc to the notary's clerk, is the origin of the very common surname Leclerc.

clergeresse.label: Clergeresse
clergeresse.summary: Woman elected to head a female guild or occupational community, for example that of the linen-workers.
clergeresse.text: The clergeresse ran the affairs of a community or guild of women practising the same trade, such as the linen-workers, a role close to that of a prud'homme but reserved for female guilds, governed by the rules of Ancien Régime confraternities.

clicheur.label: Clicheur (stereotyper)
clicheur.summary: Printing worker who prepared the metal plates (clichés) used for printing.
clicheur.text: The clicheur pours molten metal into moulds to produce clichés — relief printing plates — used in typography, a stereotyping technique that allowed the same text or image to be reproduced quickly. The word "cliché", today a synonym for a commonplace, comes directly from this printing vocabulary.

clignotant.label: Clignotant
clignotant.summary: Railway employee responsible for operating signals and points on Belgian lines.
clignotant.text: The clignotant operates light signals and railway points, a railway-safety function attested notably in Belgian railway vocabulary.

clissier.label: Clissier
clissier.summary: Basket-maker specialized in making clisses, woven trays used notably in cheesemaking.
clissier.text: The clissier weaves clisses, light trays of willow or rush used as draining moulds by cheesemakers, but also for packaging bottles or fragile objects. This fine basket-weaving trade differs from ordinary basketry by the fineness of its weaves.

clocheron.label: Clocheron
clocheron.summary: Church bell-ringer, responsible for announcing services and parish events.
clocheron.text: The clocheron rings the church bells to announce religious services, but also significant events of parish life (births, deaths, alerts), a function often carried out by the sacristan or beadle.

clocheteur.label: Clocheteur
clocheteur.summary: Town crier ringing a small bell to announce news or notices, notably for the deceased.
clocheteur.text: The clocheteur walked the streets ringing a small bell to draw attention before announcing a public notice. The "clocheteur des trépassés" had the particular task of announcing at night the deaths that had occurred in the parish, inviting residents to pray for the deceased's soul.

clochetier.label: Clochetier
clochetier.summary: Bell founder, a craftsman specialized in casting bronze for church bells.
clochetier.text: The clochetier casts church bells in bronze, a technical craft requiring great mastery of smelting and moulding. Bell founders often worked itinerantly, setting up their temporary foundry right next to the bell tower to be equipped.

closier.label: Closier (tenant farmer)
closier.summary: Tenant of a closerie, a small enclosed farm worked under a contract close to sharecropping.
closier.text: The closier farms a closerie, a small farm enclosed by hedges or low walls of about 5 to 10 hectares, held from its owner under a tenancy contract close to sharecropping — unlike the métayer, the closier generally has only cows and not a team of oxen. This agrarian status, intermediate between the day-labourer and the métayer (with whom he could blend as he gained wealth up to the rank of laboureur), is particularly documented in Anjou, where it corresponds to the bordager of neighbouring Maine. The term is sometimes spelled clozier.

clotier.label: Clôtier
clotier.summary: Craftsman specialized in making and installing fences.
clotier.text: The clôtier builds and installs agricultural or domestic fences, of wood, dry stone or living hedge depending on locally available materials. Not to be confused with the closier, tenant of an enclosed farm.

cloutier.label: Cloutier (nailer)
cloutier.summary: Blacksmith craftsman making nails by hand, often as a rural supplementary trade.
cloutier.text: The cloutier forges nails by hand on a small anvil, a light-forge craft activity very widespread in certain rural regions (Vosges, Forez, Pays de Bray) where it supplemented income from farm work, before being supplanted by mechanized industrial production in the 19th century. The term is also found in the forms cloitrier or clotrier, notably in northern Périgord.

cocher.label: Cocher (coachman)
cocher.summary: Driver of a coach or carriage, responsible for driving the team and its passengers.
cocher.text: The cocher drives a coach, a carriage or any other horse-drawn vehicle, a position that required good mastery of driving a team and enjoyed, notably in great households, a certain prestige within the domestic staff.

cocher_du_corps.label: Cocher du corps
cocher_du_corps.summary: Coachman driving the carriage of a person of royal blood.
cocher_du_corps.text: The cocher du corps drives the carriage in which a person of royal blood ordinarily rides, a position of trust within the royal stable.

cocherel.label: Cocherel
cocherel.summary: Merchant selling roosters and poultry at markets.
cocherel.text: The cocherel sold roosters and, more broadly, poultry at local markets, a small local food trade.

cochetier.label: Cochetier
cochetier.summary: Naval carpenter specialized in building ships' hulls.
cochetier.text: The cochetier is a specialized naval carpenter, whose name evokes work on the ship's hull, as opposed to other naval carpenters responsible for rigging or interior fitting.

coeffeur.label: Coëffeur
coeffeur.summary: Craftsman responsible for hairdressing, hair care and making wigs.
coeffeur.text: The coëffeur handles hairdressing and hair care, and also makes wigs, then very much in vogue in Ancien Régime society of the 17th and 18th centuries. This trade, organized into the guild of master wigmaker-barber-bathhouse-keeper-steam-bath attendants, is the direct forerunner of the modern hairdresser.

coffretier.label: Coffretier
coffretier.summary: Craftsman making chests, trunks and suitcases for storage or travel.
coffretier.text: The coffretier makes wooden chests, trunks and suitcases, often reinforced with ironwork and covered in leather, intended for storing linen and valuables or for carrying them while travelling.

cogniticien.label: Cogniticien (knowledge engineer)
cogniticien.summary: Specialist in knowledge engineering, responsible for modelling human expertise for expert systems.
cogniticien.text: The cogniticien is a specialist in knowledge engineering ("cognitique"), a field born in the 1980s with the rise of expert systems in artificial intelligence. His role consists of gathering and formalizing the know-how of human experts to transpose it into computer systems.

coiffeur.label: Coiffeur (hairdresser)
coiffeur.summary: Modern profession of hair care and styling, in a hairdressing salon.
coiffeur.text: The coiffeur cuts, styles and shapes his clients' hair in a hairdressing salon, a modern personal-service trade, to be distinguished from the Ancien Régime coëffeuse, more geared toward wig-making.

collassier.label: Collassier
collassier.summary: Saddlery craftsman specialized in certain leather equipment, probably related to harness-making.
collassier.text: The collassier is a leather craftsman close to saddlery, whose exact specialty remains uncertain but which may be related to the colleron, maker of draught-animal harness collars.

collecteur.label: Collecteur
collecteur.summary: Person responsible for collecting taxes, dues or various levies.
collecteur.text: The collecteur collects the taxes and dues owed to the State, the lord or the Church (tithe), a function often entrusted annually to a parish resident under the Ancien Régime, tasked with recovering the sums owed by his neighbours.

colleron.label: Colleron
colleron.summary: Harness maker specialized in making harness collars for draught animals.
colleron.text: The colleron makes the padded collars worn by draught horses and oxen, an essential harness piece that distributes the pulling effort over the animal's shoulders. The invention and spread of the padded shoulder collar, from the early Middle Ages, allowed a marked increase in usable draught power in agriculture.

colletier.label: Colletier
colletier.summary: Leather craftsman making colletins, a kind of jerkin or protective leather piece.
colletier.text: The colletier makes colletins, garment or protective pieces of leather covering the torso or shoulders, a craft close to saddlery and soft-leather work.

colleur.label: Colleur
colleur.summary: Textile worker who applies a glue or gum sizing to the warp threads before weaving.
colleur.text: The colleur applies a sizing — a preparation based on glue or gum — to the warp threads before they are mounted on the loom, in order to strengthen them and ease the passage of the shuttle during weaving.

colon.label: Colon
colon.summary: Tenant of a farm under sharecropping, farming an owner's land in exchange for a share of the harvest.
colon.text: In rural France, the colon is a farm tenant who works another's land under a system close to sharecropping ("colonage partiaire"), sharing harvests or income with the owner. In a colonial context, the same word denotes an entirely different status, that of the settler established in a French colony (the Antilles, Algeria), which calls for checking the document's context.

colon_partiaire.label: Colon partiaire
colon_partiaire.summary: Sharecropper paying his landlord in kind with a share of the harvest not fixed at one-half.
colon_partiaire.text: The colon partiaire is a sharecropper who pays his landlord in kind with part of the harvest, without that share necessarily being one-half as in classic sharecropping.

coloriste.label: Coloriste
coloriste.summary: Worker specialized in preparing and applying colours, in textiles or printmaking.
coloriste.text: The coloriste prepares and applies colours, whether in printed-cotton ("indienne") manufactories (printed cotton cloth, as at Mulhouse or Rouen) or for the hand-colouring of prints and engravings before polychrome printing became widespread.

colporteur.label: Colporteur (peddler)
colporteur.summary: Itinerant merchant selling small goods from village to village.
colporteur.text: The colporteur travels villages and countryside to sell small goods — haberdashery, almanacs, prints, chapbooks of the Bibliothèque bleue — carried on his back or in a pack. This itinerant trade, famous for its networks originating in Savoy, the Auvergne and the Pyrenees, contributed to the spread of print in the French countryside into the 19th century.

come.label: Côme
come.summary: Officer commanding and overseeing the convicts on a galley, also called comite.
come.text: The côme (more commonly spelled "comite") commands the chiourme of a galley: he directs the manoeuvring of the convict rowers, ensures their discipline and sets the rowing pace, under the captain's authority. This term, of Italian origin ("comito"), belongs to the vocabulary of the 16th–18th-century Mediterranean royal galleys.

comissario_do_santo_oficio.label: Comissário do Santo Ofício (commissary of the Inquisition)
comissario_do_santo_oficio.summary: Cleric who represented the Inquisition locally and conducted inquiries on its behalf.
comissario_do_santo_oficio.text: The comissário do Santo Ofício is a cleric, often a parish priest or canon, representing the Portuguese Inquisition in a town or region: he receives denunciations, hears witnesses and conducts the inquiries for the qualification of familiares and other officers of the tribunal. Like the familiares, he was subject to a qualification process investigating his ancestry.

commandeur.label: Commandeur
commandeur.summary: Overseer responsible for directing gangs of enslaved workers in the French colonies.
commandeur.text: The commandeur directed and oversaw teams of enslaved people at work on plantations in the French colonies (notably the Antilles), a supervisory function often entrusted to a trusted enslaved person or a freedman, an intermediary between the master and the enslaved workers.

commensale.label: Commensale
commensale.summary: Household employee housed and fed by her employer, sharing his table.
commensale.text: The commensale is a domestic housed and fed at her employer's home, literally "she who shares his table" (from the Latin "mensa"), a common condition for female servants and household employees under the Ancien Régime.

commercant.label: Commerçant (tradesman, shopkeeper)
commercant.summary: Person who bought and resold goods.
commercant.text: The commerçant bought and resold goods, whether as a wholesale merchant, a shopkeeper or a trader. It is a generic term covering a wide variety of commercial activities depending on the period and the scale of the trade carried on.

commercant_en_tissus.label: Commerçant en tissus (cloth merchant)
commercant_en_tissus.summary: Merchant specialized in selling cloth and fabrics.
commercant_en_tissus.text: The commerçant en tissus sells fabrics retail or wholesale, a trade often linked to haberdashery or drapery depending on the range of fabrics offered.

commercial.label: Commercial (sales representative)
commercial.summary: Modern employee responsible for a company's sales and business development.
commercial.text: The commercial is responsible, within a modern company, for prospecting, selling and following up with clients, a contemporary job title covering functions once denoted by terms such as representative or travelling salesman.

commeteur.label: Commeteur
commeteur.summary: Rope-making worker who twists together strands of tarred hemp to form a rope.
commeteur.text: The commeteur works in a ropewalk, where he "commets" — that is, twists together — strands of caret (tarred hemp yarn) to form the strands and then the cordage, a technical operation essential to the strength of ropes intended for shipping.

commis.label: Commis (clerk)
commis.summary: Subordinate employee assisting a merchant, a notary or an administration in everyday tasks.
commis.text: The commis assists an employer — merchant, notary, court clerk — with everyday administrative and commercial tasks, a generic term found in a great many trades (commis marchand, commis greffier, commis de bureau).

commis_a_la_descente_des_trains.label: Commis à la Descente des Trains
commis_a_la_descente_des_trains.summary: Employee handling the hauling of timber rafts at the confluence of two rivers via a pulley system.
commis_a_la_descente_des_trains.text: At the confluence of two rivers, the commis à la descente des trains is the employee responsible for hauling timber rafts using a system of pulleys and cables, replacing manual hauling.

commis_aux_fermes.label: Commis Aux Fermes
commis_aux_fermes.summary: Agent of the Ferme générale, responsible for collecting royal indirect taxes.
commis_aux_fermes.text: The commis aux Fermes worked for the Ferme générale, the company of financiers who leased from the king the collection of indirect taxes (gabelle, aides, internal customs, tobacco). These agents, responsible for surveillance and collection, were particularly unpopular because of the fight against smuggling they carried out, notably against salt smuggling.

commis_aux_gabelles.label: Commis Aux Gabelles
commis_aux_gabelles.summary: Agent responsible for collecting and enforcing the gabelle, the royal salt tax.
commis_aux_gabelles.text: The commis aux gabelles collected and enforced the gabelle, the royal tax on salt, one of the most hated of the Ancien Régime because of its unequal character and the severe repression of smuggling ("faux-saunage") it entailed.

commis_surveillant.label: Commis Surveillant
commis_surveillant.summary: Clerk responsible for overseeing weavers working from home on behalf of a merchant.
commis_surveillant.text: The commis surveillant visited and checked the work of weavers scattered across the countryside or suburbs, employed at home by the same merchant-manufacturer under the "scattered manufactory" system characteristic of the pre-industrial textile industry.

commissaire.label: Commissaire
commissaire.summary: Officer entrusted with a specific administrative or judicial mission on behalf of a higher authority.
commissaire.text: The commissaire carries out a temporary or permanent mission entrusted by an authority (king, town, court), in varied fields: judicial inquiries, police, administration. The title covered many functions under the Ancien Régime (commissaire du Châtelet, commissaire enquêteur) before specializing in the 19th century into the police sense.

commissaire_aux_montres_de_la_marechauss.label: Commissaire aux Montres de la Maréchaussée
commissaire_aux_montres_de_la_marechauss.summary: Gendarmerie officer of the Ancien Régime.
commissaire_aux_montres_de_la_marechauss.text: The commissaire aux montres de la maréchaussée is a gendarmerie officer responsible for the inspection (the "montre") of the personnel and equipment of the maréchaussée companies.

commissaire_de_police.label: Commissaire de police (police superintendent)
commissaire_de_police.summary: Police officer in charge of the police services of a district.
commissaire_de_police.text: The commissaire de police directed the police services of a town or an arrondissement. The institution took shape in France from the 19th century onwards and was heir to the former commissaires of the Châtelet under the Ancien Régime.

commissaire_examinateur_au_chatelet.label: Commissaire Examinateur au Châtelet
commissaire_examinateur_au_chatelet.summary: Parisian judicial officer responsible for fighting crime.
commissaire_examinateur_au_chatelet.text: The commissaire examinateur au Châtelet is a judicial officer responsible, within the jurisdiction of the Châtelet, for fighting crime in Paris.

commissionnaire.label: Commissionnaire (commission agent)
commissionnaire.summary: Intermediary responsible for carrying messages or handling business on behalf of others.
commissionnaire.text: The commissionnaire carries out commissions on behalf of a third party — carrying messages, errands — but can also denote a broader commercial intermediary, handling the buying, selling or transport of goods for a commission.

commissionnaire_de_roulage.label: Commissionnaire de Roulage
commissionnaire_de_roulage.summary: Delivery agent bringing to the end customer goods delivered wholesale by the rouliers.
commissionnaire_de_roulage.text: The commissionnaire de roulage is a delivery agent responsible for bringing goods delivered wholesale by the rouliers to the end customer.

communier.label: Communier
communier.summary: Member of a rural family community jointly farming an estate, with no personal income.
communier.text: The communier belongs to a "communauté taisible", an extended family association collectively farming an agricultural estate with no individual division of property or income, a rural organization particularly documented in central France (Bourbonnais, Nivernais, Berry) into the 19th century.

compagnon_de_riviere.label: Compagnon de rivière
compagnon_de_riviere.summary: Trained rafting worker, member of a guild, taking part in floating timber down rivers.
compagnon_de_riviere.text: The compagnon de rivière is a timber-floating worker, a technique that involved moving logs or assembled timber rafts along waterways to towns, notably to supply Paris with firewood from the Morvan via the Yonne. The term "compagnon" indicates the status of a skilled worker, often organized into a guild, as opposed to a mere day-labourer. This dangerous, seasonal trade vanished with the development of the railway in the 19th century.

compassier.label: Compassier
compassier.summary: Instrument-making mechanic making and repairing compasses and other precision instruments.
compassier.text: The compassier is a precision-instrument mechanic responsible for making and repairing compasses, intended for drafting, measurement or navigation. The trade is attested in Paris as early as the Ancien Régime, held by masters organized into a guild alongside other makers of scientific instruments.

complanteur.label: Complanteur
complanteur.summary: Person responsible for planting vines, often under a complant contract.
complanteur.text: The complanteur plants vine stock on land he does not own, under a contract known as "bail à complant": in exchange for his work planting and tending the vines over several years, he receives a share of the harvest or of the property once the vineyard is productive. This contractual system greatly contributed to the expansion of vineyards in southwestern France in the 17th and 18th centuries.

comporteur.label: Comporteur
comporteur.summary: Old form of the word colporteur, denoting an itinerant merchant selling small goods.
comporteur.text: Comporteur is actually the old form of the word: it is colporteur that is an alteration of "comporteur", by popular association with "porter sur le col" (to carry on the neck). The colporteur/comporteur sells small goods — haberdashery, almanacs, books, remedies — from village to village, often carried on the back in a pack or basket. This itinerant trade played an important role in spreading ideas and manufactured objects in the countryside into the 19th century.

compositeur.label: Compositeur (compositor)
compositeur.summary: Typesetting worker assembling movable type to set a text for printing.
compositeur.text: In the vocabulary of Ancien Régime and 19th-century printing, the compositeur (or compositeur typographe) is the worker who manually assembles movable lead type, letter by letter, to form the lines and then the pages intended for printing. A skilled trade, organized into a guild, distinct from the pressier, who operates the press. The term can be confused with the music composer, unrelated to this workshop trade.

compteur.label: Compteur
compteur.summary: Person responsible for counting, checking or tallying quantities of goods or people.
compteur.text: The compteur is responsible for tallying and checking quantities — goods, sacks, casks, coins — notably in ports, market halls or warehouses. The function covers very variable realities depending on period and place, ranging from a simple quay checker to a sworn official responsible for guaranteeing accurate measures.

comys_a_la_geolle.label: Comys à la geolle
comys_a_la_geolle.text: The comys à la geôle is a servant in the service of a prison keeper, responsible for subordinate tasks in the gaol.

concierge.label: Concierge (caretaker)
concierge.summary: Keeper responsible for the watch and upkeep of a building or an estate.
concierge.text: The concierge is responsible for guarding, maintaining and sometimes opening and closing a building: town house, château, apartment block or public establishment. Under the Ancien Régime, the term often denoted an officer responsible for guarding a royal or seigneurial building, before more generally denoting the building caretaker from the 19th century.

conciliateur.label: Conciliateur
conciliateur.summary: Person responsible for amicably bringing parties together and resolving a dispute.
conciliateur.text: The conciliateur steps in to help two parties in dispute reach an amicable agreement, without going to trial. In France, the office of court conciliator, voluntary and attached to the courts, has existed since the 20th century, but older forms of conciliation already existed under the Ancien Régime in consular and seigneurial jurisdictions.

conducteur.label: Conducteur
conducteur.summary: Person responsible for driving vehicles or teams, or for supervising works, depending on context.
conducteur.text: The term conducteur covers several realities: driver of a stagecoach or public carriage, works supervisor in building or road-and-bridge construction, or machine operator in early industry. The precise sense depends heavily on the context of the record and the period.

conducteur_d_hotel.label: Conducteur d'hôtel
conducteur_d_hotel.summary: Driver providing a shuttle service between a hotel and the station or tourist areas.
conducteur_d_hotel.text: The conducteur d'hôtel is a driver responsible for transporting guests, shuttling between the hotel and the station or tourist areas.

conducteur_d_omnibus.label: Conducteur d'omnibus
conducteur_d_omnibus.summary: Employee directing the manoeuvres, stops and departures of a passenger transport carriage.
conducteur_d_omnibus.text: The conducteur d'omnibus is the employee of a transport company who directs the manoeuvres, stops and departures of a passenger carriage and collects the fares.

conducteur_de_gabare.label: Conducteur de gabare
conducteur_de_gabare.summary: Boatman driving a gabare, a flat-bottomed craft used for river transport of goods.
conducteur_de_gabare.text: The conducteur de gabare pilots a gabare, a flat-bottomed boat typical of the rivers of southwestern France (Dordogne, Garonne, Lot), used to carry wine, timber, stone or other goods to seaports such as Bordeaux or Libourne. This river trade declined with the rise of the railway at the end of the 19th century.

conducteur_de_trains_de_bois.label: Conducteur de trains de bois
conducteur_de_trains_de_bois.summary: Worker steering assembled timber rafts downstream during floating.
conducteur_de_trains_de_bois.text: The conducteur de trains de bois guides a "train de bois", an assembly of logs or billets bound together, along rivers to their destination, a technique called floating. This trade required good knowledge of the waterway and its dangers (rapids, mills, bridges) and vanished with the development of rail transport.

conducteur_des_ouvrages_du_roi.label: Conducteur des Ouvrages du Roi
conducteur_des_ouvrages_du_roi.summary: Under the Ancien Régime, an official leading a maintenance crew for bridges, roads and canals.
conducteur_des_ouvrages_du_roi.text: Under the Ancien Régime, the conducteur des ouvrages du roi is an official who, at the head of a crew of workers, is responsible for maintaining royal bridges, roads and canals.

confectionneuse_de_fourreaux_a_bouteille.label: Confectionneuse de Fourreaux à Bouteilles en Fil de Laiton
confectionneuse_de_fourreaux_a_bouteille.summary: Female worker making brass-wire netting at home to decorate cognac bottles.
confectionneuse_de_fourreaux_a_bouteille.text: The confectionneuse de fourreaux à bouteilles en fil de laiton makes brass-wire netting to decorate cognac bottles, a supplementary activity carried out exclusively at home.

confesseur.label: Confesseur (confessor)
confesseur.summary: Priest authorized to hear confession and administer the sacrament of penance.
confesseur.text: The confesseur is a priest who hears the faithful's confession and grants them absolution in the Church's name. Some confesseurs, called appointed confessors, were attached to a great noble or royal household to give their employer spiritual guidance.

confiseur.label: Confiseur (confectioner)
confiseur.summary: Craftsman making confectionery, sugared almonds, candied fruit and other sweets.
confiseur.text: The confiseur works sugar to produce sugared almonds, sweets, candied fruit, fruit pastes and other sweets. This trade, distinct from the pastry cook, became organized into a guild from the 17th century and thrived particularly in towns known for their sugar specialties, such as Verdun for its sugared almonds.

congreganiste.label: Congréganiste
congreganiste.summary: Member of a religious congregation or a pious association attached to it.
congreganiste.text: The congréganiste is a member of a congregation: this may be a religious brother or sister belonging to an institute without solemn vows (teaching, care), or, in an older sense, a pupil affiliated with a Marian congregation (a pious student association) in a school run by Jesuits or other teaching orders.

connetable.label: Connétable (constable)
connetable.summary: Highest military dignitary of the Kingdom of France, commander-in-chief of the royal armies.
connetable.text: The connétable de France is the crown's premier officer, commander-in-chief of the royal armies and responsible for military justice, an office dating back to the Middle Ages. The function was abolished in 1627 under Richelieu after the death of the last holder, the Duke of Lesdiguières. By extension, the term also denoted, in certain towns or lordships, a local officer responsible for the watch or the police.

conreeur_de_robes_de_basane.label: Conréeur de robes de basane
conreeur_de_robes_de_basane.text: The conréeur de robes de basane curries basane, tanned sheepskin, more common and less costly than cordovan.

conreeur_de_robes_de_cordouan.label: Conréeur de robes de cordouan
conreeur_de_robes_de_cordouan.text: The conréeur de robes de cordouan curries cordovan leather, tanned from goatskin, prized for its suppleness and quality.

conseiller_d_administration.label: Conseiller d'administration
conseiller_d_administration.summary: Member of a board of directors taking part in running a company or an institution.
conseiller_d_administration.text: The conseiller d'administration sits on the board of directors of a company, association or public institution, taking part in strategic decisions and oversight of management. A rather modern function, linked to the development of company law from the 19th century.

conseiller_municipal.label: Conseiller municipal (town councillor)
conseiller_municipal.summary: Local elected official sitting on a commune's municipal council.
conseiller_municipal.text: The conseiller municipal is an elected official who takes part, alongside the mayor, in administering the commune: voting the budget, deliberating on local affairs. The election of municipal councils by universal suffrage became general in France from the 1884 law.

conseiller_rapporteur_du_point_d_honneur.label: Conseiller-Rapporteur du Point d'Honneur
conseiller_rapporteur_du_point_d_honneur.summary: Royal officer investigating, for the marshals of France, disputes of honour between gentlemen.
conseiller_rapporteur_du_point_d_honneur.text: The conseiller du roi rapporteur du point d'honneur is an office created by an edict of October 1704 attached to each lieutenant of the marshals of France, in every bailiwick and seneschalsy. He investigates matters falling under the 1679 edict on the point of honour: disputes between gentlemen or men of war concerning honorific rights, precedence or quarrels of honour, within the justice of the marshals of France, intended to prevent recourse to duelling. In the lieutenant's absence, this magistrate could exercise all his powers.

conservateur.label: Conservateur (curator)
conservateur.summary: Official keeper and manager of property, archives or public collections.
conservateur.text: The conservateur keeps and manages property entrusted to his responsibility: the collections of a museum or a library, forests (conservateur des eaux et forêts), or property deeds (conservateur des hypothèques, responsible since 1798 for registering real-estate transactions). The precise sense thus depends heavily on the institution mentioned in the record.

consignataire.label: Consignataire (consignee)
consignataire.summary: Intermediary responsible for receiving and managing goods entrusted on deposit by a shipper.
consignataire.text: The consignataire receives goods shipped by a third party (the consignor) to sell or store them in his name, for a commission, without owning them. The function is particularly common in maritime trade, where the ship's consignee represents the shipowner in a port.

constructeur.label: Constructeur (builder)
constructeur.summary: Worker or contractor specialized in construction, notably metal framework.
constructeur.text: The constructeur is a building or public-works worker, whose specialty varies by context: from the 19th century, the term frequently denotes an iron builder, responsible for making and assembling metal frameworks and structures (market halls, bridges, glass roofs), a specialty booming with the industrial use of iron and then steel.

consul.label: Consul
consul.summary: Elected judge responsible for settling commercial disputes, or municipal magistrate in the south of France.
consul.text: Under the Ancien Régime, consul denotes the elected judge of a consular jurisdiction, responsible for settling disputes between merchants, forerunner of the commercial court. In the south of France, the term also denotes, since the Middle Ages, the elected municipal magistrates who administer a town, equivalent to the échevins of the north.

contador.label: Contador (Spanish accountant)
contador.summary: Person responsible for keeping and auditing the accounts of an institution, estate or business.
contador.text: The contador kept and examined the income and expenditure accounts of a town council, a noble house, a cathedral chapter, a Crown institution or a business. The Castilian treasury had its own accounting offices (contadurías mayores), whose contadores supervised the collection of royal revenues.

continueuse.label: Continueuse
continueuse.summary: Cotton-mill worker operating a continuous spinning frame.
continueuse.text: In a cotton mill, the continueuse works on a cotton-spinning machine called a continuous spinning frame, a 19th-century mechanical innovation.

contramaestre.label: Contramaestre (Spanish boatswain)
contramaestre.summary: Petty officer who directed the crew's manoeuvres under the orders of the ship's officers.
contramaestre.text: The contramaestre was the seaman in charge of directing the crew during manoeuvres, looking after the rigging, anchors and stores, and keeping discipline on board under the orders of the captain and officers. In shipyards and workshops, the term also designates the head of a group of workers.

contrebandier.label: Contrebandier (smuggler)
contrebandier.summary: Person practising the illicit trade of goods between territories with different tax laws.
contrebandier.text: The contrebandier illicitly trades goods between countries or provinces with different laws and taxes on products, thereby avoiding payment of duties.

contrepointier.label: Contrepointier
contrepointier.summary: Maker of mattresses, quilted blankets or embroidered hangings.
contrepointier.text: The contrepointier makes mattresses, quilted blankets or embroidered hangings, a trade related to those of the courtepointier and the mattress-maker.

contreporteur_de_jusses.label: Contreporteur de jusses
contreporteur_de_jusses.summary: Liège porter carrying jugs, barrels and other loads.
contreporteur_de_jusses.text: The contreporteur de jusses is a "raflier" (Liège porter) carrying jugs (djusses), barrels and other heavy loads.

controleur.label: Contrôleur
controleur.summary: Agent responsible for checking and controlling deeds, accounts or goods.
controleur.text: The contrôleur performs a checking function, whose precise domain depends on context: control of notarial deeds (a tax formality introduced in 1693), of weights and measures, of an administration's accounts, or later of transport tickets and passes. Under the Ancien Régime, many controller offices were created to levy taxes on legal deeds.

controleur_de_personnel.label: Contrôleur de Personnel
controleur_de_personnel.summary: Agent responsible, within a company, for managing time cards, leave and pay.
controleur_de_personnel.text: The contrôleur de personnel is an agent responsible, within a company, for managing employee time cards, leave and payroll.

controleur_des_aides.label: Contrôleur des Aides
controleur_des_aides.summary: Official collecting the Aides, sums owed to the sovereign, the old equivalent of today's tax inspector.
controleur_des_aides.text: The contrôleur des Aides is the old equivalent of today's tax inspector. The Aides were originally sums paid to the sovereign for particular needs, which became a regular tax.

controleur_des_exploits.label: Contrôleur des Exploits
controleur_des_exploits.summary: Official responsible for registering the civil, criminal and financial deeds of ministerial officers.
controleur_des_exploits.text: The contrôleur des exploits is responsible for registering every civil, criminal or financial deed drawn up by notaries, bailiffs and sergeants.

controleur_des_impots.label: Contrôleur des impôts (tax inspector)
controleur_des_impots.summary: Tax-administration agent responsible for checking and collecting taxes.
controleur_des_impots.text: The contrôleur des impôts is a tax-administration official responsible for checking returns and ensuring the collection of direct and indirect taxes. The function became progressively structured from the Revolution, with the creation of a unified tax administration.

controleur_des_traites.label: Contrôleur des Traites
controleur_des_traites.summary: Under the Ancien Régime, an official collecting duties on goods transported between provinces, the equivalent of today's customs officer.
controleur_des_traites.text: The contrôleur des Traites is the old equivalent of today's customs officer. The Traites were, under the Ancien Régime, duties levied on goods transported between provinces or states.

copiste.label: Copiste (copyist)
copiste.summary: Person responsible for copying out texts, manuscripts or deeds by hand.
copiste.text: The copiste reproduces texts by hand — manuscripts, legal deeds, musical scores — before printing and then the typewriter became widespread. In medieval monasteries, copyists, often monks, ensured the transmission of ancient texts in the scriptoria.

coq.label: Coq
coq.summary: Cook aboard a ship, responsible for preparing the crew's meals.
coq.text: The coq is a ship's cook, a term borrowed from the Dutch "kok". Aboard merchant or warships, he prepares the crew's meals under often rudimentary conditions, with limited provisions during long voyages.

coqueleux.label: Coqueleux
coqueleux.text: The coqueleux raises cocks intended for cockfighting, a traditional practice in certain regions of northern France.

coquetier.label: Coquetier
coquetier.summary: Itinerant merchant collecting eggs, poultry and small farm produce to resell in town.
coquetier.text: The coquetier is a merchant, often itinerant, who collects eggs and poultry from surrounding farms to resell them at urban markets. The term, not to be confused with the object of the same name (the small egg cup), is attested in many regions under varied dialectal forms.

corailleur.label: Corailleur
corailleur.summary: Person who harvests or works coral.
corailleur.text: The corailleur harvests coral at sea, notably in the Mediterranean, or works it in a workshop to make jewellery and ornamental objects.

corbelier.label: Corbelier
corbelier.text: The corbelier is a basket-maker specialized in making willow-woven baskets.

cordelier.label: Cordelier
cordelier.summary: Craftsman making ropes and cordage from plant fibres.
cordelier.text: The cordelier, or cordier, makes ropes, twine and cordage by twisting together fibres of hemp, flax or esparto. The trade was often practised outdoors, in long walkways called ropewalks, where the craftsman walked backward while twisting his thread. Not to be confused with the Cordeliers, the Franciscan religious order bearing the same name because of the triple-knotted cord girding their habit.

cordoneuse.label: Cordoneuse
cordoneuse.summary: Openwork embroiderer tracing the curved shapes of the work with a small cord.
cordoneuse.text: The cordoneuse is an openwork embroiderer who traces, using a small cord, the curved shapes to be given to the work before the openwork proper.

cordonnier.label: Cordonnier (shoemaker)
cordonnier.text: The cordonnier makes new leather shoes, to be distinguished from the cobbler, who only repairs them. The term comes from "cordouan", a tanned goatskin originating from Cordoba much used for fine footwear. It is one of the most common craft trades in civil records; old spelling and surname variants such as Corvisier, Courvisier or Courvoisier are found.

cordouannier.label: Cordouannier
cordouannier.summary: Shoemaker working cordovan, goatskin leather from Cordoba.
cordouannier.text: The cordouannier is a shoemaker specialized in working cordovan, goatskin leather from Cordoba, a noble material of old shoemaking.

cornet.label: Cornet
cornet.summary: Musician playing the cornet, a wind instrument used notably in brass bands and orchestras.
cornet.text: Cornet denotes the musician playing the cornet à pistons, or, more anciently, the cornett ("cornet à bouquin"), a wind instrument used in municipal brass bands, orchestras and sometimes military bands, notably from the 19th century.

cornetier.label: Cornetier
cornetier.summary: Craftsman working cattle horn to make combs, buttons or lanterns.
cornetier.text: The cornetier prepares and works cattle or other animal horn, softened by heat and then moulded or cut, to make combs, buttons, powder flasks, knife handles or lantern panes, before horn was supplanted by other materials such as celluloid.

corratier.label: Corratier
corratier.summary: In Haute-Loire, a wine broker and merchant checking quality, quantity and provenance.
corratier.text: The corratier is, in Haute-Loire, a wine broker and merchant responsible for checking the quality, quantity and provenance of wine.

corregedor.label: Corregedor (royal district magistrate)
corregedor.summary: Royal magistrate who inspected justice and administration in the municipalities of a district (comarca).
corregedor.text: The corregedor is appointed by the king to a comarca, a district grouping several municipalities, where he oversees the conduct of judges and councils, hears certain cases and appeals, keeps public order and reports to the Crown. He toured the district on inspection (correição). The office disappeared with the liberal judicial and administrative reforms of the 1830s.

corregidor.label: Corregidor (Spanish royal magistrate)
corregidor.summary: Spanish royal officer who presided over a city council and held governmental and judicial powers there.
corregidor.text: Appointed by the king, the corregidor presided over the council of a city or district and combined government, policing and first-instance justice. Generalised in Castile by the Catholic Monarchs, he could be a lawyer (corregidor de letras) or a soldier or gentleman (corregidor de capa y espada). The institution was abolished in the 19th century with the reform of local administration.

corroyeur.label: Corroyeur (currier)
corroyeur.summary: Craftsman who softens and finishes leather after tanning.
corroyeur.text: The corroyeur takes over after the tanner: he softens, thins, smooths and dyes tanned leather to make it usable by leatherworkers (shoemakers, saddlers, glovers). Currying comprises beating, degreasing and smoothing operations that determine the final quality of the leather.

corsetier.label: Corsetier
corsetier.text: The corsetier makes corsets, a boned undergarment intended to shape and slim the figure.

cortijero.label: Cortijero (Andalusian farmstead keeper)
cortijero.summary: Person who lived on an Andalusian cortijo and looked after it and its work.
cortijero.text: The cortijero lived on a cortijo, the large farming estate typical of Andalusia, which he looked after on behalf of the owner or tenant, overseeing the work, the livestock and the implements. Depending on the area, the term also designates the tenant of the cortijo.

cotier.label: Côtier
cotier.summary: Agent helping omnibus or stagecoach teams climb hills.
cotier.text: The côtier assisted horse-drawn teams — omnibuses, stagecoaches — on difficult climbs, by temporarily adding reinforcing horses (the reinforcing team generally numbered three horses) for the duration of the hill. The term derives from "côte" (hill), and is found mainly in towns with marked relief in the 19th century.

cotonier.label: Cotonier
cotonier.summary: Textile worker employed at the various stages of preparing and spinning cotton.
cotonier.text: The cotonier works cotton from raw material to thread: carding, combing, spinning, then weaving depending on the workshop. The term spread with the rise of the French cotton industry from the 18th century, particularly in Normandy and the Vosges.

cotrier.label: Cotrier
cotrier.summary: Worker who carries cotrets — small bundles of wood — from the cutting site to the forest edge.
cotrier.text: The cotrier removes the wood and bundles (cotrets) felled by woodcutters and carries them to the edge of the forest, where they are piled before being loaded by carters for transport to town or points of sale. The name derives from "cotret", a small bundle of firewood.

coulie.label: Coulie
coulie.summary: Small shopkeeper practising high-interest lending to miners.
coulie.text: The coulie keeps a shop near mining operations and practises credit or usury toward mine workers, often as wage advances repayable in kind or in labour. This rare term reflects the debt practices common in mining basins.

coulier.label: Coulier
coulier.summary: Porter of the Garonne river ports, responsible for loading and unloading boats.
coulier.text: The coulier is a porter working in the river ports of the Garonne, responsible for loading and unloading gabares and other trading boats. This handling trade, sometimes organized into a port guild, declined with falling river traffic in the face of the railway.

coulissier.label: Coulissier
coulissier.summary: Unofficial broker operating at the Paris Bourse, on the margins of licensed stockbrokers.
coulissier.text: The coulissier trades securities at the Paris Bourse without holding the official office of stockbroker, operating "à la coulisse", that is, in the corridors and outside the official trading floor. This parallel market, tolerated and then regulated, notably handled securities not listed on the official floor, until the two markets merged in the 20th century.

coultre.label: Coultre
coultre.summary: Sacristan responsible for the upkeep of the church and sacristy.
coultre.text: The coultre, or coutre, is a sacristan, responsible for the upkeep of the place of worship, the keeping of sacred objects and assisting the priest during services. The term derives from the Old French "costre" (keeper, then sacristan), of which "coltre"/"coultre" is an attested variant.

coupeur_de_cheveux.label: Coupeur de cheveux
coupeur_de_cheveux.summary: Itinerant craftsman who bought peasant women's hair to resell it to wigmakers.
coupeur_de_cheveux.text: The coupeur de cheveux travelled the countryside to buy and cut women's hair, often in exchange for small change or ribbons, in order to resell it to makers of wigs and hairpieces. This trade, attested mainly in the 18th and 19th centuries, particularly affected the poorest peasant families.

coureur.label: Coureur
coureur.summary: Messenger travelling fast on foot to carry news or letters.
coureur.text: The coureur is a foot messenger, responsible for quickly carrying news, letters or small parcels over short or medium distances, before the horse post and then modern means of transport became widespread.

coureur_de_chien.label: Coureur de Chien
coureur_de_chien.summary: Miner responsible for pushing mine carts, called "dogs".
coureur_de_chien.text: The coureur de chien pushes mine carts, nicknamed "mine dogs" because of the noise they made, reminiscent of barking.

couronnier.label: Couronnier
couronnier.summary: Craftsman making wreaths, notably for religious or funeral ceremonies.
couronnier.text: The couronnier makes wreaths intended for ceremonies: bridal wreaths, funeral wreaths, or religious ornaments. This trade, often linked to floristry or passementerie, gained importance with the fashion for mourning wreaths in the 19th century.

courratier.label: Courratier
courratier.summary: Broker specialized in negotiating and trading wine.
courratier.text: The courratier is a wine broker, an intermediary between producers and merchants, responsible for tasting, appraising and bringing buyers and sellers together. The term, a regional variant of "courtier", is particularly attested in the Bordeaux vineyard, where the wine-broker function remains regulated today.

courrier.label: Courrier
courrier.summary: Official carrier of messages, dispatches or mail.
courrier.text: The courrier officially carries messages, dispatches or correspondence, on foot, on horseback or by relay of post horses. Under the Ancien Régime, royal couriers ensured the fast transmission of orders and information over the network of post relays, the forerunner of the modern postal administration.

courrier_de_cabinet.label: Courrier de cabinet
courrier_de_cabinet.text: The courrier de cabinet is a royal courier responsible for carrying the sovereign's official correspondence.

courtaut.label: Courtaut
courtaut.summary: Shop employee occupied with sedentary work, by ellipsis of "courtaud de boutique".
courtaut.text: The courtaut is a journeyman employed in a shop for sedentary work, a term formed by ellipsis of the expression "courtaud de boutique". The word "courtaud" originally evokes clothing shorter than that worn by nobles and the wealthy bourgeoisie, hence the idea of a modest status.

courtepointier.label: Courtepointier
courtepointier.summary: Craftsman making courtepointes, quilted and padded coverlets.
courtepointier.text: The courtepointier makes courtepointes, ceremonial quilted and padded coverlets intended to adorn beds, as well as hangings and caparisons for ceremonies. The trade, regulated by guilds under the Ancien Régime, is sometimes denoted by the spelling variant "coutepointier".

courtier.label: Courtier (broker)
courtier.summary: Licensed intermediary bringing sellers and buyers together for a commission.
courtier.text: The courtier acts as an intermediary in a commercial transaction — goods, real estate, insurance, securities — bringing sellers and buyers together for a commission, without becoming the owner of the goods traded. Under the Ancien Régime, many brokerages were venal royal offices regulated by trade body (wine brokers, horse brokers, goods brokers).

courtier_en_marchandises.label: Courtier en marchandises (commodity broker)
courtier_en_marchandises.summary: Broker specialized in negotiating goods between merchants.
courtier_en_marchandises.text: The courtier en marchandises brings together buyers and sellers of commercial goods — foodstuffs, raw materials, manufactured products — for a commission, without trading on his own account.

courtillier.label: Courtillier
courtillier.summary: Gardener cultivating a courtil, a small enclosed garden for vegetables and fruit.
courtillier.text: The courtillier cultivates a courtil, a modest enclosed garden located on the outskirts of villages or towns, devoted to vegetables, fruit and sometimes a little livestock. This type of small market-garden supplied local markets, notably around towns such as Paris.

couseur.label: Couseur
couseur.summary: Worker specialized in sewing work, notably in garment-making or bookbinding.
couseur.text: The couseur performs sewing work by hand or machine, whether in garment-making (assembling clothes), shoemaking (sewing shoe uppers) or bookbinding (sewing a book's gatherings). The precise sense depends on the field of activity mentioned in the record.

couseuse_en_lainges.label: Couseuse en lainges
couseuse_en_lainges.summary: Seamstress of household linen: sheets, towels, dishcloths.
couseuse_en_lainges.text: The couseuse en lainges makes and repairs household linen: sheets, towels, dishcloths and other domestic linen pieces.

coussier.label: Coussier
coussier.summary: Craftsman making hose, a garment covering the legs.
coussier.text: The coussier makes hose, a medieval and early-modern garment covering the legs, ancestor of trousers and stockings, before this term came to denote more specifically, from the 16th century, only the part covering the foot and calf.

coustier.label: Coutier
coustier.summary: Maker or merchant of ticking, a tightly woven cloth used for mattresses and cushions.
coustier.text: The coutier works ticking, a tightly woven linen or cotton cloth, resistant to feathers or horsehair working through it, used to make mattresses, cushions and bolsters. The term is found under several related spellings (coustier, coutière) depending on region and record.

coutal.label: Coutal
coutal.summary: Driver of mules for transporting goods.
coutal.text: The coutal (or coutaud) drives loaded mules for transporting goods, notably in mountainous or foothill areas where these pack animals were better suited than horses to steep paths. The term, of Occitan origin, is found mainly in the south of France.

coutelier.label: Coutelier (cutler)
coutelier.summary: Craftsman making knives and other cutting instruments.
coutelier.text: The coutelier forges and shapes knives, scissors and cutting instruments, a trade organized into a guild as early as the Middle Ages and particularly flourishing in towns such as Thiers or Nogent. The term sometimes appears in the old form "coustelier", from the Old French "coustel" or "coutel" (knife).

coutilier.label: Coutillier
coutilier.summary: 14th–15th-century foot soldier armed with a lance and a coutille (a broad dagger).
coutilier.text: The coutillier, or coutilier, is a late-medieval foot soldier (14th–15th centuries), fitted with a mail hauberk topped by a brigandine, fighting with lance and coutille, a short, broad dagger with an "ox-tongue" blade. He formed the light infantry of feudal armies and mercenary companies, charging with the lance in melees, finishing off fallen combatants with the dagger, defending positions and taking part in sieges.

couturier.label: Couturier
couturier.summary: Craftsman responsible for sewing pieces of cloth or leather cut by others.
couturier.text: In the division of labour of Ancien Régime guilds, the couturier is responsible for sewing and assembling pieces of cloth or leather previously cut by the tailor or the shoemaker, a specialization that faded over time to more broadly denote one who makes clothes. The old spelling "cousturier" is common in old records.

couturier_de_livre.label: Couturier de Livre
couturier_de_livre.summary: Printing employee responsible for sewing a book's pages before binding.
couturier_de_livre.text: The couturier de livre works in printing, where he sews the gatherings of pages together before the binding operation proper.

couverturier.label: Couverturier
couverturier.summary: Craftsman or merchant making and selling bed blankets.
couverturier.text: The couverturier makes or sells woollen blankets intended for bedding, a trade linked to working cloth and carded wool, often practised in regions with a textile tradition.

couvreur.label: Couvreur (roofer)
couvreur.summary: Craftsman who builds and repairs roofs.
couvreur.text: The couvreur builds and maintains roofs, using materials available depending on the region: tile, slate, wood shingles, thatch or stone slabs. A trade worked at height, regulated by guild in towns, whose specialties (slate roofer, thatcher) are sometimes distinguished in records.

couvreur_d_ardoise.label: Couvreur d'ardoise
couvreur_d_ardoise.summary: Roofer specialized in laying slate roofs.
couvreur_d_ardoise.text: The couvreur d'ardoise lays and repairs slate roofs, a material characteristic of regions such as Anjou, Brittany or the Ardennes, where slate extraction fed a whole craft chain linked to construction.

couvreur_de_lauzes.label: Couvreur de lauzes
couvreur_de_lauzes.summary: Roofer using flat stones (lauzes) for roofing.
couvreur_de_lauzes.text: The couvreur de lauzes lays roofs of flat stones called lauzes, a traditional technique of certain mountainous regions (Cévennes, Quercy).

couvreur_en_chaume.label: Couvreur en chaume (thatcher)
couvreur_en_chaume.summary: Roofer specialized in laying thatched roofs.
couvreur_en_chaume.text: The couvreur en chaume lays thatched roofs (rye straw, reed or rushes depending on the region), a traditional technique widespread in the French countryside until its gradual decline in favour of tile and slate from the 19th century.

couvreur_en_esseurions.label: Couvreur en esseurions
couvreur_en_esseurions.summary: In the Nièvre, a roofer using wooden shingles (oak or chestnut).
couvreur_en_esseurions.text: In the Nièvre, the couvreur en esseurions lays wooden shingles of a particular species, perhaps oak or chestnut, to cover roofs.

coyratier.label: Coyratier (leather currier)
coyratier.summary: Craftsman who dressed and finished leather after tanning.
coyratier.text: The coyratier worked leather after tanning, a role close to that of the currier ("corroyeur"). The term, a rare and probably regional spelling, remains poorly documented in genealogical sources.

craquelinier.label: Craquelinier
craquelinier.summary: Baker-pastry cook specialized in making craquelins, small crisp breads or dry cakes.
craquelinier.text: The craquelinier makes craquelins, small breads or dry biscuits of boiled and then baked dough, braided or knotted, a specialty attested notably in northern France, Belgium and Alsace, close to the pretzel in certain traditions.

craquelottiere.label: Craquelottière
craquelottiere.summary: Preparer of craquelots, lightly salted and smoked herring.
craquelottiere.text: The craquelottière prepares craquelots, fresh herring lightly salted and then hot-smoked, a specialty of Normandy fishing ports such as Dieppe and Fécamp, where herring preparation employed a large female workforce as soon as the boats landed.

crazalher.label: Crazalher
crazalher.summary: Craftsman making wooden troughs for agricultural or domestic use.
crazalher.text: The crazalher makes wooden troughs, used for feeding livestock or various domestic and craft uses. This rare and probably regional term is little documented in general genealogical sources.

credencier.label: Crédencier
credencier.summary: Person in charge of distributing provisions within a community or institution.
credencier.text: The crédencier is responsible for distributing food and provisions in a community — convent, school, hospital — a role close to that of the steward or bursar, often practised within religious institutions.

cremier.label: Crémier (dairyman)
cremier.summary: Merchant of fresh dairy products: milk, butter, cream, cheese.
cremier.text: The crémier sells fresh dairy products — milk, cream, butter, fresh cheese — often collected directly from surrounding farms. The dairy-shop trade developed particularly in towns from the 19th century, with the rise of organized milk collection.

crepinier.label: Crépinier
crepinier.summary: Maker of crépine, a woven fringe trimming beds and canopies.
crepinier.text: The crépinier makes crépine, a kind of fringe woven and worked at the top, used to trim beds and canopies.

crepinier_de_fil_et_de_soie.label: Crépinier de fil et de soie
crepinier_de_fil_et_de_soie.summary: Passementerie craftsman making crépines, ornamental fringes of thread or silk.
crepinier_de_fil_et_de_soie.text: The crépinier de fil et de soie makes crépines, passementerie works made of an openwork woven band from which short, dense fringes hang, often made of gold or silver thread. Highly prized in the 18th century to adorn royal and bourgeois furnishings, crépines were also used to trim hangings, clothing and harness.

crespinier.label: Crespinier
crespinier.summary: Weaving craftsman making light, sheer fabrics: crepe, gauze, fine silk.
crespinier.text: The crespinier makes light fabrics of silk, crepe or gauze, a textile trade distinct from the crépinier, who works in passementerie. The term derives from "crespe", an old form of the word crêpe denoting a light, rippled cloth.

criblier.label: Criblier
criblier.summary: Craftsman making sieves and screens to sort grain.
criblier.text: The criblier makes sieves, open-mesh instruments, often of woven willow, perforated skin or pierced sheet metal, used to sort grain, separate wheat from chaff or grade various materials. Crubelier and cruvelier are regional variants of the same trade, the word "cruvèl" being an Occitan form of "crivèl" (sieve).

crieur.label: Crieur (town crier)
crieur.summary: Person responsible for publicly announcing news, notices and goods aloud.
crieur.text: The public crieur announces aloud, in the streets and squares, official notices, sales, found or lost items, and goods for sale (wine crier, fish crier). An old function, regulated in many towns, the crieur was the main channel of information before the press.

crinier.label: Crinier
crinier.summary: Craftsman who prepares and works animal hair for various uses.
crinier.text: The crinier prepares horsehair — from the mane and tail of horses, or cattle hair — used to stuff seats and mattresses, to make fabric (woven horsehair), brushes or bow hair.

crinquallier.label: Crinquallier
crinquallier.summary: Merchant of hardware and metal objects.
crinquallier.text: The crinquallier sells hardware — nails, tools, metal implements — the term being an old variant of "quincaillier", itself derived from "clinquaille", formerly denoting scrap iron and small metal items.

cristallier.label: Cristallier
cristallier.summary: Prospector and cutter of rock crystal, notably in the Alpine ranges.
cristallier.text: The cristallier searches for and extracts rock crystal (quartz) from rock fissures, a traditional activity of Alpine massifs such as Mont Blanc, before also more broadly denoting the craftsman who cuts and shapes crystal objects.

crocheteur.label: Crocheteur
crocheteur.summary: Porter using a hook or a basket to carry loads.
crocheteur.text: The crocheteur carries heavy loads using a hook worn over the shoulder or a basket, notably in the markets and ports of Paris (the crocheteurs of Les Halles). This trade of strength, often organized into a sworn guild, was one of the most gruelling in urban handling.

crochetier.label: Crochetier
crochetier.summary: Craftsman making hooks for carrying or various uses.
crochetier.text: The crochetier makes metal hooks used for carrying loads (by porters), hanging goods, or other domestic and craft uses.

crocteur_de_gres.label: Crocteur de grès
crocteur_de_gres.summary: Worker extracting and breaking sandstone in a quarry.
crocteur_de_gres.text: The crocteur de grès (also called croqueteur or croqueur in dialect) breaks sandstone extracted in a quarry into small pieces, a material used for paving, construction and millstones. This gruelling quarry work is found in regions rich in sandstone deposits, such as northern France.

croise.label: Croisé
croise.summary: Combatant who took part in a crusade, enlisted under the sign of the cross.
croise.text: The croisé is one who has "taken the cross", that is, vowed to take part in a crusade, a religious military expedition organized between the 11th and 13th centuries toward the Holy Land or other targets designated by the Church. The term may appear in noble genealogies claiming crusader ancestry, often difficult to establish with certainty.

croquetier.label: Croquetier
croquetier.summary: Itinerant merchant related to the coquetier, collecting eggs, butter, cheese and poultry to resell in town.
croquetier.text: The croquetier is an itinerant merchant related to the coquetier: he travels farms to buy fresh produce — eggs, butter, cheese, poultry — then carries it to urban markets to resell it retail. This rural intermediary trade vanished with the development of modern distribution networks.

crossier.label: Crossier
crossier.text: The crossier makes stocks, the wooden parts, of firearms, a trade linked to gunsmithing that combines woodworking with knowledge of the dimensions required to fit the barrel and the weapon's mechanism.

cruysier.label: Cruysier
cruysier.summary: Potter making terracotta objects, notably jugs.
cruysier.text: The cruysier shapes terracotta objects, notably jugs and utilitarian vessels, a trade related to that of the potter. The term probably derives from "cruche" (jug).

cto.label: CTO
cto.summary: Executive responsible for a company's technology strategy and choices.
cto.text: The CTO (Chief Technology Officer), or technical director, is the executive responsible for technology choices, systems architecture and innovation within a company, particularly in the digital and technology sectors. A contemporary function, with no equivalent among old trades.

cuadrillero.label: Cuadrillero (Spanish rural patrolman)
cuadrillero.summary: Member of the armed patrols of the Spanish Santa Hermandad who pursued criminals.
cuadrillero.text: The cuadrillero belonged to the patrols of the Santa Hermandad, charged with pursuing highwaymen and criminals on roads and in the countryside and bringing them before the alcaldes of the Hermandad. Recruited among the townspeople, these patrols were one of the earliest rural police forces of Castile.

cubillier.label: Cubillier
cubillier.summary: Cooper specialized in making buckets and vats of various sizes.
cubillier.text: The cubillier makes wooden buckets and vats of various sizes, intended for storing liquids, winemaking or domestic and craft uses, a specialty close to that of the cooper.

cueilleur.label: Cueilleur
cueilleur.summary: Person responsible for harvesting natural produce: fruit, plants, or other resources.
cueilleur.text: The cueilleur harvests natural produce by hand — fruit, flowers, medicinal plants, mushrooms or other wild or cultivated resources — often seasonal work supplementing other farm activities.

cueilleur_de_jambe.label: Cueilleur de Jambe
cueilleur_de_jambe.summary: Glassworker who gathers the viscous glass forming the stem of a glass from the furnace.
cueilleur_de_jambe.text: The cueilleur de jambe is a glassworker who gathers from the furnace, using a punty, the viscous glass that will form the stem of the glass, and presents it to the stem-setter.

cueilleur_de_pied.label: Cueilleur de Pied
cueilleur_de_pied.summary: Glassworker who gathers the viscous glass forming the foot of a glass piece from the furnace.
cueilleur_de_pied.text: The cueilleur de pied is a glassworker who gathers from the furnace, using a punty, the viscous glass that will form the foot of the glass piece, and presents it to the foot-setter.

cueilleur_de_simples.label: Cueilleur de simples
cueilleur_de_simples.summary: Gatherer of food or medicinal plants.
cueilleur_de_simples.text: The cueilleur de simples harvests plants ("simples") intended for food or medicinal use.

cuilleriste.label: Cuilleriste
cuilleriste.summary: Craftsman making spoons and other wooden table utensils.
cuilleriste.text: The cuilleriste makes spoons and small table utensils, mainly of wood, a craft often practised in rural or forested areas where wood was readily available. The term is also found in the accented spelling "cuillériste".

cuilleronnier.label: Cuilleronnier
cuilleronnier.text: The cuilleronnier, also called cuillerier, makes tableware, particularly spoons of metal (tin, silver) or horn, a trade distinct from the cuilleriste, who works wood more.

cuiratier.label: Cuiratier
cuiratier.summary: Craftsman working leather, whose guild held a leading rank among municipal trades.
cuiratier.text: The cuiratier is a worker who works leather. According to Littré, the cuiratiers held first rank in the municipal body among the trade guilds of certain towns, a sign of the economic importance of leather preparation and trade under the Ancien Régime.

cuireur.label: Cuireur
cuireur.summary: Saddlery worker responsible for covering the wooden frames of saddles with leather.
cuireur.text: The cuireur takes part in saddle-making: he covers the saddle tree, a wooden structure previously shaped by the saddle-tree maker, with leather, a specialized step of traditional saddlery.

cuironnier.label: Cuironnier
cuironnier.summary: Craftsman working leather to make various objects, related to the cuilleronnier.
cuironnier.text: The cuironnier shapes various leather objects, a trade related to the cuilleronnier, sometimes combining leatherwork with that of other materials to make utensils or accessories.

cuiseur.label: Cuiseur
cuiseur.summary: Worker responsible for firing or cooking materials: charcoal, metals or other substances.
cuiseur.text: The cuiseur carries out firing operations requiring controlled heat treatment: charring wood to produce charcoal, heating metals at the forge, firing lime or brick depending on context.

cuiseur_de_paquest_de_fer.label: Cuiseur de Paquest de Fer
cuiseur_de_paquest_de_fer.summary: Cutlery worker responsible for forging raw iron bars to preform them.
cuiseur_de_paquest_de_fer.text: The cuiseur de paquest de fer is a cutlery worker responsible for forging raw iron bars to preform them before their final shaping.

cuisinier.label: Cuisinier (cook)
cuisinier.summary: Person responsible for preparing meals, professionally or domestically.
cuisinier.text: The cuisinier prepares meals, whether in a bourgeois or noble household, an inn, or on his own account. Under the Ancien Régime, great households employed a "queux" or "oyer" (kitchen officer) responsible for organizing meals, while in towns, caterers and roast-meat sellers sold cooked meat and prepared charcuterie.

culler.label: Culler
culler.summary: Port inspector responsible for setting the sale price of cod.
culler.text: The culler is a port official responsible for assessing and setting the price of landed cod, a role linked to cod-fishing ports such as those of Brittany or Normandy.

culotteur_de_pipes.label: Culotteur de Pipes
culotteur_de_pipes.summary: Person who seasons new pipes before their sale by tobacconists.
culotteur_de_pipes.text: The culotteur de pipes seasons (progressively smokes to blacken the bowl of) new pipes, which are then sold thus seasoned by the tobacconists he works for.

culottier.label: Culottier
culottier.summary: Craftsman specialized in making leather breeches.
culottier.text: The culottier makes exclusively leather breeches, a men's garment of leather or chamois-dressed skin covering the lower body to the knee, particularly worn by soldiers and horsemen before trousers became widespread.

culottiere.label: Culottière
culottiere.summary: Seamstress specialized in making men's clothing, notably breeches.
culottiere.text: The culottière makes breeches and other men's clothing, a sewing specialty distinct from the leather breeches worked by the culottier, geared toward cloth rather than leather.

cultivateur.label: Cultivateur
cultivateur.summary: Farmer who works his own land himself.
cultivateur.text: The cultivateur farms land, whether as owner, tenant or sharecropper, a term that became widespread in the 19th century, gradually replacing "laboureur" to denote the farmer, regardless of wealth.

cura_economo.label: Cura ecónomo (Spanish acting parish priest)
cura_economo.summary: Priest who administered a vacant parish or one whose parish priest was incapacitated.
cura_economo.text: The cura ecónomo was appointed by the bishop to administer temporarily a vacant parish, or one whose own parish priest could not serve, until the post was filled. In the sacramental registers he signed entries with this title, which distinguishes him from the incumbent priest.

curatolo.label: Curatolo (Sicilian farm overseer)
curatolo.summary: In Sicily, the overseer of the work and staff of a masseria, especially the herd and the cheese-making.
curatolo.text: The curatolo directed, on behalf of the owner or the gabelloto, the shepherds, cowherds and farm boys of the masseria, and supervised the livestock and the processing of the milk. He was a trusted wage earner ranking above the ordinary labourers.

cure.label: Curé (parish priest)
cure.summary: Priest responsible for a parish, in charge of religious services and keeping the registers.
cure.text: The curé is the priest in charge of a parish, responsible for celebrating services, administering the sacraments and, until the Revolution, keeping the parish registers of baptisms, marriages and burials — the main genealogical source before civil registration was established in 1792.

curial.label: Curial
curial.summary: Officer or secretary attached to a court of law.
curial.text: The curial is an officer attached to a court or jurisdiction, performing secretarial or registry functions, the term deriving from the Latin "curia" (court, tribunal).

custos.label: Custos
custos.summary: Keeper and sacristan of a church, often mentioned in its Latin form in old records.
custos.text: Custos is the Latin term, common in parish registers written in Latin, denoting the keeper or sacristan of a church, responsible for guarding sacred objects and maintaining the place of worship.

cuvelier.label: Cuvelier
cuvelier.summary: Craftsman making vats and wooden containers, spelling variant: cuvetier.
cuvelier.text: The cuvelier (or cuvetier) makes large wooden vats and containers, intended for winemaking, brewing or various industrial and domestic uses, a trade related to coopering and largely vanished with industrialization and the replacement of wood by other materials.

cwiercrolnik.label: Ćwierćrolnik (quarter-holding peasant)
cwiercrolnik.summary: Peasant farming a quarter of a full peasant holding in old Poland.
