grenetier.text: The salt warehouse manager administers a salt warehouse, royal warehouse where salt had to be purchased by inhabitants under the salt tax (gabelle), keeping sales registers and ensuring quota and tax regulation compliance.

grenier.label: Grain merchant (grenier)
grenier.summary: Merchant of grain, and also of flowers, shrubs and bulbs.
grenier.text: The grain merchant is, according to old ordinances, a merchant of grain, but also of flowers, shrubs and bulbs.

gribanier.label: Somme barge operator (gribanier)
gribanier.summary: Bargeman of the Somme transporting goods on a gribane.
gribanier.text: The Somme barge operator is a Somme bargeman who transports goods on a gribane, a sailing boat of about fifty tons.

griendwerker.label: Griendwerker (osier bed worker)
griendwerker.summary: Labourer who cut and processed willow rods in the osier beds.
griendwerker.text: Grienden are plots of coppiced willow in the river area, such as the Biesbosch, where the osier workers cut the rods. The wood was used for fascines and mattresses in hydraulic engineering, for barrel hoops and for baskets. The workers often lived the whole season in simple huts in the osier beds.

grillageuse.label: Wire-grid weaver (grillageuse)
grillageuse.summary: Worker braiding wire grids mounted in a winnowing machine.
grillageuse.text: The wire-grid weaver braids wire grids mounted in a winnowing machine, an agricultural device for sorting grain.

grillou.label: Tinware peddler (grillou)
grillou.text: The tinware peddler is an itinerant tinware maker, selling and repairing tin objects from village to village.

grosseur.label: Comb-teeth cutter (grosseur)
grosseur.summary: Comb-maker who cuts coarse teeth after the rough-shaper.
grosseur.text: The comb-teeth cutter is a comb-maker who, after the rough-shaper's work, cuts the large teeth of the comb.

grueur_d_orge.label: Barley-groat miller (grueur d'orge)
grueur_d_orge.summary: Miller making groats from barley grains stripped of their husk.
grueur_d_orge.text: The barley-groat miller is a miller who makes groats, coarsely ground flour, from barley grains stripped of their thin covering.

grumete.label: Grumete (Spanish ship's boy)
grumete.summary: Boy or young man who served aboard ship while learning the seaman's trade.
grumete.text: The grumete was a young crew member who helped the sailors with the ship's work while learning the trade; in the crews of the 16th to 18th centuries he ranked immediately below the seaman and above the pages. After a few years at sea he could be promoted to seaman.

gualano.label: Gualano (Apulian ploughman)
gualano.summary: In Apulia and Molise, a permanent farmhand of a masseria, employed mainly in ploughing with oxen.
gualano.text: The gualano, usually hired for a year, drove the oxen and worked the fields of the large grain farms of the Tavoliere and neighbouring areas, often living on the masseria itself. He differed from the day labourer in the stability of his engagement.

guarda_fiscal.label: Guarda-fiscal (customs guard)
guarda_fiscal.summary: Member of the Guarda Fiscal, the military corps responsible for customs surveillance of coasts and borders.
guarda_fiscal.text: The guarda-fiscal belongs to the Guarda Fiscal, a militarised corps created in 1885 to watch the coasts and land borders, suppress smuggling and support the collection of customs duties. Guards often lived with their families at isolated posts along the frontier or the sea, which explains their frequent presence in the registers of border and coastal parishes. The Guarda Fiscal was merged into the National Republican Guard (GNR) in 1993.

guardia_civil.label: Guardia civil (Spanish Civil Guard)
guardia_civil.summary: Member of the Guardia Civil, the military-status police force created in Spain in 1844.
guardia_civil.text: The Guardia Civil was created in 1844, under the direction of the Duke of Ahumada, to keep order in the countryside and on the roads. Its members, subject to military discipline, lived with their families in barracks-houses (casas-cuartel) and were often posted far from home, which explains why their children were born in widely scattered places.

guardiamarina.label: Guardiamarina (Spanish naval cadet)
guardiamarina.summary: Cadet training to become an officer of the Spanish navy.
guardiamarina.text: The guardiamarina was a young man training to become a naval officer. In Spain the Royal Company of Guardias Marinas was created in Cádiz in 1717 and for a long time required proofs of nobility for admission, which makes its files a valued genealogical source.

gueberschwihr.label: Gueberschwihr (place name, not an occupation)
gueberschwihr.summary: Name of a municipality in Haut-Rhin (Alsace); does not correspond to an occupation — likely a data-entry error or place of origin.
gueberschwihr.text: Gueberschwihr is a municipality in Haut-Rhin, in Alsace, and not an occupation name. Its presence in an occupation field of a document or genealogical database likely results from a data-entry error or confusion with a place of birth, residence or origin of the person concerned.

guetrier.label: Gaiter maker (guêtrier)
guetrier.text: The gaiter maker makes gaiters, cloth or leather pieces protecting the lower leg.

guida_alpina.label: Guida alpina (mountain guide)
guida_alpina.summary: Professional who leads climbers in the mountains.
guida_alpina.text: The guida alpina leads climbers on ascents and ensures their safety. The profession arose in the 19th century with the development of mountaineering, in places such as Courmayeur, Valtournenche, Macugnaga and the Dolomite valleys, where guides organised themselves into companies; porters served as their assistants.

guimpier.label: Gold-wire maker (guimpier)
guimpier.summary: Gold-wire drawer making the gold thread for the gold-thread spinner.
guimpier.text: The gold-wire maker is a gold-wire drawer who makes gold thread, raw material then worked by the gold-thread spinner.

gumienny.label: Gumienny (barn keeper)
gumienny.summary: Keeper of the threshing floor and barns of a Polish manor farm.
gumienny.text: The gumienny guarded the gumno, the barns and threshing floors of a manor farm, supervised threshing and kept account of the grain threshed. He belonged to the lower manor staff, alongside the karbowy and the włodarz.

gutsinspektor.label: Estate manager (Gutsinspektor)
gutsinspektor.summary: Salaried manager of the farming operations on a large estate.
gutsinspektor.text: The Gutsinspektor runs, on behalf of the owner or tenant, the day-to-day farming of a large estate: allocating the workforce, tilling, harvest, livestock and accounts. The position was widespread above all east of the Elbe and often served young agriculturists as a stepping stone to a tenancy or the purchase of an estate of their own.

gypsier.label: Gypsum quarryman (gypsier)
gypsier.text: The gypsum quarryman operates a gypsum quarry, a rock used for making plaster.

habilleur.label: Cod dresser (habilleur)
habilleur.summary: Fishing sailor who prepares cod on the deck of a cod ship: opening, gutting, removing the backbone.
habilleur.text: The cod dresser receives cod already decapitated and gutted by the cleaner, then opens it flat, completes gutting and removes the dorsal bone before passing it to the salter who puts it in brine. This highly specialized post formed part of the fish-processing chain organized aboard Newfoundland ships from the 16th to 20th century. The word also designates, in a wholly different modern context, the theatre professional who helps artists costume.

haeusler.label: Cottager (Häusler)
haeusler.summary: Villager owning a small house with little or no land, living from day labour or a craft.
haeusler.text: The Häusler owns a small house of his own but little or no farmland, placing him in the lowest layer of village house owners, below farmers and smallholders. He earns his living as a day labourer, domestic weaver or village craftsman. The term is especially common in east-central Germany, Silesia, Bohemia, Bavaria and Austria; the Leerhäusler ("empty" Häusler) owned no land at all.

hajduk.label: Hajduk (manor attendant)
hajduk.summary: Manor servant in Hungarian-style dress, acting as guard, messenger or footman.
hajduk.text: From the seventeenth to the nineteenth century the hajduk was a servant at a magnate’s or noble’s court, wearing Hungarian-style dress. He served as bodyguard, messenger, usher or footman accompanying his master on journeys. The name comes from the Hungarian mercenary infantry formerly employed in Poland.

halbbauer.label: Half farmer (Halbbauer)
halbbauer.summary: Farmer working half a farm or half a hide of land.
halbbauer.text: The Halbbauer owns a farm amounting to only half a full farm holding and ranks in the village hierarchy between the full farmer and smallholders such as Kötter or Kossäten. Depending on the region he is called Halbhufner (northern Germany), Halberbe (Westphalia) or Halbmeier (Lower Saxony). This classification determined dues, labour services and rights of use on the common land.

haleur.label: Barge hauler (haleur)
haleur.summary: Worker pulling a boat upstream by means of a cable from the bank.
haleur.text: The barge hauler pulls, alone or in a team, a loaded boat upstream by pulling a cable from a towpath laid along the bank. Before animal traction then motorization, this exhausting work long ensured the upstream passage of river convoys on rivers like the Seine or Loire.

hannekemaaier.label: Hannekemaaier (seasonal German mower)
hannekemaaier.summary: Seasonal worker from Westphalia or Lower Saxony who came to the Low Countries in summer to mow or cut peat.
hannekemaaier.text: From the 17th to the 19th century, thousands of men from Westphalia and Lower Saxony travelled each year to the Dutch coastal provinces to mow hay, cut peat or work in the harvest. They returned home with their earnings at the end of the season. Some eventually settled in the Low Countries, which is how they appear in baptism and marriage registers.

hanouard.label: Paris salt/fish carrier (hanouard)
hanouard.summary: Parisian porter specialized in transporting salt and sea fish, enjoying ancient corporate privileges.
hanouard.text: The hanouard carries salt and sea fish through the streets of Paris, an activity organized into a corporation from the Middle Ages onward and endowed with special privileges — notably the right to bear the coffin of the deceased king to the first cross on the road to Saint-Denis. The word would have Celtic origin, linked to Breton or Welsh roots designating the salt merchant.

harenguier.label: Herring merchant (harenguier)
harenguier.summary: Merchant of herrings and other sea fish, sold notably at retail in market halls.
harenguier.text: The herring merchant commercializes herring and other sea fish, fresh, smoked or salted according to seasons and available preservation methods. Its feminine form, the "harengère," designated more specifically female market vendors, whose crude and loud speech gave rise to the proverbial expression "to quarrel like fishwives." "Haranguier" is a spelling variant.

haricotier.label: Small farmer (haricotier)
haricotier.summary: Small peasant owning reduced team animals, between day laborer and ploughman.
haricotier.text: The small farmer occupies an intermediate position in the Ancien Régime peasant hierarchy: unlike the ploughman, he owns only an incomplete team (one or two animals) and works a smaller surface. He distinguishes himself from the day laborer or manual worker, who own no draft animals and hire only their labour. The term appears in notarial and parish documents to designate these small-scale farmers of northern and eastern France.

haringvisser.label: Haringvisser (herring fisher)
haringvisser.summary: Fisherman who sailed in the herring fishery on the North Sea.
haringvisser.text: For centuries the great herring fishery was one of the main industries of the Low Countries. From the 15th century onwards busses and later loggers sailed from the ports of Holland and Zeeland to the North Sea, where the herring was gutted, salted and packed in barrels on board. The herring fishermen worked long seasons at sea in harsh conditions.

harnacheur.label: Harness maker (harnacheur)
harnacheur.summary: Craftsman making and repairing horse harness and equipment.
harnacheur.text: The harness maker makes collars, bridles, saddles and other horse-harnessing pieces for draft and riding horses. The trade, close to that of the leather-worker and saddler, is particularly present in garrison towns and horse-breeding regions. It declines with transport motorization in the 20th century.

haubergeon.label: Mail-coat maker (haubergeon)
haubergeon.summary: Craftsman making hauberks (mail coats) or holder of a mail-coat fief.
haubergeon.text: The term designates both the armourer specialized in making the haubert, the mail coat protecting the torso of medieval combatants, and by extension the holder of a "haubert fief," a feudal tenure requiring its holder to military service on horseback, armed with this haubert. The word thus covers both an artisanal reality and a social-status reality, both attested in old documents.

haut_le_pied.label: Light-footed (haut-le-pied)
haut_le_pied.summary: Agent, animal or vehicle moving 'empty', without load or cargo to transport.
haut_le_pied.text: The old expression "haut-le-pied" literally means "with foot raised," that is, ready to run or escape quickly; by extension it qualifies what moves "not mounted, not loaded." Applied to a person, it designates an agent (military, courier, relay rider) available and without fixed load to transport; the term survives in modern railway vocabulary for a locomotive or train running empty, without passengers or goods.

haute_contre.label: Countertenor (haute-contre)
haute_contre.summary: Singer at a high masculine vocal register, pillar of French Baroque opera repertoire.
haute_contre.text: The haute-contre is a male voice at very high pitch, close to the modern tenor but using head voice extensively; it is the title role of the hero in French Baroque opera (Lully, Rameau). The term also designates, in church choirs and singing schools, the singer holding this part in liturgical choirs.

haute_lissier.label: High-warp weaver (haute-lissier)
haute_lissier.summary: Tapestry weaver working on a loom with vertical warp (high-warp).
haute_lissier.text: The high-warp weaver weaves tapestry on a vertical loom, called "high-warp," where warp threads are stretched horizontally facing the weaver — a technique employed notably in the Gobelin workshops. It opposes "low-warp," where the loom is horizontal, a technique favoured in Aubusson and Beauvais. The term covers several old spelling variants encountered in records.

havenmeester.label: Havenmeester (harbour master)
havenmeester.summary: Official who supervised traffic, berths and order in a harbour.
havenmeester.text: The harbour master assigned ships their berths, supervised arrivals and departures, collected harbour dues and enforced the harbour regulations. In larger ports he was assisted by subordinate officials.

haveur.label: Coal hewer (haveur)
haveur.summary: Underground miner specialized in cutting coal at the working face.
haveur.text: The coal hewer is the worker who, in coal mines, attacks the coal seam with a pick (then later a mechanical coal cutter) to detach it from the rock. It is a skilled and physically demanding post, distinct from that of the cart-pusher, charged with transporting cut coal to the shaft.

heaumier.label: Helmet maker (heaumier)
heaumier.summary: Weapon-craftsman specialized in making heaumes and helmets.
heaumier.text: The helmet maker is an armourer specialized in making the heaume, a helmet completely enclosing the medieval knight's head, as well as other head-protection pieces. The trade, organized into a corporation in Paris from the Middle Ages, declines with weapons and armour evolution from the 15th century onward.

heemraad.label: Heemraad (water board member)
heemraad.summary: Member of the governing board of a Dutch water board, responsible for dikes, sluices and water levels.
heemraad.text: Together with the dijkgraaf (dike reeve), the heemraden formed the board that governed a water board or high water board. They inspected dikes, watercourses and structures, levied the rates due from the landowners and judged breaches of the water board's by-laws. The office was usually held by well-to-do landowners from the district.

heibaas.label: Heibaas (pile-driving foreman)
heibaas.summary: Foreman of a gang that drove wooden piles into the ground for foundations.
heibaas.text: In the soft soil of the Low Countries, houses, bridges and sluices had to be founded on wooden piles. The pile drivers jointly hauled a heavy block up with ropes and let it drop onto the pile, while the foreman set the rhythm, often with pile-driving songs. Steam pile drivers replaced the manual work from the late 19th century.

heimbuerge.label: Village official (Heimbürge)
heimbuerge.summary: Village official in Hesse, Franconia, Thuringia and the Rhineland who managed communal affairs.
heimbuerge.text: The Heimbürge is elected or appointed by the community, often annually, and manages the communal treasury, collects dues, oversees roads, wells and common property and represents the village externally; in some places he was the actual village head, elsewhere he served beside the Schultheiß. The office is attested above all in Hesse, Franconia, Thuringia and the Rhineland.

herbilleur.label: Weeder (herbilleur)
herbilleur.summary: Farm worker charged with manual weeding of crops.
herbilleur.text: The weeder is employed in hoeing and pulling weeds in cultivated fields, seasonal work often entrusted to women and children in traditional agriculture. The term occasionally appears in civil-status documents to qualify an unskilled agricultural worker.

herboriste.label: Herbalist (herboriste)
herboriste.summary: Merchant specialized in selling medicinal plants and herbal remedies.
herboriste.text: The herbalist sells dried plants and preparations from plants for therapeutic purposes, an activity long distinct from that of the apothecary then the pharmacist, with whom he maintains centuries-old regulatory rivalry. The profession, regulated then progressively restricted in France in the 20th century, survives today in regulated form.

hercheur.label: Coal-cart pusher (hercheur)
hercheur.summary: Miner charged with pushing coal cars through the galleries.
hercheur.text: The coal-cart pusher (or herscheur, hiercheur according to regional spellings in the north France-Pas-de-Calais coal basin) ensures transport of coal cut by the coal hewer, pushing or pulling ore cars along galleries to the extraction shaft. Émile Zola makes him a central character in Germinal, where this work is often entrusted to adolescents.

herdier.label: Communal shepherd (herdier)
herdier.summary: Sheep-raiser practising collective raising with common pasture and winter shelter.
herdier.text: The communal shepherd (or hertier) groups his sheep flock with those of other villagers for common summer grazing and collective winter housing, an organization typical of certain Ancien Régime rural communities. The term is close to that of shepherd, but emphasizes the collective and community dimension of flock-keeping.

heuerling.label: Tenant cottager (Heuerling)
heuerling.summary: Landless tenant of north-western Germany renting a house and land from a farmer and paying partly in labour.
heuerling.text: The Heuerling rents a small tenant house with some land from a farmer and pays the rent largely in labour on the landlord's farm at agreed times. The Heuerling system was widespread around Osnabrück, in the Münsterland, Minden-Ravensberg and the Oldenburg Münsterland; many Heuerlinge supplemented their income with linen weaving or as seasonal workers in Holland (Hollandgänger) and emigrated in large numbers to America in the 19th century.

hidalgo.label: Hidalgo (Spanish lesser noble)
hidalgo.summary: Member of the lowest rank of the Castilian nobility, exempt from the taxes paid by commoners.
hidalgo.text: The hidalgo belonged to the untitled nobility of blood, exempt from the personal taxes (pechos) paid by commoners. The status was proved by immemorial possession or through a lawsuit before the hidalguía court of the Chancillerías, which issued a certificate of nobility (ejecutoria de hidalguía). Very numerous in northern Spain, hidalgos appear as such in census lists and registers regardless of their trade or wealth.

hintersasse.label: Dependent tenant or non-citizen resident (Hintersasse)
hintersasse.summary: Peasant dependent on a landlord or, in Switzerland, a resident without communal citizenship.
hintersasse.text: In older German usage the Hintersasse is a peasant who holds his land from a landlord and owes him dues and services. In Switzerland, until the 19th century, Hintersäss denotes an inhabitant living in a commune without holding its citizenship, and therefore excluded from the citizens' benefits and liable to a residence fee. The exact meaning follows from the region and period of the source.

hirudiniculteur.label: Leech breeder (hirudiniculteur)
hirudiniculteur.summary: Breeder of leeches intended for medical use.
hirudiniculteur.text: The leech breeder raises leeches in pools or artificial marshes to supply the medical profession, leech-bleeding having enjoyed considerable therapeutic vogue in the 19th century. The profession declines with the waning of this medical practice from the late 19th century onward.

historiographe_de_france.label: Royal historian (historiographe de France)
historiographe_de_france.summary: Officer charged with writing the official history of the realm for the king.
historiographe_de_france.text: The royal historian (or king's historian) is an honorary office instituted under the Ancien Régime to record the great deeds of the reign and realm; Racine and Boileau jointly held the position under Louis XIV. The office, mostly honorary, was granted to recognized men of letters rather than historians in the modern sense.

hollandeur_de_plumes.label: Quill-feather processor (hollandeur de plumes)
hollandeur_de_plumes.summary: Worker specialized in treating goose feathers for making writing quills.
hollandeur_de_plumes.text: The quill-feather processor prepares goose feathers intended for writing — sorting, degreasing, hardening — in writing-quill workshops, a thriving activity before mechanical pen generalization in the 19th century. The name would refer to a Dutch technique or origin of the treatment process.

hollandgaenger.label: Seasonal worker in Holland (Hollandgänger)
hollandgaenger.summary: Seasonal worker from north-western Germany who went yearly to work in the Netherlands.
hollandgaenger.text: The Hollandgänger usually came from Westphalia, the Emsland, the Osnabrück area or Oldenburg and, from the 17th into the 19th century, went every year for a few months to the Netherlands to mow grass, cut peat, help with the harvest or sign on as sailor and whaler. Many Hollandgänger were Heuerlinge or Kötter whose small holdings alone could not feed the family.

homme_de_vigie.label: Lookout (homme de vigie)
homme_de_vigie.summary: Sailor charged with surveillance at sea from the tops, operating high sails.
homme_de_vigie.text: The lookout is posted in the rigging, at the tops, to watch the horizon (land, reefs, ships) and participates in handling the high sails of the main mast. This post requires agility and good vision, and often constitutes a step in the topman's advancement within the crew.

homme_incombustible.label: Fireproof performer (homme incombustible)
homme_incombustible.summary: Juggler who protects himself, by artifices, from the action of hot bodies he manipulates.
homme_incombustible.text: The fireproof performer is a fairground juggler who, by certain artifices, protects himself from the action of hot bodies he manipulates in performance.

homme_sandwich.label: Sandwich man (homme sandwich)
homme_sandwich.summary: Advertising walker carrying advertising panels on back and chest.
homme_sandwich.text: The sandwich man walks the streets carrying two advertising panels, one on his chest and one on his back, hence his name given by analogy with the sandwich. Appearing in the 19th century as a low-cost form of advertising, this street trade is also called sign-man.

hongreur.label: Animal gelder (hongreur)
hongreur.summary: Specialist in castrating domestic animals, sometimes practising as an empirical veterinarian.
hongreur.text: The animal gelder practices castration of horses, bulls and other farm animals, a technical operation performed before the existence of regulated veterinary profession. Lacking access to a veterinary graduate, he often also provided other empirical animal care in the countryside.

hongroyeur.label: Alum-and-tallow tanner (hongroyeur)
hongroyeur.summary: Craftsman tanner working leather by the so-called 'Hungarian' technique, with alum and tallow.
hongroyeur.text: The alum-and-tallow tanner tans hides (especially cattle and horse) by a process combining alum and tallow rather than classical vegetable tannin, a method reputed to come from Hungary and yielding supple leather used for straps and soles. This tannery specialty forms a corporation distinct from that of ordinary tanners.

hoofdingeland.label: Hoofdingeland (principal polder landowner)
hoofdingeland.summary: Landowner in a polder who represented the landowners in the assembly of the water board.
hoofdingeland.text: The ingelanden were the owners of the land in a polder, who contributed to the costs of drainage and dike maintenance in proportion to their holdings. The largest of them, or their elected representatives, sat as hoofdingelanden in the assembly that approved the board's accounts and decided on major works. The term appears in records as the social standing of prosperous farmers and landowners.

hopplukker.label: Hopplukker (hop picker)
hopplukker.summary: Seasonal worker who picked hop cones in late summer.
hopplukker.text: In the hop-growing regions, such as the area around Poperinge in West Flanders, many pickers, often women and children from the surrounding villages or further afield, were hired every year to pick the hops by hand. The picking lasted a few weeks and ended with a celebration.

horbilleur.label: Timber-frame filler (horbilleur)
horbilleur.summary: Normandy craftsman specialized in creating timber-frame infill with straw and earth.
horbilleur.text: The timber-frame filler is a Normandy craftsman who fills the timber framing of half-timbered houses with daub made of straw and earth (wattle-and-daub), a traditional Normandy rural building technique. The trade is closely related to that of the daub-maker.

horchatero.label: Horchatero (Spanish horchata maker)
horchatero.summary: Person who made or sold horchata.
horchatero.text: The horchatero prepared and sold horchata, a refreshing drink traditionally made in Valencia from tiger nuts, water and sugar. In the cities, horchateros sold the drink in refreshment shops, at street stalls or as hawkers during the hot months.

horloger.label: Watchmaker (horloger)
horloger.summary: Craftsman making, adjusting and repairing watches, clocks and timepieces.
horloger.text: The watchmaker designs, assembles and maintains time-measuring mechanisms, from large building clocks to pocket watches. The trade progressively splits between "large" horology (clocks, timepieces) and fine horology (watches), with renowned production centres like Besançon and Franche-Comté in France.

hortelain.label: Vegetable gardener (hortelain)
hortelain.summary: Old dialectal form of 'gardener', cultivator of vegetable gardens.
hortelain.text: Hortelain is an old and regional form (northern France, Wallonia) of the word gardener, derived from Latin hortus (the garden). Unlike the floating-garden gardener, specifically linked to the floating vegetable gardens of the Amiens region, the hortelain more generally designates any vegetable gardener, in town or country.

hortillon.label: Floating-garden gardener (hortillon)
hortillon.summary: Market gardener cultivating the floating gardens (hortillonnages) of the Amiens marshes.
hortillon.text: The floating-garden gardener exploits small vegetable plots surrounded by canals in the Somme marshes, around Amiens — the famous "hortillonnages," accessible only by boat. This form of marsh market gardening, attested since the Middle Ages, persists today at reduced scale, partly for tourism.

hospitalier.label: Hospital worker (hospitalier)
hospitalier.summary: Person charged with care of the sick and poor within a hospital.
hospitalier.text: The term hospitalier designates, before modern medicalization of hospitals, a person — often religious or lay affiliated to a confraternity — charged with receiving and caring for sick people, the poor and pilgrims in a hotel-Dieu or hospice. It also refers to members of hospitaller orders, such as the Order of Saint John of Jerusalem, devoted to this same mission.

hoste.label: Innkeeper (hoste)
hoste.summary: Old spelling of 'host', keeper of an inn or lodging house.
hoste.text: The hoste (old spelling of host) kept an inn or hostelry where he lodged and fed travellers for payment, an activity regulated from the Middle Ages by corporate statutes specific to stage-towns and fair-towns. The term is the direct ancestor of the modern hotelier.

hotelier.label: Hotelier (hôtelier)
hotelier.summary: Professional providing paid lodging and food to travellers.
hotelier.text: The hotelier operates an establishment offering lodging and board to travellers for remuneration, an activity directly inherited from the old hoste or medieval host. The profession structures and modernizes strongly from the 19th century with tourism and railway development.

hotteur.label: Basket carrier (hotteur)
hotteur.summary: Itinerant porter transporting goods or materials in a basket on his back.
hotteur.text: The basket carrier (or hottier, hoti, hotlî according to regions) transports on his back, using a basket, various goods — grapes, fish, ore, wood — according to local contexts. The term designates both a small urban itinerant trade and a loading post in vineyards or mines.

houblonnier.label: Hop grower (houblonnier)
houblonnier.text: The hop grower cultivates hops, a climbing plant whose cones serve to flavour and preserve beer. This labour-intensive cultivation, for trellising and picking, is historically concentrated in certain brewing regions like Alsace and northern France.

houilleur.label: Coal miner (houilleur)
houilleur.text: The coal miner works at coal (mineral coal) extraction in mines, a generic term covering several specialized posts like coal hewer or cart-pusher. The word is particularly frequent in records of coal-mining basins of the north, Pas-de-Calais and Loire in the 19th and 20th centuries.

houppier.label: Wool preparer (houppier)
houppier.summary: Worker who 'houppes' wool: washing, carding and degreasing before spinning.
houppier.text: The wool preparer washes, cards and degresses raw wool to prepare it for spinning, a task the Diderot and d'Alembert Encyclopedia places notably in woollen works in Amiens and Abbeville, where the term was sometimes synonymous with comber. Not to be confused with the modern sense of 'houppier,' which today denotes the crown of tree branches in forestry.

hourdeur.label: Daub-maker (hourdeur)
hourdeur.summary: Mason specialized in daub, filling timber-frame walls.
hourdeur.text: The daub-maker fills timber framing (the wooden structure of walls) with daub made of various materials — wattle-and-daub, rubble, bricks — traditional building technique widespread before generalization of solid stone or brick walls. The trade is close to that of the mason and Normandy timber-frame filler.

houtzaagmolenaar.label: Houtzaagmolenaar (sawmill miller)
houtzaagmolenaar.summary: Miller who ran a sawmill in which logs were sawn into planks by wind power.
houtzaagmolenaar.text: The wind-driven sawmill, in use since the end of the 16th century, made it possible to saw logs into beams and planks far faster than by hand. The sawmill millers, especially numerous in the Zaan region, supplied timber for shipbuilding and construction. The trade declined with the rise of steam sawmills in the 19th century.

hucher.label: Chest maker (hucher)
hucher.summary: Joiner specialized in making chests and storage furniture.
hucher.text: The chest maker makes chests — boxes notably intended for kneading and storing bread — and other wooden storage furniture. This specialized joinery trade is the ancestor of the cabinetmaker and differs from the huchier-crier, a homonym whose name comes from the verb "hucher" (shout loudly) and who designates a public crier.

huchier_crieur.label: Public crier (huchier-crieur)
huchier_crieur.summary: Public crier charged with proclaiming official announcements aloud.
huchier_crieur.text: The public crier, whose name comes from the old verb "hucher" (to call, shout loud), proclaims in streets and public squares official announcements, sales, notices and municipal bans, at a time when written posting reached a mostly illiterate population. The trade, organized into a sworn corporation in several towns, should not be confused with the hucher, a joiner making chests.

huetejunge.label: Herd boy (Hütejunge)
huetejunge.summary: Child or youth who tended livestock on the pasture.
huetejunge.text: The Hütejunge tends cows, sheep, pigs or geese on the pasture, often from spring to autumn in return for board, clothing and a small wage. Herding was frequently the first job of children from poor families and a step towards later service as a farmhand or maid.

huettenmann.label: Smelter worker (Hüttenmann)
huettenmann.summary: Worker at a smelting works who reduced ores to metal.
huettenmann.text: The Hüttenmann works in a smelter (Hütte), where silver, lead, copper or iron ores are roasted and smelted into metal in furnaces; as a Schmelzer he tends the furnaces, while other smelter hands supply charcoal and fluxes and tap the furnace. Smelter workers formed an occupational group of their own beside the miners, with their own regulations, for example in the Harz, the Ore Mountains and the Mansfeld area; the Hüttenmeister managed the works.

hufner.label: Full farmer (Hufner)
hufner.summary: Farmer holding a full hide (Hufe) of land and a full member of the village community.
hufner.text: The Hufner (Hüfner) works an entire Hufe, the traditional land unit of a farm, and so belongs to the upper layer of village farmers with full communal rights and a team of draught animals. The term is common in northern Germany, Schleswig-Holstein and eastern Germany; in Hesse and Silesia the form is Hübner, in the south Huber (holder of a Hube). Below him rank the half and quarter Hufner, the Kossäten and the Kätner.

huilier.label: Oil presser (huilier)
huilier.summary: Craftsman making and selling edible and household oils.
huilier.text: The oil presser presses and sells vegetable oils (walnut, olive, rapeseed, poppy seed according to regions) intended for eating, lighting or maintenance. The trade organizes around the oil mill, often held by lease or collective ownership in the countryside.

huissier.label: Door maker (huissier)
huissier.text: The huissier, in its old artisanal sense, is a door maker — a sense distinct from the officer of the same name.

huissier_a_verge.label: Rod-bearing bailiff (huissier à verge)
huissier_a_verge.summary: Junior court officer at the Châtelet of Paris, bearing a rod as an authority insignia.
huissier_a_verge.text: The rod-bearing bailiff is a junior justice officer attached to the Châtelet of Paris, recognizable by the rod (baton) he carries as a mark of his function during service of acts and executions of justice. This type of bailiff constitutes one of the many rungs of Ancien Régime lower justice.

huissier_au_parlement.label: Parliament bailiff (huissier au parlement)
huissier_au_parlement.summary: Officer charged with maintaining order and making convocations within an Ancien Régime parliament.
huissier_au_parlement.text: The parliament bailiff ensures order at hearings, introduction of parties and service of decrees within a provincial parliament or the Paris Parliament, the realm's highest court of justice. His office, often venial under the Ancien Régime, was transmitted or purchased like an office.

huissier_audiencier.label: Courtroom bailiff (huissier audiencier)
huissier_audiencier.summary: Justice officer charged with calling cases and maintaining order at hearings.
huissier_audiencier.text: The courtroom bailiff ensures the smooth material running of tribunal hearings: calling of cases, introduction of parties, maintenance of order in the room. This function differs from that of the justice bailiff, charged with service of acts and execution of decisions outside the tribunal.

huissier_aux_traites_foraines.label: Forfeited-trade bailiff (huissier aux traites foraines)
huissier_aux_traites_foraines.summary: Customs officer charged with collecting rights on goods in transit at provincial borders.
huissier_aux_traites_foraines.text: The forfeited-trade bailiff collects "forfeited trades," interior customs duties levied on goods moving between realm provinces before customs unification. This system of internal barriers, progressively abolished at the Revolution, generated abundant local administration of which this office formed a part.

huissier_de_justice.label: Bailiff of justice (huissier de justice)
huissier_de_justice.summary: Ministerial officer charged with serving legal acts and executing justice decisions.
huissier_de_justice.text: The bailiff of justice serves summonses, judgements and other procedural acts, and carries out seizures and evictions ordered by justice. Holder of a royal office then a regulated ministerial charge, he constitutes one of the essential mechanisms of judicial execution from the Ancien Régime to today (commissioner of justice since 2022).

huissier_de_la_chaine.label: Chain-bearing bailiff (huissier de la chaîne)
huissier_de_la_chaine.summary: Bailiff of the king's council, bearing a gold chain adorned with the royal medal.
huissier_de_la_chaine.text: The chain-bearing bailiff serves at the king's council and distinguishes himself by wearing a gold chain to which hangs a medal with the sovereign's effigy, insignia of his proximity to royal power. This high-ranking bailiff office illustrates the highly codified internal hierarchy of the Ancien Régime bailiff corps.

huissier_de_la_chancellerie.label: Chancellery bailiff (huissier de la chancellerie)
huissier_de_la_chancellerie.summary: Bailiff attached to a royal or provincial chancellery.
huissier_de_la_chancellerie.text: The chancellery bailiff ensures order and transmission of acts within a chancellery, the administration charged with sealing and registering the official acts of the king or a parliament. His office, like most Ancien Régime bailiff offices, could be purchased and transmitted.

huissier_de_soiree.label: Evening bailiff (huissier de soirée)
huissier_de_soiree.summary: Bailiff charged with announcing guests at social receptions.
huissier_de_soiree.text: The evening bailiff announces, often by crying out their names and titles, guests arriving at a reception, ball or social evening, a representative function characteristic of great aristocratic and bourgeois households of the 19th and early 20th century. The role is purely ceremonial, unrelated to the judicial functions of other bailiffs.

huissier_fabricant.label: Door maker (huissier-fabricant)
huissier_fabricant.text: This huissier is nothing judicial: he is a joiner specialized in making huis, an old term for door, and their frames. The word comes from the same root as huis-clos and huisserie, still employed today to denote a door frame.

huissier_priseur.label: Auctioneer-bailiff (huissier-priseur)
huissier_priseur.summary: Ministerial officer authorized to appraise and sell moveable goods by auction.
huissier_priseur.text: The auctioneer-bailiff inventories, appraises and sells at public auction moveable goods and objects, notably during successions, seizures or liquidations. The function arises from the 1576 edict fusing offices of appraiser-master and bailiff; it survives in towns lacking a judicial appraiser until the 2015 Macron law fusing justice bailiffs and judicial appraisers into a single profession of justice commissioner, effective since 2022.

huttier.label: Marsh-dwelling hut dweller (huttier)
huttier.summary: Inhabitant of the Poitevin Marshes traditionally living in a hut beside canals.
huttier.text: The marsh-dwelling hut dweller resides in a hut, traditional dwelling of earth and reeds typical of the Poitevin Marshes, and lives by fishing, waterfowl hunting and cultivating small plots accessible by boat (the "flat-bottomed boat"). This amphibious way of life, once common in wet areas of western France, has largely disappeared in the 20th century.

illumineur.label: Manuscript illuminator (illumineur)
illumineur.summary: Artist specialized in illumination and decoration of manuscripts.
illumineur.text: The illuminator (or manuscript illuminator) adorns medieval manuscripts with paintings, illuminated letters and gilding, often working in a workshop serving a monastery scriptorium or a lay bookseller-publisher from the 13th century onward. The trade declines with printing's spread from the late 15th century onward.

impiraressa.label: Impiraressa (Venetian bead stringer)
impiraressa.summary: In Venice, a woman who strung glass seed beads (conterie) at home into strands and bundles.
impiraressa.text: The impiraressa, using a fan of long thin needles, quickly threaded the tiny glass beads made in Murano and Venice into strands for trade and export. Paid by the piece and done mostly at home or on the doorstep, the work occupied thousands of Venetian women from the 19th to the 20th century.

implanteur.label: Hair implanter (implanteur)
implanteur.summary: Postiche worker specialized in implanting hair on wigs.
implanteur.text: The hair implanter works in the wig and postiche industry, knotting or implanting lock by lock hair (natural or synthetic) on a tulle or net base. The trade falls within wig-making, a flourishing activity under the Ancien Régime then refocused on theatre, cinema and medical-hair needs.

imprimeur.label: Printer (imprimeur)
imprimeur.summary: Craftsman or industrialist operating a press to reproduce texts and images.
imprimeur.text: The printer operates a press (typographic, then lithographic or offset) to reproduce in series texts and images on paper. Since Gutenberg, the trade structures into corporations then industry, with multiple specializations: printer-bookseller, intaglio printer, lithographic printer, each corresponding to a particular technique or production.

imprimeur_en_taille_douce.label: Intaglio printer (imprimeur en taille-douce)
imprimeur_en_taille_douce.summary: Printer specialized in printing engravings from copper plates cut in intaglio.
imprimeur_en_taille_douce.text: The intaglio printer pulls prints from copper plates engraved in intaglio (as opposed to wood engraving, in relief), a technique allowing great fineness of line used for portraits, maps and luxury illustrations. The process requires a specific intaglio press, different from the classical typographic press.

imprimeur_lithographe.label: Lithographic printer (imprimeur lithographe)
imprimeur_lithographe.summary: Printer specialized in reproduction by lithography, drawing on limestone.
imprimeur_lithographe.text: The lithographic printer reproduces texts and images through lithography, a process invented by Aloys Senefelder at the late 18th century, based on the repulsion between greasy ink and water applied to a limestone stone engraved with a greasy crayon. The process, less costly than engraving, enjoys great success in the 19th century for posters and illustration.

indiano.label: Indiano (Spanish returnee from the Americas)
indiano.summary: Emigrant who returned from the Americas, often after making a fortune.
indiano.text: The indiano was an emigrant who, after years in the Americas (Cuba, Mexico, Argentina and elsewhere), returned to his home region, often wealthy. Common in Asturias, Cantabria, Galicia, the Canary Islands and Catalonia, where he was also called "americano", he left his mark in houses, schools and charitable foundations paid for in his native village. The term appears in census lists and documents as a descriptor of the person.

indienneur.label: Cotton-print worker (indienneur)
indienneur.summary: Worker specialized in printing coloured patterns on cotton fabrics called indiennes.
indienneur.text: The cotton-print worker prints coloured patterns, often floral, on cotton fabrics called "indiennes" because initially imported from India; cotton-print manufacturing established itself in France (Rouen, Mulhouse, Jouy-en-Josas with Oberkampf) from the 18th century despite long protectionist prohibition. The trade declines with mechanization of textile printing in the 19th century.

industriante.label: Industriante (self-employed small trader)
industriante.summary: In northern Italian records, a person living by small trade or craft work on his own account.
industriante.text: The description industriante, frequent in 19th-century civil records and censuses of Lombardy and Piedmont, designates someone who runs a small trading or craft business on his own account, being neither a wage earner nor a landowner. A generic term, it must be interpreted according to local context.

industriel.label: Industrialist (industriel)
industriel.summary: Owner or manager of an industrial production enterprise.
industriel.text: The industrialist owns or directs a manufactory, a factory or any mechanized production enterprise, a term that generalizes in the 19th century with industrial revolution. He distinguishes himself from the craftsman by production scale and employment of numerous salaried workers.

infanzon.label: Infanzón (Aragonese or Navarrese lesser noble)
infanzon.summary: Member of the lesser nobility in Aragon and Navarre, equivalent of the Castilian hidalgo.
infanzon.text: The infanzón belonged to the lower nobility of the kingdoms of Aragon and Navarre, with tax and legal privileges comparable to those of the Castilian hidalgo. The status was established through infanzonía proceedings before the courts of the kingdom, whose files often contain genealogies spanning several generations.

infirmier.label: Nurse (infirmier)
infirmier.summary: Healthcare professional providing care to the sick, under medical responsibility.
infirmier.text: The nurse provides care to patients in health establishments or at home, a profession that strongly professionalizes from the late 19th century, partly heir to religious hospital orders. A state diploma has regulated the profession in France since 1922.

ingenieur.label: Engineer (ingénieur)
ingenieur.summary: Professional applying technical sciences to the design and implementation of works.
ingenieur.text: The engineer designs and supervises the implementation of works, machines or technical processes, a title long reserved for graduates of great schools (Bridges and Highways, École Polytechnique, Arts and Crafts) created from the 18th century onward. The term later generalizes to many technical and industrial specialties.

ingenieur_technico_commercial.label: Sales engineer (ingénieur technico-commercial)
ingenieur_technico_commercial.summary: Engineer combining technical skills and commercial sales functions.
ingenieur_technico_commercial.text: The sales engineer ensures the sale and technical advice on complex products or equipment, a hybrid post appearing with industrialized-goods complexification in the 20th century, requiring both technical understanding and commercial skills.

inquiridor.label: Inquiridor (examiner of witnesses)
inquiridor.summary: Court officer who examined witnesses in lawsuits.
inquiridor.text: The inquiridor is the court officer responsible for hearing witnesses and putting their statements in writing in civil and criminal proceedings. The post, often filled by royal or seigneurial appointment and sometimes held together with that of clerk or court accountant, was part of the ordinary staff of the courts under the Ancien Régime.

inquisidor.label: Inquisidor (Spanish Inquisition judge)
inquisidor.summary: Ecclesiastical judge of a tribunal of the Spanish Inquisition.
inquisidor.text: The inquisidor was one of the judges of the district tribunals of the Spanish Inquisition, created in 1478 and finally abolished in 1834, which answered to the Council of the Suprema and the inquisitor general. A cleric trained in law or theology, he investigated and judged cases of faith with the help of prosecutors, secret notaries, commissioners and familiars.

inspecteur_des_manufactures.label: Manufactures inspector (inspecteur des manufactures)
inspecteur_des_manufactures.summary: Royal official charged with controlling the state of arts and manufactures in the provinces.
inspecteur_des_manufactures.text: The manufactures inspector is a royal agent, established notably under Colbert, charged with controlling manufacturing-quality and compliance with corporate regulations in the manufactures of a generalship, within the mercantilist policy of Ancien Régime industrial development.

inspecteur_des_telegraphes.label: Telegraph inspector (inspecteur des télégraphes)
inspecteur_des_telegraphes.summary: In Chappe's telegraph company, agent visiting posts and repairing equipment.
inspecteur_des_telegraphes.text: In Chappe's telegraph company, the inspector visits network posts, repairs equipment and pays the operators.

inste.label: Estate labourer (Inste)
inste.summary: Estate labourer engaged by the year with a dwelling and land, in Schleswig-Holstein, Mecklenburg and East Prussia.
inste.text: The Inste (Instmann) is a farm labourer who binds himself to an estate or large farm for a year and receives as wages a dwelling, a plot of land, pasture for a cow and a share of the harvest. In East Prussia he often had to supply an additional worker (Hofgänger or Scharwerker), usually a family member. The Instleute made up a large part of the rural population north and east of the Elbe in the 18th and 19th centuries.

instituteur.label: Primary teacher (instituteur)
instituteur.summary: Primary-school teacher, particularly in public secular schools.
instituteur.text: The primary teacher teaches in primary school, a title that generalizes with the Guizot laws (1833) then Ferry laws (1881-1882) making primary instruction public, free and mandatory. He succeeds the old-regime schoolmaster or master, now with training and status regulated by the State through teacher-training schools.

instituteur_prive.label: Private primary teacher (instituteur privé)
instituteur_prive.summary: Primary teacher working in a private, often religious-affiliated, establishment.
instituteur_prive.text: The private primary teacher teaches in a free school, most often run by a religious congregation, in parallel with the public network issuing from the Ferry laws. The coexistence of the two networks, source of recurrent tensions (school disputes), durably structures the French education system.

instituteur_public.label: Public primary teacher (instituteur public)
instituteur_public.summary: Primary teacher employed by the State in public secular schools.
instituteur_public.text: The public primary teacher teaches in a municipal school funded by the State and municipality, a status consolidated by the Ferry laws of 1881-1882 instituting free, mandatory and secular primary education. He is trained in a departmental teacher-training school.

intendant.label: Royal administrator (intendant)
intendant.summary: High royal official charged with administering a generalship, or manager of a great household.
intendant.text: Under the Ancien Régime, the administrator of justice, police and finances represents royal power in a generalship, combining administrative, judicial and fiscal functions — one of the principal architects of monarchical centralization. The term also designates, in a domestic context, the manager charged with running a great estate or noble house.

intendant_de_la_chapelle.label: Chapel administrator (intendant de la chapelle)
intendant_de_la_chapelle.summary: Officer charged with administration and operation of a royal or seigneurial chapel.
intendant_de_la_chapelle.text: The chapel administrator manages liturgical materials, personnel and organization of services in a royal, princely or seigneurial chapel, a domestic function close to that of a household manager but applied to private religious service.

introducteur.label: Master of ceremonies (introducteur)
introducteur.summary: Officer of the Royal Household charged with presenting foreign ambassadors at royal audiences.
introducteur.text: The master of ceremonies is a Royal Household officer charged with protocol for receiving foreign diplomats, presenting them to the sovereign and ensuring proper conduct of official audiences. The office, prestigious, illustrates the importance of ceremony in Ancien Régime diplomacy.

islandais.label: Icelandic fisherman (islandais)
islandais.summary: Fishing sailor embarked for long cod-fishing campaigns on Iceland banks.
islandais.text: The Icelandic fisherman is the sailor who embarked, from around 1850 until the 1930s, aboard schooners, dundees or three-masters for cod-fishing campaigns of six to eight months off Iceland. Dunkerquois long remained the only French to frequent these waters, before Paimpol shipowners sent their own schooners from 1852; Pierre Loti's novel, Icelandic Fisherman, made famous this fishing, distinct from that of the Newfoundland ships exploiting Newfoundland banks.

ivoirier.label: Ivory carver (ivoirier)
ivoirier.summary: Craftsman specialized in working and carving ivory.
ivoirier.text: The ivory carver sculpts and shapes ivory (elephant tusks, more rarely bone or mother-of-pearl) to make art objects, handles, fans, boxes or statuettes. The trade knows particular growth in Dieppe, a great French centre of small wares and ivory-work from the 17th to 19th century.

jagot.label: Auvergnat tinker (jagot)
jagot.summary: Itinerant tinsmith from Auvergne, repairing copper utensils from village to village.
jagot.text: The Auvergnat tinker is an itinerant Auvergnat tinsmith who travels the countryside repairing pots, cauldrons and other copper or tin utensils, seasonal activity typical of temporary labour migration from the Massif Central to other regions. The term is close to that of magnien or maignan, designating the same type of itinerant craftsman.

janteleur.label: Wheel-rim maker (janteleur)
janteleur.summary: Craftsman making metal circles used for binding cart-wheel rims.
janteleur.text: The wheel-rim maker makes and fits the iron circles (bandages) that reinforce the wooden rim of cart and wagon wheels, an operation performed hot to ensure perfect tightness upon cooling. The trade is closely linked to those of the wheelwright and farrier.

jardinier.label: Gardener (jardinier)
jardinier.summary: Person cultivating and maintaining a garden, vegetable or ornamental.
jardinier.text: The gardener cultivates vegetables, fruits or flowers, whether for his own account as an independent gardener or in service to an estate, castle or institution. The term covers great diversity of statuses, from the small suburban gardener to the head gardener of a great park.

jardinier_en_prinvaux.label: Prinvaux gardener (jardinier en prinvaux)
jardinier_en_prinvaux.summary: Cultivator of the viticultural and market-garden zone of Prinvaux, near Saint-Dizier.
jardinier_en_prinvaux.text: The Prinvaux gardener works the market-garden and viticultural lands of the Prinvaux quarter, at Saint-Dizier (Haute-Marne), a very localized designation found in documents of this municipality.

jarlier.label: Wooden-vessel maker (jarlier)
jarlier.summary: Craftsman making jarles and gerles, wooden vessels for wine or laundry.
jarlier.text: The wooden-vessel maker makes jarles (or gerles), from Latin gerula, large wooden vats or baskets used for grape harvest, wine storage or laundry. The surname derived from it is notably attested in Haute-Loire, in the Massif Central, a region where this type of rustic cooperage was widespread.

jattier.label: Wooden-bowl turner (jattier)
jattier.summary: Wood turner specialized in making bowls and wooden dishes.
jattier.text: The wooden-bowl turner turns wood on a pedal or bow-driven lathe to produce bowls, dishes and other common tableware, rural craft activity widespread in forested regions before metal or earthenware tableware generalization.

jaugeur.label: Barrel measurer (jaugeur)
jaugeur.summary: Officer charged with measuring and verifying the capacity of barrels and containers.
jaugeur.text: The barrel measurer measures the capacity (the gauge) of barrels, casks and other containers, notably for wine trade and taxed liquids, an sworn function essential to calculation of Ancien Régime tax rights.

joaillier.label: Jeweller (joaillier)
joaillier.summary: Craftsman and merchant making jewellery set with precious stones.
joaillier.text: The jeweller works gold and silver to create jewellery set with precious stones, distinguishing himself from the jeweller whose production uses more modest materials or metal alone. Joyaulier is the old spelling of the same word, attested in old documents.

jocquier.label: Postillion groom (jocquier)
jocquier.summary: Domestic driving a carriage while riding one of the horses, as a postillion.
jocquier.text: The postillion groom is a domestic who drives a carriage as a postillion, that is, riding one of the team horses rather than seated on a coach seat, to guide and direct the equipage. The term thus designates a horse-driving trade rather than an artisan craft.

jouattier.label: Jouattier (toy maker)
jouattier.summary: Craftsman who made traditional wooden toys.
jouattier.text: The jouattier made wooden toys by traditional craft methods, an activity often carried on alongside other joinery work in rural areas before the industrialisation of toy making in the 19th and 20th centuries.

joueur_d_instruments.label: Musician (joueur d'instruments)
joueur_d_instruments.summary: Professional musician playing one or several musical instruments.
joueur_d_instruments.text: The musician is a professional musician performing at celebrations, balls, religious or civic ceremonies, a generic term used in old documents without always specifying the instrument (vielle, bagpipe, violin, oboe according to regions).

jouguier.label: Yoke maker (jouguier)
jouguier.summary: Craftsman making youks, wooden pieces for yoke of draft animals.
jouguier.text: The yoke maker shapes youks, wooden pieces placed on the neck of oxen to yoke them in pairs to the plough or cart, rural craft closely linked to animal-traction agriculture.

journalier.label: Day labourer (journalier)
journalier.summary: Agricultural worker paid by the day, without land or own specialization.
journalier.text: The day labourer hires out his labour day to day, most often in agriculture, without owning land or team animals, which places him at the bottom of the peasant hierarchy, below the small farmer and ploughman. The term, one of the most frequent in parish and civil-status records, knows many regional variants like journayeur, and its feminine form journalière.

journaliste.label: Journalist (journaliste)
journaliste.summary: Professional writing and disseminating information in written or audiovisual press.
journaliste.text: The journalist researches, writes and disseminates current events, a profession that truly structures with the rise of press in the 19th century and professionalizes in France with the press card instituted in 1935.

juge.label: Judge (juge)
juge.summary: Magistrate charged with administering justice in the name of the king or state.
juge.text: The judge renders justice decisions, civil, criminal or seigneurial according to era and jurisdictions; under the Ancien Régime, the function covers great diversity of titles (justice-of-peace, seneschal judge, forest judge...) according to the matter and court level concerned.

juge_aux_traites_foraines.label: Forfeited-trade judge (juge aux traites foraines)
juge_aux_traites_foraines.summary: Magistrate charged with judging disputes related to interior customs duties.
juge_aux_traites_foraines.text: The forfeited-trade judge resolves disputes related to collection of interior customs duties, those duties levied on goods moving between realm provinces, a fiscal system abolished at the Revolution.

juge_d_armes.label: Juge d'armes (judge of arms)
juge_d_armes.summary: Heraldic officer who checked and validated coats of arms and titles of nobility.
juge_d_armes.text: The juge d'armes de France examined and authenticated coats of arms and noble titles, ensuring that heraldic rules were respected and that claims to nobility were legitimate. The office was created in the 17th century in connection with the inquiries into nobility ordered by the monarchy.

juge_de_paix.label: Juge de paix (justice of the peace)
juge_de_paix.summary: Local magistrate dealing with minor civil disputes and conciliation, until 1958.
juge_de_paix.text: The juge de paix, created in 1790, dispensed local justice in his canton for minor civil cases and favoured conciliation between the parties. The institution was abolished in 1958 and its powers transferred to the "tribunal d'instance".

juge_gruyer.label: Juge gruyer (forest judge)
juge_gruyer.summary: Forest magistrate who tried offences committed in royal or seigneurial forests.
juge_gruyer.text: The juge gruyer presided over the court of the "gruerie", a tribunal specialising in forest offences (illegal felling, poaching, unlawful grazing) committed in royal or seigneurial woods, an institution characteristic of forest administration under the Ancien Régime.

juge_senechal.label: Juge sénéchal (seneschal's judge)
juge_senechal.summary: Magistrate who dispensed justice in the name of the lord or the king within a seneschalsy.
juge_senechal.text: The juge sénéchal exercised justice within a "sénéchaussée", a judicial district characteristic of southern and western France (the equivalent of the "bailliage" in the north), in the name of the king or of a great lord.

juhas.label: Juhas (mountain shepherd)
juhas.summary: Shepherd on Carpathian mountain pastures, working under the baca.
juhas.text: The juhas grazed and milked the sheep on the mountain pastures and helped the baca make cheese, living in the shepherds’ hut for the whole season. The job was often done by young men from the mountain villages of Podhale and the Beskids.

juiz_de_fora.label: Juiz de fora (royal judge from outside)
juiz_de_fora.summary: University-trained magistrate appointed by the king to preside over the council and administer justice in a municipality.
juiz_de_fora.text: The juiz de fora, so called because he came from outside the locality, is a law-trained magistrate appointed by the Crown to administer justice in a municipality and preside over its council, in place of the locally elected ordinary judges. Introduced in the Middle Ages and spread in the following centuries, the office was abolished by the liberal judicial reforms of the 1830s. He often also held the duties of judge of orphans.

juiz_de_vintena.label: Juiz de vintena (village judge)
juiz_de_vintena.summary: Village judge who settled small cases orally in places distant from the seat of the municipality.
juiz_de_vintena.text: The juiz de vintena was chosen in villages and hamlets far from the seat of the municipality that had at least twenty households, to judge orally, without written proceedings, small civil cases of low value and to keep good local order. Provided for in the Ordinances of the Kingdom, he represented the lowest rung of Portuguese local justice.

juiz_do_povo.label: Juiz do povo (judge of the people)
juiz_do_povo.summary: President of the Casa dos Vinte e Quatro, representing the craftsmen before the municipal council.
juiz_do_povo.text: The juiz do povo was elected annually by the representatives of the trades gathered in the Casa dos Vinte e Quatro, over which he presided, and defended the craftsmen's interests before the council and sometimes before the king himself. The institution existed in Lisbon and other towns of the kingdom until its abolition in 1834, with the end of the guild system.

juiz_dos_orfaos.label: Juiz dos órfãos (judge of orphans)
juiz_dos_orfaos.summary: Judge in charge of probate inventories and partitions involving minors, and of appointing their guardians.
juiz_dos_orfaos.text: The juiz dos órfãos watches over the persons and property of orphaned minors: he orders inventories and partitions of estates where there are minor heirs, appoints guardians and curators, supervises their management and authorises marriages and emancipations. The orphans' inventories (inventários orfanológicos) produced by his court, rich in information on families and their property, are first-rate genealogical sources.

juiz_ordinario.label: Juiz ordinário (elected local judge)
juiz_ordinario.summary: Locally elected judge, not necessarily trained in law, who administered justice in the municipality.
juiz_ordinario.text: The juiz ordinário was chosen from among the leading men of the municipality, usually by annual election, to administer first-instance justice and preside over the council, in municipalities where there was no juiz de fora. He was not required to have legal training and often served in pairs. The office disappeared with the liberal judicial reforms of the 19th century.

jurat.label: Jurat (sworn town magistrate)
jurat.summary: Sworn municipal magistrate, an elected member of the town council in southern France.
jurat.text: In certain towns of southern France, the jurat was a municipal magistrate who had taken an oath (from the Latin juratus), the local equivalent of the "échevin" of the north. In Bordeaux, the "jurade" comprised twelve jurats elected by their peers for one year and headed by a mayor; under the Ancien Régime it managed the upkeep of the streets, the water and market supplies, and the guarding of the ramparts and the security of the city.

jure.label: Juré (sworn guild warden)
jure.summary: Elected member of a guild responsible for enforcing the trade's regulations.
jure.text: The juré (or "garde-juré") was a master elected by his peers within a trade guild to ensure that its statutes were respected, to inspect the quality of work and to settle disputes between members. The term is also found in specific sworn offices outside the guilds (juré-crieur, juré-compteur, etc.), denoting any office exercised under oath.

jure_compteur.label: Juré compteur (sworn timber counter)
jure_compteur.summary: Sworn officer who counted timber transported by floating.
jure_compteur.text: The juré compteur officially counted the pieces of timber floated down the rivers to their ports of arrival, a sworn office essential to the trade in firewood and building timber destined for the towns, notably Paris via the Yonne and the Seine.

jure_crieur.label: Juré crieur (sworn town crier)
jure_crieur.summary: Sworn crier responsible in particular for announcing deaths and supplying funeral hangings.
jure_crieur.text: The juré-crieur, and in particular the "crieur de corps", proclaimed in the streets the deaths of inhabitants and invited the population to the funeral, while in some towns also supplying the drapes and funeral ornaments needed for the ceremony. This sworn office thus combined a role of public announcement with a commercial activity connected with mourning.

jure_en_sel.label: Juré en sel (sworn salt officer)
jure_en_sel.summary: Sworn officer responsible for inspecting and distributing salt.
jure_en_sel.text: The juré en sel supervised the sale and distribution of salt at the "grenier à sel" (salt warehouse), under the tightly controlled regime of the Ancien Régime gabelle, an indirect tax on salt whose collection and control required a large administration.

jure_moleur_de_buches.label: Juré moleur de bûches (sworn firewood measurer)
jure_moleur_de_buches.summary: Sworn officer who measured firewood by the unit known as the mole.
jure_moleur_de_buches.text: The juré moleur de bûches checked and counted the firewood delivered to the towns using the unit of measure called the "mole", a sworn office related to that of the juré compteur in the river trade in timber.

kaasdrager.label: Kaasdrager (cheese porter)
kaasdrager.summary: Member of the guild that carried cheeses on barrows to the weigh house and the ships.
kaasdrager.text: At the cheese markets of North Holland, such as Alkmaar, the cheese porters carried the cheeses in pairs on a barrow from the market to the weigh house and on to the buyers' boats or carts. They were organised in a guild with its own teams, recognisable by the colour of their hats. In Alkmaar the guild survived as a tradition into the 21st century.

kanonik.label: Kanonik (canon)
kanonik.summary: Cleric belonging to a cathedral or collegiate chapter.
kanonik.text: The kanonik sat in the chapter of a cathedral or collegiate church, taking part in the liturgy and the administration of the diocese, and drew in return the income of a benefice (prebend). The title of honorary canon was also granted to distinguished parish priests.

kapelan.label: Kapelan (chaplain)
kapelan.summary: Cleric serving a chapel, manor, hospital, convent or army unit.
kapelan.text: The kapelan provided pastoral care outside the parish structure: in a manor chapel, a hospital, a prison, a convent or a regiment. Manor chaplains were often maintained by the landowner.

karbowy.label: Karbowy (field overseer)
karbowy.summary: Overseer of serf or hired labour on a Polish manor farm.
karbowy.text: The karbowy supervised in the fields the work of peasants performing labour service or of manor labourers. The name comes from the karb, a notch cut in a wooden tally stick with which he recorded the days worked. He answered to the steward (ekonom) or the włodarz.

karczmarz.label: Karczmarz (village innkeeper)
karczmarz.summary: Keeper of a village inn, lodging house and tap room.
karczmarz.text: The karczmarz ran the karczma, the hub of village social life, where beer and vodka from the lord’s brewery or distillery were sold, travellers were lodged and their horses stabled. Inns usually belonged to the landowner, who leased them to an arendarz or installed an innkeeper on set terms.

kastner.label: Granary official (Kastner)
kastner.summary: Official in Bavaria and Austria who managed the lord's granary and dues in kind.
kastner.text: The Kastner heads a Kastenamt and manages the Kasten, the granary of a territorial ruler, monastery or lordship: he receives the land dues paid in grain and other kind, stores them, sells or distributes them and keeps the accounts. The office is attested especially in Bavaria and Austria from the late Middle Ages to the early 19th century; the surname Kastner recalls it.

kienrussbrenner.label: Lampblack burner (Kienrußbrenner)
kienrussbrenner.summary: Forest craftsman who produced lampblack by burning resinous pine wood.
kienrussbrenner.text: The Kienrußbrenner burns resinous pine and spruce wood (Kien) or resin residues with little air in a soot hut and collects the soot in a chamber. The lampblack was used to make printer's ink, drawing ink, paint and shoe polish and was sold by pedlars in small wooden kegs (Rußbutten). The trade was widespread in the Thuringian Forest, the Black Forest, the Bavarian Forest and the Palatinate.

kiepkerel.label: Kiepkerel (basket pedlar)
kiepkerel.summary: Itinerant pedlar who carried his wares in a kiep, a basket worn on the back.
kiepkerel.text: The kiepkerels mostly came from Westphalia and travelled on foot through the eastern Netherlands to sell small wares such as thread, ribbon, earthenware or foodstuffs. They carried their goods in a large back basket, the kiep. The figure remained well known in the folk imagination of the border region.

kinesitherapeute.label: Kinésithérapeute (physiotherapist)
kinesitherapeute.summary: Health professional providing treatment through movement and therapeutic massage.
kinesitherapeute.text: The kinésithérapeute treated motor, respiratory or post-traumatic disorders through movement, massage and various manual techniques. It is a regulated profession in France, whose state diploma was established in 1946, having grown out of the former practice of masso-kinesitherapy.

klucznik.label: Klucznik (keeper of the keys)
klucznik.summary: Manor servant keeping the keys to the pantry and stores.
klucznik.text: The klucznik (a woman: klucznica) kept the keys to the pantries, cellars and storerooms of a manor house or monastery, issued provisions and kept account of them. The post required the master’s trust and was often given to older, long-serving servants. Latin sources call him “claviger”.

kmiec.label: Kmieć (full-holding peasant)
kmiec.summary: Peasant holding a full farm (a łan or a large part of one) in old Poland.
kmiec.text: The kmieć was the most prosperous layer of the peasantry in the old Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth: he held a full farm, usually a łan (a Polish land unit) or half of one, and owned his own draught team, for which he owed labour service with his animals and dues to the lord. Latin parish registers call him “cmetho” or “colonus”; the term faded in the nineteenth century with the enfranchisement of the peasants, giving way to “gospodarz”.

knappschaftsaeltester.label: Miners' fund elder (Knappschaftsältester)
knappschaftsaeltester.summary: Representative elected by miners in the Knappschaft, their sickness and invalidity fund.
knappschaftsaeltester.text: The Knappschaftsältester is elected by the miners of a district and represents them in the Knappschaft, the miners' community and fund existing since the Middle Ages, which provided support in case of sickness, accident, invalidity and death. He visited sick members, examined claims and took part in running the fund; the office carried prestige and was usually given to experienced hewers.

koetter.label: Cottager (Kötter)
koetter.summary: Smallholder of north-western Germany working a cottage holding (Kotten) with little land.
koetter.text: The Kötter lives on and works a Kotten, a small holding with little land, ranking below the full and half farmers (Vollerbe, Halberbe) in the rural hierarchy of Westphalia and Lower Saxony. He often supplemented his living with day labour, linen weaving or a craft; older Erbkötter are distinguished from later Markkötter, who settled on the common land. In Schleswig-Holstein and Mecklenburg the corresponding smallholder is called a Kätner.

komendarz.label: Komendarz (acting parish priest)
komendarz.summary: Cleric temporarily administering a parish without the full rights of a parish priest.
komendarz.text: The komendarz ran a parish whose priest had died or been transferred, or whose benefice was vacant, as well as parishes dependent on a monastery. He carried out all pastoral duties and kept the parish registers without being canonically the parish priest.

komornik.label: Komornik (rural lodger)
komornik.summary: Landless villager lodging in someone else’s house in old Poland.
komornik.text: The rural komornik had neither land nor a house of his own: he lodged in a corner of a farmer’s home, often in exchange for work, and lived from hired labour. Latin parish registers call him “inquilinus” (a woman: “inquilina”). He must not be confused with the court bailiff, also called komornik in Polish.

koniuszy.label: Koniuszy (master of the horse)
koniuszy.summary: Manager of the stables and horses at a royal or noble court or on an estate.
koniuszy.text: The koniuszy ran the stables, stud and stable staff, overseeing the breeding, purchase and care of horses and carriages. At the royal court the koniuszy was a high officer, while on noble estates the post was held by a trusted estate official.

korendrager.label: Korendrager (grain porter)
korendrager.summary: Member of the guild that carried sacks of grain between ships, warehouses and markets.
korendrager.text: In port towns with a large grain trade, such as Amsterdam, the grain porters held the right to unload grain from ships, carry it in sacks and take it to lofts and warehouses. They worked closely with the sworn grain measurers and were organised in a guild that regulated the sharing of work and the rates.

kossaet.label: Cottager (Kossät)
kossaet.summary: Smallholder of Brandenburg, Pomerania and Saxony-Anhalt with a cottage and little land, owing manual services.
kossaet.text: The Kossät (from Low German Kotsasse, cottage dweller) holds a small farmstead with little arable land and ranks below the full farmer (Hüfner) who kept a team of draught animals. Towards the manor he usually owed manual labour rather than team services. The term is typical of the Mark Brandenburg, Pomerania and neighbouring areas and appears frequently in parish registers and land-tax rolls.

kraankind.label: Kraankind (treadwheel crane worker)
kraankind.summary: Worker who powered a treadwheel crane by walking inside the wheel.
kraankind.text: In the ports of the Low Countries heavy loads were unloaded with wooden cranes driven by men walking inside a large treadwheel. These workers were called kraankinderen and in some towns were organised in a guild. The crane and its crew played a central role in handling wine, stone and other heavy goods.

kuhmagd.label: Cow maid (Kuhmagd)
kuhmagd.summary: Maidservant who tends the livestock and milks the cows on a farm.
kuhmagd.text: The Kuhmagd is responsible for work in the byre: feeding and watering the cattle, mucking out and above all milking, often also making butter and cheese. On larger farms she ranked below the head maid (Großmagd) in the servants' hierarchy. The term is frequent in parish registers and lists of farm servants.

kunstknecht.label: Pump attendant (Kunstknecht)
kunstknecht.summary: Miner who operated a mine's water-powered pumping and hoisting machinery (Künste).
kunstknecht.text: In the mines of the Harz and the Ore Mountains the machines driven by water wheels and rod systems for draining the workings were called "Künste". The Kunstknecht watches over and greases this machinery, replaces pump parts and reports damage so that the mine does not flood; the Kunststeiger supervises him, while the Kunstmeister designs and builds the installations.

laboratrice.label: Laboratrice (female farm labourer)
laboratrice.summary: Female farm worker employed in the fields by the day.
laboratrice.text: The laboratrice worked in the fields as a female agricultural day labourer, the term denoting a mere worker paid by the task who owned neither land nor a plough team. She should not be confused with the "laboureuse", the feminine form of "laboureur", a well-off farmer who owned a draught team.

laboron.label: Laboron (fortification labourer)
laboron.summary: Labourer employed on the fortification works of towns.
laboron.text: The laboron was an unskilled worker assigned to urban fortification works (earthmoving, carrying materials), a rare term found in some old records connected with fortified towns.

laboureur.label: Laboureur (ploughman-farmer)
