laboureur.summary: A comparatively well-off farmer who owned a plough team and worked his own land.
laboureur.text: A "laboureur" owned (or rented) a team of oxen or horses together with a plough, which made him one of the wealthier members of the Ancien Régime peasantry. He is distinct from the simple farmhand or day-labourer, who owned no plough team and hired out his labour instead. The term appears very frequently in French parish and civil registers from the 17th to the 19th century.

laboureur_a_boeufs.label: Laboureur à bœufs (ox ploughman)
laboureur_a_boeufs.summary: Farmer who owned a team of oxen, often a tenant of his land.
laboureur_a_boeufs.text: The laboureur à bœufs ploughed with a pair of oxen rather than with horses, a choice that often reflects hilly country or heavy soil (the Massif Central, Brittany) and a generally humbler condition than that of the laboureur à chevaux (horse ploughman), who was more often an owner than a tenant farmer.

laboureur_a_bras.label: Laboureur à bras (hand labourer)
laboureur_a_bras.summary: Cultivator with only his own manual strength and no draught team.
laboureur_a_bras.text: The laboureur à bras worked the land with nothing but the strength of his arms, using a hoe or a spade, without draught animals or plough. Despite his title of "laboureur", he was therefore socially closer to the labourer ("manœuvre") or day labourer ("journalier") than to the well-off laboureur who owned a full plough team.

laceur.label: Laceur (net maker)
laceur.summary: Craftsman who knotted and made hunting or fishing nets.
laceur.text: The laceur made and mended knotted-mesh nets for hunting or fishing, from braided or laced threads using techniques close to net-making ("filetage"). The word comes from the verb "lacer", which describes the action of knotting the meshes.

aliases: Laceuse de Fil et de Soie
laceur_de_fil_et_de_soie.label: Laceur de fil et de soie (thread and silk lace maker)
laceur_de_fil_et_de_soie.summary: Textile craftsman who made laces and ribbons of thread and silk.
laceur_de_fil_et_de_soie.text: The laceur de fil et de soie made laces, cords and braided ribbons of linen thread or silk for lingerie, trimmings ("passementerie") and clothing, a speciality distinct from that of the net-making laceur.

lacheur.label: Lâcheur (Paris river pilot)
lacheur.summary: Parisian river pilot who steered boats on the Seine between Bercy and Gros-Caillou.
lacheur.text: The lâcheur piloted strings of boats and rafts of floated timber on the Seine through Paris, notably between the ports of Bercy and Gros-Caillou, a delicate manoeuvre that required a good knowledge of the river and of its passages under the bridges.

lacier.label: Lacier (lace maker)
lacier.summary: Maker and seller of laces for shoes and clothing.
lacier.text: The lacier made and sold laces for shoes and various uses in clothing, a light trimmings craft often carried on alongside other textile activities.

laineur.label: Laineur (wool finisher)
laineur.summary: Textile worker who processed woollen cloth and fabrics.
laineur.text: The laineur took part in the finishing of woollen cloth — fulling, shearing, raising the nap ("lainage") — which gave the fabric its final appearance and texture before sale. Laneur is an equivalent variant of the term.

lainier.label: Lainier (wool merchant, wool worker)
lainier.summary: Wool merchant or worker specialised in processing wool.
lainier.text: The lainier traded in raw or processed wool, or worked it through the various stages of its textile transformation (sorting, carding, spinning). It is a generic term of the wool industry, which was highly developed in regions such as Picardy or Languedoc.

laitier.label: Laitier (milkman)
laitier.summary: Collector and seller of milk, an intermediary between producers and consumers.
laitier.text: The laitier collected milk from the farms and resold it to town dwellers, door to door or in a dairy shop, an essential activity before refrigeration and large-scale retail became widespread, particularly in urban and suburban areas.

lamaneur.label: Lamaneur (harbour pilot)
lamaneur.summary: Maritime pilot who guided ships in and out of harbours.
lamaneur.text: The lamaneur guided ships through the delicate manoeuvres of entering and leaving harbour, with a thorough knowledge of the local currents, shoals and channels, a role now performed by sworn maritime pilots.

lamarreur.label: Lamarreur (coastal pilot)
lamarreur.summary: Coastal pilot who navigated ships close to the shore.
lamarreur.text: The lamarreur piloted ships along the coast, in shallower and more dangerous waters than the open sea, a role similar to that of the lamaneur but exercised outside harbour limits.

lamballais.label: Lamballais (navvy from Lamballe)
lamballais.summary: Navvy from Lamballe, renowned for digging ditches and building ramparts and enclosures.
lamballais.text: By metonymy, lamballais denoted a navvy from the Lamballe area in Brittany, whose men traditionally left home to work elsewhere in western France, digging ditches and ramparts and building earth banks. A Breton saying sums up their reputation: "the Lamballais is a master at making good enclosures".

lambrisseur.label: Lambrisseur (panelling fitter)
lambrisseur.summary: Craftsman who fitted panelling on walls and ceilings.
lambrisseur.text: The lambrisseur installed panelling ("lambris"), panels of wood or other materials covering walls and ceilings for decoration and insulation, a speciality close to interior joinery and architectural cabinetmaking.

lamier.label: Lamier (heddle maker)
lamier.summary: Craftsman who made the wooden heddles used in looms.
lamier.text: The lamier shaped the wooden heddles ("lames" or "lisses") that make up the frame of the loom, the parts that separate the warp threads so that the shuttle can pass, a craft linked to textile work.

lamineur.label: Lamineur (rolling-mill worker)
lamineur.text: The lamineur passed metals (iron, steel, copper) between rollers to thin them and form them into sheets, bars or sections, a central operation of the industrial iron and steel industry from the 19th century onwards.

lampier.label: Lampier (lamp founder)
lampier.summary: Founder and maker of copper lamps and candlesticks.
lampier.text: The lampier cast and shaped copper or brass to produce oil lamps, candlesticks and other domestic lighting objects, a craft linked to copperware ("dinanderie") and founding.

lampiste.label: Lampiste (lamp maker, lamp man)
lampiste.summary: Craftsman specialised in making and maintaining lighting equipment.
lampiste.text: The lampiste made, sold or maintained lighting appliances — oil, then paraffin, then gas lamps — and on large networks (mines, railways) was responsible for distributing them and lighting them every day.

lampiste_chemins_de_fer.label: Railway lamp man (lampiste des chemins de fer)
lampiste_chemins_de_fer.summary: Railway employee who maintained acetylene or oil signal lamps.
lampiste_chemins_de_fer.text: The railway lampiste maintained and lit the signal lamps of stations and trains, a post essential to railway safety before signalling was generally electrified in the 20th century.

lancier.label: Lancier (lance maker)
lancier.summary: Craftsman who made lances and other polearms.
lancier.text: The lancier made lances, pikes and other polearms for arming troops, a craft of medieval and early modern armoury that was gradually supplanted by firearms.

landamann.label: Landamann (Swiss cantonal chief magistrate)
landamann.summary: Elected head of the government of a Swiss canton.
landamann.text: The landamann (Landammann) presided over the government of certain Swiss cantons, notably in German-speaking Switzerland and in neighbouring French-speaking cantons, a title still used today in some cantons to designate the president of the cantonal Council of State.

landjaeger.label: Rural policeman (Landjäger)
landjaeger.summary: Member of a rural police force, especially in Württemberg and in Swiss cantons.
landjaeger.text: The Landjäger belongs to a militarily organised corps responsible for public security in the countryside: patrolling roads and markets, pursuing vagrants and thieves, escorting prisoners. The term is attested above all for 19th-century Württemberg, several Swiss cantons and the Prussian Landjägerei from 1920 to 1934; in other states the corresponding force was called gendarmerie or Landreiter.

laneficier.label: Laneficier (wool worker, wool merchant)
laneficier.summary: Professional specialised in working and trading wool.
laneficier.text: The laneficier, from the Latin lanificium (wool work), denoted a professional of the wool industry, from trading the raw material to producing cloth. Lanificier is an equivalent variant of the term.

langueyeur.label: Langueyeur (pig tongue inspector)
langueyeur.summary: Health inspector who examined pigs' tongues to detect measles.
langueyeur.text: The langueyeur examined the tongues of pigs before slaughter or sale in order to detect "ladrerie" (pork measles, or cysticercosis), a parasitic disease transmissible to humans. This public health role is attested in livestock markets since the Middle Ages.

lanspessade.label: Lanspessade (lance-corporal)
lanspessade.summary: Junior military rank, an old variant of "anspessade".
lanspessade.text: The lanspessade was a junior military rank in the Ancien Régime infantry, between the private soldier and the corporal, more commonly spelt anspessade, a term borrowed from the Italian lancia spezzata.

lanternier.label: Lanternier (lantern maker)
lanternier.summary: Craftsman who made lanterns and portable lighting.
lanternier.text: The lanternier made lanterns in metal, glass or horn for portable or domestic lighting, a craft close to tinsmithing and copperware ("dinanderie").

lanternier_de_corne.label: Lanternier de corne (horn lantern maker)
lanternier_de_corne.summary: Maker of lanterns using thinned sheets of horn as panes.
lanternier_de_corne.text: The lanternier de corne made lanterns whose translucent sides were thin strips of animal horn, scraped and polished, an inexpensive alternative to glass already in use in Antiquity. The trade was organised into a guild in the Middle Ages, alongside the horners ("corniers") and comb makers ("peigniers"), other craftsmen who worked horn.

lapicide.label: Lapicide (stone carver)
lapicide.summary: Craftsman specialised in cutting and engraving stone.
lapicide.text: The lapicide (from the Latin lapicida) cut and engraved stone, notably for funerary and monumental inscriptions, a more learned and rarer term than "tailleur de pierre" (stonecutter) in everyday records.

lapidaire.label: Lapidaire (lapidary)
lapidaire.summary: Craftsman and merchant specialised in cutting and selling precious stones.
lapidaire.text: The lapidaire cut, polished and faceted precious and semi-precious stones for jewellery, an activity distinct from working building stone despite the shared Latin root (lapis, stone).

laptot.label: Laptot (African boatman, porter)
laptot.summary: Indigenous worker in the French colonies of Africa employed as a canoeman or porter.
laptot.text: The laptot was an indigenous worker engaged in the French trading posts and colonies of West Africa (Senegal in particular), employed as a canoeman, porter or labourer in the service of colonial trade and the navy; the term is of Wolof origin.

laquais.label: Laquais (footman, lackey)
laquais.summary: Liveried servant who accompanied his master on foot when he went out.
laquais.text: The laquais was a valet in livery whose duty was to accompany his master on foot or at the back of a carriage, to open doors and to perform various tasks of display, a post characteristic of domestic service in noble and bourgeois households under the Ancien Régime.

laqueur.label: Laqueur (lacquerer)
laqueur.summary: Cabinetmaking worker who applied and polished decorative lacquer on furniture.
laqueur.text: The laqueur applied coats of lacquer to furniture, panelling or objets d'art, imitating the Far Eastern lacquers that were highly fashionable in Europe in the 17th and 18th centuries, a specialised skill of luxury cabinetmaking.

lardeur.label: Lardeur (bacon curer)
lardeur.summary: Specialist in preparing and processing bacon fat and pork.
lardeur.text: The lardeur prepared and processed bacon fat ("lard"), an essential raw material of traditional pork butchery, an activity closely linked to that of the charcutier and the lardier.

lardier.label: Lardier (bacon curer)
lardier.summary: Craftsman specialised in processing and preserving pork fat.
lardier.text: The lardier salted, smoked or preserved pork fat ("lard"), a staple food of the French countryside before the rise of industrial charcuterie, an activity close to that of the lardeur.

lattier.label: Lattier (lath maker)
lattier.summary: Maker of split-wood laths and stakes for building and roofing.
lattier.text: The lattier split and cut wooden laths for roof framing, for roofing (as a support for tiles or slates) or for fences, a forest craft based on cleaving rather than sawing.

lauseur.label: Lauseur (stone-slab roofer)
lauseur.summary: Roofer specialised in laying lauzes, flat roofing stones.
lauseur.text: The lauseur laid lauzes, flat stones (limestone, schist or sandstone depending on the region) used in traditional roofing, a technique characteristic of certain regions such as the Quercy, the Aveyron or the Dordogne.

lavandier.label: Lavandier (scullion, kitchen washer)
lavandier.summary: Kitchen servant in a noble or royal household who washed the dishes.
lavandier.text: The lavandier washed the dishes and kitchen linen in great households and seigneurial or royal courts, a male domestic post distinct from the lavandière, who washed private individuals' linen at the wash-house.

lavandiere.label: Lavandière (washerwoman)
lavandiere.summary: Woman who washed linen at the wash-house for private individuals or establishments.
lavandiere.text: The lavandière washed, rinsed and wrung out linen, often at the municipal wash-house or on the bank of a river, arduous physical work generally done by women of humble condition until the washing machine became widespread in the 20th century. Lessiveuse and laveuse are common synonyms.

laveur.label: Laveur (ore washer)
laveur.summary: Mine worker who sorted and cleaned raw ore.
laveur.text: The laveur washed and sorted the extracted ore to separate it from the barren gangue, an operation carried out after extraction in the ore-processing installations of metal or coal mines.

lavier.label: Lavier (lava-stone roofer)
lavier.summary: Roofer who used lava stones to cover roofs.
lavier.text: The lavier covered roofs with volcanic lava stones, a material characteristic of certain parts of the Auvergne, a technique similar to that of the lauseur but using stone of a different origin.

lavrante.label: Lavrante (goldsmith-craftsman)
lavrante.summary: Goldsmith who worked and decorated pieces of gold or silver.
lavrante.text: The lavrante is a goldsmith who works and decorates precious metals — chasing, engraving or composing ornaments — to produce jewellery and goldsmith's pieces. The term, frequent in documents from northern Portugal, mainly denotes the craftsman who does the handwork, as opposed to the goldsmith who owned the shop and sold the pieces.

layeteur.label: Layeteur (box maker)
layeteur.summary: Maker of small boxes, chests and wooden packing cases.
layeteur.text: The layeteur made "layettes" — small crates and caskets of light wood — as well as various packing cases and chests, a box-making craft related to light joinery. Layetier is a spelling variant.

lego.label: Lego (Spanish lay brother)
lego.summary: Professed religious who did not receive holy orders and handled the convent's material tasks.
lego.text: The lego or lay brother belonged to a religious order but was not a priest: he took care of the kitchen, the gatehouse, the garden, alms-collecting or other manual work of the convent. In records he often appears as "fray" followed by "lego" to distinguish him from the choir religious.

leibeigener.label: Serf (Leibeigener)
leibeigener.summary: Peasant in personal bondage to a lord, tied to farm and soil.
leibeigener.text: The Leibeigener is personally dependent on a lord: he could not leave the farm without permission, needed the lord's consent to marry and owed dues such as the heriot (Besthaupt) at death. The forms and severity of serfdom varied greatly by region; in Westphalia one speaks of Eigenbehörige, in eastern Germany of Erbuntertanen. Serfdom was abolished in most German states in the late 18th and early 19th centuries.

leichenfrau.label: Layer-out of the dead (Leichenfrau)
leichenfrau.summary: Woman who washed, dressed and laid out the dead and often announced the death.
leichenfrau.text: The Leichenfrau is called at a death to wash, dress and lay out the deceased; in many places she announced the death in the neighbourhood, invited people to the funeral and kept the wake. The task was usually performed by older women or widows for a small fee, sometimes on behalf of the community or parish, and in Bavaria and Tyrol was also called Seelnonne.

lekarz.label: Lekarz (physician)
lekarz.text: The lekarz was a graduate of medical studies, entitled to treat internal diseases, unlike the barber-surgeon and the feldsher, who mainly performed procedures. In old Poland physicians were few and lived mostly in towns and at noble courts; in the nineteenth century they were employed as district and town doctors.

lenandier.label: Lenandier (linen draper)
lenandier.summary: Merchant specialised in selling linen fabrics and goods.
lenandier.text: The lenandier traded in linen fabrics and the goods made from them (household linen, cloth), a regional term of the textile trade.

lesteur.label: Lesteur (ballast loader)
lesteur.summary: Worker who loaded ballast into ships to keep them stable.
lesteur.text: The lesteur loaded and unloaded ballast (sand, stones, gravel) in ships' holds to ensure their stability and proper trim at sea, especially when the ship was sailing without cargo.

leveur.label: Leveur (charcoal-wood stacker)
leveur.summary: Charcoal burner who stacked charcoal wood into cords before it was handled by the dresseur.
leveur.text: The leveur was a charcoal burner who stacked the wood intended for making charcoal into cords, before it was used by the "dresseur".

leveur_charbonnier.label: Leveur (coal-mine haulier)
leveur_charbonnier.summary: Worker who extracted coal and brought it up from the bottom of the mine.
leveur_charbonnier.text: In the vocabulary of the coalfields, the leveur took part in extracting coal and bringing it up from the underground galleries to the surface, a generic term close to "haveur" (hewer) or "hercheur" (haulier).

leveur_de_liege.label: Leveur de liège (cork stripper)
leveur_de_liege.summary: Worker specialised in harvesting the bark of the cork oak.
leveur_de_liege.text: The leveur de liège stripped the bark of the cork oak by cutting into it, following a periodic harvesting cycle (every 9 to 12 years), a craft activity of cork-producing regions such as the Landes or Corsica.

leveur_dentelles.label: Leveur (lace worker)
leveur_dentelles.summary: Craftsman specialised in making and mending lace.
leveur_dentelles.text: In the lace industry, the leveur worked at lifting the threads on the loom or at finishing and mending pieces of lace, a term found in regions with a lace-making tradition such as Le Puy-en-Velay or Calais.

leveuse.label: Leveuse (female porter)
leveuse.summary: Woman employed to lift and carry various loads at work.
leveuse.text: The leveuse carried out handling tasks — lifting and carrying loads — in various industrial or craft settings, a generic term for an unskilled female worker assigned to this kind of physical work.

libraire.label: Libraire
libraire.text: Le libraire vend, et anciennement louait également, des livres, un métier lié de près à l'imprimerie et à l'édition.

libraire_editeur.label: Libraire-éditeur (bookseller and publisher)
libraire_editeur.summary: Book professional who combined publishing and selling.
libraire_editeur.text: The libraire-éditeur handled both the publication (printing, financing) and the sale of books, a combination of activities that was very common before the modern separation of publishing and bookselling, characteristic of the book trade under the Ancien Régime and in the 19th century.

licenciado.label: Licenciado (Spanish licentiate)
licenciado.summary: Holder of the university degree of licentiate, a title placed before the name in Spanish documents.
licenciado.text: The licenciado had obtained from a university the licentiate degree, between the bachelor's degree and the doctorate, which qualified him for professions such as law or medicine. In documents from the 16th to the 19th century the title precedes the name ("el licenciado…"), sometimes abbreviated "Ldo." or "Lic.", and usually indicates a lawyer, a physician or an educated cleric.

licheur_de_couleurs.label: Licheur de couleurs (colour preparer)
licheur_de_couleurs.summary: Craftsman specialised in preparing and applying decorative colours.
licheur_de_couleurs.text: The licheur de couleurs prepared and applied colours and pigments for decorative or artistic purposes, a rare term found in certain art-craft workshops.

liegeur.label: Liégeur (cork worker)
liegeur.summary: Craftsman who worked cork, a regional variant of the cork maker.
liegeur.text: The liégeur worked cork to make stoppers or other objects, a regional variant of the term "bouchonnier" (cork maker), an activity concentrated in producing regions such as the Landes, Corsica or Roussillon.

lieutenant.label: Lieutenant (lieutenant, deputy officer)
lieutenant.summary: Junior military officer, or deputy to a civil or judicial officer.
lieutenant.text: The term lieutenant denotes both a junior military rank (the captain's assistant) and a civil or judicial deputy assisting a senior officer (bailiff, seneschal, judge), the word coming from the Latin locum tenens, "one who holds the place of". Many Ancien Régime offices derive from it: lieutenant de louveterie, lieutenant criminel, lieutenant des charrois, and so on.

lieutenant_criminel_de_robe_courte.label: Lieutenant criminel de robe courte (criminal lieutenant of the short robe)
lieutenant_criminel_de_robe_courte.summary: Ancien Régime law officer specialised in suppressing crime and carrying out sentences.
lieutenant_criminel_de_robe_courte.text: The lieutenant criminel de robe courte investigated criminal cases and arrested wrongdoers, the "short robe" (as opposed to the long robe of the court magistrates) indicating a role that was more executive than strictly judicial, close to that of a police officer.

lieutenant_d_ordre.label: Lieutenant d'ordre (lieutenant of order)
lieutenant_d_ordre.summary: Officer responsible for maintaining order and public discipline.
lieutenant_d_ordre.text: The lieutenant d'ordre assisted a senior military or administrative officer in maintaining public order and discipline, a generic title covering various subordinate police offices of the Ancien Régime.

lieutenant_de_louveterie.label: Lieutenant de louveterie (wolf-hunting officer)
lieutenant_de_louveterie.summary: Royal officer responsible for destroying wolves and vermin.
lieutenant_de_louveterie.text: The lieutenant de louveterie organised and led hunts for wolves and other vermin in his district, an office instituted under the Ancien Régime, abolished at the Revolution, re-established by Napoleon I in 1814 and still in existence today on a voluntary basis.

lieutenant_des_charrois.label: Lieutenant des charrois (lieutenant of carriage)
lieutenant_des_charrois.summary: Officer responsible for organising and supervising transport by cart.
lieutenant_des_charrois.text: The lieutenant des charrois supervised the organisation of overland transport by carts and wagons, notably in the service of the armies or the royal administration, a logistical office of the Ancien Régime.

lieutenant_en_justice.label: Lieutenant en justice (deputy judge)
lieutenant_en_justice.summary: Deputy magistrate exercising judicial functions under the authority of a principal judge.
lieutenant_en_justice.text: The lieutenant en justice assisted a titular judge (bailiff, seneschal, provost) in the exercise of his judicial functions, ensuring the continuity of local justice in his absence or in addition to his work.

liftier.label: Liftier (lift attendant)
liftier.summary: Employee who operated and looked after a lift.
liftier.text: The liftier operated the lift car by hand and welcomed its users, a job that appeared with the spread of lifts in department stores and large buildings at the end of the 19th century and gradually disappeared as lifts became automatic.

ligneur.label: Ligneur (fishing-line maker)
ligneur.summary: Craftsman who made fishing lines and fine cords.
ligneur.text: The ligneur made fishing lines and fine cords braided from plant fibres, a rope-making craft applied to fishing tackle. Lignotier is a spelling variant.

ligotier.label: Ligotier (tie maker)
ligotier.summary: Craftsman specialised in making ties and cords for fastening.
ligotier.text: The ligotier made ties and cords for tying loads, livestock or bundles of firewood. The word comes from "ligot" (tie, cord), from Gascon or Provençal, itself from the Latin ligare (to bind) — a term close to but distinct from ligneur, which refers to the maker of fishing lines.

limeur.label: Limeur (filer)
limeur.summary: Craftsman specialised in filing and sharpening metal tools.
limeur.text: The limeur worked metal with a file to fit, deburr or sharpen it, an essential finishing operation in craft metalworking and locksmithing.

limeur_de_platines.label: Limeur de platines (plate filer)
limeur_de_platines.summary: Craftsman specialised in finishing watch plates and precision mechanisms.
limeur_de_platines.text: The limeur de platines fitted the plates (the metal plates that carry the wheel train) of watches and clocks to a tenth of a millimetre, a fine speciality of watchmaking that demanded great manual precision.

limonadier.label: Limonadier (lemonade seller, café keeper)
limonadier.summary: Merchant who made and sold lemonades and refreshing drinks.
limonadier.text: The limonadier made and sold lemonades and other refreshing drinks, an activity that in the 18th and 19th centuries extended to running cafés and drinking establishments, the term then becoming almost synonymous with "cafetier" (café owner).

limousin.label: Limousin (migrant mason)
limousin.summary: Mason from the Limousin who worked as a seasonal migrant.
limousin.text: By regional metonymy, limousin denoted a mason from the Limousin (and from the Creuse in particular) who migrated seasonally to Paris and other large cities to work on building sites, a tradition of labour migration well documented from the 18th to the 20th century.

lingere.label: Lingère (linen maid, seamstress)
lingere.summary: Female merchant or craftswoman specialised in selling and caring for linen.
lingere.text: The lingère sold, made or looked after household linen and underwear, an activity that, depending on the case, covered commercial functions (lingère marchande) or craft sewing work (lingère couturière).

lingere_couturiere.label: Lingère couturière (linen seamstress)
lingere_couturiere.summary: Seamstress specialised in making and mending household and church linen.
lingere_couturiere.text: The lingère couturière made and mended household linen, underwear and sometimes liturgical linen, a fine sewing activity distinct from dressmaking proper.

lingere_marchande.label: Lingère marchande (linen merchant)
lingere_marchande.summary: Female merchant specialised in selling fine fabrics, lace and lingerie.
lingere_marchande.text: The lingère marchande traded in fine fabrics, lace and lingerie, an activity belonging to the luxury textile trade rather than to garment making itself.

linier.label: Linier (linen merchant or maker)
linier.summary: Merchant or manufacturer specialised in linen fabrics.
linier.text: The linier traded in or made linen fabrics and their derivatives, an activity linked to flax growing, which was important in regions such as Normandy, Brittany and Flanders.

linotier.label: Linotier (flax worker)
linotier.summary: Worker specialised in working and processing textile flax.
linotier.text: The linotier worked flax through its various stages of processing (retting, scutching, spinning), a traditional rural craft of the flax-producing regions.

linotypiste.label: Linotypiste (linotype operator)
linotypiste.summary: Print worker who set texts using the linotype machine.
linotypiste.text: The linotypiste set texts for printing on a linotype, a machine invented in 1884 that mechanically cast whole lines of lead type, revolutionising typesetting until the advent of phototypesetting in the 20th century.

liquoriste.label: Liquoriste (liqueur maker)
liquoriste.summary: Manufacturer specialised in producing liqueurs and fine spirits.
liquoriste.text: The liquoriste made liqueurs and flavoured spirits, distinct from the plain brandies produced by the home distiller ("bouilleur de cru"), a craft and commercial activity that would give rise to the great liqueur houses of the 19th century. Licoriste is an equivalent old spelling.

liseur_de_dessins.label: Liseur de dessins (pattern reader)
liseur_de_dessins.summary: Textile worker who guided the setting up of looms according to the desired patterns.
liseur_de_dessins.text: The pattern reader (liseuse de dessins) deciphered the design of a weaving pattern and guided the mounting of the threads on the loom accordingly, a role essential to the Lyon silk industry before the automation brought by the Jacquard loom.

lisseur_peaux.label: Lisseur de peaux (hide smoother)
lisseur_peaux.summary: Tannery worker specialised in smoothing tanned hides.
lisseur_peaux.text: The lisseur de peaux cut and smoothed tanned hides along the animal's backbone to prepare them for sale or processing, a finishing operation in the tanning process.

lisseur_repasseur.label: Lisseur-repasseur (presser, ironer)
lisseur_repasseur.summary: Craftsman specialised in smoothing and ironing textiles.
lisseur_repasseur.text: The lisseur-repasseur smoothed and ironed fabrics and garments, a regional variant of the ironer's trade ("repasseur"), a term found notably in the vocabulary of laundering and garment making.

lissier.label: Lissier (heddle maker)
lissier.summary: Maker of heddles, equipment for looms.
lissier.text: The lissier made heddles, frames fitted with vertical threads that separate the warp threads on a loom, a supply craft for the textile industry.

lithographe.label: Lithographe (lithographer)
lithographe.summary: Artist or engraver specialised in the technique of lithography on stone.
lithographe.text: The lithographe drew with ink or greasy crayon on a limestone slab, exploiting the repulsion between grease and water to print the image in several copies, a process invented by Senefelder in 1796 and widely used for posters and illustration in the 19th century.

livreur.label: Livreur (delivery man)
livreur.summary: Person who delivered goods or parcels to homes or shops.
livreur.text: The livreur carried and handed over ordered goods, on foot, by bicycle, by cart and later by motor vehicle depending on the period, an essential commercial function linked to the development of distance selling and urban trade.

livreur_de_bains.label: Livreur de bains (bath deliverer)
livreur_de_bains.summary: Tradesman who delivered baths and hot water to homes before public baths became widespread.
livreur_de_bains.text: The livreur de bains brought a portable bathtub and the necessary hot water to people's homes, an urban service common in the 19th century before public baths and later private bathrooms became widespread.

livreur_jure.label: Livreur juré (sworn deliverer)
livreur_jure.summary: Deliverer who had taken the guild oath and obtained the mastership of his trade.
livreur_jure.text: Under the Ancien Régime guild system, the livreur juré had taken an oath before his guild and obtained the title of master, a status that gave him certain rights and responsibilities in carrying on his delivery trade.

lizzatore.label: Lizzatore (marble sledge worker)
lizzatore.summary: Worker in the Apuan marble quarries who lowered blocks downhill on a wooden sledge (lizza).
lizzatore.text: In the quarries of Carrara and the Apuan Alps, the lizzatore brought marble blocks down the steep slopes on a wooden sledge called a lizza, which slid over soaped beams and was held back by ropes wound around wooden posts. One of the most dangerous jobs in the quarries, it was practised until the mid-20th century.

locatier.label: Locatier (tenant farmer)
locatier.summary: Peasant of the Massif Central who farmed leased land.
locatier.text: The locatier leased land and farmed it according to local custom, a tenancy status widespread in the Massif Central (Rouergue, Auvergne), comparable to the sharecropper ("métayer") but with terms of payment that varied from region to region.

lombard.label: Lombard (moneylender, pawnbroker)
lombard.text: The lombard was a banker or pawnbroker from northern Italy (Lombardy) who settled in French towns from the Middle Ages onwards to practise lending and money-changing, activities then forbidden to Christians by the Church. The term gave its name to the rue des Lombards in Paris and to the modern expression "crédit lombard" (Lombard loan).

lormier.label: Lormier (loriner, bit maker)
lormier.summary: Craftsman who made metal riding equipment: bits, stirrups, spurs.
lormier.text: The lormier made the metal parts of horse harness — bits, stirrups, spurs, buckles — a craft organised as a guild (the "lormerie") in Paris from the Middle Ages, closely linked to the work of the saddler and the spur maker.

lotero.label: Lotero (Spanish lottery seller)
lotero.summary: Seller of lottery tickets or keeper of a Spanish lottery office.
lotero.text: The lotero sold tickets and shares in the lottery, established in Spain as a state revenue in the 18th century and extended with the National Lottery from 1811. Some worked in a lottery office with fixed premises, others sold tickets in the streets.

louager.label: Louager (horse and carriage hirer)
louager.summary: Businessman who hired out horses and carts, forerunner of the car hire firm.
louager.text: The louager hired out horses, carts and horse-drawn carriages, a commercial activity that was the direct ancestor of modern vehicle hire, carried on notably in staging towns and large cities.

louageur_de_voitures.label: Louageur de voitures (carriage hirer)
louageur_de_voitures.summary: Person who hired out horses and carts.
louageur_de_voitures.text: The louageur de voitures hired out horses and carts, the old equivalent of today's car hire firm.

loueur_de_cabine.label: Loueur de cabine (bathing-hut hirer)
loueur_de_cabine.summary: Businessman who hired out sea-bathing huts in the early 20th century.
loueur_de_cabine.text: The loueur de cabine hired out bathing huts, sometimes horse-drawn, which allowed bathers to change and reach the sea, an activity typical of the budding seaside tourism of the Belle Époque.

loueur_de_carrosses.label: Loueur de carrosses (coach hirer)
loueur_de_carrosses.summary: Businessman who hired out luxury carriages, with or without horses and coachmen.
loueur_de_carrosses.text: The loueur de carrosses hired out luxury horse-drawn carriages, with or without a team and staff, for ceremonies, journeys or travel around town by well-off people who did not keep their own equipage.

louvetier.label: Louvetier (wolf hunter)
louvetier.summary: Professional hunter or officer of a hunt specialised in wolf hunting.
louvetier.text: The louvetier led or took part in a wolf hunt, the organised destruction of a predator considered harmful to livestock, a role close to that of the lieutenant de louveterie but which could denote a professional hunter rather than a titled officer.

luiselier.label: Luiselier (coffin maker)
luiselier.summary: Maker of coffins, from the old word "luisel", which originally meant a shroud.
luiselier.text: The luiselier made coffins, a craft close to joinery. The word derives from the Old French "luisel", itself from the Latin linteolum (small cloth, linen), which originally meant a shroud before the meaning shifted to the coffin that encloses it.

luminier.label: Luminier (church lighting keeper)
luminier.summary: Person responsible for maintaining church lighting and liturgical supplies.
luminier.text: The luminier looked after the candles, lamps and other lighting of a church and managed the supply of wax and other materials needed for worship, a charge often entrusted to a churchwarden ("fabricien") or a parish employee.

lunetier.label: Lunetier (spectacle maker)
lunetier.summary: Optician craftsman who made and sold spectacles and optical instruments.
lunetier.text: The lunetier made and sold corrective spectacles and other optical instruments, a trade that developed from the 13th century onwards and gradually became a true optician's profession from the 19th century.

lupinaire.label: Lupinaire (lupin seller)
lupinaire.summary: Merchant specialised in selling lupins, a legume grown in the south of France.
lupinaire.text: The lupinaire sold lupin seeds, a legume formerly eaten as a popular snack after soaking in brine, a crop widespread in the southern regions of France.

luthier.label: Luthier (stringed-instrument maker)
luthier.summary: Craftsman who made stringed musical instruments.
luthier.text: The luthier made and repaired stringed instruments — violins, cellos, violas, guitars — an art craft associated in France with renowned centres such as Mirecourt in the Vosges, where instrument making developed from the 17th century onwards.

luzny.label: Luźny (unattached labourer)
luzny.summary: Person without a fixed home or employment, hiring out for casual work.
luzny.text: The luźni (also hultaje) were people in the old Commonwealth not attached to any farm or lord, without a fixed home, hiring themselves out for seasonal work in the country and in towns. The law regarded them with suspicion and repeatedly ordered them to settle or take permanent employment.

macaire.label: Macaire (cattle owner, dairy farmer)
macaire.summary: Owner of a herd of cattle, and by extension a milk and cheese producer.
macaire.text: The macaire owned a herd of cattle, a term extended to the milk and cheese production that resulted from it. The word thus covers both the status of livestock owner and the activity of processing milk.

maccaronaro.label: Maccaronaro (street macaroni seller)
maccaronaro.summary: In Naples, a street seller of cooked macaroni.
maccaronaro.text: The maccaronaro boiled macaroni in large cauldrons in the open air and sold them in the street, dressed with cheese or sauce, to working-class customers who ate them with their hands. A characteristic figure of Neapolitan street life in the 18th and 19th centuries, he was widely depicted by painters and photographers.

macon.label: Maçon (mason)
macon.summary: Building craftsman who built walls and structures in stone or masonry materials.
macon.text: The maçon built and maintained walls and buildings in stone, rubble, brick or cob, one of the oldest building trades and one of the most frequent in civil registers. Some regions, such as the Limousin or the Creuse, specialised in supplying migrant masons to the large cities.

maculaire.label: Maculaire (coal retail clerk)
maculaire.summary: Belgian employee responsible for the retail sale of coal at collieries.
maculaire.text: The maculaire supervised and managed the retail sale of the coal extracted at a colliery, a commercial role in Belgian mining, distinct from the extraction posts proper.

madreur.label: Madreur (vat stirrer)
madreur.summary: Worker who stirred the mixtures in vats in paper mills and soap works.
madreur.text: The madreur stirred and mixed the materials in vats in paper mills (paper pulp) or soap works (soap paste), an intermediate operation in craft-based industrial manufacturing.

maelzer.label: Maltster (Mälzer)
maelzer.summary: Craftsman who germinated and kiln-dried barley to make malt for brewers and distillers.
maelzer.text: The Mälzer steeps barley (more rarely wheat), lets it germinate on the malting floor, turns the sprouting grain regularly and then dries it on the kiln, producing malt, the raw material of beer and grain spirits. Malting was long part of the brewer's trade; with the growth of breweries in the 19th century separate maltings with specialised workers appeared.

maestra_de_amiga.label: Maestra de amiga (Spanish dame-school teacher)
maestra_de_amiga.summary: Woman who taught young girls to read, pray and sew in her home.
maestra_de_amiga.text: The maestra de amiga, or simply "amiga", took young girls and small children into her home to teach them Christian doctrine, reading and, for the girls, needlework, in return for a small fee from the families. These home schools were common in Spanish towns from the 17th to the 19th century, before public schooling spread.

magasinier_des_sels.label: Magasinier des sels (salt warehouse keeper)
magasinier_des_sels.summary: Royal official responsible for guarding and running the salt warehouses.
magasinier_des_sels.text: The magasinier des sels kept and managed the "grenier à sel", the royal warehouse where salt had compulsorily to be bought under the gabelle, the indirect tax emblematic of Ancien Régime taxation, abolished in 1790.

magister.label: Magister (village schoolmaster)
magister.summary: Schoolmaster providing elementary teaching before the modern state school was established.
magister.text: The magister taught reading, writing and arithmetic in the parish or village schools of the Ancien Régime, often combining this role with that of cantor or sexton for lack of sufficient pay. He was the direct predecessor of the "instituteur" (primary teacher) created by the school laws of the 19th century.

magistere.label: Magistère (teaching office, magisterium)
magistere.summary: Higher teaching office or dignity within a religious or academic institution.
magistere.text: The magistère denoted a high-level teaching office or an honorary dignity within a religious institution (order, chapter) or an academic one, often implying recognised doctrinal or teaching authority.

magnanarelle.label: Magnanarelle (silkworm rearer)
magnanarelle.summary: Woman who reared silkworms, notably in the Cévennes.
magnanarelle.text: The magnanarelle reared silkworms in a "magnanerie" (silkworm house), overseeing their feeding on mulberry leaves until they formed the cocoons destined for the spinning mill, a women's activity characteristic of the Cévennes and other silk-producing regions of southern France in the 18th and 19th centuries.

magnien.label: Magnien (itinerant tinker)
magnien.summary: Itinerant coppersmith, often from the Auvergne, who repaired copper utensils.
magnien.text: The magnien repaired and tinned copper and pewter utensils from village to village, an itinerant craft traditionally associated with the mountain people of the Auvergne and the Limousin. Magnin and maignan are dialect variants very common in old records.

mailleur.label: Mailleur (net maker)
mailleur.summary: Craftsman specialised in making meshwork and nets.
mailleur.text: The mailleur made meshwork — nets, hairnets, braided cords — a craft close to that of the laceur, applied notably to fishing and net-making.

maillocheur.label: Maillocheur (flail thresher)
maillocheur.summary: Thresher of cereals using the traditional flail.
maillocheur.text: The maillocheur threshed cereals with a flail (the "mailloche" or "maillot") to separate the grain from the ear, a manual threshing technique gradually replaced by the mechanical threshing machine from the 19th century onwards.

maioral.label: Maioral (head herdsman, southern Portugal)
maioral.summary: Head of the shepherds or herdsmen of a flock or herd on a large estate of southern Portugal.
maioral.text: The maioral is responsible for a flock of sheep, a drove of pigs or a herd of cattle or horses, and for the shepherds and helpers who guard it, on the estates of the Alentejo and Ribatejo. He reports to the owner or the steward. The rabadão and the helpers work under his orders.

maire.label: Maire (mayor)
maire.summary: Elected chief magistrate of a commune, responsible for municipal administration and civil registration.
maire.text: The maire is the chief magistrate of the commune, at once an agent of the State (registrar of civil status and officer of the judicial police) and the executive of the municipal council. The office, established in its modern form by the French Revolution in 1789, very often appears in civil registers as signatory or informant. Before 1789, comparable municipal functions existed under other titles (consul, échevin, syndic) depending on the region. The title "bourgmestre" denotes the same office in regions and countries where that name has survived: Belgium, the Netherlands, German-speaking Switzerland and certain border areas of northern France.

mairenier.label: Mairenier (timber merchant, carpenter)
mairenier.summary: Timber merchant or carpenter, from the Old French "mairien", building timber.
mairenier.text: In Old French, the mairenier was either a merchant of building timber or the carpenter himself — the two meanings coexist depending on the text. The word derives from "mairien", meaning building timber, and was also used as a verb meaning to build in wood or to split stave wood ("merrain", cooperage timber). It is attested in Frédéric Godefroy's dictionary of Old French. The variant mairineur is probably a late misspelling of it.

maiselier.label: Maiselier (wooden vessel maker)
maiselier.summary: Woodworker who made household vessels and utensils (kneading troughs, bread bins).
maiselier.text: The maiselier, also spelt maselier, was a woodworker who made household containers — "mases", bread bins ("huches"), various vessels — for domestic use, as distinct from the cooper, who worked on hooped pieces. The term is rare and is found mainly in old regional records.

maisonnier.label: Maisonnier (house steward)
maisonnier.summary: Servant or steward responsible for the day-to-day running of a bourgeois or noble house.
maisonnier.text: The maisonnier was a senior servant, or steward, responsible for the management of a household: running the staff, the provisions and the upkeep of the house on behalf of a bourgeois or noble master. Depending on the region, the term could also denote a sharecropper occupying a house on a landowner's estate.

maitre.label: Maître (master craftsman)
maitre.summary: Title of a craftsman who had completed his apprenticeship and masterpiece and could keep his own shop.
maitre.text: Under the Ancien Régime guild system, the title of maître was granted on the successful completion of a masterpiece after an apprenticeship and often a period as a journeyman. Only the master could open a shop in his own name, employ journeymen and train apprentices, as opposed to the mere worker or journeyman. In records the word very often precedes the name of a trade (maître boulanger, maître menuisier, etc.), indicating this status rather than an occupation in itself.

maitre_a_danser.label: Maître à danser (dancing master)
maitre_a_danser.summary: Teacher of dance and deportment who taught steps and good manners to the nobility.
maitre_a_danser.text: The maître à danser taught court dances and bodily deportment, skills considered indispensable to the education of the nobility and the bourgeoisie under the Ancien Régime. He often also worked as a fencing or music master, the polite accomplishments being grouped together in a single course of instruction.

maitre_boucher.label: Maître boucher (master butcher)
maitre_boucher.summary: Butcher who had attained mastership, entitled to keep a stall and train apprentices.
maitre_boucher.text: The maître boucher had completed his apprenticeship and, in towns with guilds, his masterpiece, which allowed him to keep a shop and to slaughter and cut up meat in his own name. Butchery was a powerful and regulated guild, often passed down from father to son.

maitre_boulanger.label: Maître boulanger (master baker)
maitre_boulanger.summary: Master of the baker's trade, entitled to run a bakehouse and shop in his own name.
maitre_boulanger.text: The maître boulanger had met the requirements of the bakers' guild (apprenticeship, journeyman years, masterpiece) and could run his own bakehouse. The baker's trade, strictly regulated under the Ancien Régime (price and weight of bread), appears very frequently in urban civil registers.

maitre_charpentier.label: Maître charpentier (master carpenter)
maitre_charpentier.summary: Master of the carpenter's craft, directing a building site and journeymen.
maitre_charpentier.text: The maître charpentier directed carpentry works — building frames, roof structures, or ships depending on the region — and supervised journeymen and apprentices. Carpentry, an old and well-organised guild, drew a clear distinction between the master, who alone could enter into contracts, and the ordinary wage-earning carpenter.

maitre_chirurgien.label: Maître chirurgien (master surgeon)
maitre_chirurgien.summary: Surgeon who had obtained mastership, authorised to practise and to train apprentices.
maitre_chirurgien.text: The maître chirurgien had served an apprenticeship and then passed an examination before the surgeons' guild (separate from that of the physicians until the 18th century), which authorised him to practise and open a shop. Surgery, long regarded as a manual craft close to barbering, only drew closer to learned medicine from the Enlightenment onwards.

maitre_coureur.label: Maître coureur (master courier)
maitre_coureur.summary: Person responsible for carrying messages and dispatches between localities, forerunner of the postal service.
maitre_coureur.text: The maître coureur was responsible for carrying messages and dispatches between localities before the royal postal service was organised. He sometimes announced his arrival with a horn, which may explain the origin of the term "coureur" (runner).

maitre_couvreur.label: Maître couvreur (master roofer)
maitre_couvreur.summary: Master of the roofer's trade, directing the laying of roofs (tile, slate, thatch).
maitre_couvreur.text: The maître couvreur had attained mastership of the roofing trade (tile, slate or thatch depending on the region) and could direct a site in his own name. Roofing, a dangerous and technical job, often formed a separate guild, sometimes linked to that of the carpenters.

maitre_d_armes.label: Maître d'armes (fencing master)
maitre_d_armes.summary: Instructor who taught fencing and the handling of edged weapons.
maitre_d_armes.text: The maître d'armes taught fencing and the handling of edged weapons, a skill sought after by the nobility and the military under the Ancien Régime. Established in an academy or fencing hall, he could, like the dancing master, be one of the masters of the polite accomplishments taught to young gentlemen.

maitre_d_ecole.label: Maître d'école (schoolmaster)
maitre_d_ecole.summary: Ancien Régime schoolmaster, often lay or religious, who taught reading, writing and the catechism.
maitre_d_ecole.text: The maître d'école taught the village children reading, writing, arithmetic and the catechism, often alongside another role (sexton, cantor). Under the Ancien Régime, schooling was neither compulsory nor universal, and the schoolmaster frequently depended on the parish or the local lord for his pay.

maitre_d_hotel.label: Maître d'hôtel (steward of the table)
maitre_d_hotel.summary: In noble or bourgeois households, the person in charge of everything to do with the table.
maitre_d_hotel.text: In noble or bourgeois households, the maître d'hôtel was the man in charge of everything to do with the household's table: organising meals, serving and provisioning.

maitre_de_bateau.label: Maître de bateau (boatmaster)
maitre_de_bateau.summary: Master of a boat, responsible for handling it and for its crew.
maitre_de_bateau.text: The maître de bateau was the master responsible for handling a vessel, on rivers or at sea depending on the context, and for the crew that assisted him. The title is the equivalent of captain for vessels of smaller tonnage.

maitre_de_chaloupe.label: Maître de chaloupe (launch master)
maitre_de_chaloupe.summary: Master of a chaloupe, a light boat used for coastal transport or fishing.
maitre_de_chaloupe.text: The maître de chaloupe commanded a "chaloupe", a small light boat under sail or oars used for coasting, inshore fishing or serving large ships. The title belongs to the same maritime hierarchy as the boatmaster or the master fisherman.

maitre_de_courrier.label: Maître de courrier (courier master)
maitre_de_courrier.summary: Person responsible for organising the mail and messenger service at a relay.
maitre_de_courrier.text: The maître de courrier organised and supervised the carrying of mail and messages, often from a post house. The role partly overlaps with that of the postmaster, the distinction lying mainly in the scale of the service managed.

maitre_de_cuite.label: Maître de cuite (boiling master)
maitre_de_cuite.summary: Person in charge of boiling or firing in a processing industry (sugar works, salt works, glassworks).
maitre_de_cuite.text: The maître de cuite directed the boiling or firing operations in a processing industry — sugar refinery, salt works, glassworks or earthenware factory depending on the context — a delicate technical stage on which the quality of the final product depended.

maitre_de_digue.label: Maître de digue (dyke master)
maitre_de_digue.summary: Person responsible for building and maintaining the dykes that protected land and polders.
maitre_de_digue.text: The maître de digue supervised the building and upkeep of flood defences — dykes, embankments — particularly in marshland or polder regions (Flanders, the Marais Poitevin, the Camargue), where controlling the water was a precondition of farming life.

maitre_de_forges.label: Maître de forges (ironmaster)
maitre_de_forges.summary: Owner or manager of an ironworks producing cast iron and iron.
maitre_de_forges.text: The maître de forges ran a metallurgical enterprise — blast furnace and forge — producing cast iron and iron from ore. An important social figure from the Ancien Régime and above all in the industrial 19th century, he employed a large workforce and often held a position as a local notable.

maitre_de_haute_justice.label: Maître de haute justice (lord of high justice)
maitre_de_haute_justice.summary: Lord or officer holding the right to try the most serious crimes, including capital ones.
maitre_de_haute_justice.text: Under the Ancien Régime, high justice was the highest degree of seigneurial justice, empowering its holder to try crimes punishable by death or mutilation, as opposed to middle and low justice, which dealt with minor civil cases. This right, often held by the lord himself or by his judge (bailiff, seneschal), should be distinguished from the maître des hautes œuvres, the executioner who physically carried out the sentence.

maitre_de_heu.label: Maître de heu (hoy master)
maitre_de_heu.summary: Master of a heu, a type of fishing or cargo boat used in northern ports.
maitre_de_heu.text: The maître de heu commanded a "heu" (or hoy), a fishing or small coasting vessel used notably in the ports of the Channel and the North Sea. The term belongs to regional maritime vocabulary rather than to an administrative port function.

maitre_de_marais.label: Maître de marais (salt-marsh master)
maitre_de_marais.summary: Person in charge of working a salt marsh for salt production.
maitre_de_marais.text: The maître de marais ran the working of a salt marsh, organising the work of the salt makers ("sauniers") and the salt harvest according to the rhythm of the seasons. The role, common on the Atlantic coast (Guérande, the Île de Ré, and the Camargue for its southern equivalent), required good technical knowledge of how to shape the evaporation pans.

maitre_de_montagne.label: Maître de montagne (mountain works master)
maitre_de_montagne.summary: Person in charge of mining or forestry operations in mountain regions.
maitre_de_montagne.text: The maître de montagne supervised an operation in mountainous country, either mining (iron, lead, silver mines) or forestry depending on the region, a role attested notably in the Pyrenees and the Alps, where summer pasturing and the exploitation of the subsoil shaped the local economy.

maitre_de_plate.label: Maître de plate (flat-boat master)
maitre_de_plate.summary: Master of a plate, a flat-bottomed boat used on rivers, lagoons and marshes.
maitre_de_plate.text: The maître de plate commanded a "plate", a flat-bottomed boat well suited to navigation in shallow water — marshes, lagoons, rivers — such as those found in the Camargue or on coastal rivers. This nautical sense should not be confused with "plate" meaning gold or silver tableware, which has nothing to do with this trade.

maitre_de_postes.label: Maître de postes (postmaster)
maitre_de_postes.summary: Keeper of a post house who supplied fresh horses and organised the royal postal service.
maitre_de_postes.text: The maître de poste kept a relay on the great royal roads, supplying fresh horses and postilions to travellers and couriers. Often a venal and hereditary office under the Ancien Régime, it gave its holder considerable social standing; he was generally also an innkeeper or a local notable.

maitre_de_pressoir_a_huile.label: Maître de pressoir à huile (oil-press master)
maitre_de_pressoir_a_huile.summary: Person in charge of a press, running the production of oil (olive, walnut, rapeseed) depending on the region.
maitre_de_pressoir_a_huile.text: The maître de pressoir à huile ran a communal or seigneurial press, where the peasants came to have their olives, walnuts or oilseeds pressed. As the press was often a banal right (a lord's monopoly), the master who worked it might be the lessee of that right.

maitre_de_psallette.label: Maître de psallette (choir-school master)
maitre_de_psallette.summary: Music director who trained choirboys in liturgical singing in a psallette.
maitre_de_psallette.text: The maître de psallette directed the "psallette", a singing school attached to a cathedral or collegiate church, where he trained the choirboys in plainchant and liturgical music. Both a teaching and a musical role, it produced many composers who had been trained in these institutions from childhood.

maitre_des_barques.label: Maître des barques (bargemaster)
maitre_des_barques.summary: Master of a small boat providing river or coastal transport.
maitre_des_barques.text: The maître des barques commanded a "barque", a small boat used to carry goods or passengers on rivers and along the coasts, a role comparable to that of a boatman ("marinier") or master fisherman depending on the context.

maitre_des_basses_oeuvres.label: Maître des basses œuvres (nightman, cesspit emptier)
maitre_des_basses_oeuvres.summary: Term for the cesspit emptier, who cleared out privies and removed filth.
maitre_des_basses_oeuvres.text: The maître des basses œuvres was the euphemistic name given to the cesspit emptier ("vidangeur"), whose task was to clean out cesspits and carry the faecal matter out of the towns, work regarded as the vilest of all (hence "low" works). He should not be confused with the maître des hautes œuvres, the executioner of capital sentences: the two titles, built as mirror images, refer to radically different trades, one linked to urban hygiene, the other to criminal justice.

maitre_des_comptes.label: Maître des comptes (master of accounts)
maitre_des_comptes.summary: Officer of the Chambre des comptes responsible for auditing public accounts.
maitre_des_comptes.text: The maître des comptes was an officer of the Chambre des comptes, the financial court responsible for auditing the accounts of the royal accounting officers (receivers, treasurers) and ensuring the proper management of public funds. The office, venal under the Ancien Régime, placed its holder among the high-ranking officers of the robe.

maitre_des_hautes_uvres.label: Maître des hautes œuvres (executioner)
maitre_des_hautes_uvres.summary: Euphemistic name for the executioner of high works, who carried out capital sentences.
maitre_des_hautes_uvres.text: The maître des hautes œuvres was the executor of the sentences of criminal justice, responsible in particular for capital and corporal punishments. The office was hereditary in certain families (the Sansons being the most famous example) and was exercised with a highly marginalised social status despite its official character. It should not be confused with the maître des basses œuvres, who was responsible for cleaning out cesspits.

maitre_des_ponts.label: Maître des ponts (bridge master)
maitre_des_ponts.summary: Specialist in taking boats under bridges, using flettes and towing teams.
maitre_des_ponts.text: The maître des ponts organised the perilous passage of boats under the arches of bridges, where the currents were narrowed and dangerous, using "flettes" (small handling boats) and teams of haulers. The term locman, of Flemish origin, denotes a similar role in the ports and waterways of the north.

maitre_es_arts.label: Maître ès arts (Master of Arts)
maitre_es_arts.summary: University degree qualifying the holder to teach the liberal arts (grammar, philosophy, rhetoric).
maitre_es_arts.text: The maître ès arts (magister artium) held a university degree recognising the study of the liberal arts, obtained after the licence in the faculty of arts, the classic prerequisite for higher studies in theology, law or medicine. The title qualified its holder to teach these basic disciplines, notably in the colleges.

maitre_fondeur.label: Maître fondeur (master founder)
maitre_fondeur.summary: Craftsman skilled in melting and casting metals in moulds.
maitre_fondeur.text: The maître fondeur directed the melting of metals and their casting in moulds to produce bells, cannon, statues or mechanical parts according to his speciality. The trade required great technical mastery of alloys and melting temperatures.

maitre_forgeron.label: Maître forgeron (master blacksmith)
maitre_forgeron.summary: Blacksmith who had attained mastership, running a forge and training apprentices.
maitre_forgeron.text: The maître forgeron ran a forge where he shaped iron to produce the tools, weapons and metal parts needed by the rural community. A central trade of the Ancien Régime village economy, the forge was often one of the few workshops in the village, alongside the mill.

maitre_fourreur.label: Maître fourreur (master furrier)
maitre_fourreur.summary: Craftsman who prepared and worked furs for garments and trimmings.
maitre_fourreur.text: The maître fourreur prepared and shaped fur skins to make garments, linings and trimmings, a luxury craft tightly regulated by its guild under the Ancien Régime, furriery being a trade distinct from tanning.

maitre_fromager.label: Maître fromager (master cheesemaker)
maitre_fromager.summary: Craftsman skilled in making and maturing cheeses.
maitre_fromager.text: The maître fromager made and matured cheeses, a regional craft that varies greatly across France according to the milks and local traditions. The title of master, when it appears, distinguishes the recognised producer from the ordinary dairy farmer.

maitre_jure_des_ponts.label: Maître juré des ponts (sworn bridge master)
maitre_jure_des_ponts.summary: Sworn municipal officer responsible for inspecting and maintaining a town's bridges.
maitre_jure_des_ponts.text: The maître juré des ponts was a sworn ("juré") municipal officer responsible for inspecting, maintaining and repairing a town's bridges, structures of strategic importance for trade and defence.

maitre_marechal.label: Maître maréchal (master farrier)
maitre_marechal.summary: Farrier who had attained mastership, entitled to keep a forge and train apprentices.
maitre_marechal.text: The maître maréchal had passed through the stages of the farriers' guild (apprenticeship, masterpiece) and could keep a forge in his own name. As in the other trades, the title of master distinguished the master craftsman from the ordinary shoeing smith.

maitre_menuisier.label: Maître menuisier (master joiner)
maitre_menuisier.summary: Joiner who had completed his masterpiece, entitled to run a joinery workshop.
maitre_menuisier.text: The maître menuisier had completed his masterpiece before the joiners' guild and could thereafter keep a workshop and train apprentices. Joinery, distinct from carpentry (structural work) and cabinetmaking (veneered furniture), covered the making of simple furniture, doors, windows and panelling.

maitre_perruquier.label: Maître perruquier (master wigmaker)
maitre_perruquier.summary: Master of the wigmaker's craft, who made and maintained wigs.
maitre_perruquier.text: The maître perruquier made and maintained wigs, an indispensable hair accessory of male and female elegance from the 17th to the 18th century. The guild of wigmakers-barbers-bathkeepers, highly organised in the towns, declined sharply after the Revolution as the powdered wig was gradually abandoned.

maitre_serger.label: Maître serger (master serge weaver)
maitre_serger.summary: Master weaver specialised in making serge, a twilled woollen cloth.
maitre_serger.text: The maître serger wove serge, a twill-weave woollen cloth used for everyday clothing, and in that capacity ran his own loom. The term is common in regions with a woollen textile tradition (Normandy, Languedoc).

maitre_tailleur.label: Maître tailleur (master tailor)
maitre_tailleur.summary: Tailor who had attained mastership, entitled to keep a shop and train apprentices.
maitre_tailleur.text: The maître tailleur had passed his masterpiece before the guild of tailors and could make made-to-measure clothes in his own name. Cutting and making up clearly distinguished the tailor from the ordinary seamstress or the linen maid ("lingère").

maitre_tanneur.label: Maître tanneur (master tanner)
maitre_tanneur.summary: Master of the tanner's craft, directing the transformation of hides into leather.
maitre_tanneur.text: The maître tanneur directed the tanning operations, a long and foul-smelling process that turned raw hides into leather using tan (crushed oak bark). Because of the nuisance they caused, tanneries were generally relegated to the outskirts of towns, near watercourses.

malfillier.label: Malfillier (fat-rendering worker)
malfillier.summary: Worker who made oils and stearin in the fats industry.
malfillier.text: The malfillier worked at processing fats (tallow, animal or vegetable fats) into oils and stearin, used notably for making candles. The term, fairly rare, is found in regions with industrial activity linked to fats (soap works, candle works).

malletier.label: Malletier (trunk maker)
malletier.summary: Craftsman specialised in making trunks and travel luggage.
malletier.text: The malletier made trunks and travelling chests of wood reinforced with leather and ironwork, designed to carry personal belongings. The trade, close to those of the casket maker ("coffretier") and the harness maker ("bourrelier"), enjoyed its golden age with the growth of travel in the 18th and 19th centuries.

malteiro.label: Malteiro (itinerant farm worker, Alentejo)
malteiro.summary: Itinerant worker of the Alentejo, part of a "malta", who moved from estate to estate looking for work.
malteiro.text: The malteiro belongs to a "malta", a group of workers without steady employment who wandered the Alentejo from estate to estate in search of seasonal tasks (harvesting, weeding, cutting wood or cork), often with no fixed abode. The figure, linked to the precariousness of rural work in the South, is evoked in the 19th and 20th centuries.

mamposteiro.label: Mamposteiro (alms collector for the redemption of captives)
mamposteiro.summary: Collector of alms for a pious purpose, particularly the ransom of captives.
mamposteiro.text: The mamposteiro is appointed to collect in a locality the alms intended for a specific pious work, above all the ransom of Christian captives held in North Africa (mamposteiro dos cativos), but also for hospitals or shrines. In return he enjoyed certain privileges and exemptions. The office appears frequently in documents from the 16th to the 18th century.

mamsell.label: Estate housekeeper (Mamsell)
mamsell.summary: Housekeeper on an estate supervising kitchen, dairy, poultry and maids.
mamsell.text: The Mamsell (from French "mademoiselle") runs the household of an estate, above all in Mecklenburg, Pomerania and East Prussia: kitchen and stores, dairy, poultry, slaughtering and preserving, supervising the maids in the process. The post was usually held by unmarried women and enjoyed considerable standing on the estate.

manadier.label: Manadier (Camargue herdsman)
manadier.summary: Camargue breeder of horses and bulls raised in semi-freedom.
manadier.text: The manadier ran a "manade", a herd of horses and above all of Camargue bulls raised in semi-freedom in the marshes and pastures of the Camargue. These bulls were, and still are, destined for Camargue bull races and bullfighting, making the manadier an emblematic figure of regional identity.

manajeiro.label: Manajeiro (gang foreman, Alentejo)
manajeiro.summary: Foreman who directed a gang of workers at the harvest or weeding in the Alentejo.
manajeiro.text: The manajeiro is the head of a gang (rancho) of farm workers, charged by the farmer with directing and overseeing harvesting, weeding or other collective tasks, and often with recruiting the workers too. He usually worked alongside the gang, setting its pace. The term is characteristic of the Alentejo.

manchonnier.label: Manchonnier (cylinder glass blower)
manchonnier.summary: Glassworker who made glass cylinders to be flattened into window panes.
manchonnier.text: The manchonnier blew and shaped cylindrical glass sleeves ("manchons") which, once cooled, split and flattened, became sheets of window glass — the so-called cylinder-blown glass technique, in use before plate glass became widespread.

mandatariusz.label: Mandatariusz (manorial magistrate)
mandatariusz.summary: Manorial official in Galicia exercising administration and justice on the landowner’s behalf.
mandatariusz.text: Under Austrian rule in Galicia, from the 1780s to the mid-nineteenth century, the mandatariusz was an official paid by the landowner but approved by the state authorities, who exercised administration and lower justice over the subjects in the owner’s name. He also handled labour service, conscription and taxes in the villages under his authority.

mandelier.label: Mandelier (basket maker)
mandelier.summary: Basket maker specialised in making large wicker hampers and baskets called mandes.
mandelier.text: The mandelier wove wicker to make "mandes", large baskets or hampers used to carry farm produce (fruit, vegetables, grape harvests). The term, derived from "mande", is related to but should not be confused with the neighbouring vocabulary of the "mannes" woven by the mannelier.

mandeur.label: Mandeur (village summoner, crier)
mandeur.summary: Communal usher or crier responsible for summonses and public announcements in a village.
mandeur.text: The mandeur summoned the inhabitants to communal assemblies and made public announcements, a role close to that of the town crier or the rural policeman ("garde champêtre") depending on the region. The term "mande commun" denotes the same office in certain Pyrenean valleys, where it belonged to the traditional organisation of the village community.

mandier.label: Mandier (public officer)
mandier.summary: Old French term for a kind of public officer; the exact nature of the office is not detailed in the sources.
mandier.text: The mandier is attested in Frédéric Godefroy's dictionary of Old French as a "kind of public officer", without the precise nature of the office being described further. The word is related to "mande" and "mandeor", which in Old French denote an usher or sergeant responsible for summoning parties to court — the word family therefore belongs to the field of summoning and carrying out the orders of an authority.

mandrier.label: Mandrier (large-basket maker)
mandrier.summary: Basket maker who produced large wickerwork.
mandrier.text: The mandrier was a basket maker specialising in large pieces (big baskets, cages, hurdles), a regional term close to those of mandelier and mannelier without necessarily being the same.

manetier.label: Manetier (hamper maker)
manetier.summary: Basket maker who made mannes, large flat wicker baskets with handles.
manetier.text: The manetier (variants mannelier, mannequinier) wove wicker to make "mannes", large flat baskets with handles used to carry produce, linen or goods at the markets. In this old sense the word "mannequin" denoted the same kind of basket before taking on its modern meaning.

mangonnier.label: Mangonnier (fishmonger)
mangonnier.summary: Retail fish seller in Languedoc who sold fresh fish at the markets.
mangonnier.text: The mangonnier sold fresh fish retail at the markets of Languedoc, a regional role close to that of the fishmonger ("poissonnier") elsewhere in the kingdom.

manieur.label: Manieur (grain turner)
manieur.summary: Worker at the grain ports who turned the grain to drive out moisture.
manieur.text: The manieur, a term attested notably in the grain ports of Paris, stirred and turned the stored wheat to air it and drive out moisture, an operation essential to keeping the grain in good condition before it was sold or transported.

manijero.label: Manijero (Spanish gang foreman)
manijero.summary: Foreman who hired and directed a gang of agricultural day labourers.
manijero.text: The manijero recruited a gang of day labourers for a given task (reaping, weeding, olive picking), directed it in the field and often paid it on the owner's behalf. A typical figure of the Andalusian countryside, he worked alongside the labourers himself.

manilier.label: Manilier (churchwarden)
manilier.summary: Churchwarden in the Dauphiné and the Lyonnais, responsible for the upkeep and management of a church.
manilier.text: Manilier was the name given in the Dauphiné and the Lyonnais to the churchwarden ("marguillier") responsible for managing the property and the material upkeep of a parish church — a regional variant of an office widespread elsewhere under other names (marguillier, marglier).

manissier.label: Manissier (marl digger)
manissier.summary: Worker who extracted marl, a limy soil improver for farmland, from marl pits.
manissier.text: The manissier worked in the "marnières", pits from which marl was extracted, a limy soil improver used to enrich farmland before chemical fertilisers came into general use.

manoeuvre.label: Manœuvre (labourer)
manoeuvre.summary: Unskilled worker doing heavy tasks that required no particular technical skill.
manoeuvre.text: The manœuvre was a worker with no particular qualification, employed for heavy work — earthmoving, building sites, carrying — and paid by the day. He differed from the skilled worker or the craftsman in having had no training or apprenticeship, and stood at the bottom of the wage scale in the working world.

manouvion.label: Manouvion (day labourer)
manouvion.summary: Berry term for a day labourer, a farm worker paid by the task or by the day.
manouvion.text: Manouvion (also manouvrion) was the name given in the Berry to the day labourer, a farm worker with no land of his own who sold his labour by the day according to the needs of neighbouring farms, the local equivalent of the manouvrier.

manouvrier.label: Manouvrier (landless day labourer)
manouvrier.summary: Landless farm worker who worked by the day for other farmers.
manouvrier.text: The manouvrier, a very common term in rural civil registers, denotes a farm worker who owned little or no land and hired out his labour by the day to the laboureurs and tenant farmers of the neighbourhood. He stood at the bottom of the peasant ladder, just above the mere beggar.

mansjonarz.label: Mansjonarz (mansionary priest)
mansjonarz.summary: Cleric bound to regular celebration of services at a particular church.
mansjonarz.text: The mansjonarz belonged to a college of clerics (mansionarii) founded at a cathedral, collegiate or parish church and bound to sing the hours and say mass daily, especially in honour of the Virgin Mary. He lived on the endowment set aside for this purpose.

manutentionnaire.label: Manutentionnaire (warehouseman)
manutentionnaire.summary: Employee responsible for handling, storing and moving goods in a warehouse.
manutentionnaire.text: The manutentionnaire loaded, unloaded and stored goods in warehouses, shops or railway stations. A modern term (industrial, then commercial), it appears mainly in records of the 19th and 20th centuries as wholesale trade and department stores developed.

maquignon.label: Maquignon (horse dealer, cattle dealer)
maquignon.summary: Livestock dealer, an intermediary between breeders and buyers at fairs and markets.
maquignon.text: The maquignon bought and resold livestock, especially horses, at fairs and markets, acting as an intermediary between breeders and buyers. Renowned for his sometimes unscrupulous bargaining skills, the word eventually took on in everyday French a pejorative sense of crafty haggling.

maraboutier.label: Maraboutier (tinsmith)
maraboutier.summary: Tinsmith specialised in making marabouts, metal containers with a handle.
maraboutier.text: The maraboutier worked tinplate to make "marabouts", small metal containers with a handle used in households, a speciality of tinsmithing.

maragato.label: Maragato (muleteer from Maragatería)
maragato.summary: Native of Maragatería (León, Spain), famous for its muleteers carrying goods between Galicia and Castile.
maragato.text: The maragatos, natives of the Maragatería district of León, specialised in the 18th and 19th centuries in carrying goods with mule trains, transporting fish, wine, cloth and other merchandise between Galicia, Castile and Madrid. In many documents the name of origin alone is enough to indicate this carrier's trade.

maragon.label: Maragon (salt-marsh worker)
maragon.summary: Salt-marsh worker who harvested and produced salt.
maragon.text: The maragon worked in the salt marshes, taking part in the salt harvest under the authority of the salt maker ("saunier") or the salt-marsh master. The term and its variant marayon are typical of the vocabulary of the Atlantic salt-producing regions.

marbreur.label: Marbreur (glass gatherer)
marbreur.summary: Glassworker who gathered the molten glass and began shaping the pieces.
marbreur.text: The marbreur was a glassworker who gathered the molten glass on the end of the blowpipe and began shaping it on the "marbre" (a metal plate on which the gather was rolled), before the piece passed into the hands of the glassblower. The name comes from this tool and has nothing to do with building marble.

marbrier.label: Marbrier (marble mason)
marbrier.summary: Craftsman who sawed, polished and shaped marble for decorative and funerary work.
