marbrier.text: The marbrier sawed, polished and carved marble to make chimneypieces, paving, funerary monuments and ornaments. A luxury trade linked to architecture and sculpture, it developed particularly from the 17th century with the taste for marbled interiors.

marchand.label: Marchand (merchant)
marchand.summary: Generic term for anyone engaged in trade, without a specified speciality.
marchand.text: The word marchand, used on its own in records, simply denotes a person who lived by trade without his speciality being specified. It covers a very wide variety of social situations, from the rich wholesale merchant to the modest shopkeeper or pedlar, and is found at all periods in parish and civil registers.

marchand_bladier.label: Marchand bladier (corn merchant)
marchand_bladier.summary: Dealer in wheat and cereals, an intermediary between producers and consumers.
marchand_bladier.text: The marchand bladier (from "blad", wheat in Occitan and Old French) traded wheat and cereals between producers, millers and urban consumers. This trade, essential to supplying the towns, was closely watched by the authorities in times of dearth.

marchand_boucher.label: Marchand boucher (butcher and cattle dealer)
marchand_boucher.summary: Tradesman who sold meat, combining dealing with slaughtering.
marchand_boucher.text: The marchand boucher bought livestock, slaughtered it and sold the meat retail, thus combining the functions of cattle dealer and stall-keeping butcher.

marchand_briffon.label: Marchand briffon (cattle dealer)
marchand_briffon.summary: Livestock dealer of Anjou and Maine, specialised in trading farm animals.
marchand_briffon.text: The marchand briffon dealt in livestock in the Anjou and Maine regions, a regional term for a local horse or cattle dealer ("maquignon").

marchand_d_arlequins.label: Marchand d'arlequins (leftovers seller)
marchand_d_arlequins.summary: Seller of meal leftovers collected from restaurants and resold cheaply to the poor.
marchand_d_arlequins.text: The marchand d'arlequins collected meal leftovers (meat, vegetables) from the kitchens of Parisian restaurants and hotels and resold them to the poorest, mixed into a dish nicknamed "arlequin" (harlequin) because of its motley appearance. This trade, attested in the 19th century in the working-class districts of Paris, illustrates the economy of urban poverty before the rise of social welfare.

marchand_d_avoine.label: Marchand d'avoine (oats merchant)
marchand_d_avoine.summary: Dealer specialised in trading oats, a staple of horse feed.
marchand_d_avoine.text: The marchand d'avoine sold oats, a fodder cereal indispensable for feeding horses, a commodity in heavy demand before the motorisation of transport and agriculture.

marchand_d_hommes.label: Marchand d'hommes (substitute broker)
marchand_d_hommes.summary: In the 19th century, a supplier of military substitutes for conscription.
marchand_d_hommes.text: In the 19th century, the marchand d'hommes supplied a substitute to men who had drawn an unlucky number in the conscription ballot and were therefore obliged to do their military service.

marchand_d_oing.label: Marchand d'oing (axle-grease seller)
marchand_d_oing.summary: Seller of rendered pork fat used for greasing axles.
marchand_d_oing.text: The marchand d'oing sold rendered pork fat ("oing"), used to grease the wheel axles of wagons and carriages.

marchand_d_oublies.label: Marchand d'Oublies (marchand_d_oublies)
marchand_d_oublies.text: Le marchand d'oublies vend, en marchand ambulant, des oublies, pâtisseries légères en forme de gaufrettes roulées.

marchand_de_bestiaux.label: Marchand de bestiaux (livestock dealer)
marchand_de_bestiaux.summary: Dealer who bought and resold livestock at markets and fairs.
marchand_de_bestiaux.text: The marchand de bestiaux, a common synonym of maquignon, bought and resold livestock (cattle, sheep, pigs) at fairs and markets, acting as an intermediary between breeders and butchers or other breeders.

marchand_de_blanc.label: Marchand de blanc (tinware seller)
marchand_de_blanc.summary: Tradesman who sold tinplate utensils, an activity close to that of the tinsmith.
marchand_de_blanc.text: The marchand de blanc sold utensils made of tinplate (containers, boxes), a commercial activity linked to the work of the tinsmith, whose production he sometimes sold himself.

marchand_de_boeufs.label: Marchand de bœufs (ox dealer)
marchand_de_boeufs.summary: Dealer specialised in buying and reselling oxen at fairs.
marchand_de_boeufs.text: The marchand de bœufs traded specifically in draught or beef cattle at fairs, a specialisation of the more general livestock dealer ("maquignon").

marchand_de_bourrette.label: Marchand de bourrette (coarse-cloth dealer)
marchand_de_bourrette.summary: Dealer in bourrette, a coarse fabric of wool, silk, hemp or linen depending on the region.
marchand_de_bourrette.text: The marchand de bourrette sold "bourrette", a second-quality fabric woven from waste fibres (wool, silk, hemp or linen depending on the region), intended for a working-class clientele.

marchand_de_cade.label: Marchand de cade (cade seller)
marchand_de_cade.summary: Toulon street vendor of cade, a chickpea-based speciality.
marchand_de_cade.text: The marchand de cade sold in the streets of Toulon "cade" (or "cadeuil"), a baked flatbread made from chickpea flour and olive oil, a popular culinary speciality of the Provençal coast.

marchand_de_cafe.label: Marchand de café (coffee seller)
marchand_de_cafe.summary: Tradesman who sold coffee beans or ground coffee, or kept a drinking establishment.
marchand_de_cafe.text: The marchand de café sold coffee, an imported commodity that became very popular from the 18th century onwards, either as beans or ground for home consumption, or prepared in a drinking establishment.

marchand_de_charbon.label: Marchand de charbon (coal merchant)
marchand_de_charbon.summary: Fuel dealer (charcoal or coal), subject to strict rules of sale.
marchand_de_charbon.text: The marchand de charbon sold charcoal and later, as industrialisation progressed, coal, a fuel essential for heating and industry. The trade was often regulated (obligation to unload quickly, prices displayed) to prevent speculation in cold weather.

marchand_de_coco.label: Marchand de coco (liquorice-water seller)
marchand_de_coco.summary: Street vendor of coco, a refreshing liquorice drink served in the streets.
marchand_de_coco.text: The marchand de coco sold "coco" in the street, a refreshing drink made of water, liquorice and sometimes orange-flower water, carried on the back in a decorated fountain and served in beakers — a popular and picturesque figure of French streets until the early 20th century.

marchand_de_coke.label: Marchand de coke (coke merchant)
marchand_de_coke.summary: Dealer in coke, a coal-derived fuel used for heating and industry.
marchand_de_coke.text: The marchand de coke sold coke, the solid residue obtained by distilling coal, widely used as an industrial and domestic fuel from the 19th century onwards.

marchand_de_crepins.label: Marchand de crépins (shoemakers' supplier)
marchand_de_crepins.summary: Tradesman who sold tools and supplies for shoemakers.
marchand_de_crepins.text: The marchand de crépins supplied shoemakers with the tools, leathers and small materials needed for their trade, the term "crépin" referring to Saint Crispin, patron saint of shoemakers.

marchand_de_croquets.label: Marchand de croquets (biscuit seller)
marchand_de_croquets.summary: Seller of croquets, dry crunchy biscuits, often made with gingerbread.
marchand_de_croquets.text: The marchand de croquets sold "croquets", hard crunchy biscuits (often of gingerbread or almond), a traditional confection sold at markets and funfairs.

marchand_de_darioles.label: Marchand de darioles (dariole seller)
marchand_de_darioles.summary: Pastry cook who sold darioles, small custard tarts made with flour, butter, eggs and milk.
marchand_de_darioles.text: The marchand de darioles made and sold "darioles", small custards or tartlets made with flour, butter, eggs and milk, a medieval and Ancien Régime pastry whose recipe dates back to the Middle Ages.

marchand_de_fleurs.label: Marchand de fleurs (flower seller)
marchand_de_fleurs.summary: Tradesman who sold flowers, often from a street stall in markets and squares.
marchand_de_fleurs.text: The marchand de fleurs sold cut or potted flowers, generally from a stall or as a street vendor in town squares and markets, an activity that developed above all with the urbanisation of the 19th century.

marchand_de_fripes.label: Marchand de fripes (old-clothes dealer)
marchand_de_fripes.summary: Tradesman who sold used clothes and objects, forerunner of the modern second-hand clothes dealer.
marchand_de_fripes.text: The marchand de fripes, or fripier, bought and resold second-hand clothes and objects, a popular trade essential before cheap new ready-to-wear clothing became widespread, often located in dedicated districts such as the Paris old-clothes market.

marchand_de_fromages.label: Marchand de fromages (cheesemonger)
marchand_de_fromages.summary: Tradesman who sold cheeses, often alongside other dairy produce.
marchand_de_fromages.text: The marchand de fromages sold cheeses retail at markets or in a shop, a trade distinct from that of the producer (maître fromager), even though the two roles could be combined in the same person in rural areas.

marchand_de_fruits.label: Marchand de fruits (fruiterer)
marchand_de_fruits.summary: Tradesman who sold fruit, generally from a market stall.
marchand_de_fruits.text: The marchand de fruits sold fresh fruit at markets or in a shop, a retail activity linked to local market gardening and fruit growing.

marchand_de_henons.label: Marchand de Hénons (marchand_de_henons)
marchand_de_henons.summary: Vendeur de coques et coquillages divers destinés à la consommation.
marchand_de_henons.text: Le marchand de hénons vend des hénons, coques et petits coquillages comestibles récoltés sur l'estran, un commerce de proximité typique des régions littorales.

marchand_de_loge.label: Marchand de loge (Marseille exchange merchant)
marchand_de_loge.summary: Marseille merchant attached to the commercial exchange, active in Mediterranean trade.
marchand_de_loge.text: The marchand de loge was a Marseille merchant who belonged to the Loge of the commercial exchange, an institution bringing together the merchants engaged in international trade, especially Mediterranean trade, from the great Phocaean port.

marchand_de_maree.label: Marchand de marée (fresh-fish dealer)
marchand_de_maree.summary: Fishmonger who sold fresh sea fish, known as "marée", brought in from the ports.
marchand_de_maree.text: The marchand de marée sold fresh sea fish — the "marée" — carried swiftly from the fishing ports to inland markets, a trade that formerly required a fast transport chain (relays of horses) before the advent of the railway and artificial refrigeration.

marchand_de_nouveautes.label: Marchand de nouveautés (fancy-goods draper)
marchand_de_nouveautes.summary: Tradesman specialised in women's fashion goods: fabrics, haberdashery, ribbons, lingerie.
marchand_de_nouveautes.text: The marchand de nouveautés sold fashionable articles of women's dress: new fabrics, haberdashery, ribbons, lace and lingerie. This trade, booming in the 19th century, foreshadowed the department stores that grew out of it (Bon Marché, Printemps).

marchand_de_peaux_de_lapins.label: Marchand de peaux de lapins (rabbit-skin collector)
marchand_de_peaux_de_lapins.summary: Itinerant collector of rabbit skins, resold for furriery and felt.
marchand_de_peaux_de_lapins.text: The marchand de peaux de lapins went through the streets collecting rabbit skins from households (often in exchange for small objects), which he then resold to furriers and makers of felt for hats — one of the many small itinerant salvage trades of the 19th century.

marchand_de_peilles.label: Marchand de peilles (rag dealer)
marchand_de_peilles.summary: Rag-and-bone man who resold the rags (peilles) he collected to paper mills for papermaking.
marchand_de_peilles.text: The marchand de peilles collected "peilles", old rags, which he resold to paper mills where they served as the raw material for papermaking before the invention of paper made from wood pulp. The term is a regional variant of "chiffonnier" (rag-and-bone man).

marchand_de_plaisirs.label: Marchand de plaisirs (wafer seller)
marchand_de_plaisirs.summary: Street vendor of plaisirs, delicate pastries such as wafers and small biscuits.
marchand_de_plaisirs.text: The marchand de plaisirs sold "plaisirs" in the street, light crisp pastries (thin wafers, "oublies"), a popular treat sold at festivals and markets.

marchand_de_porcs.label: Marchand de porcs (pig dealer)
marchand_de_porcs.summary: Dealer specialised in buying and reselling pigs at markets and fairs.
marchand_de_porcs.text: The marchand de porcs traded specifically in pigs at fairs, a specialisation of the livestock dealer ("maquignon") particularly common in pig-rearing regions.

marchand_de_ratieres.label: Marchand de ratières (rat-trap seller)
marchand_de_ratieres.summary: Seller of rat traps, designed to catch rats and mice.
marchand_de_ratieres.text: The marchand de ratières made or sold rat traps and other traps, designed to combat rodent pests in homes and lofts.

marchand_de_rouenneries.label: Marchand de rouenneries (Rouen cotton dealer)
marchand_de_rouenneries.summary: Dealer in rouenneries, printed cotton cloths from the Rouen area.
marchand_de_rouenneries.text: The marchand de rouenneries sold "rouenneries", painted or printed cotton cloths of which Rouen was, from the 18th century, one of the great centres of production, rivalling the "indiennes" (Indian-style printed calicoes).

marchand_de_sablon.label: Marchand de sablon (scouring-sand seller)
marchand_de_sablon.summary: Dealer in fine sand, used for scouring, polishing and various industrial purposes.
marchand_de_sablon.text: The marchand de sablon sold "sablon", fine sand traditionally used to scour floors and utensils or for various craft purposes, before industrial cleaning products appeared.

marchand_de_saline.label: Marchand de saline (salt-fish dealer)
marchand_de_saline.summary: Fishmonger specialised in selling salted fish and brined preserves.
marchand_de_saline.text: The marchand de saline sold fish preserved by salting (herring, cod), a preserving technique essential before refrigeration, allowing the fish to be transported and sold far from the coasts.

marchand_de_soie.label: Marchand de soie (silk merchant)
marchand_de_soie.summary: Dealer in silk fabrics and threads, a luxury textile imported or produced regionally.
marchand_de_soie.text: The marchand de soie sold silk, a luxury textile of which Lyon became, from the 16th century onwards, the great centre of production and trade in France, feeding a flourishing commerce until the 19th century.

marchand_de_vaire.label: Marchand de vaire (vair merchant, furrier)
marchand_de_vaire.summary: Furrier who traded in skins and furs, notably squirrel fur (vair).
marchand_de_vaire.text: The marchand de vaire traded in skins and furs, in particular vair, the grey and white fur of the Siberian squirrel ("petit-gris"), highly prized in the Middle Ages for trimming noble garments (hence the expression "pantoufle de vair", the glass slipper of the Cinderella tale).

marchand_de_verre.label: Marchand de verre (glass merchant)
marchand_de_verre.summary: Tradesman who sold glass objects and panes made by the glassworks.
marchand_de_verre.text: The marchand de verre sold the products of the glassworks — window panes, drinking glasses, flasks — handling the commercial distribution of a technical craft concentrated in suitable forest regions (firewood for the furnaces).

marchand_de_vin.label: Marchand de vin (wine merchant)
marchand_de_vin.summary: Wine dealer; the guild brought together tavern keepers, innkeepers and retailers.
marchand_de_vin.text: The marchand de vin sold wine retail or wholesale, an activity that under the Ancien Régime brought together tavern keepers, innkeepers and wine criers within a single guild responsible for distributing the most widely consumed drink in the kingdom.

marchand_de_volailles.label: Marchand de volailles (poulterer)
marchand_de_volailles.summary: Tradesman who sold poultry, live or oven-ready, at markets.
marchand_de_volailles.text: The marchand de volailles sold hens, ducks, geese and other poultry, live or already dressed, at urban markets, obtaining his supplies from the surrounding farms.

marchand_des_quatre_saisons.label: Marchand des quatre saisons (costermonger)
marchand_des_quatre_saisons.summary: Street vendor of seasonal fruit and vegetables who pushed a handcart.
marchand_des_quatre_saisons.text: The marchand des quatre saisons sold fruit and vegetables according to the season, pushing his handcart through the streets — an emblematic figure of Parisian itinerant petty trade in the 19th and 20th centuries, now largely vanished.

marchand_ecardeur.label: Marchand écardeur (wool carder and merchant)
marchand_ecardeur.summary: Tradesman linked to wool carding, which disentangled the fibre and cleaned it of impurities.
marchand_ecardeur.text: The marchand écardeur combined the wool trade with carding ("écardage"), the operation of combing wool and ridding it of impurities (burrs, thistles) before spinning, a preparatory stage of textile work.

marchand_farinier.label: Marchand farinier (flour merchant)
marchand_farinier.summary: Dealer in flour, an intermediary between millers and bakers or private customers.
marchand_farinier.text: The marchand farinier bought flour from millers to resell to bakers and private customers, an intermediate trade essential to the supply chain for bread, a basic necessity.

marchand_fruitier.label: Marchand fruitier (fruiterer)
marchand_fruitier.summary: Tradesman who sold fruit and sometimes dairy produce, depending on regional usage.
marchand_fruitier.text: The marchand fruitier sold fruit at the markets; in some regions the term "fruitier" also denoted the trade in dairy produce (butter, eggs, cheese), the two meanings coexisting according to local usage.

marchand_graissier.label: Marchand graissier (fat and oil seller)
marchand_graissier.summary: Tradesman who sold edible fats and oils, often also working as a grocer.
marchand_graissier.text: The marchand graissier (or gressier) sold fats and oils for cooking or lighting, an activity often combined with that of grocer or druggist in Ancien Régime shops.

marchand_grossier.label: Marchand grossier (wholesaler)
marchand_grossier.summary: Dealer who sold wholesale, as opposed to the retailer, organising distribution in large quantities.
marchand_grossier.text: The marchand grossier (or grossiste) bought and resold goods in large quantities to retailers, playing an essential intermediary role in the commercial circuits between producers and final consumers.

marchand_sabotier.label: Marchand sabotier (clog seller)
marchand_sabotier.summary: Tradesman who sold clogs, the wooden shoes worn by the peasantry.
marchand_sabotier.text: The marchand sabotier sold the clogs made by the clog maker ("sabotier"), solid wooden footwear very widespread in the French countryside until the early 20th century because of its low cost and durability.

marchand_tanneur.label: Marchand tanneur (tanner and leather merchant)
marchand_tanneur.summary: Tradesman who combined tanning hides with selling the leather produced.
marchand_tanneur.text: The marchand tanneur combined the functions of tanner (turning hides into leather) and merchant, selling directly the leather he produced.

marchande_de_cafe.label: Marchande de café (coffee seller)
marchande_de_cafe.summary: Woman who ran a coffee business, in a shop or at a street stall.
marchande_de_cafe.text: The marchande de café sold coffee, as beans, ground or ready to drink, keeping a shop or a stall, a female commercial activity attested notably in the towns from the 18th century onwards.

marchande_de_modes.label: Marchande de modes (milliner)
marchande_de_modes.summary: Female merchant specialised in women's fashion accessories: hats, ribbons, lace.
marchande_de_modes.text: The marchande de modes sold and made the accessories of women's finery — taffetas, gauzes, lace, feathers, ribbons, hats — a typically female trade very fashionable in the 18th and 19th centuries and the forerunner of the milliner ("modiste").

marcheur.label: Marcheur (clay treader)
marcheur.summary: Brickworks labourer who prepared the clay used to make bricks.
marcheur.text: The marcheur trod and prepared the clay in a brickworks, a manual stage that traditionally consisted of trampling the clay to make it even before it was moulded into bricks.

marechal.label: Maréchal (farrier)
marechal.summary: Craftsman who shod horses, cared for their hooves and did the forge work connected with them.
marechal.text: The maréchal (or maréchal-ferrant) shaped and fitted the shoes of horses, donkeys and mules and cared for their hooves, an essential trade as long as animal traction dominated transport and agriculture. Mareschal is the old spelling, common in records before the 18th century. In an entirely different context, the word maréchal could also denote a military or court dignitary, unrelated to this craft.

marechal_a_forge.label: Maréchal à forge (forge farrier)
marechal_a_forge.summary: Farrier working in an equipped forge, as opposed to itinerant shoeing.
marechal_a_forge.text: The maréchal à forge worked in a fixed, equipped forge, where he shod horses and did ironwork, as opposed to some itinerant farriers who travelled from farm to farm.

marechal_de_sa_vacation.label: Maréchal de sa vacation (farrier by trade)
marechal_de_sa_vacation.summary: Administrative formula for a farrier who practised this trade as his main occupation.
marechal_de_sa_vacation.text: In old records, the expression "de sa vacation" (of his condition, of his usual profession) specifies that the person practised the farrier's trade as his main occupation and not occasionally, a common administrative turn of phrase used to remove any ambiguity about the declarant's occupational status.

marechal_en_oeuvres_blanches.label: Maréchal en œuvres blanches (whitesmith)
marechal_en_oeuvres_blanches.summary: Smith specialised in fine work in white metals (tin, polished iron) and edged tools.
marechal_en_oeuvres_blanches.text: The maréchal en œuvres blanches worked white metals (as opposed to the "heavy works" of the heavy forge) to make fine tools, cutlery and small hardware, a more delicate speciality than rough ironwork.

marechal_expert.label: Maréchal expert (expert farrier)
marechal_expert.summary: Farrier recognised as competent for judicial expertise and veterinary assessment of horses.
marechal_expert.text: The maréchal expert acted as an expert appointed by the courts to assess the condition or value of horses, particularly in commercial disputes or accidents, combining his farrier's skills with a quasi-veterinary role before qualified veterinary medicine appeared.

marechal_ferrant.label: Maréchal-ferrant (farrier, shoeing smith)
marechal_ferrant.summary: Precise and usual name of the farrier specialised in shoeing horses.
marechal_ferrant.text: Maréchal-ferrant is the most precise and, from the 19th century onwards, the most widely used name for the craftsman who shod horses, the word maréchal on its own being otherwise liable to confusion with other meanings of the word (notably the military dignity).

marechal_grossier.label: Maréchal grossier (heavy smith)
marechal_grossier.summary: Smith specialised in heavy forge work and heavy ironwork.
marechal_grossier.text: The maréchal grossier devoted himself to the "heavy works" of the forge — farm tools, cart parts, heavy ironwork — as opposed to the finer work reserved for the maréchal en œuvres blanches.

marechal_soignant.label: Maréchal soignant (horse-doctoring farrier)
marechal_soignant.summary: Farrier who also provided basic veterinary care to horses.
marechal_soignant.text: In addition to shoeing, the maréchal soignant gave rudimentary veterinary care to horses (wounds, lameness), a common role before the qualified veterinary profession became widespread in the 19th century.

marechal_veterinaire.label: Maréchal vétérinaire (veterinary farrier)
marechal_veterinaire.summary: Farrier who had acquired advanced veterinary skills to treat horses.
marechal_veterinaire.text: The maréchal vétérinaire combined shoeing with a deeper medical knowledge of equine diseases, a transition typical of the 19th century between the traditional craft of the farrier and the emergence of scientific veterinary medicine.

marechaussee.label: Marechaussee (Dutch military police)
marechaussee.summary: Member of the marechaussee corps, responsible for policing the countryside, the borders and the army.
marechaussee.text: The Dutch marechaussee corps was established in 1814 as a military police force. Its members patrolled the countryside and border regions, tracked down smugglers, deserters and criminals and acted as police within the armed forces. The designation appears regularly in civil registration records of the 19th and 20th centuries.

maretquier_de_stil.label: Maretquier de son stil (market gardener by trade)
maretquier_de_stil.summary: Market gardener (grower on a "marais"), followed by the old formula "de son stil", meaning "by trade".
maretquier_de_stil.text: Maretquier (variants maresquier, marequier in the langue d'oc, mareschier in the langue d'oïl) is the ancestor of the word maraîcher (market gardener): originally a gardener who cultivated a "marais", low-lying damp ground laid out as a kitchen garden on the edge of towns (the Paris district of the Marais still bears the name). The words that follow, "de Stil", are a corruption of the old formula "de son stil" (or "de son estil"), from the Latin stilus, used notably in records from the Nord and the Pas-de-Calais to mean "by profession" — one likewise finds "laboureur de son stil" or "maçon de son estile". The full expression therefore simply means "market gardener by trade".

mareyeur.label: Mareyeur (fish wholesaler)
mareyeur.summary: Fish wholesaler who bought directly from fishermen for distribution inland.
mareyeur.text: The mareyeur bought fish directly from the fishermen on the quayside, at the fish auction, to organise its rapid distribution to inland markets — a trade still practised today, standing upstream of the retail fishmonger.

marglier.label: Marguillier (churchwarden)
marglier.summary: Elected layman responsible for managing a parish's temporal property and income.
marglier.text: The marguillier was a lay parishioner elected by his peers (or co-opted, depending on the place) to sit on the parish vestry ("conseil de fabrique") and manage the parish's material property and income: upkeep of the church, accounts, collections. The spellings marglier, marillier and marreglier are variants found in different regions and periods. The office, often honorary, was sought after by local notables.

margotier.label: Margotier (cord maker)
margotier.summary: Craftsman who made ties and cords for tying and lashing.
margotier.text: The margotier made ties and cords used to tie, lash or bind loads, a craft close to rope making or esparto work ("sparterie") depending on the region and the materials used.

margoulin.label: Margoulin (shady dealer)
margoulin.summary: Unscrupulous small trader who charged excessive prices or engaged in dubious dealings.
margoulin.text: The margoulin was a small trader or middleman of dubious reputation, given to overbidding, profiteering resale or dishonest commercial schemes. The term, still used today in a pejorative sense for an unscrupulous wheeler-dealer, dates back to 19th-century commercial slang.

marin.label: Marin (sailor, seaman)
marin.summary: Generic term for anyone working at sea, without a specified speciality.
marin.text: The word marin, used on its own, denotes anyone whose occupation was connected with seafaring, without specifying whether it was the merchant navy, fishing or the navy. The term is very common in the registers of coastal regions.

marin_classe.label: Marin classé (registered seaman)
marin_classe.summary: Seaman entered in the register of the Inscription Maritime, the French navy's enrolment system.
marin_classe.text: The marin classé was entered in the registers of the Inscription Maritime, a system created under Louis XIV (by Colbert) to record and mobilise seafarers for service in the royal and later national navy, in return for certain rights (pensions, fishing privileges).

marin_de_commerce.label: Marin de commerce (merchant seaman)
marin_de_commerce.summary: Seaman employed on merchant ships, as opposed to the navy.
marin_de_commerce.text: The marin de commerce sailed on merchant ships carrying passengers or goods, as opposed to the naval seaman or the fisherman.

marin_pecheur.label: Marin pêcheur (fisherman)
marin_pecheur.summary: Seaman whose main occupation was sea fishing.
marin_pecheur.text: The marin pêcheur practised sea fishing as his main occupation, aboard an inshore or deep-sea fishing boat depending on the region and the period.

marinier.label: Marinier (bargeman, boatman)
marinier.summary: Boatman who navigated rivers and canals carrying goods and passengers.
marinier.text: The marinier steered a barge or river boat carrying goods and sometimes passengers on rivers and canals. The trade, often a family and itinerant one (the family living on board), long constituted a major mode of transport before competition from the railway and later the road.

marinier_de_gabare.label: Marinier de gabare (gabare boatman)
marinier_de_gabare.summary: Boatman who steered a gabare, a flat-bottomed river boat for carrying goods.
marinier_de_gabare.text: The marinier de gabare steered a "gabare", a flat-bottomed river craft used especially on the Loire, the Dordogne and the Garonne to carry wine, timber and other goods between the interior and the seaports.

marinier_pecheur.label: Marinier pêcheur (boatman and fisherman)
marinier_pecheur.summary: Boatman who combined river navigation and fishing as a means of livelihood.
marinier_pecheur.text: The marinier pêcheur combined river transport with freshwater fishing, a dual activity common among the boatmen of the great rivers, who supplemented their income by fishing.

mariscador.label: Mariscador (shellfish gatherer)
mariscador.summary: Gatherer of shellfish (clams, cockles, mussels) on beaches and estuaries at low tide.
mariscador.text: The mariscador gathers bivalves and other shellfish by hand or with rakes and simple tools on beaches, lagoons and estuaries at low tide, for home consumption or for sale. Often carried out by women and complementary to fishing and farming, the activity was important in the northern estuaries, the Ria de Aveiro and the Ria Formosa.

markscheider.label: Mine surveyor (Markscheider)
markscheider.summary: Mining surveyor who measured mine workings and drew mine plans.
markscheider.text: The Markscheider (from Mark, boundary, and scheiden, to separate) surveys the underground workings and their position relative to the surface, draws the mine plans and fixes the boundaries of the granted mining fields so that neighbouring mines do not break into each other's workings. He was a trained official of the mining authority or of a mine; mine surveying was taught at the mining academies.

marneur.label: Marneur (marl spreader)
marneur.summary: Worker who spread marl on farmland to improve its fertility.
marneur.text: The marneur spread marl, a limy soil improver extracted from marl pits, on farmland to correct its acidity and improve yields — a farming practice widespread before chemical fertilisers came into general use.

maroquinier.label: Maroquinier (morocco-leather worker)
maroquinier.summary: Craftsman who worked morocco, tanned goatskin used for fine leather goods.
maroquinier.text: The maroquinier worked "maroquin" (morocco), tanned goatskin (originally imported from Morocco, hence the name) used to make luxury articles: bookbindings, wallets, bags. Fine leatherwork is distinguished from tanning and shoemaking by the delicacy of its products.

marquard.label: Marquard (boundary warden)
marquard.summary: Warden or keeper responsible for watching over borders, markets or common property.
marquard.text: The marquard was a local warden or keeper responsible for watching over territorial boundaries, markets or common property, a rare regional term close to the functions of the rural policeman ("garde champêtre") or of the warden of the marches (borders).

marqueteur.label: Marqueteur (marquetry worker)
marqueteur.summary: Craftsman who created decorative wooden patterns by assembling veneers, known as marquetry.
marqueteur.text: The marqueteur practised marquetry, the technique of assembling thin sheets of wood (veneers) of different colours and species to create decorative patterns on furniture, an art close to cabinetmaking that appeared in France in the 17th century.

marqueteur_de_paille.label: Marqueteur de paille (straw marquetry worker)
marqueteur_de_paille.summary: Craftsman who practised straw marquetry, a decorative technique using coloured straw.
marqueteur_de_paille.text: The marqueteur de paille created decorative patterns by assembling flattened, coloured straws on a wooden or cardboard base, a decorative technique widespread notably in the Berry and Poitou in the 17th and 18th centuries.

marqueur.label: Marqueur (excise marker)
marqueur.summary: Tax officer who stamped official marks on goods to certify that duties had been paid.
marqueur.text: The marqueur was an officer responsible for affixing official marks or stamps on goods, certifying that they had paid the duties and taxes in force (iron, cloth, leather depending on the period and place), a fiscal control function typical of the Ancien Régime.

marqueur_de_cuir.label: Marqueur de cuir (leather marker)
marqueur_de_cuir.summary: Craftsman who marked finished leathers, guaranteeing their quality and origin.
marqueur_de_cuir.text: The marqueur de cuir affixed an official mark on finished skins and leathers, guaranteeing their quality and their compliance with the regulations of the guild of tanners and curriers.

marqueur_ferreur.label: Marqueur ferreur (ironwork marker)
marqueur_ferreur.summary: Craftsman who marked or stamped ironwork to guarantee its origin.
marqueur_ferreur.text: The marqueur ferreur stamped ironwork with a distinctive mark, guaranteeing its provenance and conformity, a quality control practice common in the metalworking guilds.

marqueur_peignier.label: Marqueur peignier (comb marker)
marqueur_peignier.summary: Craftsman who marked the combs and hairdressing tools made by the guild.
marqueur_peignier.text: The marqueur peignier affixed the mark of the comb makers' guild on the combs and hairdressing tools produced, a quality control specific to this small trade of worked horn and ivory.

marqueuse.label: Marqueuse (linen marker)
marqueuse.summary: Craftswoman who embroidered marks and decorative motifs on linen and textiles.
marqueuse.text: The marqueuse embroidered initials, monograms or decorative motifs on household linen and clothing, a female textile activity used to identify or adorn the family linen.

marquis.label: Marquis (marquess)
marquis.summary: Title of nobility, originally reserved for the lord of a march (border territory).
marquis.text: Marquis is a title of nobility, ranking between count and duke in the French noble hierarchy, originally reserved for the lord of a march, a border territory to be defended. The title, widely conferred under the Ancien Régime, appears in records concerning the nobility and its landed estates.

marreur.label: Marreur (marl digger)
marreur.summary: Worker who extracted and handled marl in marl pits.
marreur.text: The marreur worked at extracting marl in the marl pits, physical quarry work distinct from that of the marneur, who spread the already extracted marl on the fields. The term pionnier, recorded as a variant, refers to the old sense of navvy or digger.

martchoti.label: Martchotî (dialect term, uncertain meaning)
martchoti.summary: Rare dialect term denoting a craftsman or trader in foodstuffs.
martchoti.text: Martchotî is a poorly attested dialect term, probably linked to a craft or small trade in foodstuffs in an area of regional speech (a patois of northern or eastern France). Its precise meaning remains uncertain for lack of sufficient lexicographical sources.

marteleur.label: Marteleur (tree marker)
marteleur.summary: Forester who chose the trees to be worked and showed the resin tapper where to make the cut.
marteleur.text: In the forest, the marteleur chose the trees to be worked and showed the resin tapper ("gemmeur") where to make the cut for collecting the resin, marking the tree with the forester's hammer.

marteleur_forestier.label: Marteleur forestier (tree marker)
marteleur_forestier.summary: Forestry officer who marked with a hammer the trees to be felled.
marteleur_forestier.text: The marteleur forestier marked the trees selected for felling with a blow of a hammer bearing an official stamp, in accordance with the rules of forest management and planning, a function still practised today in the forestry administration.

marteleur_forgeron.label: Marteleur forgeron (hammerman)
marteleur_forgeron.summary: Forge worker specialised in hammering metals to shape them.
marteleur_forgeron.text: The marteleur forgeron hammered metal heated in the forge to give it its shape, an essential physical task in iron and steel work before mechanical steam hammers came into use.

martineteur.label: Martinéteur (tilt-hammer operator)
martineteur.summary: Worker who operated the martinet, a water-powered hammer used in metalworking.
martineteur.text: The martinéteur operated the "martinet" (tilt hammer), a heavy mechanical hammer driven by the hydraulic power of a waterwheel, used to crush or forge metal in forges and foundries before the age of steam.

martineur.label: Martineur (brazier, tilt-hammer smith)
martineur.summary: Craftsman who made brass and copper objects with the tilt hammer, the equivalent of the coppersmith.
martineur.text: The martineur shaped brass and copper objects with the tilt hammer ("martinet"), a speciality close to copperware ("dinanderie"), working the yellow metals to produce household utensils and everyday objects.

massaro.label: Massaro (Italian farm manager)
massaro.summary: Manager or tenant of a farmstead (masseria) in Italy; in some towns, keeper of communal property.
massaro.text: In southern Italy the massaro runs a masseria on his own account or for the landowner, directing the labourers, the livestock and the sowing; the word often denotes a well-off peasant who owns oxen and tools. In northern and central Italy the massaro was also a municipal or confraternity officer who kept and administered the community's property. The meaning must therefore be read according to the region and the context of the record.

massier.label: Massier (mace-bearer)
massier.summary: Court officer who carried a mace as the emblem of his office, equivalent to the royal sergeant.
massier.text: The massier was a court officer or usher who carried a mace as a sign of his office during official ceremonies, a ceremonial role close to that of the royal sergeant or the beadle depending on the context, civil or religious.

mastiqueur.label: Mastiqueur (putty worker)
mastiqueur.summary: Craftsman who applied putty and other sealants for joints and repairs.
mastiqueur.text: The mastiqueur applied putty to seal joints, repair cracks or fix window panes, common auxiliary work in building, glazing or the navy depending on the context.

matelassier.label: Matelassier (mattress maker)
matelassier.summary: Craftsman who made mattresses and stuffed bedding.
matelassier.text: The matelassier made mattresses, cushions and other bedding stuffed with wool, horsehair or feathers, a craft linked to upholstery and bedding that flourished with the improvement of domestic comfort in the 18th and 19th centuries.

matelot.label: Matelot (sailor, deckhand)
matelot.summary: Crew member who carried out the manoeuvres aboard a ship, without any command role.
matelot.text: The matelot was a crew member responsible for routine work on board (sails, rigging, maintenance), without any command responsibility, as opposed to the officer or the master. A generic naval term, it was subdivided by seniority or speciality (matelot of the 1st, 2nd or 3rd class, topman).

matelot_de_1e_classe.label: Matelot de 1re classe (able seaman, first class)
matelot_de_1e_classe.summary: Sailor's rank corresponding to the highest level of seniority and skill.
matelot_de_1e_classe.text: The matelot de 1re classe held the highest rank in the hierarchy of seamen, recognising seniority and experience gained at sea, with higher pay than the lower classes.

matelot_de_2e_classe.label: Matelot de 2e classe (seaman, second class)
matelot_de_2e_classe.summary: Intermediate sailor's rank, between the beginner and the experienced seaman.
matelot_de_2e_classe.text: The matelot de 2e classe held an intermediate rank in the navy's hierarchy of seamen, between the novice and the most experienced matelot de 1re classe.

matelot_de_3e_classe.label: Matelot de 3e classe (seaman, third class)
matelot_de_3e_classe.summary: Beginner's sailor rank, the lowest in the seniority hierarchy.
matelot_de_3e_classe.text: The matelot de 3e classe held the lowest rank, generally given to beginners before they had acquired more seniority and experience at sea.

matelot_de_hune.label: Matelot de hune (topman)
matelot_de_hune.summary: Sailor specialised in handling the upper sails, working from the mast tops.
matelot_de_hune.text: The matelot de hune handled the ship's upper sails and kept lookout from the tops, the platforms at the head of the masts, a speciality that required agility and a head for heights.

matriculier.label: Matriculier (registrar)
matriculier.summary: Person responsible for keeping the registers and rolls of a parish or institution.
matriculier.text: The matriculier kept up to date the rolls and registers of a parish or an institution (confraternity, hospital), a record-keeping function close to, though not entirely the same as, that of the churchwarden or the vestry's procurator, the emphasis here being on keeping written records rather than on managing property.

matrone.label: Matrone (midwife)
matrone.summary: Experienced woman who assisted at childbirth, an old term for the midwife.
matrone.text: The matrone assisted women in childbirth, a role attested since Antiquity and the Middle Ages, before the profession was gradually regulated under the name of "sage-femme" (midwife) from the 17th and 18th centuries and officially recognised by a diploma.

maturier.label: Mâturier (mast maker)
maturier.summary: Craftsman who made masts for ships and other naval construction.
maturier.text: The mâturier shaped ships' masts, a specialised shipbuilding carpentry task that required selecting and assembling long, strong pieces of timber, essential in naval dockyard ports.

mayoral.label: Mayoral (Spanish head shepherd)
mayoral.summary: Head shepherd in charge of a herd; by extension, foreman of an estate or driver of a stagecoach.
mayoral.text: The mayoral was the chief shepherd in charge of a herd, particularly a transhumant one, directing the rabadanes and zagales. By extension the term also designates the foreman of the workers on an estate and, in the 19th century, the chief driver of a stagecoach or passenger carriage.

mayorazgo.label: Mayorazgo (Spanish entailed-estate holder)
mayorazgo.summary: Holder of a Spanish entailed estate that passed undivided, usually to the eldest son.
mayorazgo.text: The mayorazgo was the institution that entailed an estate so that it passed intact from generation to generation in the order set by its founder, normally to the eldest son; by extension, the term also designates its holder and the firstborn son due to inherit it. Entailed property could be neither sold nor divided. The disentailment laws of the 19th century (1820 and 1841) abolished the institution.

mazelier.label: Mazelier (butcher)
mazelier.summary: Provençal and Occitan term for the butcher, from the word "mazel" (slaughterhouse, butchery).
mazelier.text: Mazelier was the name given in Provence and in the Occitan-speaking area to the butcher — the word comes from "mazel", meaning the slaughterhouse or meat market (related to the Italian macello and the Catalan macell). The term, common in southern records of the Ancien Régime, is simply a regional equivalent of "boucher" rather than a distinct speciality.

mecanicien.label: Mécanicien (mechanic, engineer)
mecanicien.summary: Craftsman or worker who made, maintained and repaired machines and mechanisms.
mecanicien.text: The mécanicien made, maintained and repaired machines and mechanisms, a trade that developed and diversified considerably with the rise of industrialisation in the 19th century (steam engines, then motors), moving from the status of craftsman to that of skilled factory worker.

medailleur.label: Médailleur (medallist)
medailleur.summary: Engraver who made medals and commemorative metal objects.
medailleur.text: The médailleur engraved and struck medals and commemorative metal objects, an art close to goldsmithing and metal engraving, called upon for coins, decorations and official souvenirs.

medecin_de_bestial.label: Médecin de bestial (cattle doctor)
medecin_de_bestial.summary: Empirical practitioner who treated farm animals, forerunner of the modern veterinarian.
medecin_de_bestial.text: The médecin de bestial treated domestic and farm animals by largely empirical methods, before the creation of the veterinary schools (Lyon 1762, Alfort 1766) that gave rise to the profession of qualified veterinary surgeon.

medecin_veterinaire.label: Médecin vétérinaire (veterinary surgeon)
medecin_veterinaire.summary: Qualified practitioner trained at a veterinary school who treated domestic and farm animals.
medecin_veterinaire.text: The médecin vétérinaire was a practitioner trained at a veterinary school (the first in France being founded at Lyon in 1762 and then at Alfort in 1766), succeeding the empirical cattle doctors ("médecins de bestial") and bringing a scientific approach to animal care.

medico_condotto.label: Medico condotto (municipal doctor)
medico_condotto.summary: Doctor paid by an Italian municipality to treat its inhabitants and to care for the poor free of charge.
medico_condotto.text: The medico condotto was hired by the municipality under a contract called a condotta to attend the inhabitants, and especially the poor on the municipal list, often including those in the most remote hamlets. A central figure of Italian rural health care from the 19th century until the 1978 health reform, he worked alongside the municipal midwife and, for animals, the municipal veterinarian.

medico_de_partido.label: Médico de partido (municipal physician)
medico_de_partido.summary: Physician hired and paid by a municipality or an institution to treat the population, especially the poor.
medico_de_partido.text: The médico de partido is hired by a municipal council, a Misericórdia or another institution for a fixed salary (the "partido") to provide medical care to the inhabitants of an area, treating the poor free of charge. The system, which also existed for surgeons and apothecaries, long ensured the presence of practitioners in small towns and rural municipalities.

meekrapteler.label: Meekrapteler (madder grower)
meekrapteler.summary: Farmer who grew madder, a plant whose root yields a red dye.
meekrapteler.text: Madder was an important cash crop, especially in Zeeland and West Brabant. The plants usually stayed in the ground for more than a year before the roots were dug up and sold to the madder kilns. The occupation disappeared when synthetic dyes replaced natural madder.

meestoofwerker.label: Meestoofwerker (madder mill worker)
meestoofwerker.summary: Worker in a meestoof, where madder roots were processed into dye.
meestoofwerker.text: In the madder kilns (meestoven) the dried roots of the madder plant were dried further, pounded and ground into a red dye widely used in textile dyeing. The meestoof workers did this heavy and dusty work, mainly in Zeeland and West Brabant and mostly in the winter months. Cultivation and processing declined after the invention of synthetic alizarin in the second half of the 19th century.

mege.label: Mège (folk healer)
mege.summary: Folk healer, especially in the south of France, practising traditional empirical medicine.
mege.text: The mège was a folk healer, a term used mainly in the south and south-west of France, who treated people with traditional remedies, herbs or bone-setting, outside the framework of learned, qualified medicine. The word long retained a disparaging connotation of "quack" in the mouths of official physicians.

megissier.label: Mégissier (tawer)
megissier.summary: Craftsman who prepared fine skins (kid, lamb) to make supple leathers.
megissier.text: The mégissier prepared and tanned fine skins — kid, lamb, young goat — by a specific process (tawing, or "mégie", using alum and salt rather than vegetable tan) to produce supple leathers for glove making and fine leather goods. He thus differed from the tanner, who worked thicker hides (ox, cow) with tan. Mégicier is a spelling variant.

melamed.label: Mełamed (Jewish schoolteacher)
melamed.summary: Teacher in a Jewish elementary school (cheder).
melamed.text: The mełamed taught boys in the cheder, the traditional Jewish elementary school, to read Hebrew, the prayers and the basics of the Torah. He usually held school in his own home and was paid by the pupils’ parents.

melero.label: Melero (Spanish honey seller)
melero.summary: Person who sold or traded in honey.
melero.text: The melero sold honey at markets or from village to village, or bought it from beekeepers to resell. La Alcarria and other scrubland districts were known for the quality of their honey, which the meleros carried to the cities.

menager.label: Ménager (yeoman farmer)
menager.summary: Well-off peasant who owned his land and farm, managing his property on his own like a prudent householder.
menager.text: The ménager was a peasant owner or well-off farmer who managed his property "en bon père de famille" (as a prudent householder), an intermediate status between the laboureur and the ordinary sharecropper depending on the region (the term, very common in the south and south-west, often covers a reality close to that of the laboureur of the north).

menagere.label: Ménagère (housewife)
menagere.summary: Woman at home, responsible for running and looking after the household.
menagere.text: The ménagère devoted herself to running and looking after the family home — cooking, laundry, raising the children — an occupation which, though unpaid, was the main work of the many women recorded as such in civil registers, particularly in the 19th and early 20th centuries.

menagier.label: Ménagier (householder)
menagier.summary: Head of a family responsible for domestic economy and running the household.
menagier.text: The ménagier was the head of a household responsible for its domestic economy and the management of its property, an old masculine term related to ménager and ménagère, made famous notably by the well-known medieval treatise "Le Ménagier de Paris".

mendiant.label: Mendiant (beggar)
mendiant.summary: Person without resources who lived on public charity and alms.
mendiant.text: The mendiant lived on alms and public charity for lack of resources or work. Begging, sometimes tolerated and sometimes severely repressed depending on the period (the "dépôts de mendicité", or beggars' workhouses, under the Ancien Régime and in the 19th century), appears in civil registers concerning the poorest members of society.

menestrel.label: Ménestrel (minstrel)
menestrel.summary: Itinerant musician and poet who performed songs and tales at lordly courts.
menestrel.text: The minstrel was a medieval musician and poet, often itinerant, who performed songs, epic tales and poems at lordly courts and in public squares. Unlike the troubadour or trouvère, who wrote his own works, the minstrel was above all a performer in the service of a master.

menetrier.label: Ménétrier (village fiddler)
menetrier.summary: Popular musician who played traditional instruments at dances, festivities and ceremonies.
menetrier.text: The "ménétrier" played at dances, weddings and village festivals on the violin, the hurdy-gurdy or the bagpipes depending on the region. He was a popular musician indispensable to the festive life of the Ancien Régime countryside, and should be distinguished from the minstrel (ménestrel), a more lettered performer of the medieval courts.

meneur_de_moteur_a_gaz_pauvre.label: Meneur de moteur à gaz pauvre (producer-gas engine operator)
meneur_de_moteur_a_gaz_pauvre.summary: Operator who ran and maintained producer-gas engines, an industrial technology of the early 20th century.
meneur_de_moteur_a_gaz_pauvre.text: The "meneur de moteur à gaz pauvre" ran and maintained an engine fuelled by producer gas ("gaz pauvre", a gas generated by the incomplete combustion of coal or wood), an industrial technology used especially around the turn of the 20th century, before electricity became widespread.

meneur_de_rang_ardoisier.label: Meneur de rang ardoisier (slate-quarry gang leader)
meneur_de_rang_ardoisier.summary: Team leader in a slate quarry, overseeing the extraction and splitting of slate.
meneur_de_rang_ardoisier.text: The "meneur de rang" in a slate quarry led a team of workers, supervising the extraction and splitting of the slate, a way of organising work typical of the slate-producing areas (Anjou, the Ardennes, Trélazé).

meneur_de_rang_meuneuse.label: Meneur de rang, meunerie (mill gang leader)
meneur_de_rang_meuneuse.summary: Team leader in a mill, supervising the work of the mill hands.
meneur_de_rang_meuneuse.text: In the context of milling, the "meneur de rang" supervised a team of mill hands within a mill, organising the allocation and follow-up of the grinding tasks.

mentheur.label: Mentheur (mint grower and distiller)
mentheur.summary: Grower and distiller of mint, producing mint oil.
mentheur.text: The "mentheur" grew mint and distilled its essential oil, used in confectionery, perfumery or pharmacy. It was a specialised crop grown in certain favourable areas (notably Milly-la-Forêt for peppermint).

menuisier.label: Menuisier (joiner)
menuisier.summary: Woodworker who made furniture, doors, windows and panelling.
menuisier.text: The joiner worked wood to make everyday furniture, doors, windows, staircases and panelling, as distinct from the carpenter (charpentier), who built building frames, and the cabinetmaker (ébéniste), who made veneered furniture and fine marquetry. A very widespread trade, the joiner is among the craftsmen most frequently mentioned in civil registration records.

menuisier_a_livret.label: Menuisier à livret (joiner holding a worker's book)
menuisier_a_livret.summary: Wage-earning joiner required to hold a worker's book attesting to his employment and good conduct.
menuisier_a_livret.text: The "menuisier à livret" held the "livret ouvrier", a professional identity document introduced by Napoleon I in 1803 and compulsory until 1890, which recorded a wage worker's employment, certificates of good conduct and movements.

menuisier_monteur.label: Menuisier monteur (joinery assembler)
menuisier_monteur.summary: Joiner specialised in the assembly and final fitting of furniture or joinery components.
menuisier_monteur.text: The "menuisier monteur" handled the assembly and final fitting of previously shaped joinery or furniture parts, a specialisation of production-line work that emerged with the division of labour in larger workshops.

merandier.label: Mérandier (stave maker)
merandier.summary: Craftsman who split and shaped oak wood into staves for barrels.
merandier.text: The "mérandier" (also spelt "mairandier") was a craftsman specialised in making "merrain", the split oak staves that form the walls of casks and barrels. He worked upstream of the cooper, selecting and cutting the wood along the grain to make the casks watertight. The trade, closely tied to regions with oak forests (the Centre, Limousin, Burgundy), is sometimes also called "merrinier".

mercante_di_campagna.label: Mercante di campagna (Roman estate entrepreneur)
mercante_di_campagna.summary: In the Roman Campagna, an agricultural entrepreneur who leased large estates to grow grain or graze livestock with seasonal labour.
mercante_di_campagna.text: The mercante di campagna leased the vast estates of the Roman countryside from the great noble and church landowners and had them worked by hired hands and by seasonal labourers who came down from the mountains. A wealthy and influential class in the Papal States until the 19th century, these entrepreneurs combined farming with the grain and livestock trade.

mercelot.label: Mercelot (pedlar of haberdashery)
mercelot.summary: Small itinerant trader selling haberdashery and sundry goods in the villages.
mercelot.text: The "mercelot" hawked haberdashery and sundry goods from village to village on foot, carrying his wares on his back or in a basket — hence the nicknames "porte-balle" and "porte-panier" given to him in some regions.

mercier.label: Mercier (haberdasher, mercer)
mercier.summary: Merchant selling haberdashery: thread, buttons, ribbons and small sewing accessories.
mercier.text: The "mercier" sold haberdashery — thread, needles, buttons, ribbons, lace — indispensable for sewing and home dressmaking. The mercers' guild, one of the richest and most influential in Paris under the Ancien Régime (one of the "Six Corps"), covered a much broader trade than modern haberdashery alone.

mere_sage.label: Mère-sage (midwife)
mere_sage.summary: Old term for a midwife, who assisted at births and gave postnatal care.
mere_sage.text: The "mère-sage" assisted at births and gave first care to mothers and newborns. This old name was gradually replaced by "sage-femme" from the 17th and 18th centuries onwards, as the profession became organised and regulated.

merrineur.label: Merrineur (Meuse dialect term for a wood- or metalworker)
merrineur.summary: Dialect term from the Meuse area for a craftsman working wood or metal.
merrineur.text: "Merrineur" is a dialect variant attested in the Meuse area, probably denoting a craftsman working wood or metal. The term is uncommon and should not be wrongly confused with the "mérandier" (maker of staves for cooperage), although the similar sound may cause confusion.

mesoyer.label: Mésoyer (market gardener, Lorraine)
mesoyer.summary: Lorraine market gardener; in Metz, the mésoyers and the gardeners formed a single regulated trade.
mesoyer.text: The "mésoyer" grew vegetables in Lorraine, the term being a regional synonym for market gardener. In Metz, mésoyers and gardeners belonged to a single trade governed by a guild charter: anyone wishing to practise it for wages had to pay an entry fee (60 sous, reduced to 20 sous for masters' sons), and the trade's sworn officers were empowered to check the quality of the seed sold at the markets.

messager.label: Messager (messenger, carrier)
messager.summary: Person responsible for carrying and delivering messages, letters and parcels between places.
messager.text: The messenger carried and delivered messages, letters and parcels between different places, an essential function before the organisation of the royal and later national postal service. The term covers varied realities: a messenger on foot, a messenger driving a vehicle, or a messenger attached to an institution such as the university.

messager_a_pied.label: Messager à pied (messager_a_pied)
messager_a_pied.summary: Messager effectuant ses tournées à pied, sans monture ni véhicule.
messager_a_pied.text: Le messager à pied effectue ses déplacements et livraisons de courrier à pied, par opposition au messager à cheval ou en voiture, un mode de transport plus lent réservé aux liaisons de proximité.

messager_conducteur.label: Messager conducteur (carrier driver)
messager_conducteur.summary: Driver who carried goods and letters by vehicle.
messager_conducteur.text: The "messager conducteur" used a horse-drawn team or vehicle to carry goods and letters between places, a road carrier service that predates the development of the railways.

messager_des_universites.label: Messager des universités (university messenger)
messager_des_universites.summary: In the Middle Ages, official carrier of letters between a university and its distant students.
messager_des_universites.text: In the Middle Ages, the university messenger carried letters and allowances between a university's students (often far from their families) and their relatives, a recognised function sometimes protected by specific university privileges.

messier.label: Messier (crop warden)
messier.summary: Field warden responsible for watching over crops and standing harvests.
messier.text: The "messier" watched over crops and standing harvests, taking care to prevent theft, unlawful grazing or damage to the fields before the harvest, a communal office close to that of the rural policeman (garde champêtre). "Messeur" and "mussier" are regional spelling variants.

mesteiral.label: Mesteiral (guild craftsman)
mesteiral.summary: Craftsman of the mechanical trades (mesteres), organised in guilds and represented in municipal government.
mesteiral.text: The mesteiral practises one of the mechanical trades, called mesteres (shoemakers, tailors, smiths, carpenters, etc.), organised in guilds or "bandeiras". In the main towns the trades elected representatives to the Casa dos Vinte e Quatro, which in turn chose the juiz do povo and the procuradores dos mesteres who sat with the municipal council. The term appears in records to indicate artisan status, as opposed to farmers, nobles and clergy.

mesureur.label: Mesureur (timber measurer)
mesureur.summary: Specialist in a logging team who chose the trees to fell and calculated volumes.
mesureur.text: Within a team of woodcutters, the "mesureur" selected the trees to be felled and calculated the volumes of wood cut, a technical role of checking and estimation at the heart of forestry work.

mesureur_de_ble.label: Mesureur de blé (grain measurer)
mesureur_de_ble.summary: Public officer responsible for measuring the quantity and checking the quality of wheat at sales.
mesureur_de_ble.text: The "mesureur de blé" was a sworn public officer responsible for measuring the quantity and checking the quality of wheat during transactions at markets and covered market halls, ensuring fair dealing and the collection of the related dues.

mesureur_de_sel.label: Mesureur de sel (salt measurer)
mesureur_de_sel.summary: Public officer responsible for measuring the quantity and checking the quality of salt sold.
mesureur_de_sel.text: The "mesureur de sel" was a sworn public officer responsible for measuring and checking salt when it was sold, a particularly sensitive function under the Ancien Régime because of the "gabelle", a royal tax that weighed heavily on this commodity.

metari.label: Métari (salt-works hand)
metari.summary: Worker at the Arc-et-Senans salt works who kneaded the salt before it was sold.
metari.text: According to glossaries of old trades, the "métari" was a worker at the salt works of Arc-et-Senans (Doubs), where he kneaded the salt to prepare it for sale. Arc-et-Senans, where the famous Royal Saltworks were built in the 18th century, was one of the major salt-producing centres of Franche-Comté under the Ancien Régime.

metayer.label: Métayer (sharecropper)
metayer.summary: Peasant farming land owned by a landlord in exchange for a share of the harvest.
metayer.text: The sharecropper farmed land he did not own under a "métayage" contract, by which he shared the harvest (traditionally half and half) with the landowner, who often supplied part of the livestock and the buildings. This form of indirect tenure, very widespread in the South-West, the Centre and some parts of southern France until the 20th century, differs from tenant farming (fermage), in which the peasant paid a fixed rent in money rather than a variable share of the produce.

metier_de_rets.label: Métier de rets (net maker)
metier_de_rets.summary: Craftsman who made nets and fishing nets.
metier_de_rets.text: The term refers to the craftsman who made the nets ("rets") used for fishing, essential equipment in coastal and river communities. This trade overlaps with that of the "filetier" or net spinner, depending on the region and local usage in the records.

metivier.label: Métivier (harvest labourer)
metivier.summary: Seasonal farm worker employed to harvest and thresh cereals.
metivier.text: The "métivier" was a day labourer or farm worker hired for the harvest season to cut the wheat and thresh it. This kind of seasonal employment, common in the countryside under the Ancien Régime and in the 19th century, often supplemented other farming or craft activities during the rest of the year.

metteur_en_oeuvre.label: Metteur en œuvre (stone setter)
metteur_en_oeuvre.summary: Goldsmith's worker specialised in setting precious stones in jewellery.
metteur_en_oeuvre.text: In goldsmithing and jewellery, the "metteur en œuvre" was the craftsman who mounted and set precious or semi-precious stones in their metal settings, a step distinct from casting or polishing. The term "mise en œuvre" refers precisely to this final mounting of the piece.

metteuse_en_mains.label: Metteuse en mains (silk bundler)
metteuse_en_mains.summary: Silk worker who made up skeins into bundles called "mains".
metteuse_en_mains.text: In the silk industry, the "metteuse en mains" gathered silk threads or skeins into bundles of a set weight, called "mains", ready for weighing and sale. This trade, practised by women, was part of the processing chain for raw silk before weaving.

meublier.label: Meublier (furniture maker or dealer)
meublier.summary: Craftsman or merchant specialised in making and selling furniture.
meublier.text: The "meublier" made or sold furniture, a term used in France as in Quebec as an alternative to "menuisier en meubles" or "ébéniste" depending on the degree of finish. He differed from the cabinetmaker in generally less ornamental work, closer to utilitarian joinery.

meulier.label: Meulier (millstone maker)
meulier.summary: Craftsman who cut and made millstones.
meulier.text: The "meulier" quarried, cut and shaped millstones for grain mills, oil mills or other industrial uses from blocks of hard stone such as flint or buhrstone ("grès meulier"). The trade was especially common in regions with suitable quarries, such as La Ferté-sous-Jouarre in the Île-de-France.

meunier.label: Meunier (miller)
meunier.summary: Operator of a mill, responsible for grinding the villagers' grain.
meunier.text: The miller operated a water or wind mill and turned the parish's grain into flour, keeping a portion as payment (the "mouture"). The trade was often hereditary, with the mill itself rented from the local lord or abbey.

meusnier.label: Meusnier (miller)
meusnier.summary: Old spelling variant of meunier, the craftsman who ground grain at the mill.
meusnier.text: "Meusnier" is an old or dialect spelling of "meunier", the miller who ran a grain mill on behalf of a parish's inhabitants, generally keeping a share of the flour (the "droit de mouture") as payment. This spelling variant is found mainly in records earlier than the 18th century.

migautier.label: Migautier (Norman orchard farmer)
migautier.summary: In Normandy, a farmer who worked an orchard and traded in fruit and its products, notably cider.
migautier.text: The "migautier" worked an orchard in Normandy and sold the fruit and the products made from it, in particular cider, the region's traditional drink. "Migotier" is a spelling variant.

miguelete.label: Miguelete (Catalan or Basque militiaman)
miguelete.summary: Member of the Catalan armed companies of the 17th and 18th centuries, and later of provincial police corps.
miguelete.text: The migueletes (miquelets) were Catalan mountain fusiliers, organised in irregular companies that fought in the wars of the 17th and 18th centuries. In the 19th century the name also designated provincial armed corps, such as the miqueletes of Gipuzkoa, responsible for surveillance and public order.

milicien.label: Milicien (militiaman)
milicien.summary: Soldier belonging to a militia, a non-permanent auxiliary armed force.
milicien.text: The militiaman served in a militia, a local or regional armed force raised to supplement the regular army, notably under the Ancien Régime through the drawing of lots for the "milice royale" established in 1688. Unlike the professional soldier, the militiaman often remained a civilian called up temporarily for service.

militaire.label: Militaire (serviceman, soldier)
militaire.summary: Member of the armed forces, a generic term for a serving soldier.
militaire.text: "Militaire" is the generic term for anyone belonging to the army, with no indication of rank or arm. It frequently appears as an occupation in 19th- and 20th-century civil registration records, particularly for men on active service at the time of the record.

militaire_de_reserve.label: Militaire de réserve (reservist)
militaire_de_reserve.summary: Soldier attached to the army reserve, liable to be called up when needed outside active service.
militaire_de_reserve.text: The reservist belonged to the army reserve: he had received military training but was not on permanent active service, remaining liable to call-up in time of war or need. This entry appears especially in records concerning men who had completed their compulsory military service.

militaire_retraite.label: Militaire retraité (retired serviceman)
militaire_retraite.summary: Former serviceman who had left active service and drew a retirement pension.
militaire_retraite.text: The retired serviceman was a former member of the armed forces who had completed his career and, where applicable, received a military pension. The mention of this status in a record points to an earlier military career, sometimes supplemented by other details such as rank or regiment.

minageur.label: Minageur (collector of the minage toll)
minageur.summary: Officer responsible for collecting the minage due on grain sold at market.
minageur.text: Under the Ancien Régime, the "minageur" collected the "droit de minage", a tax owed on each measure ("mine") of grain sold at the public market, often for the benefit of the lord or the community. The office combined tax collection with the supervision of local grain transactions.

mineron.label: Mineron (small independent miner)
mineron.summary: Small mine operator who worked a vein he owned with his family.
mineron.text: The "mineron" worked a mineral vein on a small scale, often with his family, and owned it himself, as opposed to the wage-earning miner employed by a company. This artisanal form of mining long coexisted with industrial mining in some French mining regions.

mineur.label: Mineur (miner)
mineur.summary: Worker who extracted minerals from the ground, on the surface or in underground galleries.
mineur.text: The miner worked at extracting minerals — coal, iron, salt and so on — whether in open-cast quarries or in underground galleries. The trade grew and industrialised considerably in the 19th century with the rise of the coalfields, bringing hard and dangerous working conditions.

mineur_explosifs.label: Mineur, explosifs (shot-firer)
mineur_explosifs.summary: Worker responsible for placing and detonating explosive charges on a site.
mineur_explosifs.text: This specialised miner placed and fired the explosive charges needed to break rock, whether in mines, quarries or major earthworks (roads, tunnels, railways). The job required a specific qualification distinct from that of the ordinary underground miner.

miniaturiste.label: Miniaturiste (miniaturist)
miniaturiste.summary: Painter specialised in miniatures, painted meticulously in tiny dots of colour.
miniaturiste.text: The miniaturist painted miniatures — very small portraits or scenes, often meant to be worn in a locket or inserted in a book — using fine brushes and delicate colours. The art of the miniature reached its height in the 17th and 18th centuries before being largely supplanted by photography in the 19th century.

minotier.label: Minotier (flour-mill owner, industrial miller)
minotier.summary: Owner or operator of a flour mill, an industrial milling business.
minotier.text: The "minotier" ran a "minoterie", a mechanised industrial flour mill that appeared in the 19th century and turned grain into flour on a far larger scale than the traditional mill. The term marks the industrial transformation of the miller's trade, between small family businesses and large commercial flour mills.

miodosytnik.label: Miodosytnik (mead maker)
miodosytnik.text: The miodosytnik made mead by fermenting honey diluted with water, often with fruit juices and spices added. Mead was a common and prized drink in old Poland, and mead makers formed their own guilds in some towns.

miroitier.label: Miroitier (mirror maker)
miroitier.summary: Craftsman who made and sold looking-glasses and mirrors.
miroitier.text: The "miroitier" made, polished and sold mirrors and looking-glasses, a craft that developed particularly in France with the royal glass manufactory of Saint-Gobain from the 17th century onwards. Depending on the period and place, he might be a manufacturer or simply a dealer or fitter of mirrors.

miseur.label: Miseur (town treasurer)
miseur.summary: Municipal officer responsible for the accounts and the management of public works under the Ancien Régime.
miseur.text: In some Ancien Régime municipalities (notably in the North and in Artois), the "miseur" was the officer responsible for keeping the town's accounts and supervising expenditure on civil and military works. The office resembled that of a municipal treasurer or receiver.

moblot.label: Moblot (Mobile Guard soldier)
moblot.summary: Nickname given to soldiers of the Garde nationale mobile during the war of 1870.
moblot.text: The "moblot" was a soldier of the Garde nationale mobile, a reserve military formation created in 1868 and mobilised on a massive scale during the Franco-Prussian War of 1870–1871. The familiar term refers to these young recruits, often poorly trained, who were thrown into battle alongside the regular army.

modeleur_sur_bois.label: Modeleur sur bois (wooden pattern maker)
modeleur_sur_bois.summary: Craftsman who made the wooden patterns used to cast metal in a foundry.
modeleur_sur_bois.text: The "modeleur sur bois" made wooden patterns reproducing the shape of a part, which were then used to make the sand mould into which the molten metal would be poured. This trade, halfway between joinery and founding, demanded great precision, since the slightest flaw in the pattern reappeared on the cast part.

modiste.label: Modiste (milliner)
modiste.summary: Craftswoman specialised in designing and selling women's hats.
modiste.text: The milliner designed, made and sold women's hats and headdresses, a trade that flourished in the 19th century with the fashion for hats trimmed with ribbons, feathers and flowers. She is distinct from the hatter (chapelier), who traditionally worked mainly for a male clientele.

moireur.label: Moireur (moiré finisher)
moireur.summary: Worker who gave fabrics or metals a watered, shimmering moiré finish.
moireur.text: The "moireur" applied to fabrics (especially silk) or certain metals a treatment — pressure, heat or calendering — that produces the rippling sheen characteristic of moiré. This textile finishing trade came at the end of manufacture, to enhance fabrics intended for luxury clothing or furnishing.

moliceiro.label: Moliceiro (aquatic-weed gatherer, Aveiro lagoon)
moliceiro.summary: Boatman of the Aveiro lagoon who gathered moliço, aquatic plants used as fertiliser.
moliceiro.text: The moliceiro gathers moliço, the algae and aquatic plants of the Ria de Aveiro, using a flat-bottomed boat with a high painted prow, also called a moliceiro, and carries it to the fields, where it served as fertiliser. The activity, important until the mid-20th century, gave its name to the lagoon's emblematic boat.

molleur.label: Molleur (founder-moulder)
molleur.summary: Regional synonym for founder-moulder, a worker handling molten metal.
molleur.text: According to glossaries of old trades, the "molleur" was a founder-moulder: a foundry worker who prepared alloys, watched over the melting of the metal and poured it into moulds to produce metal parts.

molleux.label: Molleux (tile moulder)
molleux.summary: In a tile works, a worker who moulded tiles, sometimes directly on his thighs.
molleux.text: In a tile works, the "molleux" moulded the tiles by hand, sometimes directly on his thighs, before they were fired.

molleux_briqueterie.label: Molleux, briqueterie (brickworks clay worker)
molleux_briqueterie.summary: Brickworks hand who worked the soft clay before moulding.
molleux_briqueterie.text: The "molleux" prepared and worked the still-soft clay in a brickworks before it was moulded into bricks, then dried and fired. This job, upstream of the moulding proper, was common in the small-scale brickworks of the 19th and early 20th centuries.

molleux_tuilerie.label: Molleux, tuilerie (tile-works clay worker)
molleux_tuilerie.summary: Tile-works hand who worked the soft clay before the tiles were shaped.
molleux_tuilerie.text: The "molleux" in a tile works prepared the still-pliable clay used to shape the tiles, before the drying and firing stages. The job is the tile-works equivalent of the one performed in a brickworks.

monaguillo.label: Monaguillo (Spanish altar boy)
monaguillo.summary: Boy who assisted the priest at Mass and other services.
monaguillo.text: The monaguillo assisted the priest at the altar: he made the responses at Mass, carried the cruets, the censer or the cross and rang the bell. In some parishes and cathedrals he received a small payment and was trained as a future cleric or singer.

monatto.label: Monatto (plague corpse bearer)
monatto.summary: Man employed to carry and bury the dead and to move the sick during plague epidemics.
monatto.text: The monatti, recruited by the health authorities during plagues, collected corpses from houses and streets, carried them on carts to mass graves and took the sick to the lazaretto. Made famous by the description of the 1630 Milan plague in The Betrothed (I promessi sposi), they were feared for their abuses.

mondina.label: Mondina (rice-field weeder)
mondina.summary: Seasonal woman worker in the rice fields who pulled out the weeds.
mondina.text: The mondina, usually a young woman, worked in spring with her feet in the water of the rice fields of the Po plain (Vercelli, Novara and Lomellina areas) for the monda, the weeding, and sometimes for transplanting. This hard seasonal work drew thousands of women from other provinces every year, until mechanisation and chemical weeding after the Second World War.

monnayeur.label: Monnayeur (moneyer, coiner)
monnayeur.summary: Worker in a mint who struck coins.
