monnayeur.text: The moneyer worked in a mint ("hôtel des monnaies"), where he took part in making coins: preparing the blanks and striking them with a hammer or a screw press. "Monnoyeur" is an old spelling, common before modern spelling was fixed.

mont_de_piete.label: Mont-de-Piété (public pawnshop)
mont_de_piete.summary: Pawnbroking establishment run by a public or charitable institution.
mont_de_piete.text: The Mont-de-Piété was a lending establishment, often charitable or municipal in origin, that made loans on pledges — an advance of money against the deposit of an item of value. The model, born in Italy ("monte di pietà") in the 15th century, spread to France from the 16th century onwards; the associated occupation generally refers to an employee or officer of such an establishment.

monteur.label: Monteur (fitter, assembler)
monteur.summary: Worker who assembled and installed mechanical parts or building components.
monteur.text: The fitter assembled mechanical or electrical parts or structures, a generic term that diversified with industrialisation (electrical fitter, steel-frame erector, appliance fitter and so on). The exact meaning depends heavily on the context and period of the record.

montreur_d_ours.label: Montreur d'ours (bear leader)
montreur_d_ours.summary: Travelling showman who presented trained bears in street performances.
montreur_d_ours.text: The bear leader was an itinerant showman, often from the Pyrenees (especially the Ariège), who travelled through towns and villages with a trained bear to give public shows. This once-widespread travelling trade gradually disappeared in the 20th century when the training and exhibition of these animals was banned.

montreur_de_singes.label: Montreur de singes (monkey showman)
montreur_de_singes.summary: Travelling showman who presented trained monkeys in street performances.
montreur_de_singes.text: The monkey showman was an itinerant performer who exhibited trained monkeys at public shows, often alongside other fairground acts. Like the bear leader, this entertainer's trade belonged to the world of the travelling shows of former times.

morgado.label: Morgado (holder of an entailed estate)
morgado.summary: Holder of a morgadio, a body of entailed, inalienable property usually passed to the eldest son.
morgado.text: The morgado is the administrator of a morgadio (or vínculo), an estate settled so as to be inalienable and indivisible and passed, as a rule, to the eldest son, in order to preserve a family's standing and means. By extension, the word also denotes the eldest son and heir of the house. Morgadios were abolished in Portugal in 1863. The deeds founding entails and the successions of morgados are valuable genealogical sources.

mortelier.label: Mortelier (mortar maker)
mortelier.summary: Craftsman who prepared and supplied the mortar used in masonry.
mortelier.text: The "mortelier" made and supplied mortar (a mixture of lime or cement, sand and water) for masons to bind stones or bricks. The term "morteleur" is a variant referring more specifically to the labourer who prepared and applied the mortar on site.

morutier.label: Morutier (cod fisherman)
morutier.text: The "morutier" was a seafaring fisherman specialised in cod fishing, carried out notably on the Grand Banks of Newfoundland by crews from Norman and Breton ports (Fécamp, Saint-Malo, Paimpol) from the 16th to the 20th century. This distant, seasonal fishing, the "grande pêche", involved long campaigns of several months at sea.

mosaiste.label: Mosaïste (mosaicist)
mosaiste.summary: Craftsman or artist who composed mosaics from small assembled fragments.
mosaiste.text: The mosaicist assembled small fragments of stone, glass or ceramic (tesserae) to create decorative patterns on floors, walls or objects. This craft, inherited from Antiquity, enjoyed a revival in the 19th century in religious and public architecture.

mosselvisser.label: Mosselvisser (mussel fisher)
mosselvisser.summary: Fisher who dredged mussels or raised them on plots.
mosselvisser.text: Mussel fishing was practised mainly in the waters of Zeeland and later in the Wadden Sea. The fishermen gathered young mussels, laid them out on leased plots and dredged them up again after one or two years for sale.

moulangeur.label: Moulangeur (millwright)
moulangeur.summary: Carpenter specialised in building and repairing windmills and watermills.
moulangeur.text: The "moulangeur" (or "amoulangeur", "emmoulageur" depending on the region) was a carpenter specialised in building and maintaining windmills and watermills, especially their wooden mechanisms (wheels, sails, gearing). The term, not to be confused with "boulanger" (baker) despite the similar sound, is found mainly in Anjou and Loire-Atlantique.

mouleur.label: Mouleur (moulder, caster)
mouleur.summary: Craftsman who made moulds and cast pieces in various materials.
mouleur.text: The moulder made moulds and poured material into them (plaster, metal, sand, wax) to reproduce a shape in series, a trade common to many industries: founding, sculpture, ceramics, the building trade. His specialisations (plaster moulder, sand moulder, statuary moulder) indicate the material or type of piece worked.

mouleur_en_platre.label: Mouleur en plâtre (plaster caster)
mouleur_en_platre.summary: Craftsman who made plaster casts, notably ornaments and decorative figures.
mouleur_en_platre.text: The plaster caster poured plaster into moulds to produce architectural ornaments, decorative figures or reproductions of sculptures. The trade was in strong demand in the 19th century with the craze for interior decoration in stucco and moulded plaster.

mouleur_en_sable.label: Mouleur en sable (sand moulder)
mouleur_en_sable.summary: Foundry worker who made the sand moulds into which metal was cast.
mouleur_en_sable.text: In a foundry, the sand moulder prepared the mould of compacted sand that would receive the molten metal to form the desired part. This sand-moulding technique is still one of the most common methods in industrial founding today.

mouleur_statuaire.label: Mouleur statuaire (statuary moulder)
mouleur_statuaire.summary: Craftsman specialised in moulding statues and sculptural works.
mouleur_statuaire.text: The statuary moulder made, from a sculptor's original work, the moulds from which copies could be cast in plaster, bronze or another material. This trade allowed sculpted works to be distributed in series, notably for public and private decoration in the 19th century.

moulier.label: Moulier (mould maker, button moulds)
moulier.summary: Craftsman who made moulds used in particular for the production of buttons.
moulier.text: The "moulier" made small moulds used in various craft productions, in particular button making. The term is found mainly in regions where a small-scale button-making industry existed.

moulineur_mineur.label: Moulineur, mine (narrow-seam miner)
moulineur_mineur.summary: Miner who worked at extraction in narrow galleries.
moulineur_mineur.text: In mining vocabulary, the "moulineur" was a worker assigned to extraction in galleries of small cross-section ("boyaux"), particularly arduous work in a confined space. This job is distinct from that of the face miner working in the wider main galleries.

moulinier_a_draps.label: Moulinier (silk throwster)
moulinier_a_draps.summary: Textile worker who twisted and prepared yarn, notably silk, before weaving.
moulinier_a_draps.text: The "moulinier" carried out throwing ("moulinage"), the operation of twisting and combining threads (especially silk) to give them the strength needed for weaving. This trade, central to the silk industry (particularly around Lyon), could also apply to the processing of other fibres intended for cloth-making or other fabrics.

moulurier.label: Moulurier (moulding maker)
moulurier.summary: Craftsman who shaped decorative mouldings, notably in wood.
moulurier.text: The "moulurier" cut and shaped mouldings — decorative relief profiles — for the ornamentation of furniture, panelling or architectural elements. The trade is related to that of the ornamentalist and the specialised joiner.

mousquetaire.label: Mousquetaire (musketeer)
mousquetaire.summary: Soldier armed with a musket, or member of an elite company of the king's household.
mousquetaire.text: In the broad sense, the musketeer was an infantry soldier armed with a musket, a portable firearm that appeared in the 16th century. The term also refers more specifically to members of the famous companies of Musketeers of the king's military household, an elite corps of the royal cavalry created in the 17th century.

mousselinier.label: Mousselinier (muslin weaver)
mousselinier.text: The "mousselinier" wove muslin, a very light, fine cotton or silk fabric whose production developed in France in the 18th and 19th centuries, notably in the textile regions of the North and Normandy.

moussier.label: Moussier (plough smith)
moussier.summary: In southern France, a blacksmith and edge-tool maker specialised in making the charrue-mousse plough.
moussier.text: In the south of France, the "moussier" was a blacksmith or edge-tool maker specialised in making a type of plough called the "charrue-mousse", a technical development of the traditional ard. The "mousse" here refers to the tool's mouldboard, the part that turns over the ploughed soil — a meaning unrelated to the "mousse", the young apprentice sailor.

moutardier.label: Moutardier (mustard maker)
moutardier.summary: Craftsman or merchant who made and sold mustard.
moutardier.text: The "moutardier" made and sold mustard, a condiment whose craft production developed especially in Dijon, the town that gave its name to French mustard and where the guild of vinegar and mustard makers was historically organised.

mozo_de_escuadra.label: Mozo de escuadra (Catalan police officer)
mozo_de_escuadra.summary: Member of the Mossos d'Esquadra, the Catalan armed police force created in the 18th century.
mozo_de_escuadra.text: The Mossos d'Esquadra were formed in Catalonia in the early 18th century as armed squads charged with pursuing banditry and keeping order in the countryside. Linked to the administration of the Principality, the corps was dissolved and re-established several times during the 19th and 20th centuries.

mulassier_eleveur.label: Mulassier (mule breeder)
mulassier_eleveur.summary: Breeder specialised in the production of mules.
mulassier_eleveur.text: The "mulassier" bred mules, hybrid animals produced by crossing a donkey with a mare, highly sought after as pack and draught animals. Some regions, such as Poitou and the Pyrenees, specialised in this breeding, supplying a trade in mules as far as southern Europe.

muletier.label: Muletier (muleteer)
muletier.summary: Mule driver employed to carry goods and travellers.
muletier.text: The muleteer drove laden mules to carry goods or passengers, especially in mountainous regions or on roads poorly suited to wheeled vehicles. This carrier's trade, distinct from that of the mule breeder (mulassier), long accounted for a large share of overland trade in rugged areas.

mulquinier.label: Mulquinier (fine linen weaver)
mulquinier.summary: Weaver specialised in fine linen cloths such as batiste and muslin.
mulquinier.text: The "mulquinier" wove fine, light linen cloths — batiste, lawn, muslin — a craft particularly developed in the Cambrésis and the Valenciennes area from the 17th to the 19th century, where the mulquiniers formed a guild separate from the weavers of coarse cloth. Some also specialised in lace or other delicate fabrics derived from this skill.

musicien.label: Musicien (musician)
musicien.summary: Person who practised music as a profession, as an instrumentalist or singer.
musicien.text: The musician practised music professionally, as an instrumentalist, singer or conductor, in a wide range of settings (theatre, church, orchestra, military band, dances). The generic term frequently appears in records with no further detail of the speciality practised.

musicien_compositeur.label: Musicien-compositeur (musician and composer)
musicien_compositeur.summary: Musician who composed his own works as well as performing them.
musicien_compositeur.text: The musician-composer both performed music and composed original works, a dual activity that set him apart from the mere instrumentalist or performing singer.

nachtwaechter.label: Night watchman (Nachtwächter)
nachtwaechter.summary: Watchman appointed by the community who patrols the streets at night, calls the hours and watches for fire.
nachtwaechter.text: The Nachtwächter walks the streets of a town or village at night, calls out the hours at fixed times, often with a verse and a horn, and watches for fire, burglary and disturbance of the peace. He was employed by the community and poorly paid; the office was frequently held by older men or day labourers and survived in many places until the late 19th century.

nachtwaker.label: Nachtwaker (night watchman)
nachtwaker.summary: Town watchman who walked the streets at night to prevent fire and theft.
nachtwaker.text: The night watchman made his rounds through the streets of the town or village at night, called out the hours and kept watch against fire, burglary and disorder. He carried a clapper or a rattle, hence the names klapperman and ratelwacht, with which he could raise the alarm. With the introduction of street lighting and a professional police force the office disappeared during the 19th and 20th centuries.

nacrier.label: Nacrier (mother-of-pearl worker)
nacrier.summary: Craftsman who worked mother-of-pearl, notably to make buttons.
nacrier.text: The "nacrier" turned mother-of-pearl — the iridescent inner layer of certain shells — into buttons, knife handles, inlays and small decorative objects. Mother-of-pearl working developed especially around Méru in the Oise, a major centre of pearl-button making from the 18th to the 20th century.

naquetier.label: Naquetier (real-tennis marker)
naquetier.summary: Official responsible for keeping the score in games of jeu de paume.
naquetier.text: The "naquetier" refereed and kept the score in games of jeu de paume (real tennis), the ancestor of tennis, in the courts devoted to this game, which was very popular in France from the 15th to the 17th century. The office disappeared with the decline of jeu de paume from the 18th century onwards.

nattier.label: Nattier (mat maker)
nattier.summary: Craftsman who plaited plant-fibre mats to cover floors and walls.
nattier.text: The "nattier" made plaited mats, usually of straw, rush or wicker, used to cover floors or walls before carpets and parquet flooring became widespread. This inexpensive covering was common in modest dwellings as well as in some rooms of well-to-do houses.

nautonnier.label: Nautonnier (boatman)
nautonnier.summary: Boatman who carried passengers or goods on the water.
nautonnier.text: The "nautonnier" steered a boat or river craft, carrying people or goods on rivers and canals. The term, rather literary and archaic in use, also evokes the mythological figure of the ferryman (such as Charon), and its Latinising equivalent "naviculaire" is found in some records.

navetier.label: Navetier (shuttle maker)
navetier.summary: Craftsman who made the shuttles used by weavers on their looms.
navetier.text: The "navetier" made shuttles, small wooden pieces that carry the weft thread from one side of the loom to the other. This ancillary trade of the textile industry supplied a tool indispensable to every weaver in a region.

navigateur.label: Navigateur (navigator)
navigateur.summary: Crew member responsible for determining the position and course of a ship or aircraft.
navigateur.text: The navigator determined the position and the course to follow using specialised instruments, whether on board a ship or, more recently, an aircraft. This aircrew role, essential before modern positioning systems became widespread, existed as a trade in its own right in the 20th century.

negociant.label: Négociant (wholesale merchant)
negociant.summary: Wholesale merchant who bought and resold goods on a large scale.
negociant.text: The "négociant" engaged in wholesale trade, often over long distances, buying and reselling a variety of goods (colonial produce, textiles, wines, raw materials). He differed from the ordinary merchant or shopkeeper in the scale of his business and frequently in greater social standing, which made the term a mark of status in civil registration records.

niolleur.label: Niolleur (dealer in renovated old hats)
niolleur.summary: Dealer in second-hand hats made good as new, and by extension in old clothes.
niolleur.text: The "niolleur" (an old-fashioned slang term) was a dealer in "niolles", old damaged hats restored for resale, an activity typical of the Temple district of Paris in the 19th century, a centre of the second-hand clothes trade. By extension, the term could refer more broadly to a dealer in old clothes.

norretier.label: Norretier (maker of surveying instruments)
norretier.summary: Craftsman who made norres, measuring instruments used by surveyors.
norretier.text: The "norretier" made "norres", instruments used by land surveyors to take their measurements. The term "nortier" is a regional variant. Poorly documented, the trade seems to have been rare and localised.

notaire.label: Notaire (notary)
notaire.summary: Public officer who drafted and kept legal deeds.
notaire.text: The notary was a royal (later republican) public officer responsible for drafting and preserving legal deeds: marriage contracts, probate inventories, property sales, wills. Notarial records are among the richest sources for genealogy, often far more detailed than parish registers.

notaire_apostolique.label: Notaire apostolique (apostolic notary)
notaire_apostolique.summary: Church officer empowered by the Holy See to draw up deeds under canon law.
notaire_apostolique.text: The apostolic notary was appointed by papal authority to draw up deeds falling under canon law and Church administration. His office, distinct from that of the royal or seigneurial notary, was exercised within the ecclesiastical jurisdictions (officialities, chapters, bishoprics).

notaire_garde_scel.label: Notaire garde-scel (notary keeper of the seal)
notaire_garde_scel.summary: Officer responsible for keeping the seal and affixing it to notarial deeds.
notaire_garde_scel.text: The "notaire garde-scel" kept the official seal and affixed it to the deeds authenticated by the jurisdiction to which he belonged, a checking and validating function complementary to that of the notary who drafted the deed. The office existed in both royal and seigneurial administration.

notaire_royal.label: Notaire royal (royal notary)
notaire_royal.summary: Public officer appointed by the king to draw up authentic deeds within a given jurisdiction.
notaire_royal.text: The royal notary held his office directly from the king, which gave him wider competence and authority than the seigneurial notary. His minutes — marriage contracts, post-mortem inventories, sales, wills — are among the richest sources for genealogical research into the Ancien Régime.

notaire_seigneurial.label: Notaire seigneurial (seigneurial notary)
notaire_seigneurial.summary: Public officer appointed by a lord to draw up deeds within his jurisdiction.
notaire_seigneurial.text: The seigneurial notary was appointed by a lord holding high justice to draw up and authenticate legal deeds (contracts, sales, wills) within his seigneury, as opposed to the royal notary, whose authority derived directly from the Crown. The office disappeared with the abolition of seigneurial rights at the Revolution.

noueuse_de_coins_de_mouchoirs.label: Noueuse de coins de mouchoirs (handkerchief-corner knotter)
noueuse_de_coins_de_mouchoirs.summary: Woman worker who made the decorative fringes and knots at the corners of handkerchiefs.
noueuse_de_coins_de_mouchoirs.text: In the fine textile industry (notably the handkerchief making of Cambrai), the "noueuse de coins de mouchoirs" made the ornamental fringes and knots added to the corners of handkerchiefs and other pieces of fine linen. This painstaking finishing work was typically given to women working at home or in workshops.

nourrice.label: Nourrice (wet nurse)
nourrice.summary: Woman who breastfed and raised another woman's child for payment.
nourrice.text: The wet nurse breastfed and raised another woman's child for payment, a very widespread practice in France from the 17th to the early 20th century, especially for the children of well-off urban families placed with rural nurses ("mise en nourrice"). This system, regulated by the Roussel Act of 1874, left a significant trace in civil registers, as infants sometimes died far from their family of origin.

nourriguier.label: Nourriguier (children's nurse)
nourriguier.summary: Person responsible for feeding and caring for young children in a well-to-do family.
nourriguier.text: The "nourriguier" or "nourriguière" saw to the feeding and care of young children in a noble or bourgeois family, a role close to that of the wet nurse or governess depending on regional custom.

nourrisseur.label: Nourrisseur (livestock fattener)
nourrisseur.summary: Person who fattened and kept livestock on behalf of others.
nourrisseur.text: The "nourrisseur" fattened and kept farm animals — cattle, horses or other draught animals — often on behalf of third parties, an activity common near towns, where livestock were fattened on brewery or distillery residues before being sold at the urban markets.

obbligato.label: Obbligato (bound farmhand)
obbligato.summary: In Lombardy and Piedmont, a farm worker bound to a farmstead (cascina) by a yearly contract obliging him to work whenever required.
obbligato.text: The obbligato lived with his family in a house on the cascina and undertook, under a contract renewed each year (usually at Martinmas), to work by the day for the farmer whenever called upon, in return for housing, a share in kind and a daily wage. He stood between the permanent farmhand and the casual day labourer.

obywatel_ziemski.label: Obywatel ziemski (landowner)
obywatel_ziemski.summary: Owner of a landed estate, usually of noble origin.
obywatel_ziemski.text: In nineteenth-century records of the Kingdom of Poland, “obywatel ziemski” denotes the owner or leaseholder of a landed estate, usually a nobleman. The term emphasised social standing and land ownership rather than a trade.

ocrier.label: Ocrier (ochre worker)
ocrier.summary: Craftsman who extracted and prepared natural ochre for paint and dyeing.
ocrier.text: The "ocrier" extracted ochre, a natural coloured clay pigment, and prepared it (washing, grinding, drying) for use in painting, dyeing or the building trade. The Apt area and Roussillon in the Vaucluse, rich in deposits, were historic centres of this activity in France.

odreiro.label: Odreiro (wineskin maker)
odreiro.summary: Craftsman who made leather skins for carrying wine, olive oil or water.
odreiro.text: The odreiro prepares and sews whole goat skins, made watertight with pitch or resin, to make wineskins (odres) for transporting and storing wine, olive oil or water. The skin was indispensable to muleteers and to transport in regions with difficult roads, before barrels and modern containers became widespread.

odrero.label: Odrero (Spanish wineskin maker)
odrero.summary: Craftsman who made wineskins and leather flasks for wine, oil and other liquids.
odrero.text: The odrero sewed and pitched goat or other animal skins to make wineskins and leather flasks for transporting and storing wine, oil and other liquids. Skins were essential for carrying goods by pack animal on the roads of the peninsula.

oesterkweker.label: Oesterkweker (oyster farmer)
oesterkweker.summary: Farmer who raised oysters on plots in the sea and sold them.
oesterkweker.text: In Zeeland, especially around Yerseke on the Oosterschelde, oyster plots were leased from the 19th century onwards, on which the farmers laid young oysters, tended them and dredged them up again after a few years. The oysters were kept in pits and shipped at home and abroad.

official.label: Official (bishop's judge)
official.summary: Church magistrate appointed by the bishop to administer justice in matters of canon law.
official.text: The "official" was the judge delegated by the bishop to administer ecclesiastical justice in his diocese, ruling on disputes falling under canon law (marriages, benefices, discipline of the clergy). The court over which he presided, the "officialité", long formed a jurisdiction separate from royal justice.

officier_de_maree.label: Officier de marée (fish-market officer)
officier_de_maree.summary: Official responsible for supervising transactions at the fish market.
officier_de_maree.text: The "officier de marée" supervised commercial transactions and kept the registers at the fish market, notably that of Les Halles in Paris, ensuring that sales of "marée" (fresh sea fish) were properly conducted. The office belonged to the municipal administration of Ancien Régime markets.

officier_de_sante.label: Officier de santé (health officer)
officier_de_sante.summary: Medical practitioner with intermediate training, between the surgeon and the physician.
officier_de_sante.text: The "officier de santé" was a practitioner status created by the law of 19 Ventôse Year XI (1803) to make up for the shortage of qualified doctors in rural areas: his training, shorter than that of a doctor of medicine, allowed him to practise, but only in the department in which he had been admitted. The status survived until it was abolished in 1892.

officier_de_volaille.label: Officier de volaille (poultry-market officer)
officier_de_volaille.summary: Official responsible for supervising sales of poultry and game at market.
officier_de_volaille.text: The "officier de volaille" supervised transactions and kept the registers of sales of poultry and game, notably at the Paris markets, an office parallel to that of the "officier de marée" for fish.

officier_demissionnaire.label: Officier démissionnaire (resigned officer)
officier_demissionnaire.summary: Former military officer who had given up his commission while keeping his social rank.
officier_demissionnaire.text: The "officier démissionnaire" had voluntarily left his military post while keeping the mention of his former status in records, which continued to confer particular social recognition under the Ancien Régime and in the 19th century.

officier_militaire.label: Officier militaire (military officer)
officier_militaire.summary: Serviceman holding a commissioned rank, as opposed to the rank and file.
officier_militaire.text: The military officer held a commissioned rank in the armed forces (second lieutenant, lieutenant, captain and so on), as opposed to ordinary soldiers and non-commissioned officers. The exact rank is usually stated separately in records when it is known.

officieux.label: Officieux (general servant)
officieux.summary: All-purpose servant carrying out various tasks in a household.
officieux.text: The "officieux" was a servant employed for various tasks in a noble or bourgeois household, close to the valet or the odd-job man depending on the household's needs.

ogimbaire.label: Ogimbaïre (mender of utensils, Cantal)
ogimbaire.summary: In the Cantal, a craftsman who mended worn utensils.
ogimbaire.text: According to glossaries of old trades, the "ogimbaïre" was a mender of worn utensils in the Cantal, an itinerant craftsman close to the tinker or the knife-grinder, specific to this region of Auvergne.

oidor.label: Oidor (Spanish high-court judge)
oidor.summary: Judge of a Spanish royal Audiencia or Chancillería who heard and decided cases.
oidor.text: The oidor was one of the judges who made up the royal Audiencias and Chancillerías (such as those of Valladolid and Granada) and the audiencias of the American territories. His name comes from his role of hearing the parties before deciding civil cases; the alcaldes del crimen dealt with criminal cases.

oignonnier.label: Oignonnier (onion seller)
oignonnier.summary: Merchant specialised in selling onions and other bulb vegetables.
oignonnier.text: The "oignonnier" sold onions and other bulb vegetables at local markets. "Ognonnier" is a spelling variant found notably in the Bourbonnais.

oiselier.label: Oiselier (bird dealer, bird-catcher)
oiselier.summary: Breeder and dealer in domestic and ornamental birds.
oiselier.text: The "oiselier" bred, caught, trained and sold birds, whether intended for ornamental aviaries, for song or, in the case of some species, for the table. "Oiseleur" is a variant referring to the same trade.

oleder.label: Olęder (Dutch-law settler)
oleder.summary: Settler under Olęder (Dutch) law, a free hereditary tenant of land, usually on flood plains.
oleder.text: The Olędrzy were settlers, originally from the Netherlands and Frisia and later also Germans and Poles, established from the sixteenth century under Olęder law along the Vistula and other rivers. They were personally free, held land on hereditary or long leases for rent, and specialised in draining and farming wetlands.

ombrellaio.label: Ombrellaio (umbrella maker)
ombrellaio.summary: Craftsman who made, sold or mended umbrellas and parasols.
ombrellaio.text: The ombrellaio made umbrellas and parasols or, travelling from village to village, repaired them. In Italy the itinerant trade is associated in particular with the Vergante and the valleys around Lake Maggiore, from which emigrant umbrella makers, who had their own slang, set out every year.

omelettier.label: Omelettier (omelette cook)
omelettier.summary: Cook specialised in preparing omelettes in a restaurant.
omelettier.text: In a restaurant, the "omelettier" was the cook specifically responsible for preparing omelettes, a specialised culinary post peculiar to large kitchens organised by station.

onduleur.label: Onduleur (wig waver)
onduleur.summary: Postiche worker who waved and curled wigs and hairpieces.
onduleur.text: The "onduleur" worked in the wig and hairpiece industry, creating waves and curls in natural or synthetic hair made up into pieces. The trade accompanied the development of wig making and artificial hairdressing from the 18th to the 20th century.

operateur.label: Opérateur (itinerant practitioner, quack surgeon)
operateur.summary: Itinerant practitioner who performed minor surgery or sold remedies.
operateur.text: Under the Ancien Régime and up to the 19th century, the "opérateur" was an itinerant practitioner who carried out minor operations (tooth extraction, cataract operations, reduction of hernias) and sold remedies in public squares and at fairs, often without any officially recognised medical training. He was akin to the charlatan, but some, such as the oculist operators, enjoyed a solid reputation.

operateur_de_betail.label: Opérateur de bétail (livestock gelder)
operateur_de_betail.summary: Practitioner specialised in castrating domestic animals.
operateur_de_betail.text: The "opérateur de bétail" castrated farm animals, a role equivalent to that of the "hongreur" or "châtreur" (gelder), carried out as an itinerant trade in the countryside.

operateur_de_main.label: Opérateur de main (itinerant tooth-puller)
operateur_de_main.summary: Itinerant practitioner specialised in tooth extraction and minor manual surgery.
operateur_de_main.text: The "opérateur de main" performed minor manual operations, notably tooth extraction, as part of the travelling activity of the fairground operators of the Ancien Régime.

oranger.label: Oranger (orange seller)
oranger.summary: Merchant specialised in selling oranges and other citrus fruit.
oranger.text: The "oranger" sold oranges and other citrus fruit at markets, a specialisation of the fruit trade that developed as citrus fruit, long an imported luxury, became more widely available.

ordinand.label: Ordinand (ordinand)
ordinand.summary: Candidate about to receive holy orders in the Catholic Church.
ordinand.text: The ordinand is the person who receives ordination — that is, who is raised to a holy order (diaconate, priesthood and so on) — by a bishop, called the "ordinant". The term therefore refers to the recipient of ordination, not to the one who confers it.

ordynariusz.label: Ordynariusz (estate labourer paid in kind)
ordynariusz.summary: Permanent manor-farm labourer paid mostly in kind.
ordynariusz.text: The ordynariusz was a manor-farm labourer, usually with his family, hired for a year and paid largely in kind: grain, fuel, housing in a workers’ building (czworak) and a small plot, together called ordynaria or deputat. This form of employment spread on Polish estates in the nineteenth century after the abolition of serf labour and lasted until the mid-twentieth century.

orfevre.label: Orfèvre (goldsmith, silversmith)
orfevre.summary: Craftsman who made jewellery, tableware and religious objects in precious metals.
orfevre.text: The goldsmith worked gold and silver to make jewellery, tableware, religious objects (chalices, monstrances) or pieces of secular plate. The trade, tightly regulated under the Ancien Régime by strict guilds that required work to be hallmarked, is distinct from that of the jeweller (bijoutier), who worked more with set stones.

organettaro.label: Organettaro (organ grinder)
organettaro.summary: Itinerant player of a barrel organ.
organettaro.text: The organettaro went through streets and courtyards playing a barrel organ, sometimes accompanied by a small trained animal. Many organ grinders came from the Emilian Apennines and the Ciociaria and emigrated to the cities of Europe and the Americas.

organista.label: Organista (church organist)
organista.summary: Musician playing the organ during services in a parish church.
organista.text: The organista played the organ and led the singing at mass and services, and often taught children and ran the choir. In rural parishes he was one of the few literate people, so he sometimes acted as parish clerk and frequently appears in records as a witness. Latin registers call him “organarius”.

oribusier.label: Oribusier (resin-candle maker)
oribusier.summary: Craftsman who made candles or tapers from a resin called oribus.
oribusier.text: The "oribusier" made candles or tapers from "oribus", a resin used as a lighting material before wax and tallow became the common fuels for domestic lighting.

ornemaniste.label: Ornemaniste (ornamentalist)
ornemaniste.summary: Craftsman-artist specialised in the ornamental decoration of a building or object.
ornemaniste.text: The ornamentalist designed and produced ornamental decoration — sculpture, stucco, mouldings, decorative motifs — applied to architecture, furniture or goldsmiths' work. The trade combines several skills (sculpture, stucco, decorative ironwork) depending on the material worked.

orpailleur.label: Orpailleur (gold panner)
orpailleur.summary: Gold seeker who recovered flakes and nuggets from riverbeds.
orpailleur.text: The gold panner searched for and recovered native gold in the form of flakes or small nuggets in river sediments, using a pan. This activity, marginal in France, nonetheless existed on a small scale in some gold-bearing regions (the Cévennes, Limousin, Ariège).

orthophoniste.label: Orthophoniste (speech and language therapist)
orthophoniste.summary: Health professional specialised in treating language and speech disorders.
orthophoniste.text: The speech and language therapist assessed and treated disorders of speech, spoken and written language, voice or swallowing. A health profession recognised in France since the mid-20th century, it appears mainly in records concerning living or recently deceased people.

oublier.label: Oublier (wafer seller)
oublier.summary: Seller of dry pastries, wafers and oublies sold in the street.
oublier.text: The "oublier" made and sold "oublies" — thin, light wafers, often rolled into a cone — as well as other dry pastries such as "nieules", a street trade very popular since the Middle Ages, especially at fairs and religious processions (oublies were also sometimes used as hosts). "Oublayer" is a spelling variant.

ouderling.label: Ouderling (Reformed church elder)
ouderling.summary: Member of the consistory of a Protestant congregation, responsible for overseeing doctrine and conduct.
ouderling.text: Under Reformed church order, the elders formed the consistory together with the minister and the deacons. They watched over the purity of doctrine and the conduct of the members, visited families and could exercise church discipline. The office was held by lay members of the congregation, usually for a limited number of years.

ourdisseur.label: Ourdisseur (warper)
ourdisseur.summary: Textile worker who laid out the warp threads before weaving.
ourdisseur.text: The warper carried out warping, the operation of laying out and stretching the warp threads in parallel on the warping frame before mounting them on the loom. This preparatory step determines the quality and evenness of the finished fabric. "Ordisseur" is a spelling variant.

oursalier.label: Oursalier (bear trainer)
oursalier.summary: Bear hunter and trainer who exhibited bears for public entertainment.
oursalier.text: The "oursalier" captured and trained bears, which he then exhibited at public shows, a practice traditionally associated with the Pyrenean regions (Ariège, Couserans). The trade is close to that of the bear leader (montreur d'ours), a more itinerant figure who toured the villages with the trained animal.

ouvidor.label: Ouvidor (seigneurial or crown magistrate)
ouvidor.summary: Magistrate appointed by a lord-proprietor or by the Crown to administer justice in an ouvidoria.
ouvidor.text: The ouvidor administers justice in the name of a lord holding jurisdiction over lands (noble house, military order, lord-proprietor) or, in certain territories, in the name of the Crown. In seigneurial lands he played a role similar to that of the corregedor in Crown lands, hearing appeals from local judges. The office also existed in the captaincies of the islands and of Brazil, and disappeared in the 19th century with the abolition of seigneurial jurisdictions.

ouvreur_theatre.label: Ouvreur, théâtre (usher)
ouvreur_theatre.summary: Employee responsible for showing spectators to their seats in a theatre.
ouvreur_theatre.text: The usher ("ouvreur", or "ouvreuse" for a woman) welcomed spectators at the entrance of a theatre or cinema and showed them to their seats. The term "ouvreur" on its own, without further detail, most often refers to this role, although in glassmaking vocabulary it can also refer to a very different trade.

ouvreur_verrerie.label: Ouvreur, verrerie (glass cylinder opener)
ouvreur_verrerie.summary: Glassworker who opened the blown-glass "bosse" to turn it into a sheet of window glass.
ouvreur_verrerie.text: In the traditional glass industry, the "ouvreur" opened the "bosse" — a cylinder of blown glass — by splitting it and then reheating it to flatten it into a sheet to be cut into window panes. This technical trade was one of the specialised stages in making blown window glass, before the invention of drawn and later float glass.

ouvreuse_de_loge.label: Ouvreuse de loge (box attendant)
ouvreuse_de_loge.summary: Woman employed to welcome spectators and open the boxes of a theatre to them.
ouvreuse_de_loge.text: The "ouvreuse de loge" welcomed the spectators in the boxes — private and generally more expensive spaces in a theatre — and let them in, a more specialised role than that of the general auditorium usherette.

ouvrier.label: Ouvrier (worker, labourer)
ouvrier.summary: Wage-earning manual worker, a generic term used especially in industry.
ouvrier.text: "Ouvrier" is the generic term for a wage-earning manual worker, particularly frequent in records from the 19th century onwards with the rise of industry. The term is often qualified by the sector of activity (farm worker, factory worker, textile mill worker and so on).

ouvrier_a_livret.label: Ouvrier à livret (worker holding a worker's book)
ouvrier_a_livret.summary: Worker obliged, before 1890, to hold a book recording his successive jobs.
ouvrier_a_livret.text: Before the worker's book was abolished in 1890, the "ouvrier à livret" was required to hold this compulsory booklet, issued and endorsed by employers or the police, which recorded his successive jobs and allowed employers to control the mobility of the workforce. A worker without a book in order could be treated as a vagrant.

ouvrier_aux_pieces.label: Ouvrier aux pièces (piece-worker, printing)
ouvrier_aux_pieces.summary: Printing worker paid according to the work done rather than by the day.
ouvrier_aux_pieces.text: In printing, the "ouvrier aux pièces" was paid by output — by the number of characters or lines set — as opposed to the worker "en conscience", paid by the day on the basis of the trust placed in his steady work.

ouvrier_d_aout.label: Ouvrier d'août (harvest worker)
ouvrier_d_aout.summary: Seasonal farm worker hired for the harvest in August.
ouvrier_d_aout.text: The "ouvrier d'août", or "aoûteron", was a seasonal farm worker hired specifically for the harvest period at the height of summer. This temporary reinforcement of labour, often from other regions, was essential to cope with the peak of work at the grain harvest.

ouvrier_de_martel.label: Ouvrier de martel (hammer miner)
ouvrier_de_martel.summary: Miner who broke ore with striking tools in underground galleries.
ouvrier_de_martel.text: The "ouvrier de martel" broke ore with a hammer and pick in the galleries of a mine, an intensely physical task that preceded the mechanisation of cutting.

ouvrier_en_calemande.label: Ouvrier en calemande (calamanco weaver)
ouvrier_en_calemande.summary: Weaver specialised in making calamanco, a twilled, satiny woollen fabric.
ouvrier_en_calemande.text: The "ouvrier en calemande" wove calamanco ("calmande" or "calemande"), a tightly woven, glossy twilled woollen fabric with a satin-like appearance, used in particular for clothing and furnishings in the 17th and 18th centuries.

ouvrier_en_conscience.label: Ouvrier en conscience (day-rate worker, printing)
ouvrier_en_conscience.summary: Printing worker paid by the day rather than by output.
ouvrier_en_conscience.text: In printing, the "ouvrier en conscience" was paid by the day rather than by the piece, a method of payment based on trust in his regularity and reliability, as opposed to the piece-worker paid by output.

ouvrier_en_draps_de_soie.label: Ouvrier en draps de soie (silk-cloth worker)
ouvrier_en_draps_de_soie.summary: Textile worker specialised in making silk cloth.
ouvrier_en_draps_de_soie.text: The "ouvrier en draps de soie" made silk fabrics for clothing or furnishings, a skill of the silk industry, particularly that of Lyon.

ouvrier_en_fantaisie.label: Ouvrier en fantaisie (fancy-goods weaver)
ouvrier_en_fantaisie.summary: Textile worker specialised in making "fancy" fabrics with decorative patterns and textures.
ouvrier_en_fantaisie.text: The "ouvrier en fantaisie" worked on the manufacture of so-called "fancy" fabrics, characterised by patterns, textures or blends of yarn outside ordinary production, intended for decorative uses such as upholstery or luxury furnishings.

ouvrier_en_sparterie.label: Ouvrier en sparterie (esparto worker)
ouvrier_en_sparterie.summary: Worker who processed esparto, a plant fibre used for ropes and coarse fabrics.
ouvrier_en_sparterie.text: The "ouvrier en sparterie" made ropes, mats or coarse fabrics from esparto (or alfa), a Mediterranean plant fibre also used in making paper pulp and espadrille-type shoes.

ouvrier_monnaie.label: Ouvrier de la monnaie (mint worker)
ouvrier_monnaie.summary: Mint worker responsible for adjusting and cutting coin blanks.
ouvrier_monnaie.text: The mint worker prepared the blanks (metal discs) to be struck, in particular by adjusting their weight and diameter in a mint. He is distinct from the moneyer (monnayeur) proper, who carried out the striking itself.

ouvriere_en_blondes.label: Ouvrière en blondes (blonde-lace maker)
ouvriere_en_blondes.summary: Woman worker who made articles in blonde, a fine and precious silk lace.
ouvriere_en_blondes.text: The "ouvrière en blondes" made articles in "blonde", a light, lustrous silk lace, originally of unbleached natural colour (hence its name), whose manufacture developed particularly in Caen and Chantilly in the 18th and 19th centuries.

ouvriere_en_filet.label: Ouvrière en filet (net-lace worker)
ouvriere_en_filet.summary: Woman worker specialised in lacework on a net ground.
ouvriere_en_filet.text: The "ouvrière en filet" produced lace or embroidery on a meshed net ground (filet lace, also called "lacis"), an old technique consisting of embroidering a network of knotted meshes.

ovaliste.label: Ovaliste (silk throwster, Lyon)
ovaliste.summary: Woman worker in the Lyon silk industry who wound silk on an oval-shaped machine.
ovaliste.text: The "ovaliste" worked in silk preparation, winding and throwing the threads on oval-shaped machines for the manufacture of stockings, tulle and trimmings. The ovalistes of Lyon became known for a major strike in 1869, one of the first mass strikes by women workers in French industrial history.

paardenvisser.label: Paardenvisser (horseback shrimp fisher)
paardenvisser.summary: Fisher who fished for shrimp on horseback in the surf with a trawl net.
paardenvisser.text: On the Belgian coast, notably at Oostduinkerke, the horseback fishermen fish for brown shrimp at low tide with a net dragged through the surf by a draught horse. This kind of fishing used to be practised at more places along the North Sea coast. The tradition is recognised as intangible cultural heritage.

pacotilleuse.label: Pacotilleuse (woman smuggler)
pacotilleuse.summary: Woman who smuggled goods hidden on her person.
pacotilleuse.text: The "pacotilleuse" engaged in small-scale smuggling, carrying taxed goods (tobacco, salt, textiles) hidden in her clothes to evade customs checks, an activity common in border areas.

pacquetier_marchand.label: Pacquetier, marchand (pack pedlar)
pacquetier_marchand.summary: Itinerant trader who carried his goods in packs on his back.
pacquetier_marchand.text: The "pacquetier" was a pedlar who carried his goods in packs on his back, going from village to village to sell them, a modest form of itinerant trade common in the Ancien Régime countryside.

pacquetier_typographe.label: Pacquetier, typographie (compositor's packet maker)
pacquetier_typographe.summary: Printing worker who gathered set lines into packets for make-up.
pacquetier_typographe.text: In letterpress printing, the "pacquetier" gathered the lines of type set by the compositors into packets before passing them on to the make-up man, who arranged them into columns and pages.

pacqueur.label: Pacqueur (fish packer)
pacqueur.summary: Worker who sorted salted fish and packed it into barrels for preservation and shipping.
pacqueur.text: The "pacqueur" sorted and packed salted fish (especially herring) into barrels for preservation and transport, a trade of the fishing ports of the North and the Channel (Boulogne, Dieppe), where herring was salted on an industrial scale.

padleur.label: Padleur (stirrer of molten material)
padleur.summary: Worker who stirred molten metal or glass in a crucible with a long rod.
padleur.text: The "padleur" stirred the molten material — glass or metal — in a crucible or furnace with a long tool called a "padle", in order to make its composition or temperature uniform, a technical operation found in some glassworks and metalworks.

padouyer.label: Padouyer (padou ribbon maker)
padouyer.summary: Maker of padou, a silk or cotton ribbon used in dressmaking and trimmings.
padouyer.text: The "padouyer" (or "padouier") made "padou", a narrow silk or cotton ribbon used to edge or reinforce garments, named after the Italian city of Padua, where this ribbon was originally made. The rarely attested term is recorded only very locally, notably in the parish registers of the Pays de Caux in the 17th and 18th centuries. "Pasdouyer" is a regional variant.

pailler.label: Pailler (itinerant coppersmith, Normandy)
pailler.text: In Normandy, the "pailler" was an itinerant coppersmith who travelled the countryside to repair and sell metal utensils.

pailleur.label: Pailleur (straw dealer)
pailleur.summary: Supplier and carrier of straw for fodder and livestock bedding.
pailleur.text: The "pailleur" supplied and carried straw used as supplementary fodder or as bedding for horses and cattle, an activity complementary to farm work.

pailleur_au_grenier_a_sel.label: Pailleur au grenier à sel (salt-store inspector)
pailleur_au_grenier_a_sel.summary: Clerk at a salt store responsible for checking deliveries to prevent fraud.
pailleur_au_grenier_a_sel.text: The "pailleur au grenier à sel" was a clerk or inspector working in a salt store — a royal warehouse where salt was kept and sold under the gabelle — responsible for supervising operations to prevent "faux-saunage", that is, salt smuggling.

pailleuse.label: Pailleuse (straw bottle-cover maker)
pailleuse.summary: Craftswoman who made paillons, straw wrappers protecting glass bottles.
pailleuse.text: The "pailleuse" made "paillons", plaited straw wrappers designed to protect glass bottles during transport, a technique still used today for some wine or oil flasks.

pailleux.label: Pailleux (prisoner)
pailleux.summary: Prison inmate, a term found in glossaries of old trades.
pailleux.text: The term "pailleux" refers to a prison inmate — not an occupation as such, but an indication of status alluding to the straw used as bedding in the cells, sometimes found in records in place of an occupation.

pailloteur.label: Pailloteur (straw-hut builder)
pailloteur.summary: Craftsman who built paillotes, temporary straw shelters for shepherds and farm workers.
pailloteur.text: The "pailloteur" built "paillotes", temporary straw huts or shelters used by shepherds or farm workers while staying in the fields or on the pastures.

pain_d_epice.label: Pain d'épice (gingerbread maker or seller)
pain_d_epice.summary: Seller or maker of pain d'épice, a pastry speciality made with honey and spices.
pain_d_epice.text: The gingerbread seller made and sold this sweet bread made of flour, honey and spices, a speciality associated particularly with Reims and Dijon, often sold at fairs and popular festivals.

palayeur.label: Palayeur (dock worker)
palayeur.summary: Port worker responsible for loading and unloading goods on the quays.
palayeur.text: The "palayeur" worked on the quays of a port, where he loaded and unloaded ships' cargoes.

palefrenier.label: Palefrenier (groom, stableman)
palefrenier.summary: Servant responsible for caring for and looking after horses in a stable.
palefrenier.text: The groom looked after the horses in the stables of noble or bourgeois houses or of post houses: feeding, grooming, and keeping the bedding and harness in order. The trade, a lowly one in the domestic hierarchy, remained indispensable for as long as the horse was the main means of transport and traction.

palejaire.label: Palejaire (maker of wooden paddles)
palejaire.summary: Craftsman who made paddles and flat wooden implements.
palejaire.text: The "palejaire" made paddles and other flat wooden implements for various craft or household uses.

palisseur.label: Palisseur (fence builder)
palisseur.summary: Craftsman who built and maintained wooden palisades and fences.
palisseur.text: The "palisseur" built and maintained palisades, fences made of stakes or boards used to mark out a plot of land or protect a crop. In Normandy, the term "pallicier" is said by some sources to refer to the same trade.

palissonneur.label: Palissonneur (glove-leather softener)
palissonneur.text: The "palissonneur" worked in a glove factory, where he softened the skins used to make gloves.

palissonneur_ganterie.label: Palissonneur, ganterie (glove-leather staker)
palissonneur_ganterie.summary: Worker who smoothed and softened skins used to make gloves.
palissonneur_ganterie.text: In glove making, the "palissonneur" softened and smoothed tanned skins with a tool called a "palissoire", an essential step in obtaining a supple leather suitable for making gloves.

palissonneur_megissier.label: Palissonneur mégissier (tawer's leather softener)
palissonneur_megissier.summary: Worker who staked skins in the tawing industry.
palissonneur_megissier.text: The "palissonneur mégissier" softened fine skins (lamb, kid) treated by tawing, a finishing stage for light leather intended for glove making or fine leather goods.

paliteira.label: Paliteira (toothpick carver)
paliteira.summary: Craftswoman who carved toothpicks by hand, a tradition associated with Lorvão (Penacova).
paliteira.text: The paliteira carves toothpicks by hand with a small knife from willow or other light woods, sometimes decorated with delicate cut-work. This cottage industry, mostly carried on by women, is traditionally associated with Lorvão, in the municipality of Penacova, where it occupied many families and supplemented farm incomes.

palmeur.label: Palmeur (proxy pilgrim, palmer)
palmeur.summary: Professional pilgrim who made a pilgrimage to the Holy Land on behalf of others.
palmeur.text: The "palmeur" (or "palmier") made a paid pilgrimage to Jerusalem on behalf of a sponsor who could not or would not make it himself, generally bringing back a palm as proof of the journey — a medieval practice that gave rise to the surname "Palmier".

palonnier.label: Palonnier (swingletree maker)
palonnier.summary: Craftsman who made swingletrees, harness parts that spread the pulling effort.
palonnier.text: The "palonnier" made swingletrees, wooden or metal harness parts that spread the pulling effort between several harnessed animals.

paludier.label: Paludier (salt-marsh worker)
paludier.summary: Worker who harvested salt in the salt marshes.
paludier.text: The "paludier" worked a salt marsh, harvesting salt by evaporating seawater in a series of pans ("œillets"), a traditional trade emblematic of the Guérande marshes and the island of Noirmoutier.

panacher.label: Panacher (plume maker)
panacher.summary: Craftsman who prepared and fitted ornamental feather plumes on headdresses and helmets.
panacher.text: The "panacher" made and fitted plumes — bunches of ornamental feathers — on civilian or military headgear. The trade overlaps with the more widely known one of the plumassier, who worked feathers for decorative purposes in fashion and furnishing.

panetier.label: Panetier (pantler)
panetier.summary: Household officer responsible for serving bread in a royal or noble household.
panetier.text: In great royal or noble households, the "panetier" was the household officer responsible for serving bread at table, an office of honour within the household of the sovereign or the lord.

pangoussier.label: Pangoussier (baker)
pangoussier.summary: Old regional name for the baker.
pangoussier.text: According to glossaries of old trades, "pangoussier" was an old regional name for the baker, who made and sold bread. The term, now obsolete, is attested only in dictionaries of old trades.

pannasseur.label: Pannasseur (purlin repairer)
pannasseur.summary: Worker who repaired and maintained the purlins of timber frames and roofs.
pannasseur.text: The "pannasseur" worked on purlins, the horizontal timbers supporting the covering of a roof, repairing or maintaining them.

panneleur.label: Panneleur (panel maker)
panneleur.summary: Craftsman who made assembled wooden panels for building or furniture.
panneleur.text: The "panneleur" assembled wooden panels used in various constructions or fittings, a trade close to joinery.

pannereux.label: Pannereux (basket maker)
pannereux.summary: Basket maker specialised in making wicker baskets and hampers.
pannereux.text: The "pannereux" wove wicker to make baskets and hampers, a basketry craft common in the wicker-producing regions.

pannetier.label: Pannetier (maker of flat baskets)
pannetier.summary: Craftsman who made pannettes, small flat baskets used to carry produce.
pannetier.text: The "pannetier" made "pannettes", small flat baskets of wicker or split wood used to carry fruit, vegetables or other produce to market.

paonnier.label: Paonnier (peacock-feather milliner)
paonnier.summary: Hatter who used peacock feathers to adorn luxury headwear.
paonnier.text: The "paonnier" adorned luxury headwear with peacock feathers, work belonging to hat making and ceremonial finery.

papetier.label: Papetier (papermaker, stationer)
papetier.summary: Craftsman or merchant who made and sold paper.
papetier.text: The "papetier" made paper — traditionally from rags pulped in a paper mill — or sold it in a shop. "Papelier" is an old variant of the same term, used for both the maker and the seller of paper.

papetier_colleur.label: Papetier-colleur (paper sizer)
papetier_colleur.summary: Craftsman specialised in sizing and surface-treating paper.
papetier_colleur.text: The "papetier-colleur" applied a coat of size to the paper (sizing) to make it less absorbent and fit for writing in ink, a finishing stage in traditional papermaking.

paraisonnier.label: Paraisonnier (glass gatherer)
paraisonnier.summary: Glassworker who gathered the parison, the mass of molten glass, on the end of the blowpipe.
paraisonnier.text: In glassblowing, the "paraisonnier" was the worker who gathered the parison from the furnace — the mass of molten glass taken up on the end of the blowpipe — and gave it its initial shape before passing it to the blower for further shaping. "Parisonier" is a spelling variant.

parandier.label: Parandier (fuller)
parandier.summary: Textile worker who fulled woollen cloths and fabrics.
parandier.text: The "parandier" fulled woollen cloths and fabrics, an operation consisting of beating and compressing the cloth to tighten and thicken it, close to the work of the fuller (foulon).

parcheminier.label: Parcheminier (parchment maker)
parcheminier.summary: Craftsman who made parchment from animal skins.
parcheminier.text: The parchment maker prepared animal skins (calf, sheep, goat) by scraping, pumicing and stretching them to make parchment, the writing material used for official deeds and manuscripts until paper became widespread.

parementier.label: Parementier (maker of facings and trimmings)
parementier.summary: Craftsman who made facings and decorative trimmings for garments and textiles.
parementier.text: The "parementier" made "parements" — decorative borders or facings — applied to garments or other textile pieces, a trade close to that of the passementier and the maker of ornaments.

pareur.label: Pareur (cloth finisher)
pareur.summary: Textile worker who finished and smoothed woollen cloth after weaving.
pareur.text: The "pareur" worked at the end of the manufacture of a woollen cloth, dressing it (shearing, smoothing, finishing) to even out its surface and make it saleable.

pareur_de_peaux.label: Pareur de peaux (skin dresser)
pareur_de_peaux.summary: Worker who prepared and finished skins in the leather industry.
pareur_de_peaux.text: The "pareur de peaux" prepared and finished skins intended for tanning or tawing, thinning and cleaning them before the tanning stages.

parfumeur.label: Parfumeur (perfumer)
parfumeur.summary: Craftsman who created perfumes from essences and aromatic materials.
parfumeur.text: The perfumer composed perfumes by blending natural essences or, later, synthetic aromatic materials, a craft that developed particularly in Grasse, the French capital of perfume, from the 17th century.

parfumier.label: Parfumier (perfume seller)
parfumier.summary: Merchant specialised in selling perfumes and perfumery goods.
parfumier.text: The "parfumier" sold perfumes and perfumery products, a term sometimes used interchangeably with "parfumeur" depending on the period and region, but referring more specifically to the trade than to the creation.

parleuse.label: Parleuse (woman negotiator, spokeswoman)
parleuse.summary: Woman responsible for negotiating or representing others in transactions.
parleuse.text: The "parleuse" acted as an intermediary or spokeswoman in commercial transactions, playing the role of negotiator on behalf of a third party.

parlier.label: Parlier (site foreman)
parlier.summary: Foreman on a site, especially a building site, who passed on the master builder's instructions.
parlier.text: On a medieval or early modern site (especially a building site), the "parlier" was the foreman or chief assistant who passed on and saw to the execution of the master builder's instructions — hence his name, derived from "parler" (to speak). The role is well documented in the stonemasons' journeymen's associations, where it gave its name to a family of master builders (the Parler, active on several cathedrals in central Europe).

parobek.label: Parobek (farmhand)
parobek.summary: Hired farm labourer, usually a young man, working for a farmer or on a manor farm.
parobek.text: The parobek was hired, usually for a year, for work on a peasant farm or manor farm: ploughing, carting, tending livestock. He lived with his employer and received board and a small wage. Many were sons of poorer peasants before they set up their own farms.

parqueur.label: Parqueur (parquet layer, oyster farmer)
parqueur.summary: Worker who laid wooden parquet floors, or who ran an oyster bed.
parqueur.text: Depending on the context, "parqueur" refers to two distinct trades: the parquet layer in the building trade, and the oyster farmer who managed an oyster "parc" in shellfish-farming basins such as Marennes-Oléron or the Arcachon basin, a very common usage in coastal regions.

particheur.label: Particheur (goods sorter)
particheur.summary: Worker who sorted and allocated goods according to quality and destination.
particheur.text: The "particheur" sorted and allocated goods according to their quality or destination, a checking and grading function found in some trades or industries.

parurier.label: Parurier (costume-jewellery maker)
parurier.summary: Craftsman who made ornaments and costume jewellery.
parurier.text: The "parurier" assembled ornaments — necklaces, earrings, costume jewellery — a craft that developed notably in the Jura around the costume-jewellery and spectacle-making industries.

passager.label: Passager (ferryman)
passager.summary: Boatman responsible for taking travellers from one bank to the other.
passager.text: The "passager" (in the old sense, not the traveller but the one who takes people across) rowed a boat to carry people from one bank of a river to the other, a service often granted as a ferry right before bridges became widespread.

passementier.label: Passementier (trimmings maker, lace-and-braid maker)
passementier.summary: Craftsman specialised in making trimmings: braids, fringes and textile ornaments.
passementier.text: The "passementier" made trimmings ("passementerie") — braids, fringes, tassels, decorative cords — used to adorn clothing, curtains or furniture. The trade developed particularly in Lyon and Saint-Étienne, in close connection with the silk industry.

passeur.label: Passeur (ferryman)
passeur.summary: Boatman who carried people and goods from one bank to the other.
passeur.text: The ferryman carried people and goods from one bank of a river to the other in a boat, in return for a toll. "Passeur d'eau" specifies this function to distinguish it from other, more figurative uses of the word "passeur".

pastellier.label: Pastellier (woad producer, pastel maker)
pastellier.summary: Craftsman connected with the production of woad, a dye plant, or of colour sticks.
pastellier.text: Depending on the region and period, the "pastellier" was associated either with the production of woad ("pastel" or "guède"), a blue dye plant whose cultivation made the fortune of the Pays de Cocagne around Toulouse in the 15th and 16th centuries, or with the making of colour sticks used in dyeing or drawing.

pastelliste.label: Pastelliste (pastellist)
pastelliste.summary: Artist who painted in pastel, a portrait technique highly prized in the 18th century.
pastelliste.text: The pastellist produced works, especially portraits, using sticks of pure pigment applied directly to the support (pastel), a technique that enjoyed its golden age in the 18th century with artists such as Quentin de La Tour.

pasteur.label: Pasteur (shepherd; Protestant minister)
pasteur.summary: Shepherd tending flocks, or minister of religion in the Protestant churches.
pasteur.text: In the old agricultural sense, "pasteur" refers to the shepherd who led and tended flocks on the pastures. In most 19th- and 20th-century records, however, the term is used in the sense of a Protestant minister, responsible for the spiritual guidance of a Reformed parish — a meaning to be distinguished according to the context of the record.

pasteur_de_betes_a_lignes.label: Pasteur de bêtes à lignes (towing-animal keeper)
pasteur_de_betes_a_lignes.summary: Herdsman specialised in handling the draught animals used for towing boats.
pasteur_de_betes_a_lignes.text: The "pasteur de bêtes à lignes" handled the draught animals (horses, mules) used to tow boats along rivers and canals, a specialised form of livestock keeping linked to river transport.

pastilleur.label: Pastilleur (lozenge maker)
pastilleur.text: The "pastilleur" made pastilles, small sweets or sugared medicinal preparations, a craft belonging to confectionery.

patachon.label: Patachon (patache driver)
patachon.summary: Driver of a patache, a public conveyance serving rural market towns.
patachon.text: The "patachon" drove a "patache", a modest public carriage carrying passengers and mail between poorly served rural localities, before the development of the railways.

patenostrier.label: Patenostrier (rosary maker)
patenostrier.summary: Craftsman who made rosaries and devotional objects.
patenostrier.text: The "patenostrier" made rosaries ("patenôtres") and other devotional objects, a craft organised into a guild from the Middle Ages, with specialisations according to the material used (wood, bone, amber, coral). "Patenotrier" is a spelling variant of the same trade.

patenostrier_d_ambre.label: Patenostrier d'ambre (amber rosary maker)
patenostrier_d_ambre.summary: Craftsman who made amber rosaries, a precious material reserved for luxury objects.
patenostrier_d_ambre.text: The "patenostrier d'ambre" was a rosary maker specialised in making rosaries of amber, an imported and costly material reserved for a well-to-do clientele.

patenostrier_d_os.label: Patenostrier d'os (patenostrier_d_os)
patenostrier_d_os.summary: Patenôtrier fabriquant chapelets et croix exclusivement en os et en corne.
patenostrier_d_os.text: Le patenôtrier d'os est un patenôtrier spécialisé dont les chapelets et croix étaient exclusivement fabriqués en os et en corne.

patenostrier_de_corail.label: Patenostrier de corail (coral rosary maker)
patenostrier_de_corail.summary: Craftsman who made coral rosaries, a precious marine material.
patenostrier_de_corail.text: The "patenostrier de corail" made rosaries of coral, a marine material once credited with protective powers and used in particular for rosaries intended for children.

pateur.label: Pateur (pasta maker)
pateur.summary: Craftsman who made fresh and dried pasta.
pateur.text: The "pateur" made pasta, fresh or dried, a trade close to that of the vermicelli maker (vermicellier).

patinier.label: Patinier (patten maker)
patinier.summary: Maker of patins, an old term for a type of footwear.
patinier.text: The "patinier" made "patins" (pattens), an old term for a type of shoe with a wooden or thick leather sole, a trade related to that of the shoemaker or the clog maker.

patissier.label: Pâtissier (pastry cook)
patissier.summary: Craftsman who made pastries, cakes and sweet dishes.
patissier.text: The pastry cook made and sold pastries, cakes, pies and other sweet or savoury dishes made with pastry, a trade organised into a guild from the Middle Ages and distinct from the baker. "Pastoier" is an old form of the same term.

patre.label: Pâtre (herdsman, shepherd)
patre.summary: Traditional herdsman responsible for tending and driving flocks and herds.
patre.text: The "pâtre" tended and drove flocks and herds on the pastures, a literary and administrative term for the shepherd or herdsman in general, with no distinction as to the kind of animals kept.

patre_des_betes_blanches.label: Pâtre des bêtes blanches (shepherd of sheep and goats)
patre_des_betes_blanches.summary: Herdsman specialised in tending sheep and goats.
patre_des_betes_blanches.text: The "pâtre des bêtes blanches" specifically tended sheep and goats, called "white beasts" in some regional pastoral terminologies, as opposed to cattle.

patre_des_betes_rouges.label: Pâtre des bêtes rouges (cowherd)
patre_des_betes_rouges.text: The "pâtre des bêtes rouges" specifically tended cattle, called "red beasts" in some regional pastoral terminologies, as opposed to sheep and goats.

patrizio.label: Patrizio (Italian patrician)
patrizio.summary: Member of a family enrolled in a city's patriciate, with the right to hold governing offices.
patrizio.text: In the Italian republics and cities before unification (Venice, Genoa, Lucca and many towns of Tuscany and the Papal States), the patriciate comprised the families admitted by birth to the city councils. The title of patrizio often accompanies the name in records and indicates social rank rather than an occupation.

patron_d_escaffie.label: Patron d'Escaffie (patron_d_escaffie)
patron_d_escaffie.summary: Maître artisan responsable d'un atelier lié au travail d'échafaudage.
patron_d_escaffie.text: Le patron d'escaffie dirige un atelier lié à la fabrication d'échafaudages ou de structures temporaires. Le terme, rare et mal attesté, appelle une certaine prudence quant à son sens exact.

patron_de_pesca.label: Patrón de pesca (Spanish fishing skipper)
patron_de_pesca.summary: Fisherman who commanded a fishing boat and directed its crew.
patron_de_pesca.text: The patrón de pesca commanded a fishing boat, directed the crew's work and shared out the catch according to the custom of the port, often on a share basis. In Spanish ports the skippers usually belonged to the fishermen's confraternities or guilds (cofradías de mareantes), which regulated fishing and assisted their members.

patronneur.label: Patronneur (pattern maker)
patronneur.summary: Craftsman who drew and created the patterns used in trimmings and garment making.
patronneur.text: The "patronneur" designed the patterns (models, templates) used as the basis for producing pieces in trimmings or garment making.

pattier.label: Pattier (rag collector)
pattier.summary: Dealer and collector of rags intended for recycling.
pattier.text: The "pattier" collected and resold rags and old textiles for recycling, notably for papermaking before the rise of wood pulp — a trade close to that of the rag-and-bone man (chiffonnier).

paulier.label: Paulier (tithe collector's assistant)
paulier.summary: Assistant to the tithe owner, helping to collect the Church tithes.
paulier.text: The "paulier" assisted the tithe owner ("décimateur") in collecting the tithe, a Church due levied in kind on the harvest under the Ancien Régime.

paumier.label: Paumier (real-tennis equipment maker)
paumier.summary: Craftsman who made the equipment for jeu de paume: rackets, balls and accessories.
paumier.text: The "paumier" made the rackets, balls and other equipment needed for jeu de paume (real tennis), the ancestor of tennis, very popular in France from the 15th to the 17th century. The "naquetier", who refereed the games, practised a complementary trade linked to the same game.

pauvrisseur.label: Pauvrisseur (administrator of poor relief)
pauvrisseur.summary: Manager of the goods and relief intended for a parish's poor.
pauvrisseur.text: The "pauvrisseur" managed the goods and alms intended for the poor, handling the distribution of relief within the framework of Ancien Régime parish charity.

pavementeur.label: Pavementeur (stone floor layer)
pavementeur.summary: Specialist in laying stone pavements and floor coverings.
pavementeur.text: The "pavementeur" was a craftsman specialised in laying stone pavements and floor coverings, distinct from the paviour (paveur), who worked rather on public roads. The term is found in civil and parish registers referring to building workers.

paveur.label: Paveur (paviour)
paveur.summary: Worker who cut and laid paving stones for town streets.
paveur.text: The paviour cut stone setts and laid them to pave streets and roadways. The trade grew strongly with urbanisation in the 18th and 19th centuries, when municipalities systematically paved their streets. He is distinct from the "pavementeur", more concerned with interior floors.

pavisseur.label: Pavisseur (street paver)
pavisseur.summary: Worker who laid and repaired wooden blocks or paving stones in the streets.
pavisseur.text: The "pavisseur" laid and repaired surfaces, whether of wooden blocks or stone setts, especially in the streets. The term, close to "paveur", refers to a building and road-maintenance trade found in Ancien Régime registers.

peager.label: Péager (toll collector)
peager.summary: Employee responsible for collecting tolls at bridges and on roads.
peager.text: The "péager" collected, on behalf of a lord, a company or the State, the tolls due for crossing a bridge, road or canal. Levying tolls was a common feudal right under the Ancien Régime, often farmed out to private individuals, before being gradually taken over by the administration.

peaumier.label: Peaumier (real-tennis equipment maker)
peaumier.summary: Spelling variant of paumier, a maker of equipment for jeu de paume.
peaumier.text: The "peaumier", a variant of "paumier", made balls, rackets and other equipment for jeu de paume (real tennis), the ancestor of tennis, very popular from the Middle Ages to the 17th century. The trade declined as interest in the game gradually waned from the 18th century onwards.

peaussier.label: Peaussier (skin dealer, fellmonger)
peaussier.summary: Craftsman who prepared raw skins and sold them to the leather trades.
peaussier.text: The "peaussier" prepared animal skins before their final treatment and sold them to tanners, tawers and other leather craftsmen. He occupied an intermediate place in the production chain between slaughter and tanning. "Peaucier" is a spelling variant.

pecheur.label: Pêcheur (fisherman)
pecheur.summary: Person who fished at sea, in rivers or in ponds as a means of livelihood.
pecheur.text: The fisherman caught fish at sea, in rivers, ponds or lakes, for sale or for his own consumption. It is one of the oldest and most widespread trades in coastal and river regions, with many specialisations according to the technique used (net, line, traps) or the species sought, several of which appear separately in this dictionary (seine fisherman, rod fisherman and so on).

pecheur_a_engins.label: Pêcheur à engins (net and trap fisherman)
pecheur_a_engins.summary: Fisherman who used nets and other gear to catch fish.
pecheur_a_engins.text: The "pêcheur à engins" fished with nets and other catching devices, as opposed to the angler. The regulation of fishing gear (mesh size, permitted types) came under increasing administrative supervision from the 19th century onwards.

pecheur_a_la_seine.label: Pêcheur à la seine (seine fisherman)
pecheur_a_la_seine.summary: Shore fisherman who used a large net, the seine, hauled in towards the beach.
pecheur_a_la_seine.text: The seine fisherman practised a form of fishing on foot that involved setting a large net called a seine, which was then hauled back towards the shore to catch the trapped fish. This collective method, used at sea as well as in fresh water, often required several fishermen working together.

pecheur_a_verges.label: Pêcheur à verges (rod fisherman)
pecheur_a_verges.summary: Angler who used rods called verges.
pecheur_a_verges.text: The "pêcheur à verges" fished with a line using rods, called "verges", to catch fish one at a time. This technique contrasts with collective net fishing such as seine fishing or fishing with gear.

pecheur_d_ecrevisses.label: Pêcheur d'écrevisses (crayfish catcher)
pecheur_d_ecrevisses.summary: Fisherman specialised in catching freshwater crayfish.
pecheur_d_ecrevisses.text: The crayfish catcher caught this freshwater crustacean in unpolluted rivers and streams using pots or drop nets. The species, very sensitive to water quality, long provided a prized local food resource before wild populations declined in the 20th century.

pecheur_de_l_eau_du_roi.label: Pêcheur de l'eau du roi (licensed royal-water fisherman)
pecheur_de_l_eau_du_roi.summary: Privileged fisherman who worked certain royal waters under licence.
pecheur_de_l_eau_du_roi.text: The "pêcheur de l'eau du roi" enjoyed a privilege allowing him to fish certain stretches of royal rivers, notably on the Seine and the Marne, in return for a fee or a licence granted by the royal administration. This status illustrates the highly regulated system of fishing rights under the Ancien Régime.

pecheur_de_sable.label: Pêcheur de sable (sand dredger)
pecheur_de_sable.summary: Worker who gathered river sand for building.
pecheur_de_sable.text: The "pêcheur de sable" extracted sand from a riverbed, notably the Loire, using a dredge or a shovel from a boat, to meet the needs of building and industry. This river activity long supplemented the income of many boatmen.

pegoulier.label: Pégoulier (pitch maker, Provence)
pegoulier.summary: Provençal craftsman who made pitch from pine resin.
pegoulier.text: The "pégoulier" made pitch ("pego" in Provençal) from pine resin, a product used to waterproof barrels, ropes and boats. This craft trade, typical of resin-producing regions such as Provence, declined with the rise of industrial sealing products.

pegujalero.label: Pegujalero (Spanish smallholder)
pegujalero.summary: Farmer who worked a pegujal, a small plot, or owned a small number of livestock.
pegujalero.text: The pegujalero worked a pegujal, a small piece of land owned or granted to him, or owned a small herd. His holding was not enough to live on, so he supplemented his income by working as a day labourer. The term is common in the census lists and land surveys of Andalusia and Castile.

peigneur.label: Peigneur (wool comber)
peigneur.summary: Carding worker who disentangled and aligned wool fibres before spinning.
peigneur.text: The comber disentangled and aligned wool fibres with a long-toothed comb to prepare the material for spinning. This textile trade, essential in regions with a wool tradition, had many regional variants and specialisations according to the material worked (hemp, sayette, floss silk). "Pegnaire" and "Peigneur de Laisne" are regional variants referring to the same work on wool.

peigneur_de_chanvre.label: Peigneur de chanvre (hemp heckler)
peigneur_de_chanvre.summary: Carding worker specialised in combing out hemp tow.
peigneur_de_chanvre.text: The hemp heckler combed out hemp tow to prepare the fibre for spinning, an essential step in regions growing hemp for rope-making and cloth. The movement is close to that of the wool comber but adapted to a harsher fibre.

peigneur_de_chevaux.label: Peigneur de chevaux (farrier-groom treating hoof disease)
peigneur_de_chevaux.summary: Groom who treated horses suffering from crapaudine, a disease of the hoof.
