prevot_des_marchands.label: Prévôt des marchands (provost of the merchants)
prevot_des_marchands.summary: Head of the town hall in certain large cities.
prevot_des_marchands.text: The prévôt des marchands headed the town hall in certain large cities, notably Paris, where this municipal office, which grew out of the guild of river merchants ("marchands de l'eau"), was the equivalent of mayor until the Revolution.

procurador_do_concelho.label: Procurador do concelho (municipal attorney)
procurador_do_concelho.summary: Municipal officer who represented the municipality and looked after its property, revenues and public works.
procurador_do_concelho.text: The procurador do concelho, elected along with the councillors, represents the interests of the municipality: he brings before the council what serves the common good, watches over the municipality's property and revenues, public works, roads and fountains, and may sue in court on the community's behalf. In municipalities without a treasurer of their own, he could also collect revenues and pay expenses.

procurador_dos_mesteres.label: Procurador dos mesteres (representative of the trades)
procurador_dos_mesteres.summary: Representative of the mechanical trades with a seat on the municipal council.
procurador_dos_mesteres.text: The procuradores dos mesteres, usually four, were chosen from among the members of the Casa dos Vinte e Quatro to represent the trades at council meetings, where they spoke on matters of supply, prices and trade regulations. The office disappeared with the abolition of the Casa dos Vinte e Quatro in 1834.

procurador_sindico.label: Procurador síndico (Spanish community representative)
procurador_sindico.summary: Representative elected by Spanish townspeople to defend the community's interests before the council.
procurador_sindico.text: The procurador síndico general was elected by the townspeople to represent and defend the community's interests before the council: food supply, common lands, local levies. The municipal reforms of 1766 added the síndico personero del común, also elected by the residents. The office appears frequently in municipal records from the 16th to the 19th century.

procureur.label: Procureur (attorney, prosecutor)
procureur.summary: Public officer responsible for representing a third party's interests in court.
procureur.text: The procureur, formerly also called "avoué", represented in court the interests of a third party who had given him power of attorney, drawing up the procedural documents in his name. Depending on the context, the term also refers to the magistrate acting as public prosecutor (the King's prosecutor, later the "procureur de la République").

procureur_au_presidial.label: Procureur au présidial (prosecutor at a presidial court)
procureur_au_presidial.summary: Officer representing the public prosecution at a presidial court.
procureur_au_presidial.text: The procureur au présidial represented the public prosecution at a "présidial", the intermediate royal court created in the 16th century between the bailiwick and the parlement. "Procureur au siège présidial" denotes the same office.

procureur_de_fabrique.label: Procureur de fabrique (churchwarden)
procureur_de_fabrique.summary: Person responsible for the material interests of the parish vestry.
procureur_de_fabrique.text: The procureur de fabrique managed the material interests of the "fabrique", the lay body responsible for administering a parish's property and income (upkeep of the church, accounts, collections). This office, often held by a local notable, survived until the 1905 law separating the Churches and the State.

procureur_de_seigneurie.label: Procureur de seigneurie (manorial agent)
procureur_de_seigneurie.summary: Peasant responsible for receiving seigneurial dues on the lord's behalf.
procureur_de_seigneurie.text: The procureur de seigneurie received, on the lord's behalf, the dues and rents owed by the tenants, a local management office for the seigneurial estate entrusted to a trusted peasant.

procureur_des_pauvres_paroisse.label: Procureur des pauvres (overseer of the parish poor)
procureur_des_pauvres_paroisse.summary: Layman responsible in a parish for managing relief for the needy.
procureur_des_pauvres_paroisse.text: Under the Ancien Régime, each parish organised relief for the poor from alms and charitable bequests. This overseer of the poor was the layman delegated by the vestry ("fabrique") or the poor board ("bureau des pauvres") to administer these funds and distribute relief. The function is mentioned in vestry accounts and sometimes in parish and civil records as an honorific description.

procureur_des_pauvres_savoie.label: Procureur des pauvres (advocate for the poor, Savoy)
procureur_des_pauvres_savoie.summary: In Savoy, a magistrate of the Senate responsible for defending the causes of the poor in court.
procureur_des_pauvres_savoie.text: In the States of Savoy, the advocate for the poor was a judicial office attached to the Senate, responsible for pleading free of charge the cases of people without means. This legal aid institution, distinct from the parish overseer of the poor, illustrates the distinctive organisation of the Duchy of Savoy before its annexation to France.

procureur_des_trepasses.label: Procureur des trépassés (churchwarden for the dead)
procureur_des_trepasses.summary: Churchwarden specifically responsible for managing masses and foundations for the dead.
procureur_des_trepasses.text: Within a parish vestry council ("conseil de fabrique"), the procureur des trépassés administered the funds and pious foundations intended to have masses said for the repose of the souls of the dead. He kept the register of masses owed and ensured that testators' wishes were respected. This office illustrates the importance of the cult of the dead in parish life under the Ancien Régime.

procureur_du_roi.label: Procureur du roi (King's prosecutor)
procureur_du_roi.summary: Royal officer representing the King's interests before the courts of the Ancien Régime.
procureur_du_roi.text: The King's prosecutor was the public prosecutor at a royal court (bailiwick, seneschalsy, presidial court), responsible for ensuring that royal ordinances were respected and for prosecuting offences in the King's name. He was the direct ancestor of the "procureur de la République" instituted during the Revolution. The title appears frequently in notarial and parish records as a social description.

procureur_fiscal.label: Procureur fiscal (seigneurial prosecutor)
procureur_fiscal.summary: Officer of a lord of high justice responsible for defending the public interest and that of the lord.
procureur_fiscal.text: In a seigneurial court, the procureur fiscal played the same role before the lord's court as the procureur du Roi before the royal courts: he represented both the interest of the lord of high justice and the public interest, and prosecuted the offences falling under seigneurial jurisdiction. The function disappeared with the abolition of seigneurial courts in 1790.

procureur_general.label: Procureur général (Procurator General)
procureur_general.summary: Magistrate at the head of the public prosecution at a sovereign court.
procureur_general.text: The procureur général headed the public prosecution at a superior court (parlement, court of appeal, imperial court): he represented royal or state authority there, supervised the royal prosecutors of the lower courts and called for the laws to be applied. The title survives today at the head of the prosecution service of the courts of appeal and the Court of Cassation.

procureur_general_cour_imperiale.label: Procureur général (Imperial Court)
procureur_general_cour_imperiale.summary: Senior public prosecutor at the head of an Imperial Court.
procureur_general_cour_imperiale.text: Under the First and Second Empires, the courts of appeal were called Imperial Courts ("Cours impériales"); their procureur général headed the prosecution service and represented the public prosecution at the highest level of the jurisdiction. The function and its organisation remain essentially those of the procureur général of today's courts of appeal.

procureur_general_ordre_religieux.label: Procureur général (procurator general of a religious order)
procureur_general_ordre_religieux.summary: Member of a religious order responsible for representing and managing the material interests of the whole order.
procureur_general_ordre_religieux.text: In a religious order, the procureur général was the member delegated to the Holy See or the civil authorities to defend the temporal and legal interests of the whole order, as opposed to the procurator of a single house or province. He managed in particular its property, its lawsuits and its relations with Rome.

procureur_general_parlements.label: Procureur général (Procurator General of a parlement)
procureur_general_parlements.summary: Magistrate of the old parlements responsible for defending the interests of the King, the Church and minors.
procureur_general_parlements.text: At each Ancien Régime parlement, the procureur général represented the public prosecution: he made submissions in the King's name, ensured that judgments were carried out, and defended of his own motion the interests of people unable to defend themselves (minors, absentees, church establishments). It was one of the most prestigious judicial offices in the kingdom.

procureuse_du_roi.label: Procureuse du roi (wife of the King's prosecutor)
procureuse_du_roi.summary: Honorific title given to the wife of a procureur du Roi.
procureuse_du_roi.text: As with many Ancien Régime offices, the husband's title was sometimes feminised out of courtesy to designate his wife in parish or notarial records. "Procureuse du Roi" is therefore not a function exercised by the woman herself, but an honorific description reflecting her husband's social rank.

procureuse_generale.label: Procureuse générale (wife of the Procurator General)
procureuse_generale.summary: Honorific title given to the wife of a procureur général.
procureuse_generale.text: By the same courtesy usage as "procureuse du Roi", this title in old records designates the wife of a procureur général and not an office held by a woman. It reflects the Ancien Régime custom of giving the wives of legal officers the feminised title of their husbands.

professeur.label: Professeur (teacher, professor)
professeur.summary: Person who taught a subject at secondary or higher level or in private lessons.
professeur.text: A generic term for a teacher, most often at secondary or higher level, as opposed to the primary schoolteacher ("instituteur"). The word covers a wide variety of statuses and specialities depending on the period and the level of teaching.

professeur_d_histoire_geographie.label: Professeur d'histoire-géographie (history and geography teacher)
professeur_d_histoire_geographie.summary: Secondary school teacher specialising in history and geography.
professeur_d_histoire_geographie.text: A dual subject peculiar to the French school system, history and geography have been taught by the same teacher in "collèges" and "lycées" since the late 19th century, this pairing being a distinctive feature of the French national education system.

professeur_de_judo.label: Professeur de judo (judo instructor)
professeur_de_judo.summary: Qualified instructor who gave judo lessons.
professeur_de_judo.text: The professeur de judo teaches this martial art of Japanese origin, brought to France at the beginning of the 20th century, within a club or sports association; teaching is generally governed by a state diploma or a black-belt grade recognised by the federation.

professeur_de_tennis.label: Professeur de tennis (professeur_de_tennis)
professeur_de_tennis.summary: Enseignant diplômé chargé de dispenser des cours de tennis.
professeur_de_tennis.text: Le professeur de tennis donne des leçons individuelles ou collectives dans un club, activité encadrée en France par un diplôme d'État de moniteur ou d'éducateur sportif.

professeur_des_ecoles.label: Professeur des écoles (primary school teacher)
professeur_des_ecoles.summary: Teacher at the first level (nursery and primary school) in France.
professeur_des_ecoles.text: The title officially replaced that of "instituteur" in 1990, when the corps of "professeurs des écoles" was created and their training was brought into the IUFM (teacher training institutes). It designates the first-level teacher, from nursery school to the last year of primary school ("CM2").

professor_regio.label: Professor régio (royal teacher)
professor_regio.summary: Teacher paid by the State after the Pombaline education reforms.
professor_regio.text: The professor régio teaches, by appointment and at the Crown's expense, reading, writing and arithmetic or humanities subjects (Latin grammar, Greek, rhetoric, philosophy), within the public education system created by the reforms of the Marquis of Pombal, in 1759 for secondary humanities and in 1772 for elementary schooling, funded by the "subsídio literário" tax. The designation appears in records of the late 18th and first half of the 19th century.

projectionniste.label: Projectionniste (projectionist)
projectionniste.summary: Person responsible for projecting films in a cinema.
projectionniste.text: The projectionniste handles the film, assembles the reels and projects the films in the cinema. The occupation, born with the cinematograph at the end of the 19th century, has changed greatly with the move from photographic film to digital projection.

promoteur_tribunal_ecclesiastique.label: Promoteur (promoter of justice)
promoteur_tribunal_ecclesiastique.summary: In an ecclesiastical court, the officer who played the role of public prosecutor.
promoteur_tribunal_ecclesiastique.text: The promoteur de justice represented, within the diocesan court ("officialité"), the interest of canon law: he made submissions in disciplinary cases and ensured that Church law was respected, like the procureur du Roi in the civil courts.

proponent.label: Proponent (licensed preacher)
proponent.summary: Theologian licensed to preach but still awaiting a call to a congregation.
proponent.text: After studying theology and passing the preparatory examination before the classis, the proponent was allowed to preach in the Protestant churches without yet being the minister of a congregation. He waited for a call from a consistory, after which he was ordained as minister following a second examination. In the meantime he often stood in for ministers or worked as a private tutor.

proprietaire.label: Propriétaire (property owner)
proprietaire.summary: Person living on the income from land or buildings, without practising any other occupation.
proprietaire.text: In 19th-century records, "propriétaire" describes a person who owned enough land or buildings to live on, without practising a waged trade. The description indicates a certain level of social comfort, close to that of "rentier", and is found very frequently in civil registers to designate rural notables.

proprietaire_cultivateur.label: Propriétaire cultivateur (owner-farmer)
proprietaire_cultivateur.summary: Peasant who farmed the land he owned himself.
proprietaire_cultivateur.text: This double description distinguishes the peasant who owned and farmed his own land from the simple tenant farmer or sharecropper who worked someone else's property. The entry is frequent in 19th-century records, a period when small rural property was highly valued.

protecteur_chemin_de_fer.label: Protecteur (railway lookout)
protecteur_chemin_de_fer.summary: Worker in a platelaying gang who signalled the approach of trains.
protecteur_chemin_de_fer.text: Within the gangs responsible for laying and maintaining railway track, the protecteur's role was to watch the traffic and warn his colleagues of an approaching train, in order to prevent accidents during work on the line.

protecteur_de_chemin_de_fer.label: Protecteur de chemin de fer (railway lookout)
protecteur_de_chemin_de_fer.summary: In a gang of railway platelayers, the worker who warned his colleagues of approaching trains.
protecteur_de_chemin_de_fer.text: In a gang of railway platelayers, the protecteur warned his colleagues of approaching trains during work on the track.

provedor.label: Provedor (supervisor of pious legacies, or head of a Misericórdia)
provedor.summary: Official who supervised wills, chantries, confraternities and hospitals, or president of a Santa Casa da Misericórdia.
provedor.text: The provedor of a district (comarca), a royal magistrate, oversees the execution of wills and pious bequests, chantries, confraternities, hospitals and hostels, as well as the property of orphans and absentees. The title also denotes the president of the board of a Santa Casa da Misericórdia (charitable brotherhood), elected from among its brothers and usually a local notable. In records, the context makes it possible to tell these functions apart.

proxenete.label: Proxénète (broker, go-between)
proxenete.summary: Originally a go-between or broker who negotiated a deal, a marriage or a transaction.
proxenete.text: Borrowed from the Latin "proxeneta" ("broker", itself from Greek), the word originally referred to anyone acting as an intermediary in a negotiation, whether commercial or matrimonial. From the 19th century its meaning gradually narrowed to the one that is exclusive today: a person who lives off the prostitution of others (a pimp).

proyer.label: Proyer (herdsman)
proyer.summary: In some regions, a dialect variant for a shepherd or cowherd, a keeper of flocks and herds.
proyer.text: This regional term refers to a herdsman, a local variant of shepherd or cowherd; it shares its root with the name of the corn bunting ("bruant proyer"), a bird of the fields, though the only link between the two uses is life in the fields.

przeor.label: Przeor (prior)
przeor.summary: Superior of a monastery or deputy of an abbot.
przeor.text: The przeor heads a monastery in orders without abbots (such as the Dominicans, Carmelites or Paulines) or is the abbot’s deputy in an abbey. The przeorysza (prioress) has the same role in a convent.

przysiezny.label: Przysiężny (village juror)
przysiezny.summary: Member of a village court or sworn representative of the village community.
przysiezny.text: The przysiężny sat with the sołtys on the village court (ława) and took part in settling minor disputes and in the affairs of the village community. He took an oath, from which the name derives; przysiężni often appear in records as witnesses.

puddleur.label: Puddleur (puddler)
puddleur.summary: Ironworker who stirred molten pig iron to turn it into wrought iron.
puddleur.text: The puddleur worked at the puddling furnace, where he stirred by hand, using an iron rabble ("ringard"), the molten pig iron exposed to the air in order to remove its carbon and obtain malleable iron. This puddling process, developed in England at the end of the 18th century, spread to the major French iron-making regions (Nord, Lorraine, Saint-Étienne) in the 19th century; it was reputed to be among the hardest work in the iron industry.

puisatier.label: Puisatier (well digger)
puisatier.summary: Craftsman specialising in digging and maintaining wells.
puisatier.text: The puisatier dug and lined the wells that supplied water, a trade requiring both strength and skill practised throughout the countryside before piped water became widespread. The term is found under various regional spellings in old records.

puiseur.label: Puiseur (peat-pit baler)
puiseur.summary: Peat worker responsible for clearing water from the pits where peat was cut.
puiseur.text: In peat bogs worked for fuel, the puiseur bailed out the water that continually flooded the peat pits, an essential task that allowed the other workers to cut the peat.

pulpero.label: Pulpero (Spanish-American storekeeper)
pulpero.summary: In Spanish America, keeper of a pulpería, a general store and drinking place that was also a meeting point.
pulpero.text: The pulpero ran a pulpería, a type of establishment typical of the Río de la Plata, Chile, Venezuela and other parts of Spanish America, which sold food, drink, candles and sundry goods and where people drank and played games. Often isolated in the countryside, pulperías were centres of rural social life.

pureur.label: Pureur (seed sorter)
pureur.summary: In northern France, a farm worker who sorted good grain from the tares to prepare seed.
pureur.text: Before mechanical seed drills, this manual sorting of the grain intended for sowing was a careful operation entrusted to a specialised worker, who guaranteed the quality of the future harvest.

quadrilleur.label: Quadrilleur (gunstock checkerer)
quadrilleur.summary: Gunmaker's worker who carved the decorative checkering on the stocks of firearms.
quadrilleur.text: Checkering is a relief carving technique that forms a pattern of small diamonds on the wood of the stock, intended both to decorate the weapon and to improve the grip; the quadrilleur was the specialist who carried it out within the gunmaker's workshop.

quartenier.label: Quartenier (quarter officer)
quartenier.summary: Officer of the Paris citizens' militia who commanded one of the city's quarters.
quartenier.text: Under the Ancien Régime, Paris was divided administratively into quarters, each placed under the authority of a quartenier responsible in particular for the citizens' watch ("guet bourgeois"), for maintaining order and for raising the local militia. The function disappeared with the municipal reforms of the Revolution.

quartier_maitre.label: Quartier-maître (leading seaman)
quartier_maitre.summary: Junior rating in the French Navy.
quartier_maitre.text: The quartier-maître is the first rank of petty officer in the Navy, equivalent to the corporal or "brigadier" of the other arms. It is divided into quartier-maître 2nd class and then 1st class, each rank also being followed by a speciality (mechanic, stoker, helmsman, etc.).

quartier_maitre_chauffeur.label: Quartier-maître chauffeur (leading stoker)
quartier_maitre_chauffeur.summary: Naval rating specialising in running the boilers and the engine room.
quartier_maitre_chauffeur.text: On steamships, the stoker ("chauffeur") fed the boilers with coal and later monitored the propulsion plant; the quartier-maître chauffeur was the junior rating in charge within the engine-room team.

quatriesmier.label: Quatriesmier (wine tax collector)
quatriesmier.summary: Collector of a local tax on wine levied at a quarter of its price.
quatriesmier.text: This dialect term refers to the collector of the "quatrième", a local Ancien Régime tax on the sale of wine at a rate of a quarter of its value, one of the many indirect taxes levied for the benefit of a lord or a community.

questeur.label: Questeur (quaestor)
questeur.summary: Magistrate or officer responsible for the financial administration of an institution.
questeur.text: In ancient Rome, the quaestor was the magistrate responsible for public finances and the management of the treasury. The title was taken up in modern French institutions: in the National Assembly and the Senate, the quaestors are the members responsible for the administration, the budget and the internal services of their chamber.

queu.label: Queu (cook)
queu.summary: Old form of the word "queux", meaning a cook or kitchen assistant.
queu.text: "Queux" is the medieval and classical term for a cook, which survives today in the set expression "maître queux". The spelling "queu", without the x, appears in some old records to designate the same function of preparing meals, often in the service of a great house.

quincaillier.label: Quincaillier (ironmonger)
quincaillier.summary: Dealer in metal goods and tools for household and craft use.
quincaillier.text: The quincaillier kept a shop selling metal articles — nails, tools, utensils, iron fittings — intended for craftsmen and households alike. The trade grew strongly with the rise of the industrial production of hardware in the 19th century.

quintero.label: Quintero (Spanish farm tenant)
quintero.summary: Person who rented a quinta estate or worked its land as a farmhand.
quintero.text: The quintero held a quinta, a country or farming estate, on lease, or worked on it as a farmhand for the owner. The term is used mainly in central and southern Spain.

quinto.label: Quinto (Spanish conscript)
quinto.summary: Young man enlisted and drawn by lot for military service in the annual Spanish levy.
quinto.text: The quinto was the young man called up for military service under the system of quintas: the young men of each village were registered and drew lots to fill the assigned quota, and the name comes from the old practice of taking one man in five. For much of the 19th century service could be avoided by paying a redemption fee or providing a substitute, which left abundant records.

rabadan.label: Rabadán (Spanish under-shepherd)
rabadan.summary: Shepherd who, under the head shepherd, managed the flocks of a herd and directed the shepherd boys.
rabadan.text: In the shepherds' hierarchy the rabadán ranked immediately below the mayoral: he looked after one or more flocks and directed the shepherds and boys who guarded them. The figure is characteristic of Castilian transhumant stock-raising.

rabadao.label: Rabadão (assistant shepherd)
rabadao.summary: Assistant shepherd, subordinate to the head herdsman (maioral), who helped guard and drive the flock.
rabadao.text: The rabadão is the second shepherd of a flock, placed under the orders of the maioral, whom he helps in guarding the animals, driving them to pasture and caring for them, standing in for him when needed. The term is used mainly in the Alentejo, the Ribatejo and the Beiras.

rabbiner.label: Rabbi (Rabbiner)
rabbiner.summary: Jewish scholar and religious head of a congregation or rabbinical district.
rabbiner.text: The Rabbiner is a scholar trained in the Talmud and religious law who decides religious questions, teaches, preaches, officiates at marriages and divorces and supervises observance of the dietary laws. Many German states had state or district rabbis responsible for the Jewish communities of a whole area, who from the 19th century partly also supervised the keeping of Jewish civil registers.

rabin.label: Rabin (rabbi)
rabin.summary: Scholar of Jewish law, spiritual leader and judge of a Jewish community.
rabin.text: The rabin was a teacher and expert in Jewish law who decided religious questions and disputes in the community (kahal), performed marriages and supervised religious schooling. In the nineteenth-century Kingdom of Poland, rabbis and their deputies also kept, or took part in keeping, the civil registers of the Jewish population.

raboteur.label: Raboteur (planer)
raboteur.summary: Joiner or cabinetmaker's worker specialising in the use of the plane.
raboteur.text: The raboteur trued and smoothed wooden surfaces with a plane, an essential operation before the assembly or finishing of a piece of furniture or a timber frame. With industrialisation, the term applied both to the hand worker and to the operator of a mechanical planing machine.

rabouin.label: Rabouin (Gypsy)
rabouin.text: This regional term from Saintonge was used for travelling people; it shares its root with the old slang word "rabouin", a familiar name for the devil, though the connection between the two uses is not documented with certainty.

racaillon.label: Racaillon (roofer)
racaillon.text: A Lorraine dialect term for the roofer, the craftsman responsible for laying and maintaining roofs.

raccommodeur.label: Raccommodeur (mender)
raccommodeur.summary: Mender of clothes, utensils or various objects, or a miner who replaced pit props.
raccommodeur.text: This generic term refers to anyone who repaired worn objects — clothes, tools, utensils — but in mining vocabulary it also applies to the worker responsible for replacing damaged timbering in the galleries.

raccommodeur_de_coucous.label: Raccommodeur de coucous (cuckoo-clock mender)
raccommodeur_de_coucous.summary: Itinerant repairer of cuckoo clocks and other clocks.
raccommodeur_de_coucous.text: This travelling repairer went round the countryside maintaining and repairing cuckoo clocks, very common in rural homes from the 18th century, particularly those from the workshops of the Black Forest.

raccommodeux.label: Raccommodeux (pit boy)
raccommodeux.summary: Mining synonym of "galibot": a young miner or apprentice assigned to timbering work.
raccommodeux.text: The term refers to the "galibot", a young miner-carpenter responsible for setting the props in the galleries, or more broadly to the labourer and apprentice miner. Here the word has nothing to do with the mending of clothes that its form otherwise suggests.

raccoutreur_de_souliers.label: Raccoutreur de souliers (cobbler)
raccoutreur_de_souliers.text: "Raccoutrer" is an old form of "raccommoder" (to mend); the raccoutreur de souliers practised the trade of a repairing shoemaker, restoring worn shoes rather than making new ones.

raccoutreuse.label: Raccoutreuse (hosiery mender)
raccoutreuse.summary: Woman worker who repaired defects in hosiery with a needle.
raccoutreuse.text: The raccoutreuse repaired, stitch by stitch, the defects and snags in stockings and other knitted articles coming out of the factory, painstaking work typical of hosiery regions such as Champagne and the Aube.

rachaneuse.label: Rachaneuse (slag-heap coal picker)
rachaneuse.summary: Woman who gathered coal from the slag heap.
rachaneuse.text: In the mining areas of the Nord and the Pas-de-Calais, the rachaneuses gleaned from the slag heaps the pieces of coal thrown out with the waste rock, salvage work done by women and children to supplement meagre household incomes.

racheur.label: Racheur (ripper)
racheur.summary: Miner responsible for widening galleries that had become too narrow.
racheur.text: Under the pressure of the surrounding ground, mine galleries narrowed over time; the racheur stepped in to restore them to their original cross-section, hard and dangerous work underground.

racheveur.label: Racheveur (finisher)
racheveur.summary: Craftsman who gave the final touch to a worked object from a foundry, pottery or elsewhere.
racheveur.text: The racheveur stepped in at the end of manufacture to perfect the finish of an object — deburring, polishing, touching up details — before it was delivered or put on sale.

racol.label: Racol (recruiting sergeant)
racol.summary: Person responsible for enlisting recruits for the army or navy.
racol.text: Related to "racoleur", the racol went round towns and fairs to sign men up for the royal troops or the navy, often by trickery or the lure of money, before conscription was introduced.

radelier.label: Radelier (raftsman)
radelier.summary: Timber floater who drove log rafts down the rivers.
radelier.text: The radelier assembled logs into rafts ("trains de bois") and steered them down the rivers to the towns, a floating technique used in particular to supply Paris with firewood from the Morvan until the 19th century.

radeur.label: Radeur (measure leveller)
radeur.summary: Person responsible for levelling measures of salt or grain with a strickle ("radoire").
radeur.text: In the retail sale of grain or salt, the measure had to be levelled off at the rim to guarantee an exact quantity; the radeur (or "raseur") did this with a "radoire", a small board used to scrape off the excess. The term is found in several regional variants designating the same function.

raffilier.label: Raffilier (pannier carrier)
raffilier.summary: Pannier carrier from the Liège region, whose pannier was called a "rafle".
raffilier.text: In the Liège area, this porter carried loads and materials in a dialect pannier called a "rafle", hence his name. The term is found in similar spellings designating the same trade.

raffineur.label: Raffineur (refiner)
raffineur.summary: Worker specialising in refining a raw material: saltpetre, sugar or glass.
raffineur.text: Depending on the industry, the raffineur purified and improved the quality of a raw material: refining saltpetre for gunpowder, refining cane or beet sugar, or reheating and fining molten glass in a glassworks.

rafournier.label: Rafournier (lime burner)
rafournier.summary: Lime burner working at a "rafour", a lime kiln dug into limestone ground, typical of the Dauphiné.
rafournier.text: The rafour was a rudimentary lime kiln dug directly into the limestone rock, used in particular in the Dauphiné; the rafournier burned the limestone in it to produce quicklime for building or agriculture.

rais.label: Rais (head of a tuna trap)
rais.summary: Head of the crew of a tuna trap, directing the laying of the nets and the mattanza.
rais.text: The rais (from the Arabic ra'is, chief) commands the tonnaroti, decides how the nets are set and when the mattanza takes place, when the tuna, enclosed in the final chamber, are hauled aboard. A prestigious position, often handed down within families, it is characteristic of the Sicilian and Sardinian tuna traps.

ramasseur_de_crottes.label: Ramasseur de crottes (dung collector)
ramasseur_de_crottes.summary: Person who collected dog droppings used in the tanning of fine leathers.
ramasseur_de_crottes.text: Called "pure" by tanners, dog dung was used to make the "pelanage" baths that softened and tenderised fine skins, notably for glove making and tawing. The ramasseur de crottes collected it in the streets and then sold it to the tawers.

ramendeur.label: Ramendeur (net mender)
ramendeur.text: On the coast, the ramendeur (or more often the ramendeuse) repaired the torn meshes of fishing nets, work essential to maintaining the fishermen's gear.

ramonet.label: Ramonet (farm steward)
ramonet.summary: In the south of France, the steward of a farm who had it cultivated and looked after the horse and livestock on the owner's behalf.
ramonet.text: On the large farms of the south of France ("bòria" in Occitan), the ramonet held an intermediate position between the owner and the farmhands or day-labourers whom he directed; some sources describe him more specifically as responsible for the care and driving of the working horse. With his wife, who was in charge of the food budget and the running of the household, he often lived with the farm staff in an outbuilding of the farm called the "ramonetage". The word, of Occitan origin, is not listed in standard French dictionaries.

ramoneur.label: Ramoneur (chimney sweep)
ramoneur.summary: Person who cleaned chimney flues to remove the soot.
ramoneur.text: Regular sweeping of chimneys prevented fires caused by the build-up of soot. Until the 19th century the job was often done by very young boys from Savoy, the only ones able to slip into the narrow flues — the "little Savoyard sweeps" who came down to work in the towns in winter.

ramoneur_fumiste.label: Ramoneur fumiste (sweep and stove fitter)
ramoneur_fumiste.summary: Craftsman who combined chimney sweeping with installing or repairing heating appliances.
ramoneur_fumiste.text: The fumiste installed and maintained chimneys, stoves and flues; combined with chimney sweeping, this double trade ensured the complete upkeep of domestic heating installations before central heating became widespread.

rancheur.label: Rancheur (ripper)
rancheur.summary: Miner responsible for restoring the cross-section of galleries squeezed by the pressure of the ground.
rancheur.text: Under the weight of the surrounding ground, mine galleries gradually lost their usable cross-section; the rancheur stepped in to straighten them and widen them back to their original dimensions. The term is found in an equivalent phonetic variant.

rapetasseur.label: Rapetasseur (botcher, cobbler)
rapetasseur.summary: Popular name for the cobbler, a craftsman who repaired old shoes and old clothes.
rapetasseur.text: The rapetasseur (or "rataconneur") was a synonym of the "savetier": he restored worn shoes and old clothes through successive small repairs (the "pièces" or "rapetasses"), a humble trade distinct from that of the shoemaker ("cordonnier"), who made new ones.

rapeur_de_tabac.label: Râpeur de tabac (tobacco grater)
rapeur_de_tabac.summary: Tobacco factory worker who ground tobacco into powder with a rasp.
rapeur_de_tabac.text: Before snuff was produced industrially, it was prepared as a powder by grating rolls of dried tobacco with a rasp; the râpeur did this work in the royal and later state tobacco factories.

rapporteur_du_point_d_honneur.label: Rapporteur du point d'honneur (reporting counsellor of the Court of Honour)
rapporteur_du_point_d_honneur.summary: Counsellor responsible for preparing cases before the Tribunal of the Marshals of France, the judge of disputes of honour.
rapporteur_du_point_d_honneur.text: Created by the Edict of Blois of 1602 under Henri IV to stem the epidemic of duels between noblemen, the jurisdiction of the "point d'honneur" (Tribunal of the Marshals of France) employed lieutenants and reporting counsellors, hereditary offices responsible for preparing cases of honour before judgment. This special jurisdiction, which had about 370 offices at the end of the Ancien Régime, was abolished by the law of 7 September 1790.

raquettier.label: Raquettier (racket maker)
raquettier.summary: Maker of rackets for real tennis ("jeu de paume").
raquettier.text: The raquettier made the rackets used for "jeu de paume", the forerunner of tennis, widely played in France from the Middle Ages to the 17th century before the sport declined in favour of other pastimes.

raquinaudeux.label: Raquinaudeux (travelling tinker)
raquinaudeux.text: A dialect term for an itinerant coppersmith who went round the villages repairing pots, cauldrons and metal cooking utensils.

rascoyeur.label: Rascoyeur (onsetter)
rascoyeur.summary: Miner responsible for coupling the tubs at the winding shafts.
rascoyeur.text: At the pit bottom ("accrochage"), the junction between the underground galleries and the shaft, the rascoyeur coupled and uncoupled the tubs of coal or ore that were to be raised to the surface.

ratinho.label: Ratinho (migrant harvester from the Beiras)
ratinho.summary: Seasonal worker from the Beiras who went down to the Alentejo for the grain harvest.
ratinho.text: The ratinhos were rural workers from the Beiras, mainly the Beira Baixa and Beira Alta, who migrated every year in gangs to the Alentejo to work in the grain harvest, afterwards returning home. The phenomenon, well documented in the 19th and 20th centuries, met the shortage of labour on the large southern estates at harvest time. The popular-sounding name sometimes appears in local records.

rattacheur.label: Rattacheur (piecer)
rattacheur.summary: Spinning-mill worker who joined broken rovings or threads on the machines.
rattacheur.text: In a textile spinning mill, threads frequently broke on the spinning machines; the rattacheur moved between the frames to join the broken threads quickly, so that production would not be interrupted.

ravaleur.label: Ravaleur (plasterer, sett cutter)
ravaleur.summary: Mason specialising in rendering and finishing walls, or a cutter of stone setts.
ravaleur.text: "Ravalement" refers to the restoration and finishing of a façade's render; the ravaleur was the mason who carried it out. Depending on the region, the term also refers to a cutter of stone setts used to pave the streets.

ravaudeuse.label: Ravaudeuse (darner)
ravaudeuse.summary: Mender of stockings and old clothes.
ravaudeuse.text: The ravaudeuse repaired knitted stockings and worn clothes with her needle, a humble female trade that was very widespread before ready-to-wear clothing and cheap textiles became general.

ravoyeur.label: Ravoyeur (estuary net fisherman)
ravoyeur.summary: Fisherman using a net called a "ravoir", stretched between the two banks at the mouth of a river.
ravoyeur.text: The ravoir was a large fixed net stretched across an estuary to catch fish carried by the current and the tides; the ravoyeur set it, watched over it and hauled it in.

razetier.label: Razetier (serge weaver)
razetier.summary: Serge maker in Provence in the 18th century.
razetier.text: The razetier wove serge, a twill-weave woollen fabric, an activity attested in Provence in the 18th century as part of the region's large-scale textile crafts.

rebatteuse.label: Rebatteuse (tile beater)
rebatteuse.summary: Brickworks woman worker who beat the terracotta tiles on a bench.
rebatteuse.text: After moulding, terracotta tiles had to be beaten again (packed down and levelled) on a bench before firing, to make them regular; this finishing work was often given to women in brickworks and tileworks.

rebouteux.label: Rebouteux (bonesetter)
rebouteux.summary: Person renowned for healing gifts, especially for setting dislocated bones, without any medical training or qualification.
rebouteux.text: The rebouteux (literally "one who puts back into joint") treated fractures, sprains and dislocations, often in the countryside, through empirical manipulations passed down from generation to generation, outside any official medical training. Long tolerated for lack of access to regular care, this popular recourse is found under several equivalent names in old records.

recameur.label: Récameur (embroiderer in gold and silver)
recameur.summary: Embroiderer specialising in decorative embroidery, especially "récamé" in gold and silver thread.
recameur.text: Récamé was a raised embroidery technique using precious metal threads, reserved for ceremonial pieces (liturgical vestments, uniforms, hangings); the récameur was the specialist craftsman who produced it.

recarreleur.label: Recarreleur (tile relayer)
recarreleur.summary: Craftsman specialising in laying and restoring terracotta, stone or ceramic tiled floors.
recarreleur.text: The recarreleur was called in to repair or replace damaged tiled floors, an activity close to that of the tiler but aimed at renovation rather than new work.

receveur.label: Receveur (collector, receiver)
receveur.summary: Officer or employee responsible for collecting taxes, dues or payments.
receveur.text: The generic term receveur covers a multitude of fiscal or administrative posts, under the Ancien Régime as in modern times, from the collector of the taille to the bus conductor, by way of the postmaster: in every case, it refers to the person who received a payment on behalf of an institution.

receveur_a_sel.label: Receveur à sel (salt tax collector)
receveur_a_sel.summary: Officer responsible for collecting the gabelle, the indirect tax on salt.
receveur_a_sel.text: The gabelle, one of the most hated taxes of the Ancien Régime, was collected in the salt stores ("greniers à sel") by royal receivers who controlled its compulsory, taxed sale, giving rise to a vast smuggling market ("faux-saunage").

receveur_d_epices.label: Receveur d'épices (collector of court fees)
receveur_d_epices.summary: Person responsible for collecting the fee due for drawing up the record at the end of a trial.
receveur_d_epices.text: Under the Ancien Régime, "épices" were the fees paid to judges and court officers for drawing up and issuing procedural documents; the receveur d'épices collected them for the court or its officers.

receveur_de_l_octroi.label: Receveur de l'octroi (octroi collector)
receveur_de_l_octroi.summary: Person responsible for collecting the octroi duties at the entrances to towns.
receveur_de_l_octroi.text: The octroi was a local tax levied on goods (particularly food, drink and materials) entering a town, at the gates or barriers that marked its tax boundary; the receveur de l'octroi collected it, until the tax was finally abolished in 1948.

receveur_de_manufacture.label: Receveur de manufacture (factory cashier)
receveur_de_manufacture.summary: Factory employee responsible for collecting customers' payments.
receveur_de_manufacture.text: Within a manufactory, the receveur kept the till and collected the payments owed by customers for the goods delivered, an accounting function specific to large-scale crafts and to the royal manufactories.

receveur_des_aides.label: Receveur des aides (collector of excise duties)
receveur_des_aides.summary: Officer responsible for collecting the "aides", indirect taxes on wine and other drinks.
receveur_des_aides.text: Together with the gabelle and the taille, the aides were one of the great taxes of the Ancien Régime; they fell mainly on the sale of wine, cider and other drinks, and were collected by a body of specialised receivers.

receveur_des_deniers_royaux.label: Receveur des deniers royaux (collector of royal revenues)
receveur_des_deniers_royaux.summary: Officer responsible for collecting the taille locally and passing it on to the receivers general.
receveur_des_deniers_royaux.text: At the first level of collection of the taille, the main royal direct tax, the receveur des deniers royaux collected the tax owed by the parishes in his district before paying it over to the receivers general of the "généralité".

receveur_des_droits_de_l_argue.label: Receveur des droits de l'Argue (collector of wire-drawing duties)
receveur_des_droits_de_l_argue.summary: Officer collecting the taxes levied on the drawing of gold and silver wire.
receveur_des_droits_de_l_argue.text: The "argue" was the workshop where precious metals were drawn out into fine wire (wire-drawing), used in particular to make braid and embroidery; the receveur des droits de l'Argue collected the royal tax levied on this operation.

receveur_des_gabelles.label: Receveur des gabelles (salt store receiver)
receveur_des_gabelles.summary: Officer responsible for loading, unloading and storing the salt in the salt stores and for its distribution.
receveur_des_gabelles.text: Distinct from the simple receveur à sel who collected the tax, this receiver oversaw the physical handling and storage of the salt in the royal salt stores, guaranteeing the quantities put on sale under the gabelle system.

receveur_du_prieure.label: Receveur du prieuré (priory receiver)
receveur_du_prieure.summary: Monk or layman responsible for managing the income, quit-rents and annuities of a priory.
receveur_du_prieure.text: The receveur of a priory administered the temporal affairs of this monastic establishment: collecting the ground rents, tithes and quit-rents owed by the tenants, and keeping the accounts submitted to the prior or to the abbey on which the priory depended.

recommandaresse.label: Recommandaresse (registry-office keeper)
recommandaresse.summary: Woman who kept an employment office for wet nurses and servants.
recommandaresse.text: For a fee, the recommandaresse put families looking for a wet nurse or a servant in touch with women seeking such a position; these "recommanderesses" offices, very active in Paris under the Ancien Régime, were sometimes subject to regulation because of the abuses they could give rise to.

recor.label: Recors (bailiff's assistant)
recor.summary: Public officer assisting bailiffs, who could arrest debtors.
recor.text: The recors accompanied the bailiff during seizures and executions, particularly to lend a hand in case of resistance and to bear witness to the operations carried out; in this capacity he could take part in the arrest of a recalcitrant debtor.

recouvreur.label: Recouvreur (roofer)
recouvreur.summary: Craftsman who built and repaired roofs using the materials available locally (tiles, slates, shingles, thatch, stone slabs).
recouvreur.text: Recouvreur is the generic name for the roofer in some regions, designating the craftsman who laid and maintained roofs, whatever the material used according to local tradition.

recteur.label: Recteur (rector)
recteur.summary: Title borne by the head of a school or religious establishment, or, in Brittany, by the parish priest.
recteur.text: The word covers several distinct functions depending on the context: in Brittany, "recteur" is the traditional name for the parish priest, very common in Breton parish registers; in addition, the "recteur d'académie" today heads the administration of the national education system in a region, and the rector of a university presides over the institution.

recuiseur.label: Recuiseur (annealer)
recuiseur.summary: Mint worker who annealed the metal blanks to make them malleable before striking.
recuiseur.text: Before being struck into coins, the cut metal blanks had to be annealed (heated and then cooled) to regain their suppleness and prevent them from splitting under the die; the recuiseur did this work in a mint.

reculeur.label: Reculeur (mine filler)
reculeur.summary: Miner responsible for clearing the ore cut by the hewers.
reculeur.text: After the coal or ore had been cut by the hewers ("haveurs") at the face, the reculeur removed the material towards the haulage roads, a complementary task within the team at the coalface.

reder.label: Reder (shipowner)
reder.summary: Owner or part-owner of one or more merchant ships.
reder.text: The reder owned a ship or a share in a ship and bore the costs and profits of the voyages in proportion to his share. In the Dutch Republic the partenrederij, in which a ship was divided into many shares held by different owners, was a common form. The shipowner or his managing owner arranged the fitting out, the chartering and the signing on of the crew.

regardeur_de_larmes.label: Regardeur de larmes (glass skimmer)
regardeur_de_larmes.summary: In a plate-glass works, a glassworker responsible for removing impurities from the molten glass before it was spread.
regardeur_de_larmes.text: Before the molten glass for making mirrors was spread out with a roller, the regardeur de larmes (or "grapineur") removed the visible impurities with a tool — ash, unmelted particles, the "tears" ("larmes") of the glass — in order to guarantee the optical quality of the resulting plate.

regedor.label: Regedor (parish administrative officer)
regedor.summary: Representative of the administrative authority in a parish (freguesia), in the 19th and 20th centuries.
regedor.text: The regedor is appointed by the municipality's administrative authority to represent it in a parish: he maintains public order, carries out orders from above, keeps watch on strangers and vagrants, reports crimes and helps with censuses and military recruitment. Assisted by the police corporals (cabos de polícia), he was usually an influential resident of the parish. The office existed from the 19th century until the last quarter of the 20th century.

regent.label: Régent (village schoolmaster)
regent.summary: Schoolmaster who had signed a contract with a village's inhabitants to teach the children.
regent.text: Before state schools were created, many village communities themselves hired, by contract, a régent to teach the children reading, writing and the catechism, often paid in money and in kind (lodging, food). The term "recteur d'école", used in some regions, denotes the same function.

regidor.label: Regidor (Spanish town councillor)
regidor.summary: Member of the Spanish town council who took part in governing a city or town.
regidor.text: The regidor sat on the council that governed a Castilian city or town: food supply, urban policing, municipal property, public granaries and local ordinances. Depending on the place and period, the office was elective, drawn by lot or held for life; in many cities perpetual seats were bought and passed down by inheritance. The term still designates a councillor in some municipalities.

reglissier.label: Réglissier (liquorice maker)
reglissier.summary: Confectioner who made liquorice sticks and balls from the juice of liquorice roots.
reglissier.text: The réglissier prepared sweets based on liquorice root extract (Glycyrrhiza glabra), chewing sticks or pastilles, a traditional French confectionery speciality.

regratier.label: Regratier (huckster)
regratier.summary: Retail grocer selling second-hand foodstuffs, including leftovers from noble tables.
regratier.text: The regrattier sold at retail, often to the poorest, foodstuffs of inferior quality or second-hand: leftovers, surpluses or goods bought back cheaply, notably the leftovers from the tables of wealthy households.

reislaeufer.label: Swiss mercenary (Reisläufer)
reislaeufer.summary: Swiss mercenary in foreign military service.
reislaeufer.text: The Reisläufer (from Reise, campaign) is a Swiss who enters the service of a foreign ruler as a mercenary, for example France, Spain, Naples, the Netherlands or the Pope, often in regiments raised under treaties (capitulations) between cantons and foreign powers. Mercenary service was an important source of income from the 15th to the 19th century; the federal state banned new capitulations in 1848 and recruitment for foreign service in 1859, except for the Papal Swiss Guard.

rekrut.label: Rekrut (conscript)
rekrut.summary: Young man called up to the army by conscription.
rekrut.text: The rekrut was a man taken into the army by conscription, called branka in the Russian partition. Service in the nineteenth-century Russian army lasted a very long time, so that a recruit often left his home village for many years, or for good. Mentions of recruits or conscripts appear in birth records and in conscription lists.

relator.label: Relator (Spanish court reporter)
relator.summary: Lawyer attached to a Spanish court who summarised case records and read them to the judges.
relator.text: Attached to an Audiencia, Chancillería or royal council, the relator made abstracts of each lawsuit's records and reported on them to the judges before the hearing, so that they knew the content of the case. A position of trust, it required legal training and was held by appointment.

relayeur.label: Relayeur (relay carrier)
relayeur.summary: Carter specialising in the transport of goods organised by relays.
relayeur.text: On the main roads, transport by relays made it possible to change teams at regular intervals to keep up a steady speed; the relayeur provided this goods transport service between relay posts.

releveur_de_fer.label: Releveur de fer (releveur_de_fer)
releveur_de_fer.summary: Serrurier fabriquant de grandes pièces d'ornement en tôle.
releveur_de_fer.text: Ce serrurier spécialisé façonne en relief (« relevé ») de grandes pièces décoratives en tôle de fer, destinées notamment aux enseignes, grilles ou ferronneries d'ornement.

relieur.label: Relieur (bookbinder)
relieur.summary: Craftsman who assembled and bound the printed sheets of a work to make a book.
relieur.text: The relieur sewed or glued the gatherings of a book, protected them with a stiff cover (board, leather) and saw to the finishing (gilding, lettering). In Franche-Comté, the word also designated, by dialectal extension, the cooper who fitted the hoops that bind ("relie") the staves of a barrel.

remailleuse.label: Remailleuse (ladder mender)
remailleuse.summary: Woman worker who repaired ladders in stockings and tights.
remailleuse.text: Before disposable tights became general, a ladder could be repaired stitch by stitch by a remailleuse, a specialised craftswoman who often worked at home or in an alterations shop.

remetteur.label: Remetteur (drawer-in)
remetteur.summary: Textile worker who prepared and set up looms, in particular by threading the warp yarns through the heddles.
remetteur.text: "Remettage" consisted of threading each warp yarn through the heddles and the reed of the loom before the weaving itself, a painstaking operation on which the quality of the fabric depended. The feminine term "remetteuse" was particularly used in the Lyon silk industry for this preparatory work.

remonteur_de_sable.label: Remonteur de sable (sand hauler)
remonteur_de_sable.summary: In Le Havre, a worker who climbed down the cliffs to bring up sand for building.
remonteur_de_sable.text: This local occupation in Le Havre consisted of extracting sand at the foot of the coastal cliffs and hauling it up to the top; the sand was then used for mortar and building in the town.

remouleur.label: Rémouleur (knife grinder)
remouleur.summary: Itinerant craftsman who sharpened knives, scissors and other cutting tools with a grindstone.
remouleur.text: The rémouleur travelled through towns and villages with his grindstone mounted on a small cart or a bicycle, announcing his arrival in order to sharpen people's knives, scissors and tools; the image of the itinerant knife grinder remains emblematic of the vanished small street trades.

rempailleur.label: Rempailleur (chair caner)
rempailleur.summary: Chair maker who repaired straw chair seats.
rempailleur.text: The rempailleur rewove the seats of worn chairs with rye straw, a craft trade that was often itinerant and traditionally practised seasonally.

remplisseur.label: Remplisseur (colourer)
remplisseur.summary: Worker who painted or coloured the motifs sketched on faience, glass or porcelain objects.
remplisseur.text: In a ceramics or glass manufactory, the decoration was first outlined by a draughtsman, then the remplisseur applied the colour inside the motifs, one stage in a decoration line divided into specialised tasks.

renard.label: Renard (pit sawyer)
renard.summary: Forest worker specialising in ripsawing timber lengthwise with a two-handled saw worked by two men.
renard.text: Pit sawing ("sciage de long") consisted of cutting trunks into planks or beams with a two-man saw, one sawyer standing in a pit or on a trestle and the other above the timber. This itinerant trade, often practised by teams from the Massif Central or the Alps, has many regional names designating the same activity.

renovateur_de_terrier.label: Rénovateur de terrier (terrier renovator)
renovateur_de_terrier.summary: Specialist in feudal law responsible for recording the lands, rights and dues of a seigneury.
renovateur_de_terrier.text: The "terrier" was the register that listed the holdings, rights and dues owed to the lord by his tenants; its periodic "renovation", entrusted to a specialist in feudal law (often a notary or an itinerant lawyer), consisted of bringing it up to date by investigating the properties and their holders.

rentier.label: Rentier (person of independent means)
rentier.summary: Person who lived on the income from capital or annuities, without any professional activity.
rentier.text: The rentier lived on the interest from his investments, ground rents or government bonds, without working. The description, highly prized socially in the 19th century, is commonly found in civil registers in its feminine form "rentière".

rentrayeur.label: Rentrayeur (fine-drawer)
rentrayeur.summary: Textile worker who sewed or joined two pieces of cloth so that the seam could not be seen.
rentrayeur.text: "Rentraiture" was an invisible sewing technique used to mend torn fabrics or join two widths of cloth without leaving a visible trace, a skill close to invisible mending ("stoppage"). The term is found in an equivalent variant.

reparateur_de_cables_electriques.label: Réparateur de câbles électriques (electrical cable repairer)
reparateur_de_cables_electriques.summary: Technician specialising in the maintenance and repair of electrical installations and their wiring.
reparateur_de_cables_electriques.text: An occupation that appeared with the electrification of homes and industrial networks in the 20th century, it consists of diagnosing and repairing faults affecting electrical cables and circuits.

repartiteur.label: Répartiteur (tax assessor)
repartiteur.summary: Official responsible for allocating resources, goods or a tax burden among several recipients.
repartiteur.text: In the tax administration of the Ancien Régime and then of the 19th century, the term refers in particular to the officer or local notable responsible for allocating the tax (the taille, then the direct contributions) among the taxpayers of a commune, according to their presumed means.

repasseur.label: Repasseur (presser, ironer)
repasseur.summary: Craftsman specialising in ironing and finishing fabrics and clothes.
repasseur.text: The repasseur (or repasseuse) smoothed and dressed linen and clothes with an iron, a trade practised both at home and in laundries; some ironers were also dry cleaners ("dégraisseurs"), removing stains before ironing.

reperceur.label: Reperceur (piercer)
reperceur.summary: Metalworker specialising in drilling and perforating metal parts.
reperceur.text: The reperceur worked in locksmiths' or gunsmiths' workshops, drilling or re-piercing metal parts that needed precise holes or openwork.

representant_de_commerce.label: Représentant de commerce (commercial traveller)
representant_de_commerce.summary: Employee responsible for canvassing customers and selling a company's products on its behalf.
representant_de_commerce.text: The représentant de commerce ("VRP") travelled round a geographical area visiting customers, taking orders and promoting the products of one or more employers, a professional status that developed with the growth of wholesale trade in the 19th and 20th centuries.

repriseuse.label: Repriseuse (darner)
repriseuse.summary: Textile worker specialising in darning fabrics, that is, mending snags and holes.
repriseuse.text: The repriseuse closed up the tears and holes in a fabric by weaving new threads across the damaged area, a technique known as darning ("reprise"), close to invisible mending but generally applied to household linen and everyday clothes.

resarcisseuse.label: Resarcisseuse (cloth mender)
resarcisseuse.summary: Textile worker specialising in mending and repairing torn or worn fabrics.
resarcisseuse.text: From the Latin "resarcire" ("to repair, to sew up again"), this old and rare term designates a woman worker responsible for restoring damaged cloth, in the same spirit as the repriseuse or the ravaudeuse but under a more learned and localised name.

resinier.label: Résinier (resin tapper)
resinier.summary: Forest worker specialising in extracting resin from pine trees by cutting the bark.
resinier.text: The résinier (or "gemmeur") practised resin tapping ("gemmage"): he cut into the bark of maritime pines to collect the resin ("gemme"), which ran into a small terracotta pot (the "galipot") fixed to the trunk. This activity, emblematic of the Landes de Gascogne forest since the 19th century, supplied the raw material for the turpentine and rosin industry until its decline in the 20th century.

restapleur.label: Restapleur (stone packer)
restapleur.summary: Miner responsible for backfilling galleries with stones.
restapleur.text: After a face had been worked, the restapleur backfilled the voids left in the galleries by piling up waste stones in them, in order to support the ground and limit subsidence; this backfilling work complemented that of the timberman ("boiseur"), who propped the galleries with wood.

restaurateur.label: Restaurateur (restaurant keeper)
restaurateur.summary: Person who kept an establishment where meals were served for payment.
restaurateur.text: The word "restaurant" originally came from the "restaurant" (restorative) broths sold in the 18th century by health-food sellers, before it came to designate, from the end of the 18th century, the establishment itself; the restaurateur was its keeper or the cook in charge.

retameur.label: Rétameur (re-tinner)
retameur.summary: Craftsman who applied and repaired the tin lining on metal utensils.
retameur.text: The rétameur (often itinerant) coated the inside of copper or iron cooking utensils with a thin layer of tin, an operation needed to prevent the toxic oxidation of the metal in contact with food, and one that had to be renewed periodically.

retendeur.label: Rétendeur (tenterer)
retendeur.summary: Textile worker who stretched fabrics after dyeing or treatment to restore their shape.
retendeur.text: After dyeing or washing, a piece of cloth shrank and lost its shape; the rétendeur put it back under tension on a frame (the tenter, "rame") to restore its width and evenness before sale.

retordeur.label: Retordeur (doubler, twister)
retordeur.summary: Textile worker specialising in twisting, the operation of twisting several threads together to form a stronger yarn.
retordeur.text: Twisting ("retordage") increased the strength of a yarn by twisting several single strands together; the retordeur ran the twisting machines in cotton, wool or silk mills.

revendeur.label: Revendeur (retailer, dealer)
revendeur.summary: Intermediary trader who bought goods to resell them at a profit.
revendeur.text: The revendeur bought foodstuffs or objects, often second-hand or wholesale, to resell them at retail with a margin; the term covers a wide range of small intermediary trades, in food and other goods.

revendeur_d_habits.label: Revendeur d'habits (old-clothes dealer)
revendeur_d_habits.text: The revendeur d'habits bought and resold second-hand clothes, a common trade before new clothing became widely affordable, practised in a shop or at markets.

revendeuse_a_la_toilette.label: Revendeuse à la toilette (itinerant wardrobe dealer)
revendeuse_a_la_toilette.summary: Parisian street seller who sold used clothes and toilet articles from door to door.
revendeuse_a_la_toilette.text: A typical figure of the "cris de Paris" engraved in the 17th and 18th centuries, the revendeuse à la toilette went round the streets with her basket on her back or on her arm, offering second-hand clothes, lace, ribbons and small toilet articles that she had bought up and resold, often in exchange for old linen.

rhabilleur.label: Rhabilleur (clock repairer)
rhabilleur.summary: Craftsman specialising in repairing and restoring mechanical objects, especially clocks and watches.
rhabilleur.text: The horological rhabilleur dismantled, cleaned and repaired the movements of clocks and watches, a precision trade distinct from that of the clockmaker who made them. The term is also found in a form specifying the object repaired.

rhabilleur_de_meules.label: Rhabilleur de meules (millstone dresser)
rhabilleur_de_meules.summary: Recutter of millstones, which had to be dressed about every ten days.
rhabilleur_de_meules.text: The rhabilleur de meules recut millstones, whose surface wore down and had to be dressed (recut) about every ten days, a job that took two days for a pair of millstones.

ribayrier.label: Ribayrier (Rhône boatman)
ribayrier.summary: On the Rhône, a boatman who carried goods by water.
ribayrier.text: The ribayrier was a water carrier working on the Rhône, transporting up to a hundred tonnes of goods on his barges; many of them came from the dioceses of Lyon and Grenoble, particularly from Savoy. This traditional river trade declined with the arrival, from 1826, of steam tugs, which considerably shortened the time taken to travel upriver.

rietsnijder.label: Rietsnijder (reed cutter)
rietsnijder.summary: Labourer who cut reed in marshes and reedlands in winter.
rietsnijder.text: Reed was cut and bundled in winter, when the stems were dry and hard, for use as thatch, for mats or for bank revetments. The reed cutters worked in the low peat districts and river deltas, often from the ice or from flat-bottomed boats.

rifleur.label: Rifleur (executioner)
rifleur.summary: Term used in some sources for the judicial function of executioner.
rifleur.text: This rare term is sometimes recorded as a local synonym of the hangman, responsible for carrying out the death sentences and corporal punishments pronounced by Ancien Régime justice.

risaiolo.label: Risaiolo (rice-field worker)
risaiolo.summary: Worker in the rice fields, employed in the various stages of rice growing.
risaiolo.text: The risaiolo prepares the paddies, regulates the water, sows, reaps and threshes the rice in the rice-growing areas of northern Italy. The term covers both the wage labourer and the small rice grower, as distinct from the mondina, who was mainly employed for the seasonal weeding.

ristapleur.label: Ristapleur (timberman)
ristapleur.summary: Mining synonym of "boiseur": a miner who propped the galleries with timbers.
ristapleur.text: The ristapleur set the timber frames and props that supported the roof and walls of the mine galleries, essential safety work that complemented that of the restapleur, who backfilled the voids with stones.

rittergutsbesitzer.label: Manor owner (Rittergutsbesitzer)
rittergutsbesitzer.summary: Owner of a Rittergut, a landed estate with traditional seigneurial rights.
rittergutsbesitzer.text: The Rittergutsbesitzer owns a Rittergut, an originally noble estate to which certain rights were attached: seat and vote in the district and provincial diets, patronage over church and school and, until the 19th century, patrimonial jurisdiction and police powers. In Prussia commoners could also acquire Rittergüter from 1807. The title is very frequent in records of the lands east of the Elbe, Saxony and Mecklenburg.

riveron.label: Riveron (riverbank worker)
riveron.summary: In Poitou, a day-labourer or farmer responsible for maintaining riverbanks.
riveron.text: This regional Poitou term designates a farm worker assigned to maintaining the banks of rivers, an important task for preventing floods and keeping the towpaths in good order.

riveteur.label: Riveteur (riveter)
riveteur.summary: Shipyard worker specialising in riveting plates.
riveteur.text: Before welding became widespread, ships' hulls and metal structures were assembled by riveting: the riveteur heated and set the rivets that joined the plates together, a noisy and physical job typical of the great shipyards of the 19th and early 20th centuries.

robin.label: Robin (man of the robe)
robin.summary: Collective nickname given under the Ancien Régime to the "gens de robe", holders of a judicial or administrative office.
robin.text: "Robin" was a familiar term, sometimes with a mocking nuance, for the magistrates and legal officers who wore the robe (judges, advocates, prosecutors), as opposed to the nobility of the sword. The term is found in some records as a social description.

robinetaire.label: Robinetaire (tap maker)
robinetaire.summary: Craftsman specialising in making taps and valves for controlling fluids.
robinetaire.text: The robinetaire made or repaired tap and valve mechanisms, used both in domestic plumbing and in some industrial installations.

rocteur.label: Rocteur (quarryman)
rocteur.summary: Worker or operator specialising in extracting stone from a quarry.
rocteur.text: The rocteur (from "roc", rock) worked at extracting ashlar or rubble stone in a quarry, a labouring trade practised in regions rich in limestone or granite deposits. The term is found in an equivalent variant.

rodier.label: Rodier (wheelwright)
rodier.summary: Craftsman specialising in making and repairing wheeled vehicles: carts, wagons and wheels.
rodier.text: The rodier (from "roue", wheel) made and repaired wheels and horse-drawn vehicles, a trade close to that of the "charron". The term is found in an equivalent variant.

roehrmeister.label: Water-pipe master (Röhrmeister)
roehrmeister.summary: Municipal official maintaining a town's water pipes, piped fountains and pumping works.
roehrmeister.text: The Röhrmeister is responsible for the town's water supply: he lays and repairs the pipes made of bored-out tree trunks (Deicheln), lead or clay, supervises spring catchments, piped fountains and pumping works (Wasserkünste) and ensures the distribution of water to fountains and houses. Pipe labourers (Röhrknechte) worked under him; the office is attested in many German towns from the late Middle Ages to the 19th century.

rogneur.label: Rogneur (comb cutter)
rogneur.summary: Comb maker specialising in cutting out the comb shapes traced on the horn.
rogneur.text: In the craft production of horn combs, the rogneur cut out the shape of the comb previously traced by the marker ("marqueur"), one stage in a production line shared among several specialised workers.

romanier.label: Romanier (steelyard maker)
romanier.summary: Maker of "romaine" scales (steelyards), used for commercial and domestic weighing.
romanier.text: The steelyard ("balance romaine"), with its unequal beam and sliding weight, was the most widespread weighing instrument among traders before modern pan scales became general; the romanier made and repaired its mechanisms.

rondier.label: Rondier (patrolman)
rondier.summary: Security guard or watchman who made surveillance rounds.
rondier.text: The rondier went round a site (factory, warehouse, estate) at regular intervals to keep it secure, a surveillance job found both in industry and in private security.

rondier2.label: Rondier (weavers' inspector)
rondier2.summary: Clerk who visited and supervised the scattered weavers working for the same merchant.
rondier2.text: In the system of home-based textile production (the "putting-out system"), weavers worked at home on behalf of a merchant-manufacturer; the rondier made the rounds of these craftsmen scattered through the towns and villages to check the quality of the work and to hand out or collect the raw material.

rondier_surveillant_de_tisserands.label: Rondier surveillant de tisserands (weavers' inspector)
rondier_surveillant_de_tisserands.summary: Clerk who, in a large town, visited and supervised the scattered weavers working for the same merchant.
rondier_surveillant_de_tisserands.text: The rondier surveillant de tisserands was a clerk who, in a large town, visited and supervised (made the rounds of) the various scattered weavers working for the same merchant-manufacturer.

rosetier.label: Rosetier (reed maker)
rosetier.summary: Maker of "ros", wooden or iron reeds used on looms to separate the warp threads.
rosetier.text: The ros (or weaver's reed) served to space the warp threads evenly and to beat up the weft during weaving; the rosetier made its dents from wood, reed or metal depending on the period. This trade has many equivalent regional names, including "rosellier", which derives directly from the word "ros".

rosieriste.label: Rosiériste (rose grower)
rosieriste.summary: Gardener specialising in breeding and growing new varieties of roses.
rosieriste.text: The rosiériste selected, hybridised and grew rose bushes, a French horticultural speciality renowned since the 19th century with nurseries such as those of Lyon or Orléans; despite the similarity of the names, it has no connection with the rosetier who made weavers' reeds.

rotisseur.label: Rôtisseur (roaster, cook-shop keeper)
rotisseur.summary: Craftsman who, under the Ancien Régime, held the exclusive privilege of buying poultry at the market halls and cooking it for sale.
rotisseur.text: The guild of rôtisseurs held the monopoly in Paris on roasting poultry and game for resale, as opposed to caterers ("traiteurs") and butchers, whose privileges covered other preparations; this strict organisation of the food trades is typical of the Ancien Régime guild system.

roucheux.label: Roucheux (reed thatcher)
roucheux.summary: Thatcher specialising in covering roofs with reeds, using traditional techniques.
roucheux.text: This dialect term designates a thatcher working in straw or reed, the traditional roofing material of marsh and pond regions such as the Brenne, the Sologne or the Camargue.

rouennier.label: Rouennier (maker of Rouen printed cottons)
rouennier.summary: Maker or seller of printed cotton cloth, a textile speciality of the Rouen area.
rouennier.text: "Indiennes de Rouen" were cotton cloths painted or printed with coloured patterns, made in imitation of the cotton fabrics imported from India; Rouen was, with Mulhouse and Jouy-en-Josas, one of the great French centres of this industry in the 18th and 19th centuries, and the rouennier was its manufacturer or merchant.

rouisseur.label: Rouisseur (retter)
rouisseur.summary: Textile worker specialising in retting flax and hemp, the operation that isolates the textile fibres.
rouisseur.text: Retting consisted of soaking flax or hemp stalks in water (river, pond or dew) to partly decompose their tissues and free the usable textile fibres, an essential stage before scutching. This trade has many regional variants of the same name.

rouleur.label: Rouleur (barrowman, trammer)
rouleur.summary: Worker specialising in moving loads on wheels, in various trades: docker, brickmaker or pipe maker.
rouleur.text: Depending on the sector, the rouleur pushed or pulled trolleys or tubs to move loads: sacks on the quays for a docker, unfired bricks in a brickworks, or pipes in the course of manufacture in a pipe factory.

roulier.label: Roulier (carter, waggoner)
roulier.summary: Carrier of goods using horses and carts, the historical equivalent of the modern lorry driver.
roulier.text: Before the railway, the roulier carried goods by road over long distances with teams of horses or oxen pulling heavy wagons; the great royal highways structured his activity, which was sometimes organised in convoys for safety. The term is found in an equivalent variant.

roulier_d_ardoise.label: Roulier d'ardoise (slate carter)
roulier_d_ardoise.summary: Worker specialising in carting blocks of slate to the splitter's workshop.
roulier_d_ardoise.text: In the slate-producing regions (Anjou, Ardennes), the roulier d'ardoise carted the rough blocks extracted from the quarry to the workshops where the splitter ("fendeur") cut them into roofing slates.

roulier_du_chemin_de_fer.label: Roulier du chemin de fer (railway carter)
roulier_du_chemin_de_fer.summary: Carter working under contract exclusively for the railway companies.
roulier_du_chemin_de_fer.text: With the rise of the railway in the 19th century, some carters specialised in road transport complementary to the railway, under contract with a railway company, to carry goods between the stations and their final destination.

routier.label: Routier (lorry driver)
routier.summary: Professional driver of heavy goods vehicles.
routier.text: The routier drives lorries to carry goods by road, an occupation that appeared with the development of the motor vehicle and the road network in the 20th century, the modern heir to the horse-drawn roulier.

rubanier.label: Rubanier (ribbon maker)
rubanier.summary: Merchant or maker of ribbons, fringes and sewing threads for haberdashery and trimmings.
rubanier.text: The rubanier produced or sold woven ribbons for dress ornament or decoration; from the 16th century Saint-Étienne was the great French capital of ribbon making.

ruchier.label: Ruchier (beekeeper)
ruchier.summary: Beekeeper specialising in rearing bees and producing honey and wax.
ruchier.text: The ruchier kept hives to harvest their honey and wax, the latter being particularly sought after before the 20th century for making church candles and candles.

rudnik.label: Rudnik (bog-iron smelter)
rudnik.summary: Smelter extracting iron from bog ore in bloomeries and small forest ironworks.
rudnik.text: The rudnik dug bog ore from wet meadows and smelted iron from it in bloomeries or small ironworks called rudnie, usually in forests close to supplies of charcoal. Such ironworks operated in Poland from the Middle Ages to the nineteenth century, and many villages are named after them.

rusquier.label: Rusquier (cork harvester)
rusquier.summary: Person specialising in stripping cork from cork oaks.
rusquier.text: The rusquier (from "rusque", bark in Occitan) stripped the bark of cork oaks, an operation carried out every nine to twelve years without felling the tree, typical of the cork oak forests of southern France (Landes, Var, Corsica).

rzezak.label: Rzezak (ritual slaughterer)
rzezak.summary: Ritual slaughterer killing animals according to Jewish law.
