rzezak.text: The rzezak (shochet) performed the ritual slaughter of animals and poultry according to kosher rules and inspected the meat for fitness. He needed religious knowledge and a licence from the rabbi, and was employed by the Jewish community.

sableur.label: Sableur (sand moulder)
sableur.summary: Foundry worker specialising in making sand moulds for casting metals.
sableur.text: The sableur prepared foundry moulds by packing special sand around a pattern, a sand-casting technique still widely used today for casting metal parts.

sablonnier.label: Sablonnier (scouring-sand seller)
sablonnier.summary: Seller of "sablon", very fine sand used for scouring dishes and household cleaning.
sablonnier.text: Before modern cleaning products were used, fine sand served to scour pewter or copper dishes and to clean floors; the sablonnier sold it from door to door in the streets of the towns.

sabotier.label: Sabotier (clog maker)
sabotier.summary: Craftsman specialising in making clogs, wooden shoes carved from a single piece.
sabotier.text: The sabotier carved and hollowed out a block of soft wood (often beech, poplar or birch) to make a shoe from a single piece, a cheap and sturdy working shoe worn by peasants until the middle of the 20th century.

sachsengaenger.label: Seasonal farm worker (Sachsengänger)
sachsengaenger.summary: Seasonal farm worker from the eastern provinces working in sugar-beet farming in central Germany.
sachsengaenger.text: The Sachsengänger came in the late 19th and early 20th centuries from Posen, Silesia, West and East Prussia and from Russian and Austrian Poland and worked from spring to autumn on the large estates of the Province of Saxony and central Germany, above all in labour-intensive sugar-beet farming. The name derives from the Province of Saxony, the first main destination of this migrant work.

sacquier.label: Sacquier (salt measurer)
sacquier.summary: Municipal officer responsible for measuring salt in maritime trade.
sacquier.text: This office of sworn salt measurer, attested in certain Mediterranean maritime trading ports, guaranteed the accuracy of the quantities of salt sold or transhipped in the port.

sacristain.label: Sacristain (sexton, sacristan)
sacristain.summary: Person responsible for looking after the church and assisting the priest during religious ceremonies.
sacristain.text: The sacristain looked after the church, prepared the objects used in worship (linen, sacred vessels, candles) and assisted the priest during services; it was an old parish function, often combined with that of beadle or cantor in small parishes.

sacriste_de_peine.label: Sacriste de peine (funeral sexton)
sacriste_de_peine.summary: Sexton specialising in assisting the priest at burials and funeral ceremonies.
sacriste_de_peine.text: In large parishes employing several sextons, the sacriste de peine devoted himself specifically to the offices for the dead and to burials, as opposed to the sextons responsible for the other ceremonies.

sactier.label: Sactier (pack-horse carrier)
sactier.summary: Carrier of sacks of ore and charcoal on horseback in the Breton forges.
sactier.text: In the old forges of Brittany, which ran on charcoal, the sactier brought iron ore on horseback, divided into sacks of 30 to 40 kg on either side of the animal, and charcoal, which was bulkier, carried in a single sack of 50 to 60 kg, from where they were produced to the storage sheds of the blast furnace.

safranier.label: Safranier (saffron grower)
safranier.summary: Person specialising in harvesting and trading saffron.
safranier.text: The safranier grew the saffron crocus and harvested by hand the stigmas of the flower that yield this precious spice, whose cultivation flourished notably in the Gâtinais and the Quercy before it declined in the 19th century.

sagard.label: Sagard (sawmill worker)
sagard.summary: Worker specialising in cutting timber into planks in a sawmill.
sagard.text: A Vosges and Lorraine dialect term for the pit sawyer or sawmill worker who cut logs into planks, an activity closely linked to the conifer forests of the Vosges.

sage_femme.label: Sage-femme (midwife)
sage_femme.summary: Woman trained to assist women in childbirth.
sage_femme.text: The sage-femme attended pregnancy and childbirth, succeeding the empirical "matrone" of the Ancien Régime as the profession became professionalised and regulated from the 18th century, with the creation of schools and official diplomas for midwives.

sagneur.label: Sagneur (reed cutter)
sagneur.summary: In the Camargue, a reed cutter specialising in harvesting "sagne".
sagneur.text: Sagne is the reed of the Camargue marshes, traditionally harvested for roofing cabins and for thatched roofs; the sagneur carried out its seasonal cutting in the marshes.

saigneur.label: Saigneur (bloodletter)
saigneur.summary: Surgeon who performed bloodletting, or physician who prescribed this traditional treatment.
saigneur.text: Bloodletting, the deliberate removal of blood thought to rebalance the body's humours, was until the 19th century one of the most common medical procedures, performed by physicians but also by barber-surgeons; the saigneur was the person who carried it out.

saigneur_de_porc.label: Saigneur de porc (pig slaughterer)
saigneur_de_porc.summary: Specialist in slaughtering the pig on the farm, according to rural tradition.
saigneur_de_porc.text: At the annual pig killing (the "cochon qu'on tue"), a highlight of rural life in the past, the saigneur de porc came to bleed and prepare the animal before it was turned into charcuterie by the women of the house or by an itinerant pork butcher.

saintier.label: Saintier (bell founder)
saintier.summary: Craftsman specialising in casting and making bells for churches and religious buildings.
saintier.text: The saintier cast bronze church bells, an ancient skill often handed down from generation to generation within dynasties of itinerant founders, who set up their temporary furnace near the belfry to be fitted out.

salarie.label: Salarié (employee, wage earner)
salarie.summary: Person who worked for an employer in return for a wage.
salarie.text: A generic term for anyone employed for pay, as opposed to the self-employed worker or the person running his own business; it is found particularly in 20th-century records to describe an occupation without further detail.

salarie_temporaire.label: Salarié temporaire (temporary employee)
salarie_temporaire.summary: Employee paid wages for a limited period, in the military or civil administration.
salarie_temporaire.text: This description designates an agent engaged on a non-permanent basis, for wages, for a specific service or task within an administration, as opposed to the established civil servant.

saleran.label: Saleran (paper finisher)
saleran.summary: Paper-mill worker specialising in the finishing of paper: sizing, hanging, folding, smoothing, drying and cutting.
saleran.text: In a craft paper mill, after the sheet had been formed, several finishing operations were still needed before the paper could be sold; the saleran (or "sallerant") was the specialist worker who carried out these final dressing tasks.

saleur.label: Saleur (salter)
saleur.summary: Person specialising in salting foodstuffs, especially fish and meat, to preserve them.
saleur.text: Before refrigeration, salting was one of the main methods of preserving perishable foods; the saleur treated fish (herring, cod) and pork with salt in curing houses and fishing ports.

salpetrier.label: Salpêtrier (saltpetre maker)
salpetrier.summary: Worker specialising in making saltpetre (potassium nitrate), the raw material of gunpowder.
salpetrier.text: The salpêtrier extracted saltpetre from soil and rubble impregnated with organic matter (cellars, cowsheds, rubble), then purified it. Under the Ancien Régime, saltpetre making was a royal monopoly essential to supplying the armies with gunpowder, and the saltpetre makers enjoyed special rights, including that of digging on private property.

sandalier.label: Sandalier (sandal maker)
sandalier.summary: Variant of "alpargatier", a maker of espadrilles.
sandalier.text: The sandalier made sandals and espadrilles with braided rope soles, a traditional craft particularly widespread in south-western France and the Basque Country.

sanglier.label: Sanglier (spruce-bark strap maker)
sanglier.summary: In Franche-Comté, a craftsman who worked spruce bark to make straps used to hoop cheeses.
sanglier.text: Using a "plumette" (a cutting tool) and then a "cuillère" (a gouge), the sanglier took from beneath the bark of the spruce a thin strip of wood a few millimetres thick, the "sangle", whose length varied from 42 cm — the diameter of a Mont-d'Or — to more than a metre for large wheels. This strap was used to hoop and hold soft cheeses, in particular vacherin Mont-d'Or, a practice attested from the 16th century and rare today.

sans_profession.label: Sans profession (no occupation)
sans_profession.summary: Civil register entry indicating that the person had no paid occupation.
sans_profession.text: Very frequent in the registers of the 19th and early 20th centuries, this entry most often describes married women who did not work outside the home, but also children, people of independent means or elderly people with no declared activity; it does not mean an absence of unpaid domestic or farm work.

santonnier.label: Santonnier (santon maker)
santonnier.summary: Craftsman who made crib figurines, the santons.
santonnier.text: The santonnier modelled in clay, often painted by hand, the small figurines of the Provençal crib ("santoun", "little saint" in Provençal), representing the traditional figures of the Nativity and of village trades; this craft tradition, born at the turn of the 18th and 19th centuries in Provence, lives on particularly around Marseille and Aubagne.

sapeur_pompier.label: Sapeur-pompier (firefighter)
sapeur_pompier.summary: Member of a corps responsible for fighting fires and providing emergency rescue.
sapeur_pompier.text: The corps of sapeurs-pompiers, heir to the old pump guards ("gardes-pompes") and to the companies of sappers created in the 19th century, is today responsible in France for fighting fires and for a large share of rescue services for people, whether as professional, volunteer or military firefighters (Paris, Marseille).

sardiniere.label: Sardinière (sardine cannery worker)
sardiniere.summary: Woman worker in fish canneries specialising in processing sardines.
sardiniere.text: In the great sardine ports of Brittany (Douarnenez, Concarneau) and the Vendée, the sardinières worked in the canneries heading, cleaning and canning the sardines; this female workforce, numerous from the end of the 19th century, was also behind some notable workers' strikes, such as the one in Douarnenez in 1924 ("Penn Sardin").

sarger.label: Sarger (serge weaver)
sarger.summary: Maker of serge, a twill-weave woollen fabric.
sarger.text: The sarger wove serge, a sturdy twill-weave woollen fabric used for making everyday clothes, a speciality of many French cloth-making regions.

sartre.label: Sartre (tailor)
sartre.summary: Old term for a tailor of clothes.
sartre.text: Derived from the Latin "sartor" ("one who mends, who sews"), "sartre" is an old southern form of the word for tailor, known today mainly as a surname — it is notably the origin of the philosopher Jean-Paul Sartre's surname.

sassier.label: Sassier (sieve maker)
sassier.summary: Maker of objects in peeled wood veneer, such as bushel measures and sieves ("sasses").
sassier.text: The sassier made measuring bushels and sieves ("sas") used for sifting flour or grain from thin sheets of peeled wood, a craft close to that of the "boisselier".

satinaire.label: Satinaire (satin weaver)
satinaire.summary: Maker of satin, a lustrous silk fabric used for luxury clothing.
satinaire.text: The satinaire wove satin, a silk fabric with a particular weave that produces a matt back and a lustrous face, reserved for luxury clothing and furnishings, notably in the Lyon manufactories.

saucier.label: Saucier (sauce cook)
saucier.summary: Cook specialising in preparing sauces and stocks.
saucier.text: In the classic French kitchen brigade codified by Escoffier, the saucier held a key post, responsible for sauces, stews and sautéed dishes, a post reputed to require long experience and great skill.

saunier.label: Saunier (salt maker)
saunier.summary: Worker specialising in extracting and producing salt in saltworks and salt marshes.
saunier.text: The saunier harvested salt in the salt marshes (as at Guérande or on the Île de Ré) or in inland saltworks, an activity subject under the Ancien Régime to the royal monopoly of the gabelle; those who produced or sold salt while evading this tax were called "faux-sauniers" (salt smugglers) and were severely repressed. The term is found in several regional variants designating the same activity.

saussier.label: Saussier (sauce maker)
saussier.summary: Maker of sauces and spicy condiments sold to accompany dishes.
saussier.text: The saussier made and sold sauces, mustards and spicy condiments used to season food. The term appears among the food guilds of the Ancien Régime, sometimes associated with the neighbouring trade of mustard maker. He was a food craftsman-trader who appears rather rarely in records, since the making of sauces was most often a domestic or secondary activity.

saute_ruisseau.label: Saute-ruisseau (errand boy)
saute_ruisseau.summary: Junior clerk or errand boy in a notary's or attorney's office.
saute_ruisseau.text: The saute-ruisseau was the youngest clerk in a notary's, attorney's or bailiff's office, responsible for errands, delivering documents and small commissions in town. The name, which conjures up the image of the clerk leaping over the streams and gutters of the streets to get about quickly, remained in familiar use until the 20th century to designate a junior beginner in a law office.

savetier.label: Savetier (cobbler)
savetier.summary: Craftsman who mended old shoes, as opposed to the shoemaker who made new ones.
savetier.text: The savetier repaired and patched up worn shoes (hence his name, from "savate", an old shoe) by fitting them with "tacons", leather mending patches, whereas the shoemaker ("cordonnier") made new shoes — a clear distinction of status within the Ancien Régime guilds, according to the old statutes of Paris. The Parisian cobblers nevertheless rose in the hierarchy of trades, reaching fourth rank in 1581. "Savatier" is an old spelling variant, and "taconneur" a synonym designating the same shoe patcher.

savetonnier.label: Savetonnier (sheepskin shoemaker)
savetonnier.summary: Shoemaker who worked only basan, a cheap sheepskin leather.
savetonnier.text: The savetonnier was a shoemaker of modest rank who worked only basan (tanned sheepskin), a less noble and less costly material than the cowhide used by the most skilled shoemakers. The term marks an internal hierarchy within the shoemaking guild, between the workers allowed to handle only common leather and those qualified to work fine leathers.

savonneur_de_glaces.label: Savonneur de glaces (plate-glass grinder)
savonneur_de_glaces.summary: Polisher who rubbed glass plates against each other with emery in a plate-glass manufactory.
savonneur_de_glaces.text: The savonneur de glaces worked in a plate-glass (mirror) manufactory, where he rubbed the glass plates against one another with emery in order to polish them and obtain a perfectly flat and smooth surface, the last stage before silvering. This specialised post is found in the great plate-glass manufactories, such as that of Saint-Gobain, from the 17th century.

savonnier.label: Savonnier (soap maker)
savonnier.summary: Maker of soap by traditional saponification techniques.
savonnier.text: The savonnier made soap by reacting fats (olive oil, tallow) with soda or potash, a process called saponification. The trade is particularly associated with certain towns, Marseille being the most famous for its soap, where it was regulated from the Ancien Régime by guild statutes guaranteeing the quality of manufacture.

savoyard.label: Savoyard (chimney sweep, errand man)
savoyard.summary: Chimney sweep or small errand man, occupations traditionally practised by emigrants from Savoy.
savoyard.text: In records, "Savoyard" denotes not only geographical origin but an associated occupation: in the 18th and 19th centuries, many Savoyards emigrated seasonally to the large cities to work as chimney sweeps or in small jobs as errand men and porters. In some registers the term came to designate the occupation itself, regardless of the person's actual place of birth.

sayetteur.label: Sayetteur (say weaver)
sayetteur.summary: Maker of "sayettes", light woollen fabrics used for making clothes.
sayetteur.text: The sayetteur wove "sayette" (say), a light and supple worsted fabric used for everyday clothes. This textile trade is well attested in regions with a woollen tradition (Picardy, Flanders), where it was often organised as a guild separate from that of the linen weavers. The term "ceteur" is an attested regional variant.

sbirro.label: Sbirro (Italian constable)
sbirro.summary: Constable serving the courts and magistrates in the Italian states before unification.
sbirro.text: The sbirro (or birro) carried out the arrests, seizures and summonses ordered by the judges, under the command of a bargello or a captain of justice. Disliked by the population, the sbirri were a body of low social standing; the word later took on a pejorative sense for a policeman.

scagard.label: Sçagard (sawmill worker)
scagard.summary: Vosges sawmill worker who cut timber into planks.
scagard.text: The sagard (or sçagard) cut logs into planks in a sawmill, a trade well attested in the Vosges, where abundant conifer forests and water power made sawmills prosper. The word comes from the old German "sagôn" (today "sägen"), meaning to saw.

scailleteur.label: Scailleteur (slater)
scailleteur.summary: Roofer specialising in laying slates ("scailles"), a term used in Wallonia.
scailleteur.text: The scailleteur laid slates ("scailles" in Walloon) on roofs. The term is typical of the slate regions of Wallonia and northern France, the local equivalent of the slate roofer.

scailton.label: Scailton (slate miner)
scailton.summary: Miner who extracted slate in underground quarries.
scailton.text: The scailton worked deep in the slate quarries ("scailles"), where he extracted the schistose rock that would be split into roofing slates. A Walloon regional term related to "scailleteur", which refers rather to the slater than to the extractor.

scaphandrier.label: Scaphandrier (diver)
scaphandrier.summary: Diver wearing a diving suit connected to the surface for underwater work.
scaphandrier.text: The scaphandrier carried out underwater work (hull repairs, harbour works, salvage of wrecks) wearing a watertight diving suit supplied with air from the surface through a hose. The occupation developed from the middle of the 19th century with the invention of diving suits with rigid helmets, and became common in ports and naval dockyards.

scelleur.label: Scelleur (sealer)
scelleur.summary: Officer responsible for affixing official seals to documents, or a cloth inspector, depending on the context.
scelleur.text: The scelleur was most often an officer responsible for affixing the seal (royal, seigneurial or judicial) that validated an official document, a function linked to the chancery. In the context of the textile trades, the same word can also designate an inspector responsible for sealing pieces of cloth to guarantee that their quality met the guild's regulations.

schaechter.label: Ritual slaughterer (Schächter)
schaechter.summary: Ritual slaughterer who killed animals according to Jewish religious law.
schaechter.text: The Schächter (Hebrew shochet) slaughters cattle, sheep and poultry according to the rules of Jewish religious law and then examines the animals for defects that would make them unfit to eat. He needed a religious qualification to do so. In small rural communities of southern and western Germany one and the same man often held the offices of teacher, prayer leader and Schächter.

schalliste.label: Schalliste (shawl weaver)
schalliste.text: The schalliste wove shawls, a very fashionable accessory in the 19th century. The trade developed with the fashion for cashmere-style shawls, produced notably in the manufactories of Lyon and Paris.

scharfrichter.label: Scharfrichter (executioner)
scharfrichter.summary: German term for the executioner, the carrier-out of capital sentences.
scharfrichter.text: Scharfrichter (literally "sharp judge") is the German term for the executioner, responsible for carrying out capital sentences and sometimes judicial torture. It is found in the registers of Alsace, Lorraine and other regions of German culture, where the civil records frequently use German terminology.

scheepsjongen.label: Scheepsjongen (ship's boy)
scheepsjongen.summary: Boy who served on board as the lowest member of the crew and learned the seaman's trade.
scheepsjongen.text: Boys often signed on at a young age as ship's boys in the merchant navy, the fisheries or the navy. They did all kinds of light tasks on board, helped in the galley and the cabin and so learned the trade, later becoming seamen.

schelpenvisser.label: Schelpenvisser (shell fisher)
schelpenvisser.summary: Fisher who gathered shells from the sea or the sandbanks to burn them into lime.
schelpenvisser.text: Shells were dredged from the Wadden Sea and the waters of Zeeland or gathered from the sandbanks and taken to lime kilns, where they were burnt into shell lime for mortar. Later shells were also used to surface paths and as poultry feed.

schiavandaro.label: Schiavandaro (Lombard farmhand)
schiavandaro.summary: In the Lombard lowlands, a permanent farmhand of a cascina, hired by the year and paid in money and in kind.
schiavandaro.text: The schiavandaro, typical of the large irrigated farmsteads around Milan, Lodi and Pavia, was hired for a year (from Martinmas to Martinmas) and received, besides a money wage, a share of grain and firewood and housing for his family. Employed in field work, he was distinct from the bergamino, who looked after the dairy cows.

schichtmeister.label: Mine accountant (Schichtmeister)
schichtmeister.summary: Mining official who kept the accounts, wages and materials of a mine.
schichtmeister.text: The Schichtmeister keeps the accounts of a mine (Zeche) in the mining districts of the Harz, Saxony and Bohemia: he pays the miners their wages, procures and books materials such as timber, iron and powder, collects the contributions of the shareholders (Gewerken) and reports to the mining office. In the hierarchy he stood beside the Steiger, who directed the work underground.

schillenboer.label: Schillenboer (peelings collector)
schillenboer.summary: Man who collected potato peelings and food scraps from houses as pig feed.
schillenboer.text: The schillenboer went from house to house with a cart or carrier tricycle to collect potato peelings and kitchen waste, which he sold as feed to pig keepers or fed to his own pigs. The figure was well known in Dutch towns in the first half of the 20th century.

schinder.label: Schinder (knacker)
schinder.summary: Knacker responsible for flaying dead animals, a term of Germanic origin.
schinder.text: The Schinder rendered dead animals or those unfit for consumption and processed their hides and skins, a trade considered impure and socially despised in the Germanic societies of the Ancien Régime. The term is found in the registers of German-speaking regions (Alsace, Moselle).

schlitter.label: Schlitter (timber sledger)
schlitter.summary: Woodcutter who slid felled timber down mountain slopes on a "schlitte".
schlitter.text: The schlitteur (or schlitter) brought the logs cut in the forest down the steep slopes of the Vosges by means of a "schlitte", a wooden sledge sliding along a track of logs. This dangerous and physically very demanding forestry trade was emblematic of the Vosges mountains until the early 20th century.

schout.label: Schout (Dutch local officer)
schout.summary: Local officer who administered justice and police on behalf of the lord or the sovereign.
schout.text: In the northern Low Countries the schout was the officer appointed by the lord or the count for a town, village or seigniory: he acted as public prosecutor, presided over the bench of aldermen without voting on the judgement himself, and maintained public order. In Brabant and parts of Flanders the same office was called meier. It disappeared with the reform of administration and justice at the end of the 18th and the beginning of the 19th century.

schulte.label: Schulte (eastern Dutch farmer or local officer)
schulte.summary: In the eastern Netherlands, a large farmer or a local administrative officer.
schulte.text: In Drenthe the schulte was the local administrative and judicial officer of a district, comparable to the schout elsewhere. In Twente, the Achterhoek and other eastern regions the scholte originally managed a manor belonging to a lord or a monastery and collected its rents; later the name was given to the largest farmers of a hamlet.

schutter.label: Schutter (civic guard member)
schutter.summary: Burgher who belonged to the schutterij, the armed civic guard of a town.
schutter.text: The schutterij was a civic militia that guarded the town, kept order during fires and riots and helped defend it in wartime. The schutters were organised in companies under captains and lieutenants drawn from the prosperous citizens. In modified form the schutterij survived into the 19th century as a reserve of the armed forces.

schwabenkind.label: Swabian child worker (Schwabenkind)
schwabenkind.summary: Child from the Alpine valleys who went each summer to work on farms in Upper Swabia.
schwabenkind.text: The Schwabenkinder came from Vorarlberg, Tyrol, Graubünden and South Tyrol and travelled in spring, often on foot across the Alpine passes, to Upper Swabia and the Lake Constance area, where they were placed with farmers at child markets such as in Ravensburg. They worked until autumn as herders, farmhands or maids for board, clothing and a small wage. This child migration lasted from the 17th century to the early 20th century.

schwaiger.label: Dairy farmer (Schwaiger)
schwaiger.summary: Holder of a Schwaige, an Alpine farm devoted to cattle raising and cheese making.
schwaiger.text: The Schwaiger works a Schwaige (Schwaighof), a farm established by landlords in the Middle Ages at higher altitudes of Bavaria, Tyrol and Austria, geared to cattle and dairy farming and often paying its dues in cheese. The term survives in many farm and family names.

schweizer.label: Dairyman (Schweizer)
schweizer.summary: Skilled milker and cattle keeper on larger estates, regardless of his origin.
schweizer.text: In Germany, from the 18th and especially the 19th century, the term Schweizer ("Swiss") denoted the professional milker and cattle keeper of large estates, because specialists from Switzerland were initially recruited for dairy farming; the name then stuck to the occupation. The Oberschweizer ran the cowshed with Unterschweizer as assistants. In records the term must not be confused with a statement of origin.

scieur_d_aisses.label: Scieur d'aisses (stave-wood sawyer)
scieur_d_aisses.summary: Sawyer specialising in cutting "aisses", boards used for barrel staves.
scieur_d_aisses.text: The scieur d'aisses cut the wood into "aisses", thin split boards used by the cooper to make barrel staves. This forestry trade stood upstream of cooperage, in the chain for preparing stave wood ("merrain").

scieur_de_corne.label: Scieur de corne (horn sawyer)
scieur_de_corne.summary: Comb maker who cut animal horn into three pieces: throat, "biscaye" and tip.
scieur_de_corne.text: The scieur de corne was a comb maker who cut the animal horn into three pieces — throat ("gorge"), "biscaye" and tip ("pointe") — the first stage in making a horn comb.

scieur_de_long.label: Scieur de long (pit sawyer)
scieur_de_long.summary: Forest worker who cut trunks into planks with a two-handled saw.
scieur_de_long.text: The scieur de long cut logs into planks with a long two-handled saw worked by two men: the top sawyer, standing on the trunk, and his companion below. Depending on the region, the work was done over a pit dug in the ground ("en fosse") or on trestles ("sur chevalets"), hence several variants of the same itinerant trade, often practised by seasonal woodcutters.

scieur_de_pierre.label: Scieur de pierre (stone sawyer)
scieur_de_pierre.summary: Worker who sawed quarried building stone into blocks.
scieur_de_pierre.text: The stone sawyer cut up the dressed stone extracted from quarries and prepared it for the stonemason.

scieur_peignier.label: Scieur peignier (comb-wood sawyer)
scieur_peignier.summary: Sawyer specialised in cutting wood intended for comb-making.
scieur_peignier.text: The comb-wood sawyer cut blocks of wood (boxwood in particular) into thin plates for the comb-makers, who would then shape them into combs. It was a specialisation of the sawyer's trade serving one particular guild, comb-making ("peignerie").

scloneur.label: Scloneur (mine haulier)
scloneur.summary: Miner responsible for moving ore in tubs along the underground galleries.
scloneur.text: The "scloneur" pushed and guided the ore tubs along the underground galleries, between the coalface and the winding shaft. It is a regional term from the mining vocabulary of Wallonia and northern France.

scoliaste.label: Scoliaste (scoliaste)
scoliaste.summary: Copiste et annotateur critique d'œuvres classiques grecques ou latines.
scoliaste.text: Le scoliaste copie, annote et commente de façon critique les œuvres classiques grecques ou latines, rédigeant des scholies (notes explicatives).

sdjere.label: Sdjère (mower)
sdjere.text: In Auvergne, the "sdjère" was the mower, who cut grass or cereal crops with a scythe.

seareiro.label: Seareiro (grain sharecropper, southern Portugal)
seareiro.summary: Small cultivator of the Alentejo and Ribatejo who sowed grain on land of a large estate in exchange for rent or a share of the harvest.
seareiro.text: The seareiro, owning a few draught animals and implements, sowed wheat or other grain on plots of a large estate (herdade) that did not belong to him, paying the owner or leaseholder a rent or a share of the harvest. An intermediate figure between the farmer and the wage labourer, he is characteristic of the large grain-growing estates of southern Portugal in the 19th and 20th centuries.

secretaire.label: Secrétaire (secretary)
secretaire.summary: Person responsible for drafting, filing and correspondence for an individual or an institution.
secretaire.text: The secretary drafted and filed correspondence, deeds and administrative documents on behalf of an employer — a private individual, a notable, an administration or a religious institution. Under the Ancien Régime the title could denote a prestigious office (secretary to the king, secretary to a great lord); it later became commonplace and covered any clerical job.

secretaire_de_commissaire.label: Secrétaire de commissaire (police commissioner's clerk)
secretaire_de_commissaire.summary: Secretary attached to a police commissioner, responsible for writing up official reports.
secretaire_de_commissaire.text: The police commissioner's clerk assisted a "commissaire de police" in drafting official reports ("procès-verbaux"), keeping the registers and handling the administrative filing of the police station. It was a junior post within the police staff that appeared with the organisation of urban policing in the 18th and 19th centuries.

segretario_comunale.label: Segretario comunale (municipal secretary)
segretario_comunale.summary: Official who runs the offices of an Italian municipality and draws up its administrative records.
segretario_comunale.text: The segretario comunale assists the mayor and the council, writes the minutes of their decisions, keeps the archives and supervises the municipal offices, often including the civil registry. In pre-unification municipalities the duty was performed by the cancelliere comunale; after the unification of Italy the post was regulated by the municipal law and required a special licence.

seifner.label: Placer miner (Seifner)
seifner.summary: Miner who washed tin ore or gold out of stream deposits (Seifen).
seifner.text: The Seifner recovers tinstone, more rarely gold, from Seifen, ore-bearing sand and gravel deposits in valleys and stream beds, by digging up the material and washing it in channels of running water so that the heavy ore stays behind. The tin placers of the Ore Mountains, the Fichtel Mountains and Bohemia were worked from the Middle Ages and left characteristic spoil heaps.

seigneur.label: Seigneur (lord of the manor)
seigneur.summary: Holder of a seigneury, exercising justice and feudal rights over his lands.
seigneur.text: The "seigneur" owned a seigneury, an estate over which he exercised feudal rights (dues, labour services, seigneurial justice) and from which he took his title ("seigneur de X"). It was not a trade in the strict sense but a social rank, very common in Ancien Régime notarial and parish records to designate members of the local nobility or those who had purchased fiefs.

seillietier.label: Seillietier (bucket maker)
seillietier.summary: Maker of buckets and "seilles", oval grape-harvest buckets.
seillietier.text: The "seillietier" made buckets and "seilles", oval grape-harvest buckets whose base was narrower than the top, fitted with a handle on each side.

seldner.label: Smallholder (Seldner, Söldner)
seldner.summary: South German smallholder owning a Selde (Sölde), a small house with little land.
seldner.text: The Seldner or Söldner owns a Selde (Sölde), a small property usually rated at one eighth of a whole farm in the Bavarian Hoffuß system; he often lived additionally from a craft or day labour. The term is common in Bavaria, Swabia and Franconia; the Gütler ranks at a similar level. In parish registers "Söldner" here therefore means a smallholder and not a paid soldier, which should be kept in mind when reading.

sellier.label: Sellier (sellier)
sellier.summary: Fabricant et marchand de selles, souvent aussi bourrelier.
sellier.text: Le sellier fabrique et vend des selles pour chevaux, un métier souvent cumulé avec celui de bourrelier (harnais).

senateur.label: Sénateur (senator)
senateur.summary: Member of an upper legislative assembly, the Senate.
senateur.text: The senator sat in the Senate, the upper house of Parliament under various regimes (First Empire, Restoration, Third Republic, present-day regimes). The title appears in the civil registers of notable families from the 19th century onwards, the Senate having been re-established in various forms since 1799.

senechal.label: Sénéchal (seneschal)
senechal.summary: Military officer who headed justice in his district and led the nobility when summoned to the arrière-ban.
senechal.text: The seneschal was an officer of the sword ("officier d'épée") who, in certain districts, was the head of justice, and who became the leader of the local nobility whenever it was called up for the "arrière-ban".

senteuse.label: Senteuse (fish smeller)
senteuse.summary: Cannery employee who bought tuna as the boats came in and detected pieces of lesser freshness.
senteuse.text: The "senteuse" was employed by a fish cannery to buy tuna when the fishing boats came in and to detect, by smell, any pieces of doubtful freshness.

seranceur.label: Séranceur (flax hackler)
seranceur.summary: Flax dresser who refined the fibre using "sérans", boards set with iron teeth.
seranceur.text: The "séranceur" made flax fibre very fine using small boards set with teeth of thick iron wire, called "sérans".

serdeau.label: Serdeau (table clearer)
serdeau.summary: In a noble household, the officer responsible for clearing the master's table.
serdeau.text: In a noble household, the "serdeau" was the officer responsible for clearing the master's table after meals.

sergent.label: Sergent (sergeant)
sergent.summary: Junior court officer who served legal documents, or a non-commissioned army officer, depending on context.
sergent.text: Under the Ancien Régime, the "sergent" was a junior officer of justice who served summonses, carried out seizures and made arrests on behalf of a seigneurial or royal court — the forerunner of the bailiff ("huissier"). In a military context the same word also denotes a non-commissioned officer in charge of supervising troops; the exact meaning must be inferred from the context of the record.

sergent_a_verge.label: Sergent à verge (rod-bearing sergeant)
sergent_a_verge.summary: Royal sergeant of the Châtelet in Paris, carrying a rod as a badge of authority.
sergent_a_verge.text: The "sergent à verge" was a royal sergeant attached to the Châtelet in Paris, who carried a rod ("verge") as the visible symbol of his authority when executing court orders. He is distinct from the "sergent à masse", whose mace was a badge reserved for other officers of higher rank.

sergent_de_chambre.label: Sergent de chambre (aldermen's court officer)
sergent_de_chambre.summary: In the Nord, an officer of an aldermen's court who carried out judicial and police decisions.
sergent_de_chambre.text: In the Nord, the "sergent de chambre" was responsible, within an aldermen's court ("chambre échevinale"), for carrying out judicial and police decisions: arrests and formal notices.

sergent_de_ville.label: Sergent de ville (town policeman)
sergent_de_ville.summary: Municipal police officer, forerunner of the "gardien de la paix", especially in 19th-century Paris.
sergent_de_ville.text: The "sergent de ville" was an urban police officer responsible for keeping order and watching over the public highway, a force created in Paris in 1829 and recognisable by its uniform and bicorne hat. The title preceded that of "gardien de la paix", adopted at the end of the 19th century.

sergent_du_marquisat.label: Sergent du marquisat (marquisate sergeant)
sergent_du_marquisat.summary: Court sergeant serving within the jurisdiction of a marquisate, a seigneury held by a marquis.
sergent_du_marquisat.text: The "sergent du marquisat" performed the ordinary duties of a seigneurial sergeant (serving legal documents, enforcing court decisions) within the territorial jurisdiction of a marquisate. The mention of the fief to which he belonged, frequent in records, makes it possible to identify the seigneurial court concerned.

sergent_major.label: Sergent-major (sergeant major)
sergent_major.summary: Non-commissioned officer responsible for the administration of a company in the Ancien Régime army.
sergent_major.text: The sergeant major was a senior non-commissioned officer responsible for the discipline, training and day-to-day administration of an infantry company, acting as the link between the officers and the rank and file. The post, attested from the 16th century, is the forerunner of the present-day "adjudant" or "sergent-chef".

sergent_royal.label: Sergent royal (royal sergeant)
sergent_royal.summary: Court officer representing the king's authority, responsible for serving and enforcing judicial acts.
sergent_royal.text: The royal sergeant enforced court decisions (summonses, seizures, executions) in the king's name across all or part of the kingdom, as opposed to the seigneurial sergeant, whose competence was limited to a single fief. The "sergent à verge" of the Châtelet is a particular example attached to the Paris jurisdiction.

serger.label: Serger (serge weaver)
serger.summary: Maker of serge, a twill-woven woollen cloth used for clothing.
serger.text: The "serger" wove serge, a woollen cloth (sometimes mixed with silk or cotton) with a characteristic twill weave, used for everyday clothing. The trade is well represented in the wool-working regions of northern and western France.

serpent.label: Serpent (serpent player)
serpent.summary: Musician playing the serpent, an S-shaped wind instrument used in churches.
serpent.text: The serpent player accompanied plainchant in churches that had no organ; the serpent was a wooden wind instrument covered in leather, bent into several S-shaped curves, producing a deep sound close to that of the bassoon. The instrument, common from the 17th to the early 19th century, gradually disappeared as organs became widespread.

serpier.label: Serpier (billhook smith)
serpier.summary: Smith specialised in making and sharpening sickles and cutting tools.
serpier.text: The "serpier" forged and sharpened billhooks, sickles and other agricultural cutting tools, a specialisation of the edge-tool maker's trade ("taillandier") focused on curved cutting tools. The name comes directly from "serpe" (billhook).

serre_frein.label: Serre-frein (brakeman)
serre_frein.summary: Railway employee responsible for applying wagon brakes by hand.
serre_frein.text: The brakeman rode on a wagon fitted with a manual braking position, which he operated on the engine driver's orders to slow or stop the train, before continuous automatic brakes became widespread. The job, which disappeared as rolling stock was modernised, is well attested in railway workers' registers of the 19th and early 20th centuries.

serreur.label: Serreur (hide packer)
serreur.summary: Hungarian-leather worker responsible for packing hides into the treatment vats.
serreur.text: The "serreur" worked in tawing or Hungarian-leather making ("hongroierie"), where he laid and pressed the hides into the tanning or chemical treatment vats. It was a menial task in the chain of leather preparation.

serrurier.label: Serrurier (locksmith)
serrurier.summary: Craftsman who made and fitted locks, generally forged piece by piece.
serrurier.text: The locksmith made and fitted locks, bolts and wrought-iron fittings, each piece being shaped by hand before the era of industrial mass production. The trade, organised into a guild from the Middle Ages, also covered architectural ironwork (gates, railings, hinges). "Serraillieur" is a regional dialect variant, alongside other local forms such as "sarrurier" or "sarrusier".

servante.label: Servante (maidservant)
servante.summary: Female domestic employed for household work in a private home.
servante.text: The maidservant was employed, living in or by the day, to carry out domestic work (cooking, cleaning, looking after children) for a private individual, on a farm or in an establishment. The term is very common in censuses and civil registration records to describe the employment of unmarried or widowed women lodged with their employer.

servante_a_gages.label: Servante à gages (hired maidservant)
servante_a_gages.summary: Maidservant employed by a master for a fixed wage over a set period.
servante_a_gages.text: The "servante à gages" was engaged for a fixed period (often a year, following the custom of hiring fairs, "louées" and "foires d'embauche") for a wage agreed in advance, as opposed to mere occasional service. The phrase "à gages" specifies in records the salaried, contractual nature of the employment.

serveuse.label: Serveuse (waitress)
serveuse.summary: Employee serving customers in a café, restaurant or bar.
serveuse.text: The waitress welcomed and served customers in a restaurant or drinking establishment. The term, in common use since the end of the 19th century, is found mainly in 20th-century records relating to urban occupations.

serviteur.label: Serviteur (manservant)
serviteur.summary: Household employee providing domestic service to a noble or bourgeois individual.
serviteur.text: The "serviteur" was employed in the personal and domestic service of a master, in a noble or bourgeois household — the male equivalent of the maidservant, sometimes with more specialised duties (valet, coachman, odd-job man). The generic term covers very different realities depending on the status of the employing household.

sesmeiro.label: Sesmeiro (allocator of uncultivated land)
sesmeiro.summary: Official charged with distributing uncultivated or abandoned land under the sesmarias law.
sesmeiro.text: The sesmeiro is appointed by the king or the municipality to allocate uncultivated or abandoned land, applying the sesmarias law enacted by King Fernando in 1375, which obliged recipients to bring the land into cultivation within a fixed period. The sesmarias system was later carried over to the Atlantic islands and to Brazil.

siamoisier.label: Siamoisier (siamoise weaver)
siamoisier.summary: Weaver specialised in "siamoises", light cotton-and-linen fabrics in the Siamese style.
siamoisier.text: The "siamoisier" wove "siamoises", fabrics mixing cotton and linen whose name recalls the cloths imported from Siam (present-day Thailand) in the 17th century and later imitated by French manufactories. The trade developed notably around the textile centres of Normandy and Picardy.

signaleur.label: Signaleur (signalman)
signaleur.summary: Belgian railway employee responsible for watching over a section of track.
signaleur.text: The "signaleur" was responsible for a section of railway line, combining the duties of level-crossing keeper and pointsman to ensure the safe running of trains. The term was used notably on the Belgian railways.

silindreur.label: Silindreur (calenderer)
silindreur.summary: Worker who used a cylinder to soften leather or glaze fabrics.
silindreur.text: The "silindreur" passed hides or fabrics under a cylinder (calender) to soften them, smooth them or give them a sheen, the final stage before they were put on sale. It is a finishing term in the leather and textile trades.

sirgien.label: Sirgien (surgeon)
sirgien.summary: Old dialect variant of "chirurgien" (surgeon), whose usual practice was bloodletting.
sirgien.text: "Sirgien" is an old spelling variant of "chirurgien" (surgeon). Under the Ancien Régime, rural surgery was most often limited to bloodletting (the drawing of blood, considered therapeutic, performed with a lancet) and minor care, learned surgery being reserved for the towns; the country surgeon, often trained on the job or of barber origin, could also be called upon to assist at difficult births when no other practitioner was available.

sirgueiro.label: Sirgueiro (silk cord and trimmings maker)
sirgueiro.summary: Craftsman who made cords, fringes, braids and other silk goods.
sirgueiro.text: The sirgueiro works "sirgo", that is, silk: he makes silk cords, fringes, braids, buttons and trimmings for clothing, furnishings and vestments, and also sells silk in skeins. In Lisbon the sirgueiros formed an organised trade with its own regulations, close to the passementerie makers.

sixtain.label: Sixtain (sixth-share labourer)
sixtain.summary: Farm worker paid with one sixth of the harvest.
sixtain.text: The "sixtain" was a farm worker or smallholder whose pay consisted of a share of the harvest — here one sixth — under a system of partial sharecropping similar to "tiercelage" or "quartage", but with a different fraction. The term specifies the contractual method of payment, common in Ancien Régime rural leases.

smolarz.label: Smolarz (tar burner)
smolarz.summary: Maker of tar and pitch from resinous wood in forest tar kilns.
smolarz.text: The smolarz rendered tar from pine stumps and wood in smolarnie, simple forest kilns. Tar was used to caulk boats and barrels, grease carts and preserve timber. Tar burners often lived in forest settlements, and Polish place names derived from the trade are numerous.

soigneuse.label: Soigneuse (spinning-mill tender)
soigneuse.summary: Spinning-mill worker who prepared the wool bobbins for the spinning frames.
soigneuse.text: The "soigneuse" prepared the bobbins and skeins of wool ahead of spinning, making sure the yarn was even and clean before it went onto the frame. It was a typical workshop post in 19th-century woollen mills.

soiton.label: Soiton (associated smallholder)
soiton.summary: Small farmer of the Paris Basin and Normandy who worked in partnership with others.
soiton.text: The "soiton" was a smallholder who pooled his resources (land, equipment, draught animals) with other farmers in a mutual-aid partnership, a practice widespread in the Paris Basin and Normandy. The term has several regional spelling variants.

soldat.label: Soldat (soldier)
soldat.summary: Enlisted soldier, a member of the rank and file without non-commissioned or commissioned rank.
soldat.text: The soldier was an enlisted man, the base of the military hierarchy, as opposed to the ranked men (corporal, sergeant) and the officers. The term appears in large numbers in military registration registers ("registres matricules") and in the civil registration records of men of military age, especially during periods of conscription.

soldat_de_1e_classe.label: Soldat de 1re classe (private first class)
soldat_de_1e_classe.summary: Highest rank of enlisted soldier before promotion to corporal.
soldat_de_1e_classe.text: The private first class had moved up a step through seniority or merit within the ranks, without yet holding the command of a ranked man. The distinction has been common in military service books and registration registers since the 19th century.

soldat_de_2e_classe.label: Soldat de 2e classe (private)
soldat_de_2e_classe.summary: Basic rank of enlisted soldier, without particular seniority.
soldat_de_2e_classe.text: The "soldat de deuxième classe" is the initial rank of an enlisted soldier on joining, before any promotion. It is a frequent mention in military registration registers.

soltys.label: Sołtys (village headman)
soltys.summary: Head of a village, originally the founder of a village chartered under German law.
soltys.text: The sołtys was originally the locator who founded a village under German law and received in return a hereditary endowment and judicial authority over the village. Over time he became the head of the village community, mediating between the inhabitants and the lord or the authorities; in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries he was the elected head of a village within a commune. Latin sources call him “scultetus”.

sommelier.label: Sommelier (butler-steward)
sommelier.summary: Ancien Régime household officer in charge of table service, tableware and wines.
sommelier.text: Under the Ancien Régime, the "sommelier" was an officer of a noble or royal household responsible for serving and keeping the tableware, the table linen and the wines — a stewardship role much broader than the present-day meaning, which is restricted to wine. The modern sense, specialised in choosing and serving wines in restaurants, only became established from the 19th and 20th centuries.

sonnetier.label: Sonnetier (cattle-bell founder)
sonnetier.summary: Founder of "sonnailles", the large bells hung round the necks of livestock.
sonnetier.text: The "sonnetier" (or "sonnaillier") cast and shaped "sonnailles", the large bronze or brass bells hung round the necks of cattle and sheep so that the herd could be located at pasture. The trade was related to that of the church-bell founder, but geared towards smaller pieces intended for stock-rearing rather than worship, and was often handed down from father to son in families of rural craftsmen.

sonneur.label: Sonneur (bell-ringer)
sonneur.summary: Person responsible for ringing the bells and maintaining their mechanism.
sonneur.text: The bell-ringer pulled the bell ropes of a church to announce services, civil events (births, marriages, deaths) or alarms, and maintained the ringing mechanism. The duty was often carried out by the beadle or the sacristan, and was sometimes paid separately according to parish custom.

sopista.label: Sopista (poor Spanish student)
sopista.summary: Poor student who lived on charity, especially the soup handed out at convents.
sopista.text: The sopista was a penniless student at the old universities such as Salamanca or Alcalá who lived on alms and on the soup distributed at convent doors, sometimes serving wealthier students. The figure appears frequently in Golden Age literature.

sorbettiere.label: Sorbettiere (ice-cream maker)
sorbettiere.summary: Craftsman who made and sold sorbets and ice cream.
sorbettiere.text: The sorbettiere made sorbets and ice creams with ice or stored snow and salt, an art that flourished in Sicily and Naples and spread to Italian towns from the 17th century. In the 19th century itinerant ice-cream makers from Cadore and the Val di Zoldo emigrated in large numbers to German-speaking countries, where they opened ice-cream parlours.

souchier.label: Souchier (clog maker)
souchier.summary: Clog maker who made wooden shoes from a single piece.
souchier.text: The "souchier" carved one-piece clogs out of a block of wood (a "souche", or stump), as opposed to the clog maker who sometimes worked with assembled wood. It is a regional term for the clog maker's trade, with local spelling variants.

soudan.label: Soudan (mercenary soldier)
soudan.summary: Medieval mercenary soldier serving for pay.
soudan.text: The "soudan" (or "soudard") was a medieval man-at-arms who served for payment — the word comes from "solde" (pay) — as opposed to the compulsory feudal service owed by a vassal. In modern French the term later took on the pejorative connotation of a brutish soldier ("soudard").

soudeux.label: Soudeux (can solderer)
soudeux.summary: Cannery worker responsible for soldering tinplate cans.
soudeux.text: The "soudeux" closed and sealed tinplate cans by soldering them with tin, a manual operation before the seaming machine was mechanised. It was a typical trade in the canneries, particularly fish canneries, that appeared from the mid-19th century onwards.

souffletier.label: Souffletier (bellows maker)
souffletier.summary: Maker of bellows for the home, the forge, organs and other wind instruments.
souffletier.text: The bellows maker made bellows for fanning fires (domestic hearths, forges) or supplying air to instruments (organs, harmoniums). The trade, a manual craft, declined as mechanical ventilation became widespread.

souffleur_de_perles.label: Souffleur de perles (bead blower)
souffleur_de_perles.summary: Craftsman making artificial pearls from blown glass in imitation of real pearls.
souffleur_de_perles.text: The bead blower shaped artificial pearls by blowing glass around a core, then coated it with an essence made from fish scales ("essence d'Orient") imitating the nacreous lustre of real pearls. This costume-jewellery industry developed notably in the Paris region in the 18th and 19th centuries.

souffleur_de_verre.label: Souffleur de verre (glassblower)
souffleur_de_verre.summary: Glassworker who shaped hot glass by blowing through a blowpipe.
souffleur_de_verre.text: The glassblower shaped hot glass into bottles and other hollow objects by blowing by mouth through a blowpipe.

souffleur_theatre.label: Souffleur (prompter)
souffleur_theatre.summary: Person hidden near the stage who prompts the actors when they forget their lines.
souffleur_theatre.text: The theatre prompter followed the text of the play from a concealed position (often the "prompter's box" at the front of the stage) and discreetly reminded the actors of their lines when they forgot them. It was an indispensable role in the classical theatre before complete memorisation became standard practice.

souffleur_verrier.label: Souffleur (glassblower)
souffleur_verrier.summary: Glassworker who shaped molten glass by blowing through a blowpipe.
souffleur_verrier.text: The glassblower gathered molten glass on the end of a hollow blowpipe and shaped it by blowing, the basic technique of glassmaking for producing bottles, tumblers and hollow objects. It was a highly skilled trade, traditionally handed down from generation to generation in the glassworks.

sous_come.label: Sous-côme (under-overseer of convicts)
sous_come.summary: Assistant supervisor in the penal colonies or aboard the galleys.
sous_come.text: The "sous-côme" assisted the "comite" (the officer in charge of manoeuvres and discipline) aboard the galleys or in the penal colonies ("bagnes"), supervising the convicts and the oarsmen. It was a post of the old French penal and naval system that disappeared along with the galleys and the "bagne".

speakerin.label: Speakerine (television announcer)
speakerin.summary: Presenter who announced the programmes on French television.
speakerin.text: The "speakerine" announced television programmes on screen and provided the link between broadcasts — an emblematic role of French television from the 1950s to the 1970s. The term, feminine by default because the job was almost exclusively held by women, disappeared as broadcasting practices changed.

spugnaro.label: Spugnaro (sponge fisher)
spugnaro.text: The spugnaro gathered sponges from the seabed by free diving, with dragged gear or, later, in a diving suit. In Italy sponge fishing was practised mainly by Sicilian seamen, notably from Trapani and Lampedusa, including on the banks off Tunisia and Libya.

stadeur.label: Stadeur (comb-tooth cutter)
stadeur.summary: Comb-maker specialised in cutting the fine teeth of combs.
stadeur.text: The "stadeur" worked in comb-making, finely cutting the small teeth after the shaper ("façonneur") had done the preliminary work. It was a specialised post in the production chain of the comb-makers' guild.

stadtmusikus.label: Town musician (Stadtmusikus)
stadtmusikus.summary: Town musician appointed by the council with the privilege of playing at festivities and weddings.
stadtmusikus.text: The Stadtmusikus is a musician employed by the town council who, with his journeymen and apprentices (Stadtpfeifer, Kunstpfeifer), played at civic ceremonies, church services and from the tower. He usually held the privilege of playing in the town at weddings, dances and feasts, and trained musicians. The institution existed from the 16th into the 19th century.

staffeur.label: Staffeur (fibrous plasterer)
staffeur.summary: Decorative worker using staff, a mixture of plaster and plant fibres.
staffeur.text: The "staffeur" moulded and fitted decorative elements in staff — a mixture of plaster and plant fibres (hemp, jute) cast in moulds — to adorn ceilings, cornices and façades. The trade expanded greatly at the end of the 19th century with eclectic architecture and the universal exhibitions.

stationnaire.label: Stationnaire (inshore cod fisherman)
stationnaire.summary: Cod fisherman who set and hauled fixed traps, as opposed to the offshore fisherman of the Banks.
stationnaire.text: The "stationnaire" fished for cod using fixed traps (large pots submerged close to the shore, needing little supervision), a coastal technique distinct from that of the "terre-neuva", who fished offshore on the Banks from a ship on a fishing campaign. This method developed in Newfoundland and Labrador as catches declined in the areas close to the shore.

stationnaire_telegraphiste.label: Stationnaire (telegraph operator)
stationnaire_telegraphiste.summary: Chappe telegraph operator responsible for watching and relaying the optical signals of a fixed station.
stationnaire_telegraphiste.text: The Chappe telegraph "stationnaire" was posted to a fixed station on the line, where he watched the signals of the neighbouring station through a telescope and immediately reproduced them on his own apparatus to relay them, thus ensuring that messages were transmitted over long distances. Some "stationnaires" were also responsible for inspecting the stations and keeping them in technical order.

stearinier.label: Stéarinier (stearin candle maker)
stearinier.summary: Maker of candles from stearin, a purified animal fat.
stearinier.text: The "stéarinier" made candles from stearin, a purified animal fat that gradually replaced tallow and wax in the 19th century because it burned more cleanly and with less smell. The trade is linked to the rise of the chemical industry in the first half of the 19th century.

stenodactylographe.label: Sténodactylographe (shorthand typist)
stenodactylographe.summary: Office worker skilled in both shorthand and typing.
stenodactylographe.text: The shorthand typist took texts down in dictation using shorthand (a rapid abbreviated script) and then transcribed them on a typewriter. It was a typically female office job, very widespread in public administration and business in the first half of the 20th century, before dictaphones and word processing became widespread.

strandjutter.label: Strandjutter (beachcomber)
strandjutter.summary: Person who searched the beach for washed-up goods and wreckage.
strandjutter.text: After storms the beachcomber searched the beach for driftwood, cargo and other washed-up objects, often to use or sell them. By law, found goods had to be reported to the strandvonder, but beachcombing was regarded as an old customary right in the coastal villages and on the islands.

strandvonder.label: Strandvonder (receiver of wreck)
strandvonder.summary: Official responsible for washed-up goods and the rights of wreck.
strandvonder.text: The strandvonder recorded goods that washed ashore or were salvaged from stranded ships, kept them for their owners and collected the dues owed to the lord or the state. He also supervised salvage in shipwrecks. The office existed in the coastal municipalities into the 20th century.

strohflechter.label: Straw plaiter (Strohflechter)
strohflechter.summary: Home worker who plaited straw into braids for hat making.
strohflechter.text: The Strohflechter plaits split or whole straws, mostly of rye or wheat, into braids and plaits that were sewn into straw hats and bags. Straw plaiting was a widespread home industry of women and children in the 18th and 19th centuries, especially in the Black Forest and the Freiamt region of Aargau, where it was organised by merchant-employers.

strzelec_dworski.label: Strzelec dworski (estate gamekeeper)
strzelec_dworski.summary: Hunter and gamekeeper in the service of a landowner.
strzelec_dworski.text: The strzelec dworski looked after the game in the estate’s woods and fields, organised the owner’s hunts, controlled vermin and guarded against poachers. He belonged to the manor’s forest staff, alongside the forest guards and foresters.

stucateur.label: Stucateur (stuccoist)
stucateur.summary: Decorative worker using stucco, plaster mixed with marble dust.
stucateur.text: The stuccoist produced decorations in stucco — a render based on plaster and marble dust imitating the look of polished marble — to adorn interior ceilings, columns and cornices. The trade was close to that of the "staffeur" but used a different material and finish, nearer to decorative marble work.

suelfmeister.label: Salt-works operator (Sülfmeister)
suelfmeister.summary: Operator of a boiling house of the Lüneburg saltworks, usually from the town's upper class.
suelfmeister.text: The Sülfmeister operates in Lüneburg one of the boiling houses of the saltworks (the Sülze), in which brine was boiled down to salt in lead pans; the boiling houses mostly belonged to ecclesiastical and lay owners, from whom the Sülfmeister leased them. The Sülfmeister formed an influential association whose members belonged to the town's ruling class and held the council offices.

sueur.label: Sueur (shoe stitcher)
sueur.summary: Shoemaker responsible for sewing shoes cut out by the "cordouannier".
sueur.text: The "sueur" (from the Latin "sutor", one who sews) assembled and stitched shoes whose leather pieces had been cut by the "cordouannier", in an organisation of work where cutting and sewing were handled by separate specialists within the guild. The word is the origin of the surname "Sueur" or "Le Sueur", common in France.

suifeur.label: Suifeur (tallow greaser)
suifeur.summary: Shipyard worker who coated hulls with tallow for caulking and launching.
suifeur.text: The "suifeur" coated ships' hulls with a tallow-based mixture to make it easier to launch them in the shipyards and to protect the submerged timber. It was a trade of the shipyards and ports.

suisse_gardien.label: Suisse (church beadle)
suisse_gardien.summary: Guard in ceremonial dress responsible for keeping order in churches and at ceremonies.
suisse_gardien.text: The "suisse" was a guard in ceremonial dress (halberd, bicorne hat) who kept order in churches and paraded during processions and ceremonies. The name comes from the historical recruitment of Swiss guards, and the title remained attached to the post even when it was held by Frenchmen.

suisse_portier.label: Suisse (porter)
suisse_portier.summary: Porter guarding the entrance to a great lord's town house.
suisse_portier.text: The "suisse" porter guarded the carriage entrance of a great lord's town house ("hôtel particulier"), keeping watch over the comings and goings of visitors. As with the church "suisse", the name preserves the memory of the traditional recruitment of Swiss porters in great households.

superintendent.label: Superintendent (Protestant)
superintendent.summary: Protestant clergyman supervising the pastors of a church district.
superintendent.text: The Superintendent heads a church district (Superintendentur, Ephorie) in the Lutheran and United regional churches: he supervises pastors, teachers and congregations, conducts visitations, installs new pastors and is usually also pastor of the main church of his town. The Generalsuperintendent exercises oversight of a whole province or regional church; in Württemberg and Bavaria the corresponding office is called Dekan.

superviseur.label: Superviseur (supervisor)
superviseur.summary: Person responsible for overseeing and coordinating the work of a team or department.
superviseur.text: The supervisor oversaw and coordinated the execution of work by a team or workshop, a middle-management role. It is a modern term, found mainly in 20th-century records relating to industry or services.

surveillant_des_portes.label: Surveillant des portes (town-gate inspector)
surveillant_des_portes.summary: Municipal officer checking people and goods at the town gates.
surveillant_des_portes.text: The town-gate inspector checked the movement of people and goods at the entrance gates of the town, in particular to enforce the "octroi" (a tax on goods entering the town). It was a municipal post of the Ancien Régime and the 19th century, before the "octroi" was abolished.

syndic_fabricien.label: Syndic fabricien (churchwarden)
syndic_fabricien.summary: Elected layman responsible for managing the parish's material assets within the "fabrique".
syndic_fabricien.text: The "fabricien" was a layman elected by the parish to sit on the vestry council ("conseil de fabrique"), responsible for administering the church's material assets (building, furnishings, income, alms) together with the parish priest. The "syndic fabricien" was its representative or treasurer, a common office mentioned in Ancien Régime parish registers.

szames.label: Szames (synagogue beadle)
szames.summary: Synagogue attendant and beadle of a Jewish community.
szames.text: The szames looked after the synagogue, called the faithful to prayer, delivered summonses and helped with community business. His role was similar to that of a sexton or beadle, and he often served as a witness when records were drawn up.

szlachcic.label: Szlachcic (Polish nobleman)
szlachcic.summary: Member of the noble estate in the old Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth.
szlachcic.text: The szlachcic belonged to the privileged estate which, in the old Commonwealth, held full political rights, the right to own land and a voice in the regional diets. The estate was very unequal in wealth, from magnates to landless nobles. Latin parish registers distinguish nobles with the epithets “nobilis” or “generosus”.

szlachcic_czynszowy.label: Szlachcic czynszowy (rent-paying noble)
szlachcic_czynszowy.summary: Landless nobleman leasing land from another owner for rent.
szlachcic_czynszowy.text: The szlachcic czynszowy had no land of his own and farmed ground leased from a magnate or wealthier noble, paying rent but owing no labour service. After the partitions, many who could not prove their nobility were declassed by the partitioning authorities.

szlachcic_zagrodowy.label: Szlachcic zagrodowy (yeoman noble)
szlachcic_zagrodowy.summary: Petty nobleman farming his own small plot with his own hands.
szlachcic_zagrodowy.text: The szlachcic zagrodowy owned a small farm which he worked himself, without serfs, living much like well-off peasants while keeping the privileges of his estate. Such petty nobility was especially numerous in Mazovia, Podlachia and Lithuania, where it formed whole villages called zaścianki.

tabaillonneur.label: Tabaillonneur (shingle maker)
tabaillonneur.summary: Craftsman who fitted split spruce shingles ("tavaillons") on Jura roofs and façades.
tabaillonneur.text: During the winter the "tabaillonneur" split blocks of spruce with an axe into "tavaillons" (small wooden boards), then, from spring to autumn, laid them one by one as roofing or cladding on traditional houses. This wooden cladding is called "bardeau" in the Jura and Franche-Comté, and "tavillon" in the Pre-Alps (Gruyère, Pays d'En-Haut, Haute-Savoie); the craft is enjoying renewed heritage interest today.

tabakskerver.label: Tabakskerver (tobacco cutter)
tabakskerver.summary: Worker who cut tobacco leaves into smoking or chewing tobacco.
tabakskerver.text: In the tobacco-cutting works the leaves were moistened, pressed and cut with knives or machines into fine shreds for pipe or rolling tobacco. The occupation was common in towns with a tobacco industry such as Amsterdam, Rotterdam and Kampen.

tabaksplanter.label: Tabaksplanter (tobacco grower)
tabaksplanter.text: From the 17th century onwards tobacco was grown in the Low Countries, mainly around Amersfoort, on the Veluwe and in the Betuwe. Cultivation required much manual labour, from planting to harvesting and drying the leaves in barns. Domestic tobacco growing declined sharply in the 19th century owing to competition from overseas tobacco.

tabaquier.label: Tabaquier (tobacconist)
tabaquier.summary: Tobacco seller or worker in a tobacco factory.
tabaquier.text: The "tabaquier" sold tobacco in a shop or worked in a tobacco factory (preparing the leaves, making cigars or snuff). As the tobacco trade in France has been a state monopoly since Colbert, these factories employed a large workforce, much of it female.

tabellion.label: Tabellion (keeper of notarial records)
tabellion.summary: Officer responsible for keeping notarial deeds and issuing copies of them.
tabellion.text: The "tabellion" was a public officer who kept the original minutes of notarial deeds and issued engrossments (authenticated copies) of them, a role distinct from that of the notary, who drew up the deeds. The title gradually disappeared at the beginning of the 17th century, when its functions merged with those of the notary.

tabletier.label: Tabletier (maker of small wares in horn and ivory)
tabletier.summary: Craftsman making small objects in horn, bone or ivory: games, boxes, fans.
tabletier.text: The "tabletier" worked horn, bone, ivory or tortoiseshell to make small, fine objects: draughtboards, dice, games, boxes, combs, fans and tool handles. The Paris guild of "tabletiers", well attested since the Middle Ages, is one of the oldest in precision craftsmanship.

tacquier.label: Tacquier (ship's carpenter)
tacquier.summary: Ship's carpenter specialised in building and maintaining the wooden structures of vessels.
tacquier.text: The "tacquier" took part in shipbuilding, particularly in repairing and maintaining the wooden structures of hulls and rigging. It was a shipyard trade, related to that of the ship's carpenter.

tacrenier.label: Tacrenier (tan-mill operator)
tacrenier.summary: Operator of a tan mill in Touraine, grinding oak bark into powder.
tacrenier.text: The "tacrenier" ran a tan mill, a water mill in which a camshaft drove pestles that crushed dried oak (or chestnut) bark to extract tan, used by tanners to soften and waterproof hides. In Touraine, tan milling was long the second milling activity after the grinding of cereals: some thirty of these mills were still working in Indre-et-Loire in the 19th century.

taffetassier.label: Taffetatier (taffeta weaver)
taffetassier.summary: Weaver specialised in taffeta, a plain, glossy silk fabric.
taffetassier.text: The "taffetatier" (commonly spelt "taffetassier") wove taffeta, a plain, fine and glossy silk fabric obtained by a tight plain weave. Nîmes was one of the great French centres of taffeta production in the 18th century, where a worker earned on average 20 to 30 sous a day, the most skilful reaching 2 livres; in Avignon, the "taffetassiers" formed a trade body devoted to the trade in and production of cloths of gold, silver and silk from the 16th to the 18th century.

taillandier.label: Taillandier (edge-tool maker)
taillandier.summary: Smith specialised in making and sharpening agricultural cutting tools.
taillandier.text: The edge-tool maker forged, shaped and sharpened cutting tools for agriculture and the crafts: scythes, sickles, billhooks, spades, axes. Edge-tool making ("taillanderie") was a specialised branch of smithing, distinct from the farrier (who shod horses) and the armourer, with its own guilds and, later in the 19th century, its own mechanised workshops.

aliases: Taillandière en fer blanc et noir
taillandier_en_fer_blanc_et_noir.label: Taillandier en fer blanc et noir (tin and sheet-iron smith)
taillandier_en_fer_blanc_et_noir.summary: Edge-tool maker specialised in candlesticks, lanterns, strainers and various iron utensils.
taillandier_en_fer_blanc_et_noir.text: This "taillandier" made utilitarian objects in wrought iron and tinplate — candlesticks, lanterns, strainers, kitchen utensils — rather than cutting tools as such. It was a specialisation within the edge-tool makers' guild geared towards domestic hardware.

taillandier_en_uvres_blanches.label: Taillandier en œuvres blanches (cutting-tool smith)
taillandier_en_uvres_blanches.summary: Edge-tool maker specialised exclusively in cutting tools, excluding bladed weapons.
taillandier_en_uvres_blanches.text: This "taillandier" confined himself to making cutting tools for everyday work (scythes, billhooks, working knives), excluding bladed weapons as such, which were reserved for other trades (sword cutlers, armourers). It was a distinction of status within the edge-tool makers' guild.

taillandier_grossier.label: Taillandier grossier (heavy ironware smith)
taillandier_grossier.summary: Edge-tool maker producing kitchen utensils and large tools (cooking pots, pot-hangers, hammers).
taillandier_grossier.text: The "taillandier grossier" worked large pieces of hardware and kitchen utensils — cooking pots, pot-hangers, hammers — as opposed to the edge-tool makers specialised in fine tools. The qualifier "grossier" refers here to the size of the pieces, not to the quality of the work.

taillandier_vrillier.label: Taillandier vrillier (gimlet and small-tool smith)
taillandier_vrillier.summary: Edge-tool maker specialised in gimlets, files, awls, chisels and pincers.
taillandier_vrillier.text: The "taillandier vrillier" made precision steel tools: gimlets, files, awls, chisels and pincers, intended for other craftsmen. It was a fine specialisation within the edge-tool makers' guild, geared towards tooling rather than agricultural cutting pieces.

taille.label: Taille (tenor singer)
taille.summary: Church singer taking the tenor part in liturgical singing.
taille.text: In the French vocal vocabulary of the 17th and 18th centuries, "taille" denotes the register closest to the present-day tenor, between the "haute-contre" (higher) and the bass. The singer who took this part in a church choir school ("maîtrise" or "psallette") was himself called "la taille".

taillenier.label: Taillenier (taille collector)
taillenier.summary: Person responsible for collecting the "taille", a direct tax of the Ancien Régime.
taillenier.text: The "taillenier" collected the "taille", the main royal direct tax levied on commoners under the Ancien Régime, on behalf of the collector or the parish. The duty was often taken on in turn by the inhabitants of a village community and was not a permanent occupation.

tailleresse.label: Tailleresse (mint blank trimmer)
tailleresse.summary: Mint worker who trimmed the blanks to be struck into a round shape with shears.
tailleresse.text: The "tailleresse" worked in a mint alongside the adjuster ("ajusteur"): he flattened the blank (the piece of metal cut from the strip) with a hammer, and the "tailleresse" immediately rounded it off with shears to give it its regular shape before striking — hence her name, derived from "tailler les carreaux" (cutting the squares) according to the Encyclopédie of 1782. It was a specialised post in coin manufacture, almost exclusively female, attested in the royal mints of the Ancien Régime.

tailleur.label: Tailleur (tailor)
tailleur.summary: Craftsman who made made-to-measure clothes using cutting and sewing techniques.
tailleur.text: The tailor (of clothes) made made-to-measure garments for his customers, cutting the cloth and then assembling it, as opposed to the old-clothes dealer ("fripier"), who sold ready-made or second-hand clothes. It was an ancient and very widespread guild, present in every town and most market towns under the Ancien Régime. "Tailleuse" is the feminine form, used in particular for women practising the trade.

tailleur_d_amadou.label: Tailleur d'amadou (tinder maker)
tailleur_d_amadou.summary: Craftsman preparing amadou, a spongy substance obtained from the tinder fungus.
tailleur_d_amadou.text: The tinder maker prepared amadou from the tinder fungus (Fomes fomentarius), a fungus whose spongy flesh, once beaten and treated, was used to light fires by percussion (with a steel and flint) before matches were invented. It was a rural craft that has now disappeared.

tailleur_de_corps.label: Tailleur de corps (stay maker)
tailleur_de_corps.summary: Tailor specialised in making corsets for women and children.
tailleur_de_corps.text: The stay maker made boned corsets ("corps à baleines") for women and children, an essential item of the female wardrobe until the early 20th century. It was a specialisation distinct from that of the ordinary tailor, requiring its own technique.

tailleur_de_meules.label: Tailleur de meules (millstone cutter)
tailleur_de_meules.summary: Craftsman specialised in cutting millstones, both runner and bedstone.
tailleur_de_meules.text: The millstone cutter extracted and dressed millstones (the runner stone and the bedstone) from a suitable hard stone (burrstone, flint), grooving their surface to ensure efficient grinding. The trade was linked to the burrstone quarries that supplied the grain mills of an entire region.

tailleur_de_pierre.label: Tailleur de pierre (stonecutter)
tailleur_de_pierre.summary: Craftsman specialised in cutting stone for building and sculpture.
tailleur_de_pierre.text: The stonecutter cut and shaped the blocks of stone extracted from the quarry into building elements (rubble stones, voussoirs, cornices) or sculpted pieces. It was a fundamental building trade under the Ancien Régime, often distinguished from the ordinary mason by its greater technical skill.

tailleur_de_sel.label: Tailleur de sel (salt measurer)
tailleur_de_sel.summary: Clerk responsible for measuring and checking salt imported into the port of Bordeaux.
