tailleur_de_sel.text: The "tailleur de sel" was a clerk of the port of Bordeaux responsible for measuring and checking imported cargoes of salt, particularly for the collection of the taxes that weighed heavily on this commodity (the "gabelle"). It was a specialised post in the port's salt trade.

taissier_de_cadix.label: Taissier de Cadix (Cadiz-cloth weaver)
taissier_de_cadix.summary: Weaver specialised in Cadiz cloth, a linen fabric used in particular for sheets.
taissier_de_cadix.text: The "taissier de Cadix" (a variant of "texier") wove so-called "Cadiz" cloth, a linen cloth used in particular for making bed sheets. It is a regional term belonging to the family of words for weavers ("texier", "tixier").

talemelier.label: Talemelier (baker)
talemelier.summary: Old name for the baker, attested in Paris from the 13th century.
talemelier.text: The "talemelier" was originally a sifter who sifted the coarse flour coming out of the mills; having obtained the right to bake bread in the lord's communal oven, he also became an oven-keeper ("fournier"), then, once allowed to own his own oven, a "panetier" or pastry-maker — the "talemelier" is thus the direct ancestor of the baker. The trade is regulated in Étienne Boileau's Livre des métiers (1268), which codifies the Paris guild of the Talemeliers; the term remained dominant in Parisian sources until the 15th century, when "boulanger" finally prevailed. It had many regional spelling variants ("talmetier", "tamelier", "tamisier"...).

talonnier.label: Talonnier (heel maker)
talonnier.summary: Shoemaking worker specialised in making heels, or a shoemaker of modest standing.
talonnier.text: The "talonnier" made and fitted the heels of shoes, a specialised task in shoemaking. By extension the term also denotes a shoemaker of modest rank within the guild.

tamiseur.label: Tamiseur (glassworks sifter)
tamiseur.summary: Glassworks labourer who prepared and sifted the raw materials before the glass was melted.
tamiseur.text: The "tamiseur" sorted and sifted the raw materials (sand, ashes, lime) intended for melting glass, in order to remove impurities and ensure an even mixture. It was a preparation post in a glassworks.

tamisier_fabricant.label: Tamisier (sieve maker)
tamisier_fabricant.summary: Craftsman making sieves using traditional techniques.
tamisier_fabricant.text: The sieve maker made sieves (frames stretched with horsehair, silk or metal) used in milling, in the kitchen and in various crafts to sort or filter materials. It should not be confused with the "talemelier" (baker), sometimes spelt in a similar way.

tanneur.label: Tanneur (tanner)
tanneur.summary: Craftsman who treated animal hides with tan to make them rot-proof.
tanneur.text: The tanner turned raw hides into leather by treating them with tan (crushed oak bark rich in tannin), a lengthy process that made them supple and rot-proof. The trade, indispensable and foul-smelling, was traditionally carried on on the outskirts of towns, near the watercourses needed for soaking the hides.

tanqueur.label: Tanqueur (docker)
tanqueur.summary: Porter specialised in loading and unloading ships in port.
tanqueur.text: The "tanqueur" loaded and unloaded goods from ships at the quayside, a physical job of port portering before cargo handling was mechanised. It is a regional term for a porter or docker.

tapissier.label: Tapissier (tapestry and wall-hanging worker)
tapissier.summary: Worker who handled all kinds of tapestry and fabric used to cover walls.
tapissier.text: The "tapissier" worked all kinds of tapestry and fabric used to cover walls, a trade distinct from that of the upholsterer ("tapissier meublant").

tapissier_en_commode.label: Tapissier en commode (furniture liner)
tapissier_en_commode.summary: Worker who lined the inside of furniture with more or less precious fabrics.
tapissier_en_commode.text: The "tapissier en commode" lined the inside of furniture (drawers, chests) with more or less precious fabrics.

tapissier_meublant.label: Tapissier meublant (upholsterer)
tapissier_meublant.summary: Worker who decorated and covered furniture such as chairs and armchairs with fabric.
tapissier_meublant.text: The upholsterer decorated and covered furniture such as chairs and armchairs with fabric, as distinct from the wall-hanging "tapissier".

taquetier.label: Taquetier (loom picker maker)
taquetier.summary: Worker who drove nails into the pickers of a loom.
taquetier.text: The "taquetier" drove nails into pieces of wood ("taquets", pickers) fitted on a loom, an essential part of the weaving mechanism.

taqueur.label: Taqueur (cage unloader)
taqueur.summary: Miner responsible for moving ore tubs out of the cage.
taqueur.text: The "taqueur" was a miner responsible for moving the ore tubs out of the winding cage.

targeur.label: Targeur (box-side maker)
targeur.summary: Maker of wooden ware who produced the "targe", the side of wooden boxes and containers.
targeur.text: The "targeur" was a maker of wooden ware ("boisselier") specialised in making the "targe", the name given to the side of wooden boxes and containers.

tartrier.label: Tartrier (tartar gatherer)
tartrier.summary: Craftsman recovering the tartar from wine casks to produce cream of tartar.
tartrier.text: The "tartrier" recovered tartar, the crystalline deposit that forms on the inside of wine casks, and processed it to extract cream of tartar, used in pharmacy and cooking (particularly in pastry-making). The trade was linked to the wine-growing regions.

taupier.label: Taupier (mole catcher)
taupier.text: The mole catcher hunted and trapped moles, which were pests to crops and gardens.

tavernier.label: Tavernier (tavern keeper)
tavernier.summary: Keeper of a tavern serving food and drink, sometimes with lodging.
tavernier.text: The tavern keeper ran a tavern where he served wine and meals to his customers, and sometimes offered lodging to travellers — an activity regulated from the Middle Ages by local statutes fixing prices and opening hours. The word predates the modern use of "aubergiste" (innkeeper) or "cafetier" (café owner).

taxateur.label: Taxateur (postage assessor)
taxateur.summary: Person who set the charge on mail on arrival, when postage was paid by the recipient.
taxateur.text: The "taxateur" determined the charge on mail when it arrived at the post office, at a time when postage was still paid by the recipient.

taxi.label: Taxi (taxi driver)
taxi.summary: Driver of a public hire vehicle, paid by the journey.
taxi.text: The taxi driver carried passengers on demand for payment, in an identifiable vehicle. The occupation developed as the motor car became widespread in the early 20th century, succeeding the cabs and hackney coachmen.

taxidermiste.label: Taxidermiste (taxidermist)
taxidermiste.summary: Craftsman who prepared, stuffed and mounted dead animals to preserve them.
taxidermiste.text: The taxidermist skinned, treated and stuffed dead animals to give them a lifelike appearance for preservation, natural-history study or decoration. The trade became professional in the 19th century with the rise of natural-history cabinets and private collections.

teerschweler.label: Tar burner (Teerschweler)
teerschweler.summary: Forest craftsman who produced wood tar and pitch by smouldering pine wood and roots.
teerschweler.text: The Teerschweler heats resinous pine wood, especially stumps and roots, without air in a brick tar kiln and collects the wood tar that runs off; by boiling it down he obtains pitch, often with charcoal as a by-product. Tar and pitch were used to caulk ships and barrels, as axle grease and in medicine. Tar kilns were especially common in the pine heaths of Brandenburg, Lusatia and Pomerania.

teichwaerter.label: Pond keeper (Teichwärter)
teichwaerter.summary: Keeper of a lordship's fish ponds, especially in carp farming.
teichwaerter.text: The Teichwärter looks after the fish ponds of a lordship or monastery: he regulates the inflow and outflow of water, maintains the dams and sluice outlets (Mönche), feeds and protects the fish and takes part in the autumn harvesting of the ponds. Carp pond farming was especially important in Bohemia, Upper Lusatia, Silesia and Franconia; the Teichmeister supervised several ponds.

teilleur.label: Teilleur (scutcher)
teilleur.summary: Worker who separated the usable textile fibres from flax or hemp straw.
teilleur.text: The scutcher carried out scutching ("teillage"): he broke and mechanically separated the flax or hemp straw to extract the usable textile fibres, an essential step before spinning. It was seasonal work in the countryside of regions with a flax- and hemp-growing tradition (Normandy, Brittany, Flanders).

teinturier.label: Teinturier (dyer)
teinturier.summary: Craftsman who dyed fabrics and yarns using traditional processes.
teinturier.text: The dyer dyed cloth and yarn in coloured baths made from dye plants (madder, woad, weld) or, later, from chemical dyes. It was an old and regulated guild, because of the difficulty of obtaining fast colours and the pollution produced by the dye baths.

teinturier_en_grand_teint.label: Teinturier en grand teint (master dyer of fine cloth)
teinturier_en_grand_teint.summary: Dyer authorised to dye wide, high-value woollen cloth.
teinturier_en_grand_teint.text: The "teinturier en grand teint" could dye any woollen cloth more than 1.33 ells wide (about 1.60 m) and worth more than 20 sous per ell, a higher qualification than that of the "teinturier en petit teint".

teinturier_en_petit_teint.label: Teinturier en petit teint (dyer of common cloth)
teinturier_en_petit_teint.summary: Dyer authorised to dye lower-value cloth or to re-dye cloth already dyed.
teinturier_en_petit_teint.text: The "teinturier en petit teint" could dye any woollen cloth worth less than 20 sous per ell, or re-dye cloth that had already been dyed by a "teinturier en grand teint".

telegraphiste.label: Télégraphiste (telegraphist)
telegraphiste.summary: Employee responsible for receiving and transmitting messages by optical or electric telegraph.
telegraphiste.text: The telegraphist received and transmitted messages by means of a telegraph, either optical (the Chappe system) or electric.

telephoniste.label: Téléphoniste (telephone operator)
telephoniste.summary: At a telephone exchange, the person who connected telephone subscribers.
telephoniste.text: At a telephone exchange, the telephone operator, usually a woman, connected telephone subscribers by linking the lines by hand.

tellatier.label: Tellatier (cloth merchant or maker)
tellatier.summary: Merchant or maker of linen cloth.
tellatier.text: The "tellatier" was a merchant or maker of cloth, a trade related to that of the weaver and the "chanevacier" (canvas maker).

tendeur_de_basse_eau.label: Tendeur de basse eau (low-water net fisherman)
tendeur_de_basse_eau.summary: Coastal fisherman who set his nets on the shallows.
tendeur_de_basse_eau.text: The "tendeur de basse eau" was a coastal fisherman who set his nets on the shallows at low tide.

tendeur_de_draps.label: Tendeur de draps (cloth stretcher)
tendeur_de_draps.summary: Fulling worker responsible for stretching cloth to dry it.
tendeur_de_draps.text: The "tendeur de draps" was a fulling worker responsible for stretching woollen cloth to dry it after fulling.

teneur_de_tas.label: Teneur de tas (holder-up)
teneur_de_tas.summary: In a shipyard, the riveter's assistant who placed and held the rivet as it was set.
teneur_de_tas.text: In a shipyard, the holder-up ("teneur de tas") assisted the riveter by placing the rivet and holding it in position while it was set in the hull.

terminator.label: Terminator (craft apprentice)
terminator.summary: Apprentice learning a craft from a guild master.
terminator.text: The terminator learned a craft from a master for several years, usually living in his house and working in the workshop in return for board. At the end of his apprenticeship (termin) he was released before the guild as a journeyman.

terrasseur.label: Terrasseur (navvy)
terrasseur.summary: Earthworks labourer digging foundations, trenches and embankments.
terrasseur.text: The navvy carried out earthworks — digging foundations, trenches, cuttings and embankments — with pick and shovel before mechanisation. The occupation was in great demand in the 19th century for building railways, canals and roads.

terre_neuva.label: Terre-neuva (Newfoundland cod fisherman)
terre_neuva.summary: Seaman-fisherman fishing for cod off Newfoundland.
terre_neuva.text: The "terre-neuva" embarked on long cod-fishing campaigns on the Banks off Newfoundland, an activity that made the fortune of many French ports (Saint-Malo, Fécamp, Paimpol) from the 16th to the 20th century. The term denotes the seaman and sometimes the ship itself.

terzadro.label: Terzadro (third-share tenant)
terzadro.summary: Tenant farmer who shared the harvest with the owner in thirds rather than in halves.
terzadro.text: The terzeria contract, found in various parts of northern and central Italy, divided the produce into thirds, the tenant receiving one or two thirds according to local custom and the crops. The terzadro supplied the labour and part of the costs; his position was close to that of the sharecropper (mezzadro).

tesoureiro_da_bula.label: Tesoureiro da bula (treasurer of the Crusade Bull)
tesoureiro_da_bula.summary: Person charged with distributing the summaries of the Crusade Bull and collecting the corresponding alms.
tesoureiro_da_bula.text: The tesoureiro da bula distributes in a parish or municipality the summaries of the Bull of the Holy Crusade, a papal document granting indulgences and dispensations to the faithful who gave alms, and receives the sums thus collected to hand them over to the Bull's administration. A common local function from the 17th to the 19th century, it was carried out by a trusted resident.

teut.label: Teut (Kempen travelling trader)
teut.summary: Travelling trader from the Kempen who journeyed abroad with his wares.
teut.text: The teuten were traders from the Kempen who, often in organised companies, travelled abroad every year to sell goods such as copperware, textiles or horses and to mend kettles. They returned to their village after the season. The teuten trade flourished in the 17th and 18th centuries and declined in the 19th century.

thuilier.label: Thuilier (tile maker)
thuilier.summary: Maker of tiles using traditional terracotta techniques.
thuilier.text: The "thuilier" (a variant of "tuilier") shaped and fired clay tiles in a tile works, often set up near a clay deposit and a watercourse. The trade was related to that of the potter, sharing the same firing techniques.

tiari.label: Tiari (saltworks ash-raker)
tiari.summary: Saltworks labourer responsible for removing ashes from the evaporation furnaces.
tiari.text: The "tiari" worked in a saltworks (such as the one at Arc-et-Senans), where he removed the ashes from the furnaces that heated the pans in which brine was evaporated to produce salt. It was a menial post in fire-heated ("ignigène") salt production.

tillolier.label: Tillolier (Adour boatman)
tillolier.summary: Fisherman and boatman of the Bayonne area who handled a "tillole" on the Adour.
tillolier.text: The "tillolier" was at once fisherman, ferryman, carrier and expert swimmer, sailing a "tillole" (or "thillole"), a traditional boat of the Adour at Bayonne whose name is said to come from the Old Norse "tilja" (plank), by way of Gascon. The Bayonne poet Pierre Lesca (born in 1730) devoted the "Chant des Tilloliers" to them. The trade, now extinct, is also associated with the Arcachon basin, where related boats were in use.

timbalier.label: Timbalier (beaker maker)
timbalier.summary: Goldsmith or coppersmith making "timbales", metal drinking cups.
timbalier.text: The "timbalier" made "timbales", metal cups (silver, pewter or copper) often given as christening presents, using the techniques of goldsmithing or copperware ("dinanderie"). Not to be confused with the musician "timbalier", the kettledrum player.

tire_sac.label: Tire-sac (salt-store porter)
tire_sac.summary: Salt-store clerk responsible for loading and handling the salt.
tire_sac.text: The "tire-sac" handled the sacks of salt in a "grenier à sel", a royal warehouse where salt was stored before sale under the "gabelle" system. It was a menial job in the handling of salt under the Ancien Régime.

tire_sou.label: Tire-sou (penny-pincher)
tire_sou.summary: Tax collector or usurer; a term with a pejorative connotation.
tire_sou.text: Depending on the context, the "tire-sou" was an over-zealous tax collector or a usurer lending at high interest — in both cases a popular term with a pejorative connotation aimed at someone who squeezed money (the "sou") out of his fellow citizens. It is found mostly in colloquial use rather than as an official title.

tiretainier.label: Tiretainier (linsey-woolsey weaver)
tiretainier.summary: Weaver specialised in "tiretaine", a coarse drugget with a linen warp and woollen weft.
tiretainier.text: The "tiretainier" wove "tiretaine", a coarse drugget with a warp of linen or hemp yarn and a weft of locally carded wool, used for cheap working clothes. Reims also produced "tiretaines" woven entirely of wool, lighter and finer, sold under the name of "petits droguets".

tireur_d_or.label: Tireur d'or (gold-wire drawer)
tireur_d_or.summary: Craftsman who drew gold out into precious thread.
tireur_d_or.text: The gold-wire drawer drew an ingot or wire of gold through ever finer draw-plates to obtain gold thread for embroidery, trimmings ("passementerie") or goldsmiths' work. It was a high-precision trade attached to the guild of goldsmiths or of gold and silver wire drawers.

tireur_de_ficelles.label: Tireur de ficelles (draw boy)
tireur_de_ficelles.summary: In brocade workshops, the person responsible for pulling the cords of the "semple".
tireur_de_ficelles.text: In brocade workshops, the "tireur de ficelles" pulled the cords of the "semple", a device on the hand loom used to raise the warp threads according to the desired pattern.

tireur_de_pierre.label: Tireur de pierre (quarryman)
tireur_de_pierre.summary: Quarry worker responsible for extracting and moving blocks of stone.
tireur_de_pierre.text: The "tireur de pierre" extracted blocks of stone from the working face of a quarry and moved them to the place where they were cut up or shipped. It was a physical quarrying job, upstream of the stonecutter.

tireur_de_sable.label: Tireur de sable (sand digger)
tireur_de_sable.summary: Worker responsible for extracting sand from sandpits and carting it away.
tireur_de_sable.text: The sand digger extracted sand from a sandpit or riverbed and carted it to where it was to be used (building, glassmaking, foundry work). It was a manual job in the sand quarries.

tireur_epinglier.label: Tireur (pin-wire drawer)
tireur_epinglier.summary: Pinmaker who drew iron or brass wire through the draw-plate.
tireur_epinglier.text: In the pinmakers' guild, the "tireur" drew iron or brass wire through a draw-plate to give it the fine gauge needed for making pins. It was the stage before the actual shaping of the pin.

tireur_estame.label: Tireur d'estaim (worsted comber)
tireur_estame.summary: Worker who combed wool to draw out "estaim", a long yarn for "étamine".
tireur_estame.text: The "tireur d'estaim" combed wool with a large comb (a comb with long, pointed teeth) to draw out "estaim", a long, fine yarn used to weave "étamine", a light and valuable woollen cloth of the 17th and 18th centuries, sometimes mixed with silk for the finest pieces, known as "camelotées". The occupation is often misspelt "tireur d'étain" (tin) in records, by confusion with the metal, when "estaim" should be read.

tireur_mineur.label: Tireur (hewer)
tireur_mineur.summary: Miner responsible for extracting raw materials underground.
tireur_mineur.text: In mining vocabulary, the "tireur" was the worker responsible for cutting and extracting the ore or coal at the working face. It was the basic post in underground mining.

tireur_textile.label: Tireur (draw boy)
tireur_textile.summary: Textile worker who worked the cords of the "semple" when weaving brocaded fabrics.
tireur_textile.text: The "tireur" (de lacs) worked, at the weaver's command, the cords of the "semple" that raised the warp threads according to the pattern being woven, in the manufacture of figured or brocaded fabrics. It was an indispensable assistant's post before the invention of the Jacquard loom, which automated this task.

tisanier.label: Tisanier (herbal-tea seller)
tisanier.summary: Seller of herbal teas and medicinal infusions, itinerant or with a fixed stall.
tisanier.text: The "tisanier" sold herbal teas and infusions for medicinal purposes, in a shop or at markets, at a time when self-medication with plants was the norm for everyday ailments. The trade was close to that of the herbalist.

tissandier.label: Tissandier (weaver-merchant)
tissandier.summary: Merchant-weaver who both made and sold cloth.
tissandier.text: The "tissandier" combined making (weaving) and selling his cloth directly, bringing together in one person the functions of craftsman and merchant, which were usually separate. It was a more integrated organisation of production than that of the ordinary weaver working for a merchant-manufacturer.

tisserand.label: Tisserand (weaver)
tisserand.summary: Craftsman weaving linen or wool cloth on a hand loom.
tisserand.text: The weaver worked fibre (flax, hemp or wool) on a hand loom to produce cloth, frequently on commission for a merchant-clothier. Widespread in textile-producing regions (Normandy, Flanders, the Beauvaisis), the trade was often a supplementary activity alongside a small farm holding.

tisserand_de_lange.label: Tisserand de lange (swaddling-cloth weaver)
tisserand_de_lange.summary: Weaver specialised in making swaddling clothes and baby linen.
tisserand_de_lange.text: The "tisserand de lange" wove swaddling clothes and linen for infants, a domestic textile specialisation. The term has an old spelling variant, "toisseran".

tisserand_de_lin.label: Tisserand de lin (linen weaver)
tisserand_de_lin.summary: Weaver specialised in weaving flax to produce linen cloth.
tisserand_de_lin.text: The linen weaver made cloth by weaving yarn obtained from flax fibres that had first been scutched and spun. It was a common specialisation in flax-growing regions (Normandy, Flanders, Brittany), where linen cloth was a major domestic and commercial product.

tisserand_de_linge.label: Tisserand de linge (household-linen weaver)
tisserand_de_linge.summary: Weaver specialised in making household linen.
tisserand_de_linge.text: The "tisserand de linge" made cloth for household linen (sheets, tablecloths, napkins), as opposed to the weaver of cloth for garments. It was a domestic or craft production widespread in countryside with a flax-working tradition.

tisserand_de_queuvre_chefs_de_soie.label: Tisserand de queuvre-chefs de soie (silk kerchief weaver)
tisserand_de_queuvre_chefs_de_soie.summary: Medieval craftsman making silk caps and veils.
tisserand_de_queuvre_chefs_de_soie.text: This medieval weaver made "queuvre-chefs" (kerchiefs, head coverings) and veils of silk, precious items of women's headwear. It is a rare medieval term, attested in the vocabulary of the luxury textile guilds.

tisseur_de_trosse.label: Tisseur de trosse (hemp-cloth weaver)
tisseur_de_trosse.summary: Weaver specialised in weaving fabrics of hemp yarn.
tisseur_de_trosse.text: The "tisseur de trosse" wove coarse fabrics from hemp yarn (the "trosse"), intended for everyday rural use (sacks, coarse cloth). It was a rural textile specialisation linked to hemp growing.

tisseur_en_sparterie.label: Tisseur en sparterie (esparto weaver)
tisseur_en_sparterie.summary: Craftsman plaiting articles from esparto grass, a fibrous Mediterranean plant.
tisseur_en_sparterie.text: The esparto weaver plaited and wove esparto (or "sparte"), a fibrous Mediterranean plant, to make ropes, mats, bags and shoes (espadrilles). It was a traditional craft around the Mediterranean, particularly in North Africa and the south of France.

tissutier.label: Tissutier (small-ware weaver)
tissutier.summary: Craftsman making small woven articles: ribbons, laces, braids and tapes.
tissutier.text: The "tissutier" made woven haberdashery articles — ribbons, laces, braids, tapes — and was often grouped with the ribbon maker in the guild of "tissutiers-rubaniers". The trade was distinct from that of the cloth weaver, being centred on small, narrow wares.

tixolier_de_soye.label: Tixolier de soye (silk weaver)
tixolier_de_soye.text: The "tixolier de soye" (an old spelling of "tissier de soie") wove silk fabrics, a luxury craft concentrated in certain specialised centres (Lyon, Tours). It is a regional variant of the word for weaver applied specifically to silk.

toilatier.label: Toilier (linen-cloth maker or dealer)
toilatier.summary: Merchant or craftsman specialised in the trade and weaving of linen cloth.
toilatier.text: The "toilier" made and/or sold linen or hemp cloth, an activity on the border between textile craftsmanship and trade. The feminine form "toilière" denotes a woman who specialised in selling and caring for linen.

toiseur.label: Toiseur (quantity surveyor)
toiseur.summary: Person responsible for measuring building work to assess its cost.
toiseur.text: The "toiseur" measured ("toiser") completed work on a building site — masonry, carpentry, roofing — in order to draw up the quantities and hence the cost, the basis for settlement between the client and the craftsmen paid by the job. It was a technical role close to that of the present-day quantity surveyor ("métreur").

tombelier.label: Tombelier (refuse carter)
tombelier.summary: Worker responsible for carting mud and refuse out of the town.
tombelier.text: The "tombelier" removed mud, rubble and refuse from the town's streets by means of a cart (the "tombereau", tipcart), a public-health role before the modern organisation of street cleaning. The trade is attested from the Middle Ages in the large towns.

tombier.label: Tombier (tomb sculptor)
tombier.summary: Sculptor specialised in making tombs and altars in marble.
tombier.text: The "tombier" sculpted tombs, recumbent effigies and altars in marble or stone, a prestigious funerary craft often linked to commissions from the Church and the nobility. The trade is well documented in the Middle Ages and under the Ancien Régime, and was close to that of the sculptor and the marble mason.

tondeur.label: Tondeur (cloth shearer)
tondeur.summary: Worker who sheared and smoothed the surface of woollen cloth to even out the nap.
tondeur.text: The cloth shearer evened out the nap of fulled woollen cloth with large shears ("forces") to obtain a smooth, lustrous surface — the last prestigious stage of cloth manufacture, strictly regulated by the guilds. Not to be confused with the sheep shearer, who cut the wool from the animal.

tondeur_cheveux.label: Tondeur (hair buyer)
tondeur_cheveux.summary: Person who bought women's hair at fairs for making wigs.
tondeur_cheveux.text: The hair buyer travelled round fairs and markets buying women's hair, a raw material resold to wigmakers. The practice is attested up to the 19th century, the sale of hair providing extra income for poor rural families.

tonnaroto.label: Tonnaroto (tuna-trap fisherman)
tonnaroto.summary: Fisherman working at a tonnara, a fixed net installation for catching tuna.
tonnaroto.text: The tonnaroto worked seasonally in the tuna traps of Sicily, Sardinia, Calabria and Liguria, helping to lay the nets and taking part in the mattanza under the direction of the rais. The crews, recruited in coastal villages, lived in the tonnara's buildings during the season.

tonnelier.label: Tonnelier (cooper)
tonnelier.summary: Craftsman who made barrels, casks and other hooped wooden containers.
tonnelier.text: The cooper assembled wooden staves held together by metal or wooden hoops to make barrels, "muids" and casks for storing and transporting liquids (wine, cider, salted provisions). It was an old and prosperous guild, particularly in wine-growing regions.

tonnelier_futier.label: Tonnelier fûtier (cask maker)
tonnelier_futier.summary: Cooper specialised in making casks for storing liquids.
tonnelier_futier.text: The "tonnelier fûtier" concentrated on making casks ("fûts"), watertight and durable containers for ageing and transporting wine and spirits. It was a specialisation of cooperage geared to one particular size of container.

tonnelier_specialise.label: Tonnelier spécialisé (vat cooper)
tonnelier_specialise.summary: Cooper specialised in making "foudres", large vessels for ageing wine.
tonnelier_specialise.text: This cooper made "foudres", very large wooden vessels used for ageing and storing wine in large quantities, requiring particular technical mastery compared with ordinary barrels. It was a specialisation reserved for experienced coopers in the large wine cellars ("chais").

tordeur.label: Tordeur (wringer)
tordeur.summary: Worker who twisted and wrung out wool or cloth after washing or fulling.
tordeur.text: The "tordeur" wrung out and twisted wool during its preparation, or cloth as it came out of the wash after fulling, to squeeze out the excess water. It was a finishing post in cloth-making workshops.

tordeur_d_huile.label: Tordeur d'huile (oil presser)
tordeur_d_huile.summary: Oil maker who extracted oil by pressing seeds or oil-bearing fruit.
tordeur_d_huile.text: The oil presser pressed seeds (rapeseed, walnuts, linseed) or fruit (olives) in an oil mill to extract the oil by pressure, a traditional technique predating chemical extraction. The name comes from the press or the twisting system used to squeeze the oilcakes.

tordeur_de_coton.label: Tordeur de coton (cotton twister)
tordeur_de_coton.summary: Worker who twisted cotton down into yarn.
tordeur_de_coton.text: The cotton twister twisted the down surrounding the seeds of the cotton plant to form a spinnable yarn, a manual operation predating the mechanisation of cotton spinning. It was a trade of the early days of the cotton industry.

torenwachter.label: Torenwachter (tower watchman)
torenwachter.summary: Watchman who looked out from a church or town tower for fire and approaching danger.
torenwachter.text: The torenwachter lived or stayed in the tower of a church or town gate, from where he overlooked the town and its surroundings. In case of fire or threat he raised the alarm with a horn, a trumpet or the bell, and in some towns he also sounded the hours. The office disappeared with modern fire brigades and public lighting.

torqueur.label: Torqueur (tobacco twister)
torqueur.summary: Worker who spun tobacco and made it into rolls.
torqueur.text: The "torqueur" spun dried tobacco leaves and then rolled them into twists ("torques") or "carottes" of tobacco, a traditional preparation before the tobacco manufactories were industrialised. The trade was linked to the French tobacco monopoly.

tosquiador.label: Tosquiador (sheep shearer)
tosquiador.summary: Worker who sheared sheep, often in itinerant gangs in spring.
tosquiador.text: The tosquiador cuts the wool from sheep with shearing scissors in spring, before the summer heat. On the large farms of the Alentejo and the Beiras, shearing was done by gangs of shearers who moved from estate to estate, and it was an important moment of the pastoral year.

toucheur.label: Toucheur (drover)
toucheur.summary: Person who drove livestock on foot to the fair, the market or the slaughterhouse.
toucheur.text: The drover drove livestock on foot along the roads, from the farm to the fair, the market or the slaughterhouse, an itinerant trade linked to the buying, selling and transport of animals before railways and lorries became widespread. The term comes from the stick (the goad) with which he "touched" the animals to guide them.

toucheur_de_boeufs.label: Toucheur de bœufs (ox driver)
toucheur_de_boeufs.summary: Farm servant responsible for driving the oxen during ploughing.
toucheur_de_boeufs.text: The ox driver guided the team of oxen during fieldwork, particularly ploughing, walking alongside them with a goad. It was the role of a farm servant, distinct from the "laboureur", who owned or rented the team.

tourbier.label: Tourbier (peat cutter)
tourbier.summary: Worker who extracted peat, a fuel, from peat bogs.
tourbier.text: The peat cutter cut and extracted blocks of peat from the bogs, an organic material burnt for heating in regions lacking wood or coal. It was seasonal work in wetland areas (Sologne, Brière, the Nord).

touriere.label: Tourière (turn sister)
touriere.summary: Nun or convent servant in charge of the "tour" and of dealings with the outside world.
touriere.text: In a convent, the "tourière" was in charge of the "tour" — a revolving device allowing objects and messages to be passed without visual contact with the outside — as well as errands and dealings with the outside world on behalf of the enclosed community. It was an essential role in convents with strict enclosure.

tourmenteur_jure.label: Tourmenteur juré (sworn torturer)
tourmenteur_jure.summary: Executioner's assistant responsible for subjecting the accused to judicial torture.
tourmenteur_jure.text: The "tourmenteur juré" assisted the executioner in administering "the question" (judicial torture) intended to obtain confessions or the denunciation of accomplices, a legal practice under the Ancien Régime until its abolition at the end of the 18th century. It was an official and "sworn" ("juré") post, attached to the judicial apparatus.

tourneur.label: Tourneur (turner)
tourneur.summary: Craftsman who shaped objects in wood, metal or bone by rotating them on a lathe.
tourneur.text: The turner shaped cylindrical pieces (furniture legs, utensils, buttons, machine parts) by turning the material on a lathe, the cutting tool being held against the rotating work. It was a versatile trade, found in many crafts (wood, ivory, metal, bone).

tourneur_bistourneur.label: Tourneur bistourneur (gelder by torsion)
tourneur_bistourneur.summary: Empirical practitioner who castrated animals by twisting the cords.
tourneur_bistourneur.text: The "bistourneur" castrated farm animals (bulls, pigs) by "bistournage": without opening the scrotum, he twisted each spermatic cord by hand until it was closed off, which cut the blood supply and caused the testicle to atrophy. The technique was practised by itinerant rural empirics before veterinary medicine became widespread, often alongside another activity.

tourneur_de_carrousel.label: Tourneur de carrousel (merry-go-round turner)
tourneur_de_carrousel.summary: Person who turned a merry-go-round by hand before it was motorised.
tourneur_de_carrousel.text: The merry-go-round turner worked a fairground roundabout by the strength of his arms, or by pushing the mechanism, before the arrival of steam and then electric motors. It was a fairground trade that disappeared when roundabouts were motorised at the end of the 19th century.

tourneur_de_cendres.label: Tourneur de cendres (sweep washer)
tourneur_de_cendres.summary: Goldsmith's worker responsible for recovering gold dust by mercury amalgamation.
tourneur_de_cendres.text: The "tourneur de cendres" recovered the particles of gold lost in the ashes and waste of a goldsmith's workshop, treating them with mercury (amalgamation) to extract the gold. It was a specialised recovery trade on the fringes of goldsmithing proper.

tourneur_en_chaise.label: Tourneur en chaise (chair turner)
tourneur_en_chaise.summary: Craftsman who turned the legs and rungs of wooden chairs on a lathe.
tourneur_en_chaise.text: The chair turner turned the legs, rungs and cylindrical parts of wooden chairs on a lathe, before they were assembled by the joiner or chair maker. It was a specialisation of the wood turner for the furniture industry.

tourneur_en_nacre.label: Tourneur en nacre (mother-of-pearl turner)
tourneur_en_nacre.summary: Craftsman who turned mother-of-pearl to make buttons, in the Méru area.
tourneur_en_nacre.text: The mother-of-pearl turner cut discs from shells and then turned, sanded and drilled them to make buttons. The craft was concentrated around Méru, in the Oise, where peasants practised it at home from the 17th century during the agricultural slack season; industrialised in the 20th century, the Pays de Thelle became the largest European centre of mother-of-pearl button making, employing more than 10,000 people in the 1910s.

tourneur_opticien.label: Tourneur opticien (lens turner)
tourneur_opticien.summary: Worker who turned spectacle lenses on a lathe before the era of industrial optical production.
tourneur_opticien.text: The lens turner shaped corrective lenses using a hand lathe, before the arrival of industrial optical smoothing and polishing processes. The trade gradually disappeared during the 20th century with the mechanisation of spectacle making, particularly around specialised areas such as the French Jura.

tourneur_potier.label: Tourneur potier (potter's thrower)
tourneur_potier.summary: Potter who shaped clay on a wheel to form pottery.
tourneur_potier.text: The thrower was the ceramic worker who shaped the clay on a potter's wheel, as opposed to the other workers in the workshop responsible for drying, glazing or firing. The term emphasises the technical skill of throwing, which remains the most skilled stage of the potter's trade.

tourneur_sur_fer.label: Tourneur sur fer (metal turner)
tourneur_sur_fer.summary: Metalworker who machined metal parts on a lathe.
tourneur_sur_fer.text: The metal turner worked metal with a lathe, removing material to produce precise cylindrical parts (shafts, bolts, machine parts). The trade developed mainly with 19th-century industrialisation and the rise of mechanical engineering, distinguishing this turner from the wood turner or the potter's thrower, who worked different materials.

toutier.label: Toutier (river scout boatman)
toutier.summary: Boatman who went ahead in a small craft to mark out the route for large river convoys.
toutier.text: The "toutier" sailed a small boat called a "toute", which he took ahead of the large convoys of boats to sound and mark out the best channel on the river. This piloting role, attested in the vocabulary of Ancien Régime inland navigation, was essential to the safety of convoys on rivers with shifting shallows.

touzer.label: Touzer (sheep shearer)
touzer.summary: Sheep shearer; a term used in Brittany.
touzer.text: The "touzer" was the worker who sheared the wool from sheep, a dialect term used in Brittany (from the regional verb "touser", to shear). The seasonal work was often carried out alongside another farming occupation.

traankoker.label: Traankoker (train-oil boiler)
traankoker.summary: Worker who boiled whale or seal blubber to extract train oil.
traankoker.text: In the try-works, the blubber of whales and seals was boiled down into train oil, which served as lamp oil and as a raw material for soap, leather dressing and other industries. The boilers worked in the whaling ports and, in the 17th century, also in temporary try-works in the polar regions. The work was notorious for its dreadful stench.

traceur_pierre.label: Traceur de pierre (stone setter-out)
traceur_pierre.summary: Worker who marked the cutting lines on a block before it was dressed.
traceur_pierre.text: The generic term "traceur" denotes a draughtsman, in particular an industrial draughtsman, who draws up plans or technical layouts. Applied to stone, the "traceur" transferred onto the rough block the lines and marks that would guide the stonecutter, an art of setting out regarded as the most delicate stage of work on dressed stone, even before its extraction or cutting.

traffiquant.label: Trafiquant (trader)
traffiquant.summary: Itinerant merchant or dealer in various goods.
traffiquant.text: In its old sense, the "trafiquant" (or "traffiquant", the period spelling) simply meant a merchant or dealer who traded ("trafic") in various goods, often travelling from fair to fair. In old records the word does not yet have the illicit connotation it would take on later.

traginer.label: Traginer (muleteer)
traginer.summary: Driver of mules carrying goods; a Catalan term.
traginer.text: The "traginer" (from the Catalan "traginar", to carry) was a muleteer who conveyed goods on the backs of mules along mountain tracks. The term is attested mainly in regions of Catalan culture, in Roussillon and beyond the Pyrenees.

trameur.label: Trameur (weft winder)
trameur.summary: Worker who prepared the weft and tended the shuttle on a loom.
trameur.text: The "trameur" prepared the weft (the weft threads) and tended the shuttle on a loom.

trameur_pipes.label: Trameur (clay-pipe trimmer)
trameur_pipes.summary: Pipe-factory worker responsible for cleaning clay pipes as they came out of the kiln.
trameur_pipes.text: In a clay-pipe factory, the "trameur" was the worker responsible for cleaning and trimming the pipes after firing, removing the clay residue left by the moulding. The post belonged to the craft production chain of fired clay pipes, an activity that expanded greatly in the 19th century (notably at Saint-Omer and Givet).

trameur_tissage.label: Trameur (weft winder)
trameur_tissage.summary: Weaving worker who prepared the weft and kept the loom's shuttle supplied.
trameur_tissage.text: The "trameur" prepared the weft threads (the transverse thread, as opposed to the warp) and kept the loom's shuttle supplied throughout the weaving. The term is commonly found in the registers of regions with a strong textile tradition (the Nord, Normandy, the Lyonnais).

trancheur.label: Trancheur (splitter)
trancheur.summary: Cod-processing worker who opened the fish and removed the backbone.
trancheur.text: In cod-processing workshops (Newfoundland, Breton and Norman ports), the "trancheur" was the specialised worker who opened the fish and removed its backbone, one stage of assembly-line work shared with the "décolleur" (who separated the head) and the "étêteur" (header). This vocabulary of highly divided trades reflects the industrial organisation of cod fishing in the 19th and 20th centuries.

transporteur_rural.label: Transporteur rural (country carter)
transporteur_rural.summary: Peasant who used his oxen and cart for commercial haulage.
transporteur_rural.text: The country carter was a farmer who supplemented his agricultural income by hiring out his draught animals and cart to carry goods on behalf of others. This sideline, common in the countryside before the railway, sometimes appears as a declared occupation in civil registration records.

trappeur.label: Trappeur (trapper)
trappeur.summary: Hunter specialised in trapping animals for the fur trade.
trappeur.text: The trapper caught fur-bearing game with traps rather than with a gun, in order to sell the pelts. The term, popularised in French by the colonisation of North America (the fur trade), is also applied by extension to European hunter-trappers.

trasson.label: Trasson (salt carrier)
trasson.summary: Port employee who carried sacks of salt to the ship on horseback.
trasson.text: The "trasson" was an employee of the salt ports who carried the sacks of salt, with the help of a horse, from the storehouses to the ship or the boatman's barge. The term belongs to the vocabulary of the ports of western France involved in the salt trade.

travailleur_terre.label: Travailleur de la terre (farm labourer)
travailleur_terre.summary: Agricultural worker hired by the day according to seasonal needs.
travailleur_terre.text: The "travailleur de la terre" was an agricultural worker with no land or team of his own, hired by the day or by the task by farmers according to the needs of seasonal work (ploughing, harvest, grape harvest). He broadly corresponds to the day-labourer ("journalier") and is distinct from the "laboureur", who owned or rented a plough team.

trecciaiola.label: Trecciaiola (straw plaiter)
trecciaiola.summary: Woman who plaited straw for hat-making, especially in Tuscany.
trecciaiola.text: The trecciaiola worked wheat straw at home, plaiting it into strips that were then sewn into the hats known as Florentine straw hats. Widespread in the countryside around Florence and Prato between the 18th and 20th centuries, the work employed tens of thousands of women and girls and was an important supplement to peasant income.

trefileur.label: Tréfileur (wire drawer)
trefileur.summary: Craftsman who drew metal into wire, especially iron or brass ("archal").
trefileur.text: The wire drawer made metal wire by passing a metal rod through a series of draw-plates that gradually made it thinner ("tréfilage"). Depending on the material worked, a distinction is made between the iron-wire drawer and the brass-wire drawer ("tréfileur d'archal"), the latter working after the "batteur d'archal", who prepared the raw material. Some old dictionaries also record, under the spelling "tréfilier", an older sense of maker of mail armour (drawn iron wire being used to make the rings of the hauberk).

treillageur_artisan.label: Treillageur (trellis maker)
treillageur_artisan.summary: Craftsman making trellises and fences of wood or wire.
treillageur_artisan.text: The trellis maker made trelliswork: structures of wooden laths or interwoven wire used as fences, palings or supports for climbing plants in gardens. The trade, related to the techniques of basketry and light joinery, also existed as a commercial activity (selling trellises) under the name of "treillagiste".

treillageur_jardinier.label: Treillageur (trellis gardener)
treillageur_jardinier.summary: Gardener who grew plants on wooden trellises that he made himself.
treillageur_jardinier.text: This gardener built wooden trellises himself so that certain plants (vines, ornamental plants) could climb and grow on them, thus combining horticultural work with making the supports. He is distinct from the craftsman "treillageur", who sold trellis structures without necessarily tending the plants grown on them.

treilleur_minier.label: Treilleur (winch operator)
treilleur_minier.summary: Mine worker responsible for operating the winding winches.
treilleur_minier.text: In a mine, the "treilleur" operated the winches that raised ore, spoil or miners from the bottom of the shaft. The word comes from "treuil" (winch) and has nothing to do with trelliswork; the job was essential to the safety and pace of extraction.

trekschuitschipper.label: Trekschuitschipper (towed barge master)
trekschuitschipper.summary: Master of a trekschuit, a horse-drawn passenger barge on the canals.
trekschuitschipper.text: From the 17th century onwards, trekschuiten linked the towns of Holland and other provinces by specially dug canals with towpaths. The barge was pulled by a horse ridden by a boy, the jager, and ran to a fixed timetable. The trekschuit master stood at the helm and looked after the passengers; this means of transport disappeared with the coming of the railways.

trelissier.label: Trélissier (hemp-canvas weaver)
trelissier.summary: Occitan weaver specialised in the hemp cloth called "trélis".
trelissier.text: The "trélissier" wove "trélis", a three-thread hemp cloth considered the ancestor of "treillis" (drill), used in particular for sacks, tarpaulins and working clothes. The term, related to Occitan, is attested mainly in the south of France, a region where hemp was widely grown.

trepointeur.label: Trépointeur (espadrille welt stitcher)
trepointeur.summary: Espadrille worker who stitched the sole to the fabric of the shoe.
trepointeur.text: The "trépointeur" was a worker in espadrille making, responsible for stitching the welt ("trépointe", the strip joining the rope sole and the fabric upper). The trade developed in the traditional espadrille-making areas, notably in the south-west and the Basque Country.

tresorier.label: Trésorier (treasurer)
tresorier.summary: Officer responsible for collecting and managing the revenues of a lord or an institution.
tresorier.text: The treasurer was responsible for collecting, safeguarding and managing the financial revenues of a seigneury, a parish or a church institution. Under the Ancien Régime the office covered very different realities depending on scale (treasurer of a parish vestry, seigneurial treasurer, royal treasurer).

tresseur.label: Tresseur (hair braider)
tresseur.summary: Craftsman who braided hair for making wigs.
tresseur.text: The "tresseur" worked locks of hair, natural or dressed, braiding them for the making of wigs and hairpieces. This wigmaking trade reached its peak in the 17th and 18th centuries, a period when wearing a wig was an important social marker.

tressier.label: Tressier (wigmaker's assistant)
tressier.summary: Wigmaker's assistant who prepared false hairpieces and other hair work.
tressier.text: The "tressier" assisted the wigmaker in preparing hairpieces, dressing the braids of hair to be mounted on wigs. He held the position of a specialised worker within the master wigmaker's workshop.

tricoteuse.label: Tricoteuse (knitter)
tricoteuse.summary: Woman who made knitted goods (stockings, caps, garments).
tricoteuse.text: The knitter made knitted articles by hand or on a frame — stockings, caps, jumpers — an activity often carried out at home to supplement household income, particularly in rural or mountain regions. The word has remained in collective memory associated with the women who, knitting in hand, attended the sessions of the Convention and the executions during the French Revolution.

trieur_de_crottes.label: Trieur de crottes (dung sorter)
trieur_de_crottes.summary: Person who sorted dog droppings intended for tanning.
trieur_de_crottes.text: The dung sorter sorted and graded the dog droppings collected from the streets by the gatherer, according to their quality and origin. Called "pure" in the jargon of the trade, these dried droppings were sold on to tanners and tawers, who used them to soften the hides and remove the lime from them before tanning — an unsavoury but very real activity in 19th-century towns.

trieur_de_minerai.label: Trieur de minerai (ore sorter)
trieur_de_minerai.summary: In a mine, the person responsible for separating ore from stone.
trieur_de_minerai.text: In a mine, the ore sorter was responsible for separating the useful ore from the waste rock after extraction.

trieur_forestier.label: Trieur (log sorter)
trieur_forestier.summary: Worker responsible for sorting logs by their marks during timber floating.
trieur_forestier.text: During timber floating (the transport of logs by river), the log sorter identified and separated the logs according to the distinctive marks applied by each felling company, so as to direct them to the right recipient downstream. The trade disappeared with the decline of timber floating in the 20th century.

trieur_minier.label: Trieur (ore picker)
trieur_minier.summary: Mine worker responsible for separating useful ore from the barren gangue.
trieur_minier.text: The ore picker separated by hand, at the surface or underground, the workable ore from the waste rock extracted with it. This sorting work, often given to women or children in 19th-century coal mines, came before the washing and grading of the ore.

trimardeur.label: Trimardeur (tramp)
trimardeur.summary: Vagrant roaming the roads, sometimes doing casual work.
trimardeur.text: The "trimardeur" (from the slang "trimard", the road) was a man of no fixed abode who wandered from village to village, living on odd jobs or begging, particularly during the great harvests when itinerant labour was in demand. The term, popularised at the end of the 19th century, is distinct from the ordinary day-labourer because of this itinerant way of life.

tripier.label: Tripier (tripe butcher)
tripier.summary: Butcher specialised in selling tripe and offal.
tripier.text: The tripe butcher was a tradesman specialised in preparing and selling offal (tripe, liver, brains, trotters), a branch distinct from conventional butchery, which sold muscle meat. The activity, long linked to the slaughterhouses near the markets, still survives today as a specialty.

tripotier.label: Tripotier (real-tennis court keeper)
tripotier.summary: Another name for the "paumier", keeper of a real-tennis court.
tripotier.text: The "tripotier" is another name for the "paumier", the man who kept a "tripot" in the old sense of the term: a "jeu de paume" (real-tennis) establishment, the ancestor of tennis. Only later did "tripot" take on its present-day connotation of a disreputable gambling house, a secondary sense that must not be confused with the original meaning of the occupation.

triquenaire.label: Triquenaire (canal hauler)
triquenaire.summary: Hauler who guided and towed boats along the canals, especially in Belgium.
triquenaire.text: The "triquenaire" helped, by means of ropes, to guide and pull boats through the difficult passages of the canals, particularly in the northern regions and in Belgium. This towing work supplemented that of the crew or of the draught horses harnessed on the canal bank.

trollard.label: Trollard (back porter)
trollard.summary: Porter who carried parcels and goods on his back.
trollard.text: The "trollard" carried goods or parcels on his back through the streets and outskirts, at a time when many urban districts remained hard for vehicles to reach. In his role he was close to the "crocheteur" or the "portefaix" (porter).

trouvere.label: Trouvère (trouvère)
trouvere.summary: Itinerant poet-musician of northern France, the equivalent of the troubadour north of the Loire.
trouvere.text: The trouvère was a medieval poet-musician who composed and performed songs and tales in the langue d'oïl, active mainly from the 12th to the 14th century in the seigneurial courts and public squares of northern France. He was the northern counterpart of the Occitan troubadour, who expressed himself in the langue d'oc.

truchemant.label: Truchement (interpreter)
truchemant.text: The "truchement" (or "truchemant", "trussemant") translated orally between two languages, an essential role in diplomatic and commercial exchanges with the countries of the Levant. The word comes from the Arabic "tarjuman" (interpreter), which passed into French via Italian in the Middle Ages.

trufficulteur.label: Trufficulteur (truffle grower)
trufficulteur.summary: Farmer who cultivated and harvested truffles.
trufficulteur.text: The truffle grower ran a truffle plantation, often of truffle oaks or hazels, and harvested the truffles with the help of trained animals (dogs, formerly pigs) that located them underground by smell. The activity remains rooted in certain regions of south-eastern and south-western France.

trumelier.label: Trumelier (greave maker)
trumelier.summary: Armourer specialised in making "trumelières", leg armour.
trumelier.text: The "trumelier" made "trumelières", pieces of armour protecting the shin (the "trumeau" of the leg), within the armourer's workshop. This highly specialised trade of medieval armament declined with the gradual abandonment of plate armour.

tuermer.label: Tower watchman (Türmer)
tuermer.summary: Watchman living on a church or town tower who looked out for fire and gave signals.
tuermer.text: The Türmer often lives with his family in the watchman's room of a church or town tower, looks out day and night for fires and approaching riders or enemies, reports them by horn, bell or flag and sounds the hours. In many places he was also a musician (Turmbläser) attached to the town musician.

tueur_de_chiens.label: Tueur de chiens (dog killer)
tueur_de_chiens.summary: Man responsible for killing stray dogs in the streets, particularly in the 18th century.
tueur_de_chiens.text: The dog killer went through the streets, often armed with a cudgel, to kill stray dogs considered dangerous or suspected of rabies. This public-health role, performed on behalf of the municipal authorities, was part of the long-standing fight against rabies before modern health measures appeared.

tueur_de_cochons.label: Tueur de cochons (pig killer)
tueur_de_cochons.summary: Itinerant worker who killed and dressed the pig at private homes.
tueur_de_cochons.text: The pig killer went from farm to farm, usually in autumn or winter, to slaughter the family pig and help turn it into charcuterie ("cochonnailles"). This seasonal trade, often carried on alongside another activity, was long part of French rural life.

tuffelier.label: Tuffelier (tufa boatman)
tuffelier.summary: Boatman specialised in carrying tufa stone on the Loire.
tuffelier.text: The "tuffelier" carried "tuffeau" by boat, the white limestone extracted from the quarries of the Loire Valley and used to build the châteaux and houses of the region. This river trade sustained the activity of the Loire ports for several centuries.

tuilier.label: Tuilier (tile maker)
tuilier.text: The tile maker shaped and fired clay tiles in a tile works, often combined with a brickworks. This trade, essential to traditional building, was frequently carried on near workable clay deposits.

tuinder.label: Tuinder (market gardener)
tuinder.summary: Grower of vegetables for the market.
tuinder.text: The tuinder grows vegetables, and sometimes fruit, on small plots to sell them at market or to dealers. It was an important occupation in the Westland, around the towns and in Flanders; the older name warmoezenier comes from "warmoes", vegetables. From the late 19th century cultivation increasingly moved under glass.

tulliste.label: Tulliste (tulle machine operator)
tulliste.summary: Worker or technician specialised in the machine manufacture of tulle and lace.
tulliste.text: The "tulliste" operated or maintained the mechanical tulle machines in mills and lace factories, particularly in the Calais-Caudry area, the heartland of the French lace industry since the 19th century. The job required a good technical command of the complex machines used to wind and weave tulle.

tupinier.label: Tupinier (earthenware potter)
tupinier.summary: Regional synonym (Lyon area) for an earthenware potter, a maker of "tupins".
tupinier.text: The "tupinier" was an earthenware potter who made "tupins" (terracotta pots), a term specific to the Franco-Provençal linguistic area, in particular the Lyon region. The word "tupin" goes back to a Germanic root (Old Low Franconian *topp-, related to modern German Topf, pot); a letter of King Charles VII dated 1492 already attests the existence of an annual fair of the "tupiniers" in Lyon.

turfdrager.label: Turfdrager (peat porter)
turfdrager.summary: Member of the guild that unloaded peat from the boats in a town and carried it to the houses.
turfdrager.text: In towns such as Amsterdam the peat porters held the exclusive right to unload peat from the peat boats, measure it and carry it in baskets to the lofts and cellars of the buyers. They were organised in a guild with its own rules and rates. The trade disappeared as peat use declined in the 19th century.

turfmeter.label: Turfmeter (peat measurer)
turfmeter.summary: Sworn official who measured the quantities of peat sold in a town.
turfmeter.text: Because peat was sold by the ton, basket or load, towns appointed sworn peat measurers who determined the quantity when the peat boats were unloaded. This safeguarded the rights of buyers and sellers and the levying of the peat excise.

turfschipper.label: Turfschipper (peat boatman)
turfschipper.summary: Boatman who carried peat from the peat districts to the towns.
turfschipper.text: Since peat was the main fuel of the Low Countries, many peat boatmen sailed their barges from the high and low peat districts to the towns, where the peat was carried ashore by the peat porters. The trade, often carried on as a family business, gradually disappeared with the switch to coal.

turronero.label: Turronero (Spanish nougat maker)
turronero.summary: Person who made or sold turrón.
turronero.text: The turronero made or sold turrón, a sweet of almonds and honey. The turroneros of Jijona (Xixona), in Alicante, travelled throughout Spain during the Christmas season to sell the turrón made in their town, and many ended up opening shops in other cities.

typographe.label: Typographe (compositor)
typographe.summary: Printing worker who set texts from movable type.
typographe.text: The compositor set texts for printing by hand, and from the end of the 19th century on the Linotype, by assembling movable lead type. The trade, born with Gutenberg's printing press, required perfect command of spelling and layout, and gradually disappeared with phototypesetting and then computerisation in the 20th century.

ubiquiste.label: Ubiquiste (unattached doctor of theology)
ubiquiste.summary: Doctor of theology of the old University of Paris, not attached to any particular college.
ubiquiste.text: The "ubiquiste" (from the Latin "ubique", everywhere) was a doctor of theology of the University of Paris who was not attached to any particular house or college, unlike the regular doctors attached to an order. The title belongs to the university organisation of the Ancien Régime.

uhrenschildmaler.label: Clock-face painter (Uhrenschildmaler)
uhrenschildmaler.summary: Painter who decorated the painted dials (Schilde) of Black Forest clocks.
uhrenschildmaler.text: The Uhrenschildmaler paints the Schilde, the wooden and later also sheet-metal dials of Black Forest clocks, with numerals, flowers, figures and landscapes. The trade flourished in the 18th and 19th centuries in the upper Black Forest around Furtwangen, Neustadt and Triberg, often as home work in which women and whole families took part.

uhrentraeger.label: Clock pedlar (Uhrenträger)
uhrentraeger.summary: Travelling salesman who carried Black Forest clocks on his back to distant countries and sold them.
uhrentraeger.text: The Uhrenträger carried Black Forest wooden clocks on a back frame (Kraxe) and sold them as a pedlar throughout Europe and beyond. In the 18th and 19th centuries the traders joined together in clock-trading companies with permanent branches abroad, for example in England, Russia and North America; many Black Forest families lived apart for years while fathers and sons were away trading.

ulan.label: Ułan (uhlan)
ulan.summary: Light cavalryman armed with a lance.
ulan.text: The ułan was a light cavalryman armed chiefly with a lance, a sabre and firearms. The formation, which grew out of Tatar horsemen serving the Commonwealth, spread in the eighteenth century and later in the Napoleonic, Russian, Prussian and Austrian armies, and is closely tied to Polish military tradition.

uniformiste.label: Uniformiste (military tailor)
uniformiste.summary: Tailor-embroiderer specialised in making military uniforms.
uniformiste.text: The "uniformiste" made and embroidered military uniforms in accordance with the official regulations specific to each corps and rank. The trade required good knowledge of military dress regulations, which were often very detailed under successive regimes.

usinier.label: Usinier (factory worker or owner)
usinier.summary: Person who worked in a factory, or who ran one.
usinier.text: Depending on the context, the "usinier" was either a worker employed in a factory or the operator or owner of an industrial establishment (for example a mill or forge run on an industrial basis). The term became widespread with the rise of industry in the 19th century.

usurero.label: Usurero (Spanish usurer)
usurero.summary: Person who lent money at excessive interest.
usurero.text: The usurero lent money, grain or seed at interest regarded as excessive or unlawful, a practice condemned by the Church and prosecuted by law, yet widespread in rural areas, where indebted peasants relied on such loans between harvests. The term is pejorative and was rarely declared as a person's own occupation.

v_r_p.label: V.R.P. (commercial traveller)
v_r_p.summary: "Voyageur, représentant ou placier": the commercial status of travelling salesmen.
v_r_p.text: The abbreviation V.R.P. denotes a French legal status specific to sales representatives who sell on behalf of one or more firms by visiting customers. This status, governed by labour law since the 20th century, distinguishes the "voyageur" (traveller), the "représentant" (representative) and the "placier" (canvasser) according to their conditions of work.

vacher.label: Vacher (cowherd)
vacher.summary: Person responsible for minding the herd of cows, sometimes also for making cheese.
vacher.text: The cowherd minded and tended the cattle of a farm or a mountain pasture, sometimes also handling the milking and cheese-making. He is distinct from the shepherd ("berger"), who traditionally looked after sheep.

vaguemestre.label: Vaguemestre (baggage master)
vaguemestre.summary: Officer in charge of the baggage train and wagons of an army.
vaguemestre.text: The "vaguemestre" was an officer in charge of the baggage train and wagons of an army on campaign; the term later evolved to denote the person responsible for military mail.

vaguemestre_equipages.label: Vaguemestre (baggage master)
vaguemestre_equipages.summary: Officer in charge of the baggage train and wagons of an army.
vaguemestre_equipages.text: In its oldest sense, the "vaguemestre" (from the German "Wagenmeister", master of the wagons) was the officer responsible for the baggage train, wagons and baggage of an army on campaign. It is from this original, transport-related function that the better-known sense of person responsible for military mail would later derive.

vaguemestre_facteur.label: Vaguemestre (military postman)
vaguemestre_facteur.summary: Non-commissioned officer responsible for distributing mail within a military unit.
vaguemestre_facteur.text: The "vaguemestre"-postman was the non-commissioned officer responsible for receiving and distributing the soldiers' mail within a unit, which became the usual meaning of the word in the 19th and 20th centuries. This shift in meaning is explained by the fact that mail was historically carried with the army's baggage train and baggage, under the responsibility of the "vaguemestre".

valadier.label: Valadier (ditcher)
valadier.summary: Worker who dug or cleared ditches.
valadier.text: The "valadier" dug or cleared ditches (from the word "valade", ditch, in several Occitan dialects), a trade linked to the upkeep of communal or seigneurial drainage and ditch networks rather than to the more specific one of cemetery gravedigger.

valet.label: Valet (servant)
valet.summary: Young servant or helper; a generic term of Ancien Régime domestic and feudal organisation.
valet.text: In the broad sense, the "valet" was a servant or helper under the authority of a master, whether a house servant, a farm hand or, in the Middle Ages, a young nobleman in the service of a knight before attaining that rank himself (squire). The word forms the basis of many compounds denoting more specific roles ("valet de chambre", "valet de ferme", "valet de bourreau"...).

valet_bourreau.label: Valet de bourreau (executioner's assistant)
valet_bourreau.summary: Executioner's assistant, taking part in carrying out capital punishment.
valet_bourreau.text: The executioner's assistant helped the "exécuteur des hautes œuvres" (the executioner) in the exercise of his office, particularly at executions and corporal punishments. Like the executioner himself, he belonged to a category of occupations considered infamous under the Ancien Régime, which explains his frequent social exclusion.

valet_charrue.label: Valet de charrue (plough boy)
valet_charrue.summary: Farm worker who led the team while the ploughman held the plough.
valet_charrue.text: The plough boy led the oxen or horses harnessed to the plough while the "laboureur" guided the share, a typical piece of teamwork on the large cereal farms of the Ancien Régime. This subordinate role was often a stage of apprenticeship before becoming a "laboureur" oneself.

valet_commun.label: Valet commun (community officer)
valet_commun.summary: Municipal officer in charge of summonses; a Pyrenean term.
valet_commun.text: The "valet commun" was an officer in the service of a village community, responsible in particular for summoning people to assemblies and for various tasks of communal organisation. The term is attested in the Pyrenean regions, where rural communities handled a large part of their own local administration.

valet_de_chambre.label: Valet de chambre (valet)
valet_de_chambre.summary: Servant responsible for looking after the rooms and for his master's personal service.
valet_de_chambre.text: The "valet de chambre" looked after the living quarters and provided personal service (dressing, toilet) to a master, in a château, a town house or a large bourgeois household. The post, higher in the hierarchy than the other servants, could bring particular closeness to and trust from the employer.

valet_de_ferme.label: Valet de ferme (farm servant)
valet_de_ferme.summary: Live-in agricultural worker employed to help with farm work.
valet_de_ferme.text: The farm servant was hired, often by the year and lodged on the premises, to help the farmer with all agricultural tasks. He is distinct from the day-labourer ("journalier"), paid by the task, by the length and stability of his engagement. The mention "valet de ferme-commis" sometimes links this role to clerical or writing tasks on behalf of the farmer.

valet_harnais.label: Valet de harnais (harness hand)
valet_harnais.summary: Farm worker responsible for looking after the harness and tack of the draught animals.
valet_harnais.text: The "valet de harnais" (or "de harnois", the old spelling) took care of harnessing and maintaining the equipment of a farm's draught animals, a role close to that of a groom applied to the farming world. "Harnais" and "harnois" denote the same equipment, the spelling varying according to period and scribe.

valet_limier.label: Valet de limier (lymerer)
valet_limier.summary: Huntsman's assistant responsible for handling the lymer, a tracking hound.
valet_limier.text: The lymerer handled and trained the lymer ("limier"), a hound specialised in tracking game by scent, during the great seigneurial hunts (venery). He worked under the authority of the huntsman ("veneur"), within the hierarchical organisation of a hunt.

vallante.label: Vallante (lagoon fishery worker)
vallante.summary: Worker of the fishing lagoons (valli da pesca) of Comacchio and the Po delta, employed in catching and guarding eels.
vallante.text: The vallante worked in the valli da pesca, embanked brackish lagoons around Comacchio and the Po delta, where he regulated the water, maintained the banks and caught fish, especially eels, in the lavorieri, reed barriers that trapped them during their autumn migration. He often lived in the huts scattered across the lagoons and was subject to strict watch against poaching.

vannier.label: Vannier (basket maker)
vannier.summary: Craftsman who worked wicker to make baskets, back-baskets and hampers.
vannier.text: The basket maker wove wicker or other plant fibres to make utilitarian objects: baskets, back-baskets, hampers, "mannes" (large baskets). This ancient trade, practised near osier beds (notably in the Loire Valley and at Fayl-Billot), long supplied the containers indispensable to rural life.

varcollier.label: Varcollier (neckerchief maker)
varcollier.summary: Maker of neck scarves and garments protecting the neck.
varcollier.text: The "varcollier" made neck scarves and other items of clothing intended to protect the neck from the cold. The word has many spelling variants ("varcoletier", "varcolier", "vercollier") depending on region and scribe, all denoting the same clothing trade.

vasselaire.label: Vasselaire (wooden-tableware maker)
vasselaire.summary: Craftsman making tableware from beech wood.
vasselaire.text: The "vasselaire" (or "vaxelaire") shaped, by turning and fine joinery, beechwood tableware — plates, bowls, porringers — for everyday domestic use before earthenware or metal tableware became widespread. The word is attested mainly in the regions of eastern France.

vaxillaire.label: Vexillaire (standard-bearer)
vaxillaire.summary: Soldier responsible for carrying and guarding a unit's standard (vexillum).
vaxillaire.text: The "vexillaire" (from the Latin "vexillum", standard) carried and protected the flag or ensign of a regiment, a post of honour within a military unit. The term, of ancient Roman origin, was reused in later French military vocabulary to denote the standard-bearer.

veehouder.label: Veehouder (livestock farmer)
veehouder.summary: Farmer who mainly kept livestock, in particular dairy cows.
veehouder.text: The veehouder lives mainly from keeping cattle, for milk, butter and cheese or for meat, rather than from arable farming. The designation is very common in the records of the grassland regions of Holland, Friesland and Utrecht, where dairy production was the main source of income.

veenbaas.label: Veenbaas (peat foreman)
veenbaas.summary: Foreman of a gang of peat workers.
veenbaas.text: The veenbaas led a gang of peat cutters or dredgers on behalf of a peat entrepreneur, allocated the work, checked the quality of the peat and often also paid the wages. He usually worked in the bog himself.

velineuse.label: Vélineuse (Alençon lacemaker)
velineuse.summary: Woman who made Alençon lace, known as "point royal".
velineuse.text: The "vélineuse" took part in making "point d'Alençon", a renowned needle lace also called "vélin" or "point royal", inscribed on UNESCO's list of intangible cultural heritage. This extremely painstaking work, done exclusively by hand, could take several months for a single motif.

veloutier.label: Veloutier (velvet weaver)
veloutier.text: The "veloutier" wove velvet, a fabric with a short, dense pile obtained by a particular weaving technique (pile warp). The trade developed notably in renowned textile centres such as Lyon, in association with silk weaving.

vendangeur.label: Vendangeur (grape picker)
vendangeur.summary: Farm worker who harvested grapes in the vineyard.
vendangeur.text: The grape picker took part in the seasonal grape harvest ("vendange"), often as temporary labour coming to lend a hand at harvest time. This seasonal activity traditionally brought together a whole rural community, including workers from other regions.

vendeiro.label: Vendeiro (village shopkeeper and tavern keeper)
vendeiro.summary: Keeper of a venda, a small village or suburban shop selling provisions and wine.
vendeiro.text: The vendeiro runs a venda, a modest village or suburban establishment combining a grocery (foodstuffs, salt, olive oil, paraffin) and a tavern serving wine by the glass. The venda was also a meeting place and news centre for the neighbourhood, and the vendeiro often gave his customers credit.

vendeur_de_fruits.label: Vendeur de fruits (fruit seller)
vendeur_de_fruits.text: The fruit seller sold fruit at a market, in a shop or as a street trader. It was a common food trade in towns as well as in rural market towns.

vendeur_de_tisane.label: Vendeur de tisane (herbal-drink seller)
vendeur_de_tisane.summary: Itinerant or fixed seller of herbal teas and infusions.
vendeur_de_tisane.text: The "vendeur de tisane" offered refreshing or medicinal drinks made from infused plants, often crying his wares in the streets of towns. This small itinerant trade, common before other drinks became widespread, belonged to the category of street drink sellers.

vendeur_pierre_feu.label: Vendeur de pierre à feu (gunflint seller)
vendeur_pierre_feu.text: The gunflint seller dealt in gunflints, knapped flints used to produce the spark in flintlock weapons. The Meusnes area, in Touraine, was renowned for this knapped-flint industry, which supplied armies and private individuals.

vendeuse.label: Vendeuse (saleswoman)
vendeuse.summary: Woman employed in selling in a shop.
vendeuse.text: The saleswoman welcomed customers and sold goods in a shop or at a market. It is a generic term covering a very wide variety of businesses, from the grocery to the haberdashery.

veneur.label: Veneur (huntsman)
veneur.summary: Person in charge of organising a lord's hunts: estates, hounds, staff and game.
veneur.text: The huntsman directed the whole of a lord's staghunting establishment: training and management of the pack, supervision of the whippers-in and hunt servants, and upkeep of the game on the estate. Under the Ancien Régime, venery was one of the great offices of seigneurial and royal households.

verdier.label: Verdier (forest warden)
verdier.summary: Former officer of the Eaux et Forêts responsible for watching over the royal forests.
verdier.text: The "verdier" was a junior officer of the "Eaux et Forêts" (waters and forests administration) responsible for watching over royal or seigneurial forests, recording offences (illegal felling, poaching) and ensuring that the timber was properly exploited. This old forestry administration prefigured the modern forestry services.

verdurier.label: Verdurier (greengrocer)
verdurier.summary: Seller of vegetables and early produce.
verdurier.text: The "verdurier" sold green vegetables and early produce at markets, a specialisation of the food trade distinct from the fruiterer or the grocer. The term is still used today in some regions.

vergaro.label: Vergaro (head shepherd)
vergaro.summary: In the Roman Campagna and central Italy, the head shepherd who ran a sheep station for the owner of the flock.
vergaro.text: The vergaro supervised the shepherds, the processing of the milk and the transhumance of the flock between the winter pastures of the Roman Campagna and the Maremma and the summer pastures of the Apennines. A trusted and experienced man, he often received a share of the flock's profits.

vergetier.label: Vergetier (brush maker)
vergetier.summary: Craftsman who made and sold brushes and boot scrapers of animal bristle.
vergetier.text: The "vergetier" made "vergettes" — small brushes of boar or pig bristle — used to clean and brush the mud off clothes and shoes. The trade belonged to traditional brush-making, alongside the "brossier", who worked a wider range of articles.

vergeur.label: Vergeur (cask gauger)
vergeur.summary: Gauger who measured the capacity of casks with a graduated rod.
vergeur.text: The "vergeur" measured the capacity of barrels and casks using a "verge", a graduated rod whose name gave rise in the 16th century to the verbs "verger"/"vergier" (to gauge) and the word "vergeur" (gauger). The trade is synonymous with the "velteur", who carried out the same operation with a comparable instrument called the "velte".

veriere.label: Verière (bait-worm digger)
veriere.summary: Woman who dug worms from the sand or mud to serve as fishing bait.
veriere.text: The "verière" (or "verrotière") collected marine worms from the sand or mud of the beaches, which were sold to fishermen as bait. This small coastal activity, often carried out by women, supplemented the income of fishing families.

verificateur_des_poids_et_mesures.label: Vérificateur des poids et mesures (inspector of weights and measures)
verificateur_des_poids_et_mesures.summary: Official responsible for checking the accuracy of traders' measuring instruments.
verificateur_des_poids_et_mesures.text: The inspector of weights and measures checked and calibrated the scales, weights and measuring instruments used by traders, in order to prevent fraud over the quantities sold. This public inspection role was strengthened and standardised with the adoption of the metric system after the French Revolution.

verinier.label: Vérinier (stained-glass painter)
