verinier.summary: Glass painter specialised in creating and restoring stained-glass windows.
verinier.text: The "vérinier" practised the glassmaker's art as applied to stained glass, creating or restoring compositions of coloured and painted glass for religious and civil buildings. The term, a rare form, belongs to the regional vocabulary of glasswork.

vermaillou.label: Vermaillou (eel fisherman)
vermaillou.summary: Specialised eel fisherman; a regional term from the south-west.
vermaillou.text: The "vermaillou" fished for eels using traditional freshwater fishing techniques, particularly in the river basins of south-western France, where this fishery long provided an important local resource. The word probably derives from "ver" (worm), the bait used for this kind of fishing.

vermicelier.label: Vermicelier (pasta maker)
vermicelier.text: The "vermicelier" made dried pasta, in particular vermicelli, a fine thread of pasta used especially in soups. The trade, of Italian inspiration, developed in French towns from the 18th century onwards.

vernisseur.label: Vernisseur (varnisher)
vernisseur.summary: Worker who applied varnish to protect and embellish manufactured objects.
vernisseur.text: The varnisher applied one or more coats of varnish to objects of wood or metal, or to coachwork (furniture, carriages and cars, instruments), to protect them and give them a glossy finish. The trade existed in many industries, from cabinetmaking to coachbuilding, with techniques suited to each material.

vernisseur_sur_optique.label: Vernisseur sur optique (optical-instrument varnisher)
vernisseur_sur_optique.summary: Factory worker who protected the metal parts of optical instruments with varnish.
vernisseur_sur_optique.text: The optical-instrument varnisher applied a protective varnish to the metal parts of optical instruments (binoculars, telescopic sights, measuring devices) to protect them from corrosion. This specialised post is found in precision-instrument factories.

verrier_fabricant.label: Verrier (glassmaker)
verrier_fabricant.summary: Craftsman who made all kinds of glass objects.
verrier_fabricant.text: The glassmaker shaped molten glass to produce a variety of objects — tableware, flasks, window panes — by blowing or moulding, in a glassworks. The trade, which involved working a material brought to very high temperatures, was often concentrated around forests that supplied the wood needed for melting.

verrier_peintre.label: Verrier (glass painter)
verrier_peintre.summary: Medieval craftsman who designed and painted church stained glass.
verrier_peintre.text: The glass painter (also called "voirier" in Old French) designed, cut and painted the pieces of coloured glass assembled into stained-glass windows and rose windows for the religious buildings of the Middle Ages. The trade combined technical mastery of glass with genuine pictorial skill, illustrated by the great ensembles of Gothic stained glass.

verrier_peintre_de_vitraux.label: Verrier peintre de vitraux (stained-glass painter)
verrier_peintre_de_vitraux.summary: In the Middle Ages, a painter of stained glass.
verrier_peintre_de_vitraux.text: In the Middle Ages, the stained-glass painter designed and painted the stained-glass windows made for churches and cathedrals.

vertugadier.label: Vertugadier (farthingale maker)
vertugadier.summary: Maker of farthingales, frames used to spread out dresses.
vertugadier.text: The "vertugadier" made farthingales ("vertugadins"), rigid structures (originally of wicker, later with hoops) worn under dresses to spread out the skirt, fashionable in the 16th and 17th centuries. This women's fashion trade disappeared as clothing silhouettes changed.

vervener.label: Vervener (peat entrepreneur)
vervener.summary: Entrepreneur who bought or leased peat bogs and had peat dug or dredged from them.
vervener.text: The vervener exploited peatland: he acquired the rights to the peat, had it drained and dug by gangs of peat workers and sold the peat. In the high peat colonies of Groningen and Drenthe and in the low peat districts of Holland and Friesland the verveners were important entrepreneurs whose activity profoundly changed the landscape.

veslier.label: Veslier (veal butcher or calf dealer)
veslier.summary: Specialist in the calf trade, as a butcher or as a livestock dealer.
veslier.text: The "veslier" (from the regional term "vesle" for calf) was a tradesman specialising in veal. Depending on sources and regions, the word could denote either a butcher selling only veal, or, in the related form "velier", a dealer in calves on the hoof (live cattle) rather than a butcher as such; the two activities were closely linked in the rural trade.

veterinaire.label: Vétérinaire (veterinary surgeon)
veterinaire.summary: Practitioner treating animals, historically descended from the farrier's trade.
veterinaire.text: The veterinary surgeon treated animals, particularly livestock and horses. The modern profession was born in France with the founding of the first veterinary school in Lyon in 1762; before that date, animal care was often provided by "maréchaux-experts", craftsmen from the farrier's trade who had developed particular competence in equine diseases.

veterinaire_artiste.label: Vétérinaire (performing-animal vet)
veterinaire_artiste.summary: Veterinary surgeon specialised in caring for performing animals.
veterinaire_artiste.text: This veterinary surgeon looked specifically after animals used in shows (circuses, menageries, equestrian shows), a specialisation linked to the development of the great travelling circuses in the 19th and 20th centuries. It required expertise in sometimes exotic species, in addition to standard equine care.

vicaire.label: Vicaire (curate)
vicaire.summary: Priest who assisted the parish priest in running a parish.
vicaire.text: The curate was a priest who assisted the incumbent parish priest in pastoral duties and the running of a parish: masses, sacraments, keeping the parish registers. He frequently appears as the signatory of baptism, marriage and burial entries in Ancien Régime registers.

vidangeur.label: Vidangeur (nightman)
vidangeur.summary: Worker responsible for emptying household cesspits by hand.
vidangeur.text: The nightman emptied the cesspits (latrines) of houses, usually at night, in the absence of mains drainage, an indispensable but socially despised trade before sewerage networks became widespread. The collected matter, called "poudrette" once dried, was sold as agricultural fertiliser.

viertelbauer.label: Quarter farmer (Viertelbauer)
viertelbauer.summary: Farmer working a quarter of a full farm holding.
viertelbauer.text: The Viertelbauer works a holding equal to a quarter of a full farm and belongs to the small farmers, who usually kept no full team of their own. The designation follows the classification of farms into whole, half and quarter holdings, as used for example in the Bavarian Hoffuß system or with the northern German Hufen.

vietor.label: Vietor (basket maker)
vietor.summary: Basket maker, and by extension cooper; a term of Latin origin ("vietor", one who weaves).
vietor.text: The "vietor" (or "vitor") was a basket maker, a craftsman who wove wicker or other plant fibres to make baskets and woven objects; the word comes from the Latin "vietor" (from "viere", to weave). It is also attested with the meaning of cooper, the two trades historically sharing similar techniques of bending and binding wood (barrel hoops, wickerwork casing).

vif_baillif.label: Vif-baillif (deputy bailiff)
vif_baillif.summary: Deputy to the bailiff in the seigneurial judicial system.
vif_baillif.text: The "vif-baillif" assisted the "bailli" in carrying out his local judicial and administrative duties. This hierarchy of deputies reflects the organisation of the seigneurial courts of the Ancien Régime.

vigile.label: Vigile (watchman)
vigile.summary: Guard keeping watch at night, particularly over a lighthouse.
vigile.text: The "vigile" performed a surveillance and guard role, for example at a lighthouse, making sure it worked properly for the safety of shipping. The word, from the Latin "vigilia" (watch), more broadly denotes anyone responsible for keeping watch and guard.

vigneron.label: Vigneron (winegrower)
vigneron.summary: Person who cultivated vines and produced wine.
vigneron.text: The "vigneron" cultivated vines and traditionally made the wine himself, unlike the mere grape grower ("viticulteur"), who might confine himself to producing grapes, which were then sold or made into wine at a cooperative. The term has been used in all French wine-growing regions since the Middle Ages.

viguier.label: Viguier (southern provost)
viguier.summary: Judicial officer of the Midi, the southern equivalent of the provost.
viguier.text: In the regions of southern law (Languedoc, Provence), the "viguier" held an office equivalent to that of the "prévôt" in the rest of France. At first an important official in the Middle Ages, his office gradually declined until, by the end of the Ancien Régime, he was no more than a subordinate judge under the authority of the "bailli" or the seneschal.

vinaigrier_ambulant.label: Vinaigrier (vinegar hawker)
vinaigrier_ambulant.text: The vinegar hawker sold vinegar door to door or at markets, following a regular trading round. This form of itinerant trade complemented the business of the vinegar makers who kept shops.

vinaigrier_fabricant.label: Vinaigrier (vinegar maker)
vinaigrier_fabricant.summary: Craftsman who made vinegar by acetic fermentation.
vinaigrier_fabricant.text: The vinegar maker made vinegar by fermenting wine or other alcoholic liquids. Under the Ancien Régime, the vinegar makers of Paris formed a guild combined with that of the mustard makers ("vinaigriers-moutardiers-sauciers"), so closely linked were the two products.

violonaire.label: Violonaire (itinerant fiddler)
violonaire.text: The "violonaire" was an itinerant musician who played the fiddle at village festivals, dances and weddings, part of the popular rural musical traditions before organised bands appeared.

vireteur.label: Vireteur (river boat handler)
vireteur.summary: River worker responsible for manoeuvring boats through difficult passages.
vireteur.text: The "vireteur" helped to manoeuvre and turn boats on rivers and canals, particularly at awkward passages (bends, locks). This auxiliary work supplemented that of the boatman or the hauler.

visafslager.label: Visafslager (fish auctioneer)
visafslager.summary: Official who sold fish at the fish auction by Dutch auction.
visafslager.text: At the fish markets of the fishing towns the landed fish was sold by Dutch auction: the auctioneer called a high price and let it fall until a buyer called "mine". He recorded the sales and handled the settlement between fishermen and buyers.

visiteur_des_metiers.label: Visiteur des métiers (guild inspector)
visiteur_des_metiers.summary: Inspector responsible for checking the quality and conformity of a trade's work.
visiteur_des_metiers.text: The "visiteur des métiers" (or "garde-visiteur") was an officer elected by a guild to check the quality of the work produced by its members and compliance with the trade's regulations. This institution of internal control is characteristic of the guild organisation of trades under the Ancien Régime.

visiteuse.label: Visiteuse (woman inspector or visitor)
visiteuse.summary: Woman responsible for an inspection or checking task.
visiteuse.text: The "visiteuse" carried out an inspection or checking role in various activities, whether quality control in a workshop or social visiting (visitor to the sick or to needy families, depending on the context). The term remains fairly generic and depends heavily on the context of the record in which it appears.

visiteuse_de_pieces.label: Visiteuse de pièces (parts inspector)
visiteuse_de_pieces.summary: Factory worker responsible for quality control of manufactured parts.
visiteuse_de_pieces.text: The "visiteuse de pièces" inspected the parts produced in a factory to check that they conformed to manufacturing standards, a post characteristic of the industrial organisation of work from the end of the 19th century.

viticulteur.label: Viticulteur (grape grower)
viticulteur.text: The "viticulteur" devoted himself to growing vines and producing grapes, without necessarily making the wine himself, unlike the "vigneron", who traditionally also made his own wine. The distinction between the two terms became sharper with the development of cooperative wineries.

vitrier.label: Vitrier (glazier)
vitrier.summary: Craftsman who fitted panes of glass in windows and frames.
vitrier.text: The glazier cut and fitted glass panes in windows, doors and frames. The trade has existed ever since glass became the usual material for closing openings, replacing oiled paper or solid shutters.

vivandier.label: Vivandier (sutler)
vivandier.summary: Person who supplied provisions to troops on campaign or to itinerant work gangs.
vivandier.text: The sutler supplied food and drink to military troops on campaign or to gangs of itinerant workers (building sites, timber floating). This logistical role, sometimes filled by women (the famous "vivandières" of the armies), was essential to supply in the absence of a modern commissariat.

vlasboer.label: Vlasboer (flax farmer)
vlasboer.summary: Farmer or dealer who grew, processed or bought up flax.
vlasboer.text: Flax was grown on a large scale in Zeeland, Groningen, Friesland and above all in Flanders, along the Lys. The flax farmer sowed and pulled the flax, had it retted and broken, or sold it standing to dealers who handled further processing. Flax supplied the raw material for the linen industry.

voilier.label: Voilier (sailmaker)
voilier.summary: Craftsman who made the sails of boats.
voilier.text: The sailmaker cut and sewed canvas sails for boats, a specialised textile trade in sea and river ports. It should not be confused with the modern sense of the word, which denotes the sailing boat itself.

voiturier.label: Voiturier (carter)
voiturier.summary: Carrier of goods using horses and carts.
voiturier.text: The carter transported goods overland with horses and carts, the historical equivalent of the modern road haulier. The trade assumed the ownership or hire of a complete team and had many variants according to the type of transport (on the back, by water, hotel).

voiturier_a_dos.label: Voiturier à dos (pack carrier)
voiturier_a_dos.summary: Porter who loaded and carried goods on the back of a man or an animal.
voiturier_a_dos.text: The "voiturier à dos" loaded, unloaded and sometimes carried goods borne on the back, in places where wheeled vehicles had difficult access (narrow lanes, mountain tracks). In his role he was close to the "portefaix" or the "crocheteur" (porter).

voiturier_hotel.label: Voiturier (hotel valet)
voiturier_hotel.summary: Hotel employee responsible for parking and minding guests' vehicles.
voiturier_hotel.text: The hotel "voiturier" parked and minded the vehicles (formerly horse-drawn carriages, today cars) of the guests of a hotel, a service that has existed since the days of post houses and the grand hotels of the 19th century.

voiturier_par_eau.label: Voiturier par eau (water carrier)
voiturier_par_eau.summary: Boatman who carried goods and passengers on rivers and canals.
voiturier_par_eau.text: The "voiturier par eau" (or river carrier) sailed rivers and canals to carry goods and passengers, complementing the network of overland carters before the arrival of the railway. River transport was then an economical means of moving heavy goods (timber, stone, grain).

voiturin.label: Voiturin (coach driver)
voiturin.summary: Driver of a public passenger vehicle; a term of Italian origin.
voiturin.text: The "voiturin" drove a small public or hired carriage, a term derived from the Italian "vetturino" (coachman), used particularly in the border regions and tourist towns of the 19th century.

volaillier.label: Volaillier (poulterer)
volaillier.text: The poulterer raised and/or sold poultry (hens, ducks, geese, turkeys) at markets. This common food trade remains, in modernised form, one of the few occupations on the list to survive today with its name largely unchanged.

volontaire_au_service_de_la_republique.label: Volunteer in the service of the Republic (volontaire au service de la République)
volontaire_au_service_de_la_republique.summary: Soldier who enlisted voluntarily in the armies of the French Revolution.
volontaire_au_service_de_la_republique.text: This status denotes the men who enlisted voluntarily in the armies of the First Republic, particularly during the great levies of volunteers of 1791-1793 to defend the Revolution against the coalition of monarchies. The mention appears frequently in civil registration records and military registers of the revolutionary period.

voltigeur.label: Voltigeur (acrobat or light infantryman)
voltigeur.summary: Equestrian acrobat or elite light-infantry soldier, depending on the period and context.
voltigeur.text: The "voltigeur" was either an acrobat specialised in equestrian or circus vaulting, or, in Napoleonic military vocabulary, an elite infantryman of small stature forming a company specialised in marksmanship and skirmishing within each infantry regiment. The two senses coexist depending on the context of the record.

voltigeur_sur_cordes.label: Voltigeur sur cordes (rope dancer)
voltigeur_sur_cordes.summary: Acrobat performing balancing and vaulting feats on a taut rope.
voltigeur_sur_cordes.text: The rope dancer was a performer (close to the tightrope walker) who executed balancing and acrobatic figures on a taut rope, at the fairs and travelling shows of the Ancien Régime and the 19th century.

voorlezer.label: Voorlezer (Reformed church reader)
voorlezer.summary: Church official of the Reformed Church who read from the Bible and led the singing before the service.
voorlezer.text: In the Dutch Reformed Church the voorlezer read chapters of Scripture and the articles of faith before the sermon and led the psalm singing. In villages the office was often combined with that of schoolmaster, sexton or precentor, so that one man carried out the church and school duties of the community. The voorlezer sometimes also kept the baptism and marriage registers.

voulgier.label: Voulgier (vouge man)
voulgier.summary: Medieval soldier armed with the vouge, a pole weapon.
voulgier.text: The "voulgier" fought with the vouge, a pole weapon (a long shaft topped with a cutting blade) used by medieval infantry. The term belongs to the military vocabulary of feudal armies before firearms became widespread.

voyer.label: Voyer (highway surveyor)
voyer.summary: Officer responsible for administering public roads and ways.
voyer.text: The "voyer" was an officer responsible for the upkeep, alignment and supervision of the public highways (tracks, roads, streets), a public-works administration role inherited from the Ancien Régime and continued in modernised forms ("ingénieur voyer") in the 19th century.

vrillier.label: Vrillier (gimlet maker)
vrillier.summary: Edge-tool maker specialised in making gimlets, files, awls and cutting tools.
vrillier.text: The "vrillier" made small cutting and boring tools: gimlets, files, awls, chisels and pincers. This trade of craft metalworking supplied the basic tools of the other wood and metal craftsmen.

vroedschapslid.label: Vroedschap member (Dutch town council)
vroedschapslid.summary: Member of the vroedschap, the town council of the towns of Holland and other provinces under the Dutch Republic.
vroedschapslid.text: The vroedschap was the council that set municipal policy in the towns of the Dutch Republic and from whose ranks, or on whose nomination, the burgomasters and aldermen were chosen. Its members, often appointed for life and replaced by co-optation, belonged to the circle of the regents. The institution disappeared with the upheavals of the end of the 18th century.

vulcaniseur.label: Vulcaniseur (vulcaniser)
vulcaniseur.text: The vulcaniser treated rubber by vulcanisation (heating it with sulphur) to make it tougher and more elastic, an industrial process that appeared in the mid-19th century and was essential in particular for making tyres.

waagmeester.label: Waagmeester (weigh house master)
waagmeester.summary: Keeper of the municipal weigh house, where goods were officially weighed.
waagmeester.text: In many Dutch towns heavy goods such as cheese, butter, grain or metals had to be weighed at the weigh house, both for trade and for levying the weighing dues. The waagmeester ran this public weigh house, ensured the accuracy of the scales and weights and issued weighing slips. He was assisted by weigh-house servants and by the porters' guilds.

waidier.label: Waidier (woad dyer)
waidier.summary: Medieval craftsman making the blue dye obtained from the woad plant.
waidier.text: The "waidier" prepared pastel (a blue dye) from the leaves of woad ("waide"), a dye plant whose trade made the fortune of the Toulouse region during the Renaissance, before it was supplanted by indigo imported from the Indies. The term, of Germanic/Picard origin, denotes both the grower and the preparer of woad.

waisenvater.label: Orphanage master (Waisenvater)
waisenvater.summary: Head of an orphanage who cared for and brought up the orphans together with his wife.
waisenvater.text: The Waisenvater runs a municipal or church orphanage, usually together with his wife as Waisenmutter: he provides the children's lodging, food, schooling and religious upbringing, their work in the house and later their placement in an apprenticeship or service. He answered to a supervisory body of the town or foundation, to which he rendered accounts.

wapeur.label: Wapeur (rewinder)
wapeur.summary: Textile worker in the Nord who rewound large bobbins onto small ones.
wapeur.text: The "wapeur" transferred yarn from the large spinning bobbins to small bobbins intended for weaving, an intermediate operation in the textile production chain of the spinning mills of northern France.

warandeur.label: Warandeur (herring inspector)
warandeur.summary: Officer appointed by the magistrates of Dunkirk to check the salting and marking of herrings.
warandeur.text: The "warandeur" was an officer appointed by the magistrates (the aldermen, "échevinage") of the town of Dunkirk to check the quality of herring salting and to certify, together with a sworn marker, that the barrels met the standards laid down by municipal regulations before they were sold or exported. This inspection role bears witness to the economic importance of herring fishing and trade in the Flemish ports.

waretier.label: Waretier (thatcher)
waretier.summary: Craftsman who covered roofs with thatch (straw, reed or heather).
waretier.text: The "waretier" (thatcher) covered roofs with woven plant material — straw, reed or heather depending on the region — a traditional roofing technique still visible on some rural houses in northern France. The term, of dialect form, denotes the same trade as the "chaumier".

wasenmeister.label: Wasenmeister (German knacker)
wasenmeister.summary: German knacker, often also responsible for duties linked to carrying out punishments.
wasenmeister.text: In German-speaking countries, the Wasenmeister was the knacker responsible for removing and cutting up dead animals, a public-health role. Like the executioner, with whose office it was sometimes combined, he belonged to the category of so-called "dishonourable" trades (unehrliche Berufe) in the society of the Germanic Ancien Régime.

waterschout.label: Waterschout (shipping master)
waterschout.summary: Municipal official in Dutch port towns who supervised the signing on of seamen.
waterschout.text: In the Dutch port towns the waterschout registered the muster rolls of merchant ships, on which seamen bound themselves to the master, and settled disputes about wages and service. His registers record the name, origin and position of those on board and are therefore a valuable source for research into seafaring ancestors.

wattman.label: Wattman (tram driver)
wattman.text: The "wattman" drove an electric tram, a term borrowed from English (in reference to the watt, the unit of electrical power) that appeared in France with the electrification of urban tram networks at the end of the 19th century.

weesmeester.label: Weesmeester (orphan chamber master)
weesmeester.summary: Member of the orphan chamber, the municipal institution that supervised the property and guardianship of minor orphans.
weesmeester.text: In many towns of the Low Countries the orphan chamber administered the estates of minor children who had lost a parent, appointed guardians and checked their accounts. The weesmeesters, usually chosen from among the town regents, presided over this chamber. Their registers are an important source for genealogical research into estates and guardianships.

weesvader.label: Weesvader (orphanage master)
weesvader.summary: Man or woman who lived in and ran the daily life of an orphanage or almshouse.
weesvader.text: Under the supervision of the regents, the weesvader and weesmoeder, or binnenvader and binnenmoeder, looked after daily life in an orphanage or almshouse: food, clothing, discipline and the work of the inmates. They were often a married couple who lived in the institution and received a fixed salary with board and lodging.

wethouder.label: Wethouder (alderman)
wethouder.summary: Member of the executive board of a Dutch municipality, alongside the burgomaster.
wethouder.text: Since the Municipalities Act of 1851, the aldermen together with the burgomaster have formed the board that runs the day-to-day administration of a Dutch municipality. They are elected by the municipal council and each manages part of the municipal responsibilities. In older town institutions the word was also used for members of the town government.

wheeleuse.label: Wheeleuse (bobbin filler)
wheeleuse.summary: Textile worker who filled the thread bobbins in a lace factory.
wheeleuse.text: The "wheeleuse" filled and prepared the thread bobbins for the lace machines, a term borrowed from the English "wheel" (wheel, bobbin) in the lace and tulle factories of northern France.

wlodarz.label: Włodarz (manor overseer)
wlodarz.summary: Overseer of a manor farm or village on behalf of the lord, usually of peasant origin.
wlodarz.text: The włodarz ran a manor farm or village day to day on the owner’s behalf: he allocated work, watched over the harvest and livestock and enforced labour service. He was usually of peasant origin and ranked below the steward (ekonom). Latin sources call him “villicus”.

wloscianin.label: Włościanin (peasant)
wloscianin.summary: Villager belonging to the peasant estate.
wloscianin.text: Włościanin is the official nineteenth-century term for a peasant as a member of the peasant estate, frequently used in the civil registers of the Kingdom of Poland. Latin parish registers designated peasants with the epithet “laboriosus” (hard-working) or “rusticus”, in contrast with “nobilis” for the nobility and “famatus” for townspeople.

wojt.label: Wójt (commune head)
wojt.summary: Head of a rural commune or, in old towns, a judge and administrator on behalf of the lord.
wojt.text: In medieval towns chartered under German law, the wójt was the hereditary founder and judge who presided over the bench of aldermen; in villages the sołtys was his counterpart. In the Kingdom of Poland from 1864, the wójt headed a rural commune (gmina) covering several villages and often appears in records as a witness or official. Latin sources call him “advocatus”.

xystarque.label: Xystarque (xystarch)
xystarque.summary: Ancient official in charge of the athletes training in a xystus.
xystarque.text: The xystarch directed and organised the training of athletes in a xystus, a covered portico of ancient gymnasia reserved for sporting practice. This office, known in the Greek and then the Roman world, supervised the officially recognised guilds of athletes (the "xystici").

xystique.label: Xystique (xystic athlete)
xystique.summary: Ancient athlete belonging to the official guild of sportsmen training in the xystus.
xystique.text: The "xystique" was a professional athlete (runner, wrestler, pancratiast) who was a member of a guild recognised by the Roman authorities and trained in the xystus, the covered portico of the gymnasia. He should not be confused with the gladiator, who belonged to a separate institution (the ludus) and engaged in combats of an altogether different kind.

yane.label: Yane (vagrant)
yane.text: The "yane" was a vagrant wandering the roads, a rare regional term whose use is limited to certain dialect sources.

yeguero.label: Yegüero (Spanish mare herder)
yeguero.summary: Herdsman who looked after the mares of a stud herd.
yeguero.text: The yegüero tended and guarded the mares, foals and stallions of a stud herd, taking them to pasture and watching over their breeding. Many villages had a communal yegüero, paid by the residents to guard their mares together.

ymagier.label: Imagier (image carver)
ymagier.summary: Medieval craftsman who carved the images (statues) on church façades.
ymagier.text: The "imagier" (spelt "ymagier" in Old French) carved the statues and figures adorning the portals and façades of medieval churches and cathedrals. The great sculptural ensembles of Chartres, Reims or Amiens are the work of such "imagiers", whose craft combined stonecutting with a highly developed artistic sense.

ymagier_peintre.label: Imagier (image painter)
ymagier_peintre.summary: Painter of devotional images and portraits, from the Middle Ages to the Renaissance.
ymagier_peintre.text: The "imagier"-painter devoted himself to painting images, often religious (altarpieces, illuminations) but also secular (portraits), from the Middle Ages to the Renaissance. The term covers a craft close to that of the workshop painter before painting emerged as an individualised art.

ymagier_sculpteur.label: Imagier (image sculptor)
ymagier_sculpteur.summary: Sculptor of statues and religious images, from the Middle Ages to the Renaissance.
ymagier_sculpteur.text: The "imagier"-sculptor carved statues and figures in stone or wood, mainly on religious subjects, intended for places of worship. He represents the strictly sculptural branch of the "imagier" trade, alongside the "imagier"-painter.

yoleur.label: Yoleur (marsh boatman)
yoleur.summary: Boatman who steered a "yole", a small boat used in the marshes.
yoleur.text: The "yoleur" steered a "yole", a light, flat-bottomed boat suited to navigating marshes and wetlands (such as the Marais poitevin or the Brière), to carry people and goods between the island villages.

yuntero.label: Yuntero (Spanish ploughman with a team)
yuntero.summary: Peasant who owned a team of mules or oxen but little or no land, and worked the land of others.
yuntero.text: The yuntero was a farmer who had a working team but little or no land of his own, so that he cultivated rented land or hired himself out with his team. A characteristic figure of Extremadura and other regions of large estates, he stood between the day labourer and the well-off farmer.

zagrodnik.label: Zagrodnik (cottager with a garden)
zagrodnik.summary: Peasant owning a cottage with a small plot, without a full farm.
zagrodnik.text: The zagrodnik owned a house with a yard and garden and a small strip of field, not enough to support a family or a draught team. He owed labour service on foot and earned extra money as a hired hand. Latin parish registers usually call him “hortulanus”, which here does not mean a professional gardener.

zakkendrager.label: Zakkendrager (sack porter)
zakkendrager.summary: Member of the guild that carried goods in sacks between ships, warehouses and the weigh house.
zakkendrager.text: In several towns of Holland the guild of sack porters held the exclusive right to carry sacked goods such as grain, salt, sugar or coffee. The porters worked in teams under a foreman and shared the work and earnings according to the guild's rules. After the abolition of the guilds, some sack porters' associations continued to exist for a long time.

zakonnica.label: Zakonnica (nun)
zakonnica.summary: Member of a female religious congregation.
zakonnica.text: The zakonnica had taken religious vows and lived in a convent community, devoted to prayer and, in active congregations, to teaching and caring for the sick and the poor. Latin sources call her “monialis” or “religiosa”.

zakonnik.label: Zakonnik (monk, religious brother)
zakonnik.summary: Member of a male religious order, monk or lay brother.
zakonnik.text: The zakonnik had taken religious vows and lived in a monastic community under the rule of his order. He could be a priest (father) or a brother who was not ordained and did manual work or a craft in the monastery. The suppressions of religious houses in the nineteenth century, especially after 1864 in the Kingdom of Poland, dispersed many communities.

zampognaro.label: Zampognaro (bagpiper)
zampognaro.summary: Player of the zampogna, the traditional bagpipe of central and southern Italy.
zampognaro.text: The zampognaro, usually a shepherd from the Apennines of Abruzzo, Molise, Lazio or Calabria, came down to the towns during Advent to play Christmas novenas before sacred images, often paired with a shawm player (the pifferaro). A traditional figure of central and southern Italy.

zandarm.label: Żandarm (gendarme)
zandarm.summary: Member of a military force carrying out public order and police duties.
zandarm.text: The żandarm belonged to the gendarmerie, a military force responsible for public order, pursuing criminals and deserters and political surveillance. In the nineteenth century gendarmeries operated in each of the partitions of Poland, and gendarmes appear in records as parties or witnesses.

zentgraf.label: District judge (Zentgraf)
zentgraf.summary: Presiding judge of a Zent, a high-court district in Franconia and Hesse.
zentgraf.text: The Zentgraf presides over the Zent court, which in Franconia, Hesse and neighbouring areas exercised high jurisdiction, especially over serious crimes, for a district of several villages (the Zent). He was appointed by the territorial ruler and judged with lay assessors from the Zent villages; the Zent courts lasted until the early 19th century.

ziekentrooster.label: Ziekentrooster (comforter of the sick)
ziekentrooster.summary: Layman in the service of the Reformed Church who visited and comforted the sick and the dying.
ziekentrooster.text: The ziekentrooster, also called krankbezoeker, was a layman appointed by the church to visit the sick, prisoners and the dying, to pray with them and read Scripture to them. The Dutch East India Company and the West India Company took ziekentroosters on board their ships and into their settlements, where they sometimes also served as schoolmasters or readers.

zolfataro.label: Zolfataro (sulphur miner)
zolfataro.summary: Miner in the sulphur mines, especially in Sicily.
zolfataro.text: The zolfataro worked in the sulphur mines of central Sicily (provinces of Caltanissetta, Agrigento and Enna) and, to a lesser extent, of Romagna and the Marche. In Sicily the work was organised in teams: the hewer cut the ore and the carusi carried it to the surface, where it was smelted in calcaroni kilns. The very harsh working conditions were documented by 19th-century inquiries.

zordisseur.label: Zordisseur (warper)
zordisseur.summary: Textile worker who laid out the warp threads before weaving.
zordisseur.text: The "zordisseur" prepared and laid out the warp threads on the loom before the weaving proper, an operation related to warping ("ourdissage"); the term, a dialect form from the Nord, appears to be a regional variant of "ourdisseur" (warper).

zupnik.label: Żupnik (salt-mine administrator)
zupnik.summary: Administrator of the royal salt mines of Wieliczka and Bochnia.
zupnik.text: The żupnik managed on the king’s behalf the Kraków salt works, the salt mines of Wieliczka and Bochnia with their boiling houses and salt sales. It was one of the most important and lucrative fiscal posts in old Poland and was often farmed out to leaseholders. Latin sources call him “zupparius”.
